exercise.solution:
create show(secret, found):
    shown = ""
    each letter in secret:
        shown += letter if letter in found else "_"
    end
    return shown
end

main:
    secret = "comet"
    found = []
    tried = []
    lives = 6
    loop lives > 0 and "_" in show(secret, found):
        guess = input("Guess a letter: ").lower()
        if len(guess) != 1:
            print("One letter at a time, please.")
            skip
        end
        if guess in tried:
            print("You already tried {guess}.")
            skip
        end
        tried.append(guess)
        if guess in secret:
            found.append(guess)
        else:
            lives -= 1
        end
        print("{show(secret, found)}  lives: {lives}")
    end
    if lives > 0:
        print("You win! The word was {secret}.")
    else:
        print("Out of lives. The word was {secret}.")
    end
end
hints: `guess = input(...).lower()` handles capitals.
Check `len(guess) != 1` first, then `guess in tried`, each with `skip`.
Remember every guess with `tried.append(guess)`.

lessons.title: Step 6: the finished game
lessons.text:
The last step brings back the random word and adds a picture that grows
with each lost life. Run it yourself and play: this one isn't checked,
because the word is different every time.

```vyrn check
use vyrn.random

const WORDS = ["planet", "rocket", "galaxy", "comet", "nebula", "orbit", "meteor"]
const PICTURES = ["  ", " o", " o/", "\\o/", "\\o/\n |", "\\o/\n |\n/", "\\o/\n |\n/ \\"]

create show(secret, found):
    shown = ""
    each letter in secret:
        shown += letter if letter in found else "_"
    end
    return shown
end

main:
    secret = random.choice(WORDS)
    found = []
    tried = []
    lives = 6
    print("Guess the space word!")
    loop lives > 0 and "_" in show(secret, found):
        print(show(secret, found))
        guess = input("Letter: ").lower()
        if len(guess) != 1 or guess in tried:
            print("Try a new single letter.")
            skip
        end
        tried.append(guess)
        if guess in secret:
            found.append(guess)
        else:
            lives -= 1
            print(PICTURES[6 - lives])
        end
    end
    if lives > 0:
        print("You win! The word was {secret}.")
    else:
        print("Out of lives. The word was {secret}.")
    end
end
```

**Try it:** add a hint command: typing `?` reveals one hidden letter but
costs a life.

**Day 7 done.** You built a whole game in six careful steps. Tomorrow:
text in depth, and secret codes.

days.title: Day 8: Working with Text, and Secret Codes
days.intro:
Text is everywhere: names, messages, files, web pages. Today you learn
Vyrn's tools for taking text apart and putting it back together, then use
them to build the Caesar cipher, a code Julius Caesar is said to have used
for his letters.

lessons.title: Characters and positions
lessons.text:
A string is a sequence of **characters**: letters, digits, spaces,
punctuation. Like a list, each has an index from 0, and slices work the
same way:

```vyrn
main:
    word = "Vyrnlang"
    print(word[0], word[-1], len(word))
    print(word[0:4], word[4:])
    print(word[::-1])
    print(word.chars())
end
```

```text
V g 8
Vyrn lang
gnalnryV
["V", "y", "r", "n", "l", "a", "n", "g"]
```

Unlike a list, a string can't be changed in place: `word[0] = "B"` is an
error. Instead, you build a **new** string, as in `"B" + word[1:]`.

### Exercise

Print the initials of a full name, then the name backwards.

```vyrn starter
main:
    first = "Grace"
    last = "Hopper"
end
```

```text expect
Initials: G.H.
Backwards: reppoH ecarG
```

exercise.starter:
main:
    first = "Grace"
    last = "Hopper"
end
exercise.solution:
main:
    first = "Grace"
    last = "Hopper"
    print("Initials: {first[0]}.{last[0]}.")
    full = first + " " + last
    print("Backwards:", full[::-1])
end
hints: `first[0]` is the first letter.
The full name is `first + " " + last`; reverse it with `[::-1]`.

lessons.title: String methods
lessons.text:
Strings come with many methods. Each gives back a **new** string (or other
value) and leaves the original alone:

```vyrn
main:
    s = "  Hello, Vyrn World  "
    print("[" + s.strip() + "]")
    t = s.strip()
    print(t.upper(), t.lower())
    print(t.replace("World", "friends"))
    print(t.split(", "))
    print(t.startswith("Hello"), t.endswith("!"))
    print(t.find("Vyrn"), t.count("o"))
    print("-".join(["a", "b", "c"]))
    print("vyrn is fun".title(), "42".isdigit(), "abc".isalpha())
end
```

```text
[Hello, Vyrn World]
HELLO, VYRN WORLD hello, vyrn world
Hello, Vyrn friends
["Hello", "Vyrn World"]
true false
7 2
a-b-c
Vyrn Is Fun true true
```

| Method | Gives |
|---|---|
| `strip()`, `lstrip()`, `rstrip()` | the text without spaces at the ends |
| `upper()`, `lower()`, `title()`, `capitalize()` | changed capitals |
| `replace(old, new)` | every `old` replaced by `new` |
| `split(sep)` | a list of the parts between `sep`s (spaces if left out) |
| `sep.join(list)` | the list's strings joined with `sep` between them |
| `startswith(x)`, `endswith(x)` | `true` or `false` |
| `find(x)` | the index of `x`, or `-1` if it isn't there |
| `count(x)` | how many times `x` appears |
| `isdigit()`, `isalpha()`, `isspace()` | whether every character is a digit, a letter, a space |

### Exercise

Tidy up a messy name typed by a user: remove spaces at the ends, and make
it capitalised properly. The checker types `   aDA   lOVELACE  `.

```vyrn starter
main:
    raw = input("Name: ")
end
```

```text input
   aDA   lOVELACE  
```

```text expect
Name: Hello, Ada Lovelace!
```

exercise.starter:
main:
    raw = input("Name: ")
end
exercise.solution:
main:
    raw = input("Name: ")
    name = " ".join(raw.split()).title()
    print("Hello, {name}!")
end
hints: `.split()` with nothing in the brackets splits on any run of spaces, dropping the extra ones.
`" ".join(raw.split())` collapses the spaces; then `.title()`.

lessons.title: Counting words
lessons.text:
`split` and loops together answer many questions about text:

```vyrn
main:
    text = "the cat sat on the mat with the hat"
    words = text.split()
    print(len(words), "words")
    longest = ""
    each w in words:
        if len(w) > len(longest): longest = w
    end
    print("first longest:", longest)
    print("'the' appears", words.count("the"), "times")
end
```

```text
9 words
first longest: with
'the' appears 3 times
```

### Exercise

Count the vowels and the consonants in a sentence (ignore spaces and
punctuation).

```vyrn starter
main:
    sentence = "Programming is a superpower!"
end
```

```text expect
vowels: 9, consonants: 15
```

exercise.starter:
main:
    sentence = "Programming is a superpower!"
end
exercise.solution:
main:
    sentence = "Programming is a superpower!"
    vowels = 0
    consonants = 0
    each c in sentence.lower():
        if c in "aeiou":
            vowels += 1
        else if c.isalpha():
            consonants += 1
        end
    end
    print("vowels: {vowels}, consonants: {consonants}")
end
hints: Loop over `sentence.lower()`.
`if c in "aeiou":` it's a vowel; `else if c.isalpha():` it's a consonant.

lessons.title: Characters are numbers underneath
lessons.text:
Every character has a number, its **code**. `ord` gives a character's code
and `chr` turns a code back into a character. Letters are in order, so
`ord("b")` is one more than `ord("a")`:

```vyrn
main:
    print(ord("a"), ord("b"), ord("z"), ord("A"))
    print(chr(97), chr(65), chr(9731))
    print(chr(ord("c") + 1))
end
```

```text
97 98 122 65
a A ☃
d
```

(Languages like C++ and Java have a separate `char` type for one
character. In Vyrn a character is simply a string of length 1.)

### Exercise

Print the alphabet in capitals, without typing it, using `chr` and a range.

```vyrn starter
main:
end
```

```text expect
ABCDEFGHIJKLMNOPQRSTUVWXYZ
```

exercise.starter:
main:
end
exercise.solution:
main:
    letters = ""
    each code in ord("A") to ord("Z"):
        letters += chr(code)
    end
    print(letters)
end
hints: `ord("A")` is 65 and `ord("Z")` is 90.
Build it: `letters = ""` then `each code in 65 to 90: letters += chr(code)`.

lessons.title: Wrapping around with `%`
lessons.text:
The Caesar cipher shifts each letter forward in the alphabet: with a shift
of 3, `a` becomes `d`, `b` becomes `e`... and `x` becomes `a`, wrapping
around the end. `%` does the wrapping: positions go 0 to 25, and
`(position + shift) % 26` always lands back in that range.

```vyrn
main:
    alphabet = "abcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyz"
    each letter in "axyz":
        i = alphabet.find(letter)
        print(letter, "->", alphabet[(i + 3) % 26])
    end
    print(-1 % 26)
end
```

```text
a -> d
x -> a
y -> b
z -> c
25
```

`-1 % 26` is `25`: in Vyrn, `%` with a positive right side never gives a
negative answer, so shifting backwards wraps around too.

### Exercise

A clock shows hours 0 to 23. Print what time it is 50 hours after 18:00.

```vyrn starter
main:
    now = 18
    later = 50
end
```

```text expect
It will be 20:00
```

exercise.starter:
main:
    now = 18
    later = 50
end
exercise.solution:
main:
    now = 18
    later = 50
    print("It will be {(now + later) % 24}:00")
end
hints: `(now + later) % 24`

lessons.title: The Caesar cipher
lessons.text:
### Exercise

Write `encrypt(text, shift)`: shift each letter by `shift`, keep anything
that isn't a lowercase letter (spaces, punctuation) as it is.

```vyrn starter
const ALPHABET = "abcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyz"

create encrypt(text, shift):
    result = ""
    return result
end

main:
    print(encrypt("meet me at noon", 3))
    print(encrypt("zebra!", 1))
end
```

```text expect
phhw ph dw qrrq
afcsb!
```

exercise.starter:
const ALPHABET = "abcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyz"

create encrypt(text, shift):
    result = ""
    return result
end

main:
    print(encrypt("meet me at noon", 3))
    print(encrypt("zebra!", 1))
end
exercise.solution:
const ALPHABET = "abcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyz"

create encrypt(text, shift):
    result = ""
    each c in text:
        i = ALPHABET.find(c)
        if i == -1:
            result += c
        else:
            result += ALPHABET[(i + shift) % 26]
        end
    end
    return result
end

main:
    print(encrypt("meet me at noon", 3))
    print(encrypt("zebra!", 1))
end
hints: Start with `result = ""` and loop over the text.
`i = ALPHABET.find(c)`; if `i == -1` keep `c`, otherwise add `ALPHABET[(i + shift) % 26]`.

lessons.title: Decoding: reuse, don't rewrite
lessons.text:
To decode, shift *backwards*. There's no need for a second function:
`encrypt(secret, -3)` undoes `encrypt(text, 3)`, because `%` wraps
negative positions too. Spotting that one function can do both jobs is a
big part of programming well.

### Exercise

Write `caesar(text, shift, direction)` where `direction` is `"encode"` or
`"decode"`, using one shift calculation. The checker types `decode`,
`wkh fdnh lv d olh`, `3`.

```vyrn starter
const ALPHABET = "abcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyz"

main:
    direction = input("encode or decode? ")
    text = input("Message: ")
    shift = int(input("Shift: "))
end
```

```text input
decode
wkh fdnh lv d olh
3
```

```text expect
encode or decode? Message: Shift: Result: the cake is a lie
```

exercise.starter:
const ALPHABET = "abcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyz"

main:
    direction = input("encode or decode? ")
    text = input("Message: ")
    shift = int(input("Shift: "))
end
exercise.input:
decode
wkh fdnh lv d olh
3
exercise.expect: encode or decode? Message: Shift: Result: the cake is a lie
exercise.solution:
const ALPHABET = "abcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyz"

create caesar(text, shift, direction):
    if direction == "decode": shift = -shift
    result = ""
    each c in text:
        i = ALPHABET.find(c)
        result += c if i == -1 else ALPHABET[(i + shift) % 26]
    end
    return result
end

main:
    direction = input("encode or decode? ")
    text = input("Message: ")
    shift = int(input("Shift: "))
    print("Result:", caesar(text, shift, direction))
end
hints: `if direction == "decode": shift = -shift`, then encode as usual.

lessons.title: Long text and special strings
lessons.text:
Text over several lines goes between triple quotes. Every string fills in
`{...}`; when you want real braces, or backslashes, as they are, put `r`
before the quote for a **raw** string:

```vyrn
main:
    name = "Ada"
    letter = """Dear {name},
Thank you for your code.
Best wishes"""
    print(letter)
    print(r"C:\new\folder has {no} interpolation")
end
```

```text
Dear Ada,
Thank you for your code.
Best wishes
C:\new\folder has {no} interpolation
```

### Exercise

Print a small framed menu using one triple-quoted string with
`{dish}` and `{price:.2f}` filled in.

```vyrn starter
main:
    dish = "Soup"
    price = 4.5
end
```

```text expect
+-----------+
| Soup 4.50 |
+-----------+
```



**Day 8 done.** You can slice, search, change and build text, and you've
written your first cipher. Tomorrow: maps, for looking things up by name.

main:
    dish = "Soup"
    price = 4.5
end
exercise.solution:
main:
    dish = "Soup"
    price = 4.5
    print("""+-----------+
| {dish} {price:.2f} |
+-----------+""")
end
hints: Put the three lines between `"""` and `"""`.

days.title: Day 9: Maps, Tuples, Sets and Nesting
days.intro:
Lists keep things in order. But often you want to look something up by
name: a word's meaning, a player's score, a country's capital. That's what
a **map** is for. Today you also meet **tuples** (fixed groups of values)
and **sets** (collections without repeats), and build a silent auction.

lessons.title: Maps: looking things up by key
lessons.text:
A map links **keys** to **values**, written `{key: value, ...}`:

```vyrn
main:
    capitals = {"France": "Paris", "Japan": "Tokyo", "Kenya": "Nairobi"}
    print(capitals["Japan"])
    print(len(capitals))
    print("Peru" in capitals)
    print(capitals)
end
```

```text
Tokyo
3
false
{"France": "Paris", "Japan": "Tokyo", "Kenya": "Nairobi"}
```

`capitals["Japan"]` reads as "the value for the key Japan". Keys are
usually strings or numbers, and each key appears only once. (Python calls
maps *dictionaries*; Java and C++ call them *maps* or *hash maps*.)

### Exercise

Look up the number of legs for the animal the checker types (`spider`).

```vyrn starter
main:
    legs = {"cat": 4, "bird": 2, "spider": 8, "snake": 0}
    animal = input("Animal: ")
end
```

```text input
spider
```

```text expect
Animal: A spider has 8 legs.
```

exercise.starter:
main:
    legs = {"cat": 4, "bird": 2, "spider": 8, "snake": 0}
    animal = input("Animal: ")
end
exercise.solution:
main:
    legs = {"cat": 4, "bird": 2, "spider": 8, "snake": 0}
    animal = input("Animal: ")
    print("A {animal} has {legs[animal]} legs.")
end
hints: `legs[animal]`

lessons.title: Adding, changing and removing
lessons.text:
```vyrn
main:
    stock = {"apples": 10}
    stock["pears"] = 4
    stock["apples"] = 7
    stock["apples"] += 5
    print(stock)
    stock.remove("pears")
    print(stock)
    print(stock.get("kiwis", 0))
end
```

```text
{"apples": 12, "pears": 4}
{"apples": 12}
0
```

- `m[key] = value` adds a new key, or replaces the value of an existing one.
- `m.remove(key)` takes a key out.
- `m[key]` for a missing key is an error (`KeyError`), but
  `m.get(key, default)` gives the default instead.

### Exercise

Count how many times each word appears in a sentence.

```vyrn starter
main:
    text = "red blue red green blue red"
    counts = {}
end
```

```text expect
{"red": 3, "blue": 2, "green": 1}
```

exercise.starter:
main:
    text = "red blue red green blue red"
    counts = {}
end
exercise.solution:
main:
    text = "red blue red green blue red"
    counts = {}
    each word in text.split():
        counts[word] = counts.get(word, 0) + 1
    end
    print(counts)
end
hints: Loop over `text.split()`.
`counts[word] = counts.get(word, 0) + 1`

lessons.title: Looping through a map
lessons.text:
```vyrn
main:
    scores = {"Ada": 92, "Alan": 78, "Grace": 85}
    each name in scores:
        print(name)
    end
    each name, score in scores.items():
        print("{name}: {score}")
    end
    print(scores.keys(), scores.values())
    print(sum(scores.values()) / len(scores))
end
```

```text
Ada
Alan
Grace
Ada: 92
Alan: 78
Grace: 85
["Ada", "Alan", "Grace"] [92, 78, 85]
85.0
```

Looping over a map gives its keys, in the order they were added.
`.items()` gives each key with its value, and `each name, score in ...`
unpacks the pair into two variables.

### Exercise

Turn scores into grades: 90 and over `A`, 80 and over `B`, otherwise `C`.
Build a new map of grades and print it.

```vyrn starter
main:
    scores = {"Ada": 92, "Alan": 78, "Grace": 85, "Linus": 90}
    grades = {}
end
```

```text expect
{"Ada": "A", "Alan": "C", "Grace": "B", "Linus": "A"}
```

hints: `each name, score in scores.items():` and set `grades[name]`.

lessons.title: Tuples: values that belong together
lessons.text:
A **tuple** groups a fixed number of values in parentheses. Unlike a list,
a tuple can't be changed after it's made, which makes it good for things
like a point `(x, y)` or a date `(2026, 11, 11)`.

```vyrn
main:
    point = (3, 4)
    print(point[0], point[1])
    x, y = point
    print("x is {x}, y is {y}")
    a = 1
    b = 2
    a, b = b, a
    print(a, b)
end
```

```text
3 4
x is 3, y is 4
2 1
```

`x, y = point` **unpacks** the tuple into two variables, and `a, b = b, a`
swaps two variables in one line (compare that with lesson 1.6).

### Exercise

Write `min_max(numbers)` that returns the smallest and largest numbers as
a tuple, and unpack the answer.

```vyrn starter
create min_max(numbers):
    return (0, 0)
end

main:
    low, high = min_max([7, 2, 9, 4])
    print("low {low}, high {high}")
end
```

```text expect
low 2, high 9
```

exercise.starter:
create min_max(numbers):
    return (0, 0)
end

main:
    low, high = min_max([7, 2, 9, 4])
    print("low {low}, high {high}")
end
exercise.solution:
create min_max(numbers):
    return (min(numbers), max(numbers))
end

main:
    low, high = min_max([7, 2, 9, 4])
    print("low {low}, high {high}")
end
hints: `return (min(numbers), max(numbers))`

lessons.title: Sets: no repeats
lessons.text:
A **set** holds each value at most once, written `{a, b, c}`. It's the
right tool for "which different things are there?" and "what do these
have in common?":

```vyrn
main:
    visited = {"Paris", "Rome", "Paris", "Oslo"}
    print(visited, len(visited))
    visited.add("Lima")
    print("Rome" in visited)
    mine = {"pizza", "sushi", "tacos"}
    yours = {"sushi", "curry", "tacos"}
    print(mine & yours)
    print(mine | yours)
    print(mine - yours)
    print(set([3, 1, 3, 2, 1]))
end
```

```text
{"Paris", "Rome", "Oslo"} 3
true
{"sushi", "tacos"}
{"pizza", "sushi", "tacos", "curry"}
{"pizza"}
{3, 1, 2}
```

| Operation | Gives |
|---|---|
| `a & b` | what's in both |
| `a \| b` | what's in either |
| `a - b` | what's in `a` but not `b` |
| `set(list)` | the list's values without repeats |

An empty set is written `set()`, because `{}` is an empty map.

### Exercise

Print how many *different* words this sentence has, ignoring capitals.

```vyrn starter
main:
    text = "The quick fox and the lazy dog and THE cat"
end
```

```text expect
7 different words
```

exercise.starter:
main:
    text = "The quick fox and the lazy dog and THE cat"
end
exercise.solution:
main:
    text = "The quick fox and the lazy dog and THE cat"
    words = set(text.lower().split())
    print("{len(words)} different words")
end
hints: `set(text.lower().split())`

lessons.title: Nesting: collections inside collections
lessons.text:
Lists and maps can hold each other, as deep as you need. That's how real
data is shaped:

```vyrn
main:
    trips = {
        "France": {"cities": ["Paris", "Lyon"], "visits": 3},
        "Japan": {"cities": ["Tokyo"], "visits": 1},
    }
    print(trips["France"]["cities"][1])
    trips["Japan"]["cities"].append("Kyoto")
    trips["Peru"] = {"cities": ["Lima"], "visits": 1}
    each country, info in trips.items():
        print("{country}: {", ".join(info["cities"])} ({info["visits"]} visits)")
    end
end
```

```text
Lyon
France: Paris, Lyon (3 visits)
Japan: Tokyo, Kyoto (1 visits)
Peru: Lima (1 visits)
```

Read `trips["France"]["cities"][1]` left to right: the France entry, then
its cities, then the second city.

### Exercise

A list of maps is the classic shape for records. Print each student whose
average is at least 80.

```vyrn starter
main:
    students = [
        {"name": "Ada", "marks": [90, 85, 88]},
        {"name": "Ben", "marks": [60, 75, 70]},
        {"name": "Cai", "marks": [80, 82, 79]},
    ]
end
```

```text expect
Ada 87.7
Cai 80.3
```

exercise.starter:
main:
    students = [
        {"name": "Ada", "marks": [90, 85, 88]},
        {"name": "Ben", "marks": [60, 75, 70]},
        {"name": "Cai", "marks": [80, 82, 79]},
    ]
end
exercise.solution:
main:
    students = [
        {"name": "Ada", "marks": [90, 85, 88]},
        {"name": "Ben", "marks": [60, 75, 70]},
        {"name": "Cai", "marks": [80, 82, 79]},
    ]
    each s in students:
        average = sum(s["marks"]) / len(s["marks"])
        if average >= 80: print("{s["name"]} {average:.1f}")
    end
end
hints: `average = sum(s["marks"]) / len(s["marks"])`
Print with `{average:.1f}`.

lessons.title: Project: the Silent Auction
lessons.text:
Bidders type their name and bid one after another; nobody sees the others'
bids. At the end, the highest bidder wins.

Plan: keep a map from name to bid; keep asking until there are no more
bidders; then find the key with the largest value.

### Exercise

The checker enters three bidders.

```vyrn starter
main:
    bids = {}
    print("Welcome to the silent auction.")
end
```

```text input
Ana
120
yes
Bo
95
yes
Cy
140
no
```

```text expect
Welcome to the silent auction.
Name: Bid: Any more bidders? Name: Bid: Any more bidders? Name: Bid: Any more bidders? Cy wins with a bid of 140.
```



**Day 9 done.** You have all of Vyrn's basic collections: lists, maps,
tuples and sets, and you can nest them. Tomorrow: functions that give back
answers, and functions as values.

exercise.starter:
main:
    bids = {}
    print("Welcome to the silent auction.")
end
exercise.input:
Ana
120
yes
Bo
95
yes
Cy
140
no
exercise.expect:
Welcome to the silent auction.
Name: Bid: Any more bidders? Name: Bid: Any more bidders? Name: Bid: Any more bidders? Cy wins with a bid of 140.
exercise.solution:
main:
    bids = {}
    print("Welcome to the silent auction.")
    loop:
        name = input("Name: ")
        bid = int(input("Bid: "))
        bids[name] = bid
        if input("Any more bidders? ") != "yes": stop
    end
    winner = ""
    best = 0
    each name, bid in bids.items():
        if bid > best:
            best = bid
            winner = name
        end
    end
    print("{winner} wins with a bid of {best}.")
end
hints: `loop:` ... ask name and bid, store `bids[name] = bid`, and `stop` when the answer is not `yes`.
Find the winner by looping over `bids.items()`, keeping the best so far.

days.title: Day 10: Functions with Outputs
days.intro:
Functions that give back answers are the building blocks of every larger
program. Today you see how to design them well, discover that functions are
values you can store and pass around, meet **recursion** (a function that
calls itself), and build a calculator.

lessons.title: Many small functions, one clear program
lessons.text:
Compare a program that does everything in `main` with one split into
functions that each `return` one answer:

```vyrn
create average(numbers):
    return sum(numbers) / len(numbers)
end

create grade(score):
    if score >= 90: return "A"
    if score >= 80: return "B"
    if score >= 70: return "C"
    return "F"
end

create report(name, scores):
    avg = average(scores)
    return "{name}: {avg:.1f} ({grade(avg)})"
end

main:
    print(report("Ada", [95, 88, 92]))
    print(report("Ben", [72, 65, 80]))
end
```

```text
Ada: 91.7 (A)
Ben: 72.3 (C)
```

Each function can be understood, tested and fixed on its own. A good rule:
if you can't describe what a function does in one sentence, split it.

### Exercise

Write `is_palindrome(word)`: `true` if the word reads the same backwards,
ignoring capitals. Then print the palindromes in the list.

```vyrn starter
main:
    words = ["Level", "vyrn", "Racecar", "noon", "moon"]
end
```

```text expect
Level
Racecar
noon
```

exercise.starter:
main:
    words = ["Level", "vyrn", "Racecar", "noon", "moon"]
end
exercise.solution:
create is_palindrome(word):
    w = word.lower()
    return w == w[::-1]
end

main:
    words = ["Level", "vyrn", "Racecar", "noon", "moon"]
    each word in words:
        if is_palindrome(word): print(word)
    end
end
hints: `w = word.lower()` then `return w == w[::-1]`.

lessons.title: Returning several values
lessons.text:
A function can return a tuple and the caller unpacks it:

```vyrn
create divide(a, b):
    return (a // b, a % b)
end

create stats(numbers):
    return (min(numbers), max(numbers), sum(numbers) / len(numbers))
end

main:
    q, r = divide(17, 5)
    print("17 / 5 = {q} remainder {r}")
    low, high, mean = stats([4, 8, 15, 16, 23, 42])
    print(low, high, mean)
end
```

```text
17 / 5 = 3 remainder 2
4 42 18.0
```

(`divmod(17, 5)` is built in and does the same as `divide`.)

### Exercise

Write `split_name(full)` returning the first and last name, and use it.

```vyrn starter
create split_name(full):
    return ("", "")
end

main:
    first, last = split_name("Katherine Johnson")
    print("Last: {last}, first: {first}")
end
```

```text expect
Last: Johnson, first: Katherine
```

exercise.starter:
create split_name(full):
    return ("", "")
end

main:
    first, last = split_name("Katherine Johnson")
    print("Last: {last}, first: {first}")
end
exercise.solution:
create split_name(full):
    parts = full.split()
    return (parts[0], parts[-1])
end

main:
    first, last = split_name("Katherine Johnson")
    print("Last: {last}, first: {first}")
end
hints: `parts = full.split()` then `return (parts[0], parts[-1])`.

lessons.title: Functions are values
lessons.text:
A function's name, without `()`, is the function itself. You can store it
in a variable, put it in a list or map, and pass it to another function:

```vyrn
create shout(text): return text.upper() + "!"
create whisper(text): return text.lower() + "..."

create apply_to_all(f, words):
    result = []
    each w in words: result.append(f(w))
    return result
end

main:
    speak = shout
    print(speak("hello"))
    print(apply_to_all(whisper, ["HI", "THERE"]))
    styles = {"loud": shout, "quiet": whisper}
    print(styles["quiet"]("Good night"))
end
```

```text
HELLO!
["hi...", "there..."]
good night...
```

A function that takes or returns another function is called a
**higher-order function**. You'll use them all the time: `sorted(xs, key =
f)` takes one, for example.

### Exercise

Write `apply_twice(f, x)` that returns `f(f(x))`, and test it with
`double` and with `exclaim`.

```vyrn starter
create double(n): return n * 2
create exclaim(s): return s + "!"

create apply_twice(f, x):
    return x
end

main:
    print(apply_twice(double, 5))
    print(apply_twice(exclaim, "wow"))
end
```

```text expect
20
wow!!
```

exercise.starter:
create double(n): return n * 2
create exclaim(s): return s + "!"

create apply_twice(f, x):
    return x
end

main:
    print(apply_twice(double, 5))
    print(apply_twice(exclaim, "wow"))
end
exercise.solution:
create double(n): return n * 2
create exclaim(s): return s + "!"
create apply_twice(f, x): return f(f(x))

main:
    print(apply_twice(double, 5))
    print(apply_twice(exclaim, "wow"))
end
hints: `create apply_twice(f, x): return f(f(x))`

lessons.title: Small functions without a name: `=>`
lessons.text:
For a tiny function used once, write it on the spot with an arrow:
`x => x * 2` means "a function that takes `x` and gives back `x * 2`". With
more than one parameter, use parentheses: `(a, b) => a + b`.

```vyrn
main:
    double = x => x * 2
    add = (a, b) => a + b
    print(double(21), add(2, 3))
    words = ["kiwi", "fig", "banana", "apple"]
    print(sorted(words, key = w => len(w)))
    print(words.map(w => w.upper()))
    print(words.filter(w => "a" in w))
end
```

```text
42 5
["fig", "kiwi", "apple", "banana"]
["KIWI", "FIG", "BANANA", "APPLE"]
["banana", "apple"]
```

`xs.map(f)` gives a new list of `f` applied to each item; `xs.filter(f)`
keeps the items for which `f` gives `true`. Day 26 goes further with these.

### Exercise

Sort the players by score, highest first, and print their names.

```vyrn starter
main:
    players = [("Ana", 72), ("Bo", 95), ("Cy", 88)]
end
```

```text expect
["Bo", "Cy", "Ana"]
```

exercise.starter:
main:
    players = [("Ana", 72), ("Bo", 95), ("Cy", 88)]
end
exercise.solution:
main:
    players = [("Ana", 72), ("Bo", 95), ("Cy", 88)]
    ranked = sorted(players, key = p => p[1], reverse = true)
    print(ranked.map(p => p[0]))
end
hints: `sorted(players, key = p => p[1], reverse = true)`
Then `.map(p => p[0])` for the names.

lessons.title: Recursion: a function that calls itself
lessons.text:
Some problems contain smaller copies of themselves. The factorial of 5 is
`5 × 4 × 3 × 2 × 1`, which is `5 × (factorial of 4)`. A function can
solve it by calling itself on the smaller problem:

```vyrn
create factorial(n):
    if n <= 1: return 1
    return n * factorial(n - 1)
end

create countdown(n):
    if n == 0:
        print("Lift off!")
        return
    end
    print(n)
    countdown(n - 1)
end

main:
    print(factorial(5), factorial(20))
    countdown(3)
end
```

```text
120 2432902008176640000
3
2
1
Lift off!
```

Every recursive function needs a **base case** that stops it (`n <= 1`,
`n == 0`), and each call must move closer to it. Without one, the function
calls itself forever, until Vyrn stops it with a `StackOverflow` error.

### Exercise

Write `sum_digits(n)` recursively: the sum of the digits of 4096 is
4 + 0 + 9 + 6 = 19.

```vyrn starter
create sum_digits(n):
    return n
end

main:
    print(sum_digits(4096))
    print(sum_digits(7))
end
```

```text expect
19
7
```

exercise.starter:
create sum_digits(n):
    return n
end

main:
    print(sum_digits(4096))
    print(sum_digits(7))
end
exercise.solution:
create sum_digits(n):
    if n < 10: return n
    return n % 10 + sum_digits(n // 10)
end

main:
    print(sum_digits(4096))
    print(sum_digits(7))
end
hints: The last digit is `n % 10`; the rest is `n // 10`.
Base case: a single digit (`n < 10`) is its own sum.

lessons.title: Project: the Calculator
lessons.text:
Put the operations in a map from symbol to function. The calculator keeps
a running result: the person types an operator and a number, and the
result updates, until they type `=`.

### Exercise

The checker starts from `10`, then types `+ 5`, `* 3`, `/ 4` and `=`.

```vyrn starter
create add(a, b): return a + b
create subtract(a, b): return a - b
create multiply(a, b): return a * b
create divide(a, b): return a / b

main:
    operations = {"+": add, "-": subtract, "*": multiply, "/": divide}
    result = float(input("Start with: "))
end
```

```text input
10
+ 5
* 3
/ 4
=
```

```text expect
Start with: Next (like + 5, or =): 10.0 + 5.0 = 15.0
Next (like + 5, or =): 15.0 * 3.0 = 45.0
Next (like + 5, or =): 45.0 / 4.0 = 11.25
Next (like + 5, or =): Result: 11.25
```



**Try it:** add `**` for powers, and print `Unknown operator` instead of
failing when the symbol isn't in the map (`symbol in operations`).

**Day 10 done, and Unit 1 with it!** You can write real programs: they
calculate, decide, repeat, keep data in collections, and are organised into
functions. Unit 2 builds bigger games, and the tools that keep bigger
programs tidy: scope, error handling and objects.

exercise.starter:
create add(a, b): return a + b
create subtract(a, b): return a - b
create multiply(a, b): return a * b
create divide(a, b): return a / b

main:
    operations = {"+": add, "-": subtract, "*": multiply, "/": divide}
    result = float(input("Start with: "))
end
exercise.expect:
Start with: Next (like + 5, or =): 10.0 + 5.0 = 15.0
Next (like + 5, or =): 15.0 * 3.0 = 45.0
Next (like + 5, or =): 45.0 / 4.0 = 11.25
Next (like + 5, or =): Result: 11.25
exercise.solution:
create add(a, b): return a + b
create subtract(a, b): return a - b
create multiply(a, b): return a * b
create divide(a, b): return a / b

main:
    operations = {"+": add, "-": subtract, "*": multiply, "/": divide}
    result = float(input("Start with: "))
    loop:
        line = input("Next (like + 5, or =): ")
        if line == "=": stop
        symbol, number = line.split()
        n = float(number)
        new = operations[symbol](result, n)
        print("{result} {symbol} {n} = {new}")
        result = new
    end
    print("Result:", result)
end
hints: Inside a `loop:`, read a line and `stop` if it is `=`.
`symbol, number = line.split()` then `operations[symbol](result, float(number))`.

days.title: Day 11: Capstone: Twenty-One
days.intro:
Today is a capstone: a complete card game using everything from Unit 1.
In **Twenty-One**, you and the dealer are each dealt cards; you try to get
closer to 21 than the dealer without going over. Number cards count their
number, picture cards count 10, and an ace counts 11, or 1 if 11 would
take you over 21.

As on Day 7, the game is built one step at a time, and each step is
checked before the next.

lessons.title: Step 1: the deck and dealing
lessons.text:
Represent each card by its value: `[11, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 10,
10, 10]` (ace, 2 to 10, then three picture cards). Dealing means picking a
random card.

### Exercise

Write `deal()` that returns a random card, and deal two to the player.

```vyrn starter
use vyrn.random

const CARDS = [11, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 10, 10, 10]

create deal():
    return 0
end

main:
    random.seed(21)
    hand = [deal(), deal()]
    print("Your cards:", hand)
end
```

```text expect
Your cards: [10, 4]
```

exercise.starter:
use vyrn.random

const CARDS = [11, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 10, 10, 10]

create deal():
    return 0
end

main:
    random.seed(21)
    hand = [deal(), deal()]
    print("Your cards:", hand)
end
exercise.solution:
use vyrn.random

const CARDS = [11, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 10, 10, 10]

create deal():
    return random.choice(CARDS)
end

main:
    random.seed(21)
    hand = [deal(), deal()]
    print("Your cards:", hand)
end
hints: `return random.choice(CARDS)`

lessons.title: Step 2: scoring a hand
lessons.text:
The score is the sum of the cards, with one twist: while the score is over
21 and the hand holds an ace counted as 11, count that ace as 1 instead
(take 10 off).

### Exercise

Write `score(hand)`.

```vyrn starter
create score(hand):
    return sum(hand)
end

main:
    print(score([10, 7]))
    print(score([11, 10]))
    print(score([11, 11]))
    print(score([11, 9, 5]))
    print(score([10, 9, 5]))
end
```

```text expect
17
21
12
15
24
```

exercise.starter:
create score(hand):
    return sum(hand)
end

main:
    print(score([10, 7]))
    print(score([11, 10]))
    print(score([11, 11]))
    print(score([11, 9, 5]))
    print(score([10, 9, 5]))
end
exercise.solution:
create score(hand):
    total = sum(hand)
    aces = hand.count(11)
    loop total > 21 and aces > 0:
        total -= 10
        aces -= 1
    end
    return total
end

main:
    print(score([10, 7]))
    print(score([11, 10]))
    print(score([11, 11]))
    print(score([11, 9, 5]))
    print(score([10, 9, 5]))
end
hints: Count the aces: `aces = hand.count(11)`.
`loop total > 21 and aces > 0:` take 10 off the total and one off `aces`.

lessons.title: Step 3: who wins?
lessons.text:
### Exercise

Write `result(player, dealer)` taking two scores and returning one of:
`You went over. You lose.`, `Dealer went over. You win!`, `Draw.`,
`You win!`, `You lose.`. The order of the checks matters: going over is
checked first.

```vyrn starter
create result(player, dealer):
    return ""
end

main:
    print(result(23, 18))
    print(result(20, 25))
    print(result(19, 19))
    print(result(20, 18))
    print(result(17, 19))
end
```

```text expect
You went over. You lose.
Dealer went over. You win!
Draw.
You win!
You lose.
```

exercise.starter:
create result(player, dealer):
    return ""
end

main:
    print(result(23, 18))
    print(result(20, 25))
    print(result(19, 19))
    print(result(20, 18))
    print(result(17, 19))
end
exercise.expect:
You went over. You lose.
Dealer went over. You win!
Draw.
You win!
You lose.
exercise.solution:
create result(player, dealer):
    if player > 21: return "You went over. You lose."
    if dealer > 21: return "Dealer went over. You win!"
    if player == dealer: return "Draw."
    if player > dealer: return "You win!"
    return "You lose."
end

main:
    print(result(23, 18))
    print(result(20, 25))
    print(result(19, 19))
    print(result(20, 18))
    print(result(17, 19))
end
hints: `if player > 21: return ...` first, then `if dealer > 21: ...`.

lessons.title: Step 4: the player's turn
lessons.text:
The player sees their cards and one of the dealer's, then types `y` to
take another card or `n` to stop. Going over 21 ends the turn at once.

### Exercise

Write the player's turn. The checker types `y`, then `n`.

```vyrn starter
use vyrn.random

const CARDS = [11, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 10, 10, 10]

create deal(): return random.choice(CARDS)

create score(hand):
    total = sum(hand)
    aces = hand.count(11)
    loop total > 21 and aces > 0:
        total -= 10
        aces -= 1
    end
    return total
end

main:
    random.seed(3)
    player = [deal(), deal()]
    dealer = [deal(), deal()]
end
```

```text input
y
n
```

```text expect
Your cards: [7, 10], score 17. Dealer shows 10.
Another card? (y/n) You end with [7, 10, 8], score 25.
```

    end

create deal(): return random.choice(CARDS)

Show the dealer's first card with `dealer[0]`.

lessons.title: Step 5: the dealer's turn, and the whole game
lessons.text:
The dealer follows a fixed rule: keep taking cards while the score is under
17. Then the results are compared.

### Exercise

Put everything together. The checker types `n` (stand on the first two
cards).

```vyrn starter
use vyrn.random

const CARDS = [11, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 10, 10, 10]

create deal(): return random.choice(CARDS)

create score(hand):
    total = sum(hand)
    aces = hand.count(11)
    loop total > 21 and aces > 0:
        total -= 10
        aces -= 1
    end
    return total
end

create result(player, dealer):
    if player > 21: return "You went over. You lose."
    if dealer > 21: return "Dealer went over. You win!"
    if player == dealer: return "Draw."
    if player > dealer: return "You win!"
    return "You lose."
end

main:
    random.seed(8)
end
```

```text input
n
```

```text expect
Your cards: [4, 10], score 14. Dealer shows 10.
Another card? (y/n) You: [4, 10] = 14
Dealer: [10, 9] = 19
You lose.
```



**Try it:** remove the seed and play a few rounds. Then add a "play again?"
question around the whole game, and keep a running count of wins.

**Day 11 done.** You designed and built a full card game from small,
tested pieces: exactly how professional programs are made.

create score(hand):

Dealer: [10, 9] = 19
You lose.
exercise.solution:
use vyrn.random

const CARDS = [11, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 10, 10, 10]

create deal(): return random.choice(CARDS)

create score(hand):
    total = sum(hand)
    aces = hand.count(11)
    loop total > 21 and aces > 0:
        total -= 10
        aces -= 1
    end
    return total
end

create result(player, dealer):
    if player > 21: return "You went over. You lose."
    if dealer > 21: return "Dealer went over. You win!"
    if player == dealer: return "Draw."
    if player > dealer: return "You win!"
    return "You lose."
end

main:
    random.seed(8)

    dealer = [deal(), deal()]

    end

    print("Dealer: {dealer} = {score(dealer)}")

end

Finish with both hands and `print(result(score(player), score(dealer)))`.

days.title: Day 12: Scope, `let`, `var` and `const`
days.intro:
Programs get bigger, and with more names comes more chance of mixing them
up. Today you learn exactly where each name lives (its **scope**), and how
to say "this never changes" so Vyrn can hold you to it. The project is a
number-guessing game with difficulty levels.

lessons.title: Block scope
lessons.text:
A variable created inside a block (an `if`, a loop, a function) belongs to
that block and disappears at its `end`:

```vyrn check
main:
    temperature = 25
    if temperature > 20:
        advice = "wear a hat"
        print(advice)
    end
    # `advice` doesn't exist here.
end
```

Trying to use `advice` after the `end` is an error that `vyrn check`
catches before running:

```text
error: `advice` is not defined
```

When you need a value after a block, create the variable **before** it:

```vyrn
main:
    temperature = 25
    advice = "no advice"
    if temperature > 20:
        advice = "wear a hat"
    end
    print(advice)
end
```

```text
wear a hat
```

Why does Vyrn work this way? Because it keeps mistakes local: a name made
for a moment inside a loop can't accidentally clash with something
elsewhere. (Python lets block variables leak out; C++, Java and Vyrn
don't.)

### Exercise

This program should print the largest even number in the list, but it
doesn't compile. Fix it by creating `largest` in the right place.

```vyrn starter broken
main:
    numbers = [3, 8, 5, 12, 7]
    each n in numbers:
        if n % 2 == 0:
            largest = n
        end
    end
    print("Largest even:", largest)
end
```

```text expect
Largest even: 12
```

exercise.starter:
main:
    numbers = [3, 8, 5, 12, 7]
    each n in numbers:
        if n % 2 == 0:
            largest = n
        end
    end
    print("Largest even:", largest)
end
exercise.solution:
main:
    numbers = [3, 8, 5, 12, 7]
    largest = 0
    each n in numbers:
        if n % 2 == 0 and n > largest:
            largest = n
        end
    end
    print("Largest even:", largest)
end
hints: Create `largest = 0` before the loop.
Inside, only replace it when `n` is even **and** bigger: `if n % 2 == 0 and n > largest:`.

lessons.title: Function scope, and sharing without globals
lessons.text:
Each call of a function gets its own fresh variables. A function sees its
parameters, its own variables, and the file's top-level declarations
(functions, `const`s, types), but **not** the variables of `main` or of
other functions.

```vyrn
const BONUS = 5

create add_bonus(score):
    total = score + BONUS
    return total
end

main:
    score = 10
    print(add_bonus(score))
    print(add_bonus(20))
end
```

```text
15
25
```

Many languages have **global variables**, changeable from anywhere. They
make programs hard to follow: any function might change anything. Vyrn
has no global variables. Values travel in through parameters and out
through `return`, so you can always see where a value came from. Day 16
shows the other way: an **object** that keeps its own changing state.

### Exercise

`roll_total` should add up the dice, and `main` should print the total of
both rounds. Make it work by passing values in and returning them, without
any variable shared between functions.

```vyrn starter
create roll_total(rolls):
    total = 0
    each r in rolls: total += r
end

main:
    first = roll_total([3, 5, 6])
    second = roll_total([1, 2])
    print("Total of both rounds:", first + second)
end
```

```text expect
Total of both rounds: 17
```

exercise.starter:
create roll_total(rolls):
    total = 0
    each r in rolls: total += r
end

main:
    first = roll_total([3, 5, 6])
    second = roll_total([1, 2])
    print("Total of both rounds:", first + second)
end
exercise.solution:
create roll_total(rolls):
    total = 0
    each r in rolls: total += r
    return total
end

main:
    first = roll_total([3, 5, 6])
    second = roll_total([1, 2])
    print("Total of both rounds:", first + second)
end
hints: `roll_total` computes `total` but never gives it back.

lessons.title: `let` and `var`: saying what changes
lessons.text:
Plain `x = 1` is fine for short programs. In longer ones it helps to say
what you mean:

- `let name = value` creates a name that will **never** be given a new
  value.
- `var name = value` creates a variable you **plan** to change.

```vyrn
main:
    let tax_rate = 0.2
    var total = 0.0
    each price in [10.0, 20.0, 5.0]:
        total += price * (1 + tax_rate)
    end
    print("{total:.2f}")
end
```

```text
42.00
```

If you later write `tax_rate = 0.3` by mistake, Vyrn refuses, and says how
to fix it if you really meant it:

```text
error: cannot assign to `tax_rate`: it is declared with `let`
  = help: declare it with `var tax_rate` to change it
```

A `let` list can still have items added (the name keeps pointing at the
same list). What `let` forbids is pointing the name at a different value.

### Exercise

Mark each variable `let` or `var` correctly: the program should still run
and print the same.

```vyrn starter
main:
    name = "Ada"
    lives = 3
    lives -= 1
    greeting = "Hi, {name}"
    print(greeting, lives)
end
```

```text expect
Hi, Ada 2
```

exercise.starter:
main:
    name = "Ada"
    lives = 3
    lives -= 1
    greeting = "Hi, {name}"
    print(greeting, lives)
end
exercise.solution:
main:
    let name = "Ada"
    var lives = 3
    lives -= 1
    let greeting = "Hi, {name}"
    print(greeting, lives)
end
hints: Only `lives` changes after it is created.

lessons.title: `const`: values fixed for the whole program
lessons.text:
A `const` at the top of a file is fixed before the program even starts,
and every function can read it. Use it for the settings of your program:

```vyrn
const MAX_TRIES = 5
const LEVELS = {"easy": 10, "hard": 5}
const WELCOME = "Guess my number!"

main:
    print(WELCOME)
    print("Easy gives {LEVELS["easy"]} tries, the default is {MAX_TRIES}.")
end
```

```text
Guess my number!
Easy gives 10 tries, the default is 5.
```

Writing constants in CAPITALS makes them stand out. Changing one later
(say, `MAX_TRIES = 7` in `main`) is an error.

### Exercise

Replace the repeated "magic number" `0.15` with a constant `DISCOUNT`, so
it's defined in one place.

```vyrn starter
create sale_price(price):
    return price * (1 - 0.15)
end

main:
    print("Discount: {0.15:.0%}")
    print("{sale_price(40):.2f}")
end
```

```text expect
Discount: 15%
34.00
```

exercise.starter:
create sale_price(price):
    return price * (1 - 0.15)
end

main:
    print("Discount: {0.15:.0%}")
    print("{sale_price(40):.2f}")
end
exercise.solution:
const DISCOUNT = 0.15

create sale_price(price):
    return price * (1 - DISCOUNT)
end

main:
    print("Discount: {DISCOUNT:.0%}")
    print("{sale_price(40):.2f}")
end
hints: `const DISCOUNT = 0.15` at the top, then use `DISCOUNT` in both places.

lessons.title: Project: Guess the Number
lessons.text:
The computer picks a number from 1 to 100; the player chooses easy (10
tries) or hard (5 tries) and guesses, with `Too high` and `Too low` as
clues.

### Exercise

The checker picks `easy`, then plays the smart way: always guess the middle
of what's left, so each clue halves the possibilities. With the seed kept,
it guesses `50`, `75`, `62`, `68`, `71`, `69`, `70`. (Halving finds any
number from 1 to 100 in at most 7 guesses: that idea is called **binary
search**, and it comes back on Day 68.)

```vyrn starter
use vyrn.random

const TRIES = {"easy": 10, "hard": 5}

main:
    random.seed(100)
    let secret = random.int(1, 100)
    print("I'm thinking of a number between 1 and 100.")
end
```

```text input
easy
50
75
62
68
71
69
70
```

```text expect
I'm thinking of a number between 1 and 100.
easy or hard? You have 10 tries. Guess: Too low.
You have 9 tries. Guess: Too high.
You have 8 tries. Guess: Too low.
You have 7 tries. Guess: Too low.
You have 6 tries. Guess: Too high.
You have 5 tries. Guess: Too low.
You have 4 tries. Guess: Yes! It was 70.
```



`return` inside `main` ends the program early.

**Day 12 done.** You know where every name lives and how to make Vyrn guard
the ones that shouldn't change. Tomorrow: finding and handling errors.

exercise.starter:
use vyrn.random

const TRIES = {"easy": 10, "hard": 5}

main:
    random.seed(100)
    let secret = random.int(1, 100)
    print("I'm thinking of a number between 1 and 100.")
end
exercise.expect:
I'm thinking of a number between 1 and 100.
easy or hard? You have 10 tries. Guess: Too low.
You have 9 tries. Guess: Too high.
You have 8 tries. Guess: Too low.
You have 7 tries. Guess: Too low.
You have 6 tries. Guess: Too high.
You have 5 tries. Guess: Too low.
You have 4 tries. Guess: Yes! It was 70.
exercise.solution:
use vyrn.random

const TRIES = {"easy": 10, "hard": 5}

main:
    random.seed(100)
    let secret = random.int(1, 100)
    print("I'm thinking of a number between 1 and 100.")
    var left = TRIES[input("easy or hard? ")]
    loop left > 0:
        let guess = int(input("You have {left} tries. Guess: "))
        if guess == secret:
            print("Yes! It was {secret}.")
            return
        else if guess > secret:
            print("Too high.")
        else:
            print("Too low.")
        end
        left -= 1
    end
    print("Out of tries. It was {secret}.")
end
hints: `var left = TRIES[input("easy or hard? ")]`
`loop left > 0:` read a guess; if it's right, print and `return`; otherwise give a clue and take a try away.
After the loop, the player has run out of tries.

days.title: Day 13: Finding and Handling Errors
days.intro:
Every programmer spends a lot of time on **bugs**: programs that stop with
an error, or worse, run and give the wrong answer. Today you learn to read
errors, to hunt down wrong answers, and to make programs that recover
gracefully when something goes wrong.

lessons.title: Reading a runtime error
lessons.text:
Some mistakes only show up while the program runs. Vyrn then stops and
reports the **kind** of error, a message, where it happened, and the chain
of function calls that led there:

```vyrn
create average(numbers):
    return sum(numbers) / len(numbers)
end

main:
    print(average([4, 6]))
    print(average([]))
end
```

```text
5.0
error: DivisionByZero: division by zero
```

In a terminal you see more:

```text
error: DivisionByZero: division by zero
 --> avg.vyrn:2
  |
2 |     return sum(numbers) / len(numbers)
  |
  = help: check that the number you divide by is not 0
  in average (avg.vyrn:2)
  in main (avg.vyrn:7)
```

Read the bottom lines from the bottom up: `main` on line 7 called
`average`, which failed on line 2. The fix belongs in whichever of them
should have handled an empty list.

### Exercise

Make `average` return `0` for an empty list instead of failing.

```vyrn starter
create average(numbers):
    return sum(numbers) / len(numbers)
end

main:
    print(average([4, 6]))
    print(average([]))
end
```

```text expect
5.0
0
```

exercise.starter:
create average(numbers):
    return sum(numbers) / len(numbers)
end

main:
    print(average([4, 6]))
    print(average([]))
end
exercise.solution:
create average(numbers):
    if len(numbers) == 0: return 0
    return sum(numbers) / len(numbers)
end

main:
    print(average([4, 6]))
    print(average([]))
end
hints: `if len(numbers) == 0: return 0` before dividing.

lessons.title: The usual suspects
lessons.text:
| Error kind | Typical cause | Typical fix |
|---|---|---|
| `IndexError` | `xs[5]` on a shorter list | check `i < len(xs)` |
| `KeyError` | `m["x"]` when `"x"` isn't a key | `m.get("x", default)` or `"x" in m` |
| `DivisionByZero` | dividing by `0` | check first |
| `ValueError` | `int("abc")`: text that isn't a number | check, or catch it (lesson 13.4) |
| `TypeError` | the wrong kind of value, like `none + 1` | find where the value came from |
| `StackOverflow` | recursion without a base case | add the base case |

```vyrn
main:
    stock = {"apples": 3}
    print(stock.get("pears", 0))
    print(stock["pears"])
end
```

```text
0
error: KeyError: key "pears" is not in the map
```

### Exercise

The program crashes on the last word. Make it print `?` for words that are
not in the dictionary.

```vyrn starter
main:
    spanish = {"cat": "gato", "dog": "perro"}
    each word in ["cat", "dog", "bird"]:
        print(word, "->", spanish[word])
    end
end
```

```text expect
cat -> gato
dog -> perro
bird -> ?
```

exercise.starter:
main:
    spanish = {"cat": "gato", "dog": "perro"}
    each word in ["cat", "dog", "bird"]:
        print(word, "->", spanish[word])
    end
end
exercise.solution:
main:
    spanish = {"cat": "gato", "dog": "perro"}
    each word in ["cat", "dog", "bird"]:
        print(word, "->", spanish.get(word, "?"))
    end
end
hints: `spanish.get(word, "?")`

lessons.title: Hunting wrong answers
lessons.text:
The hardest bugs don't crash: the program runs and prints the wrong thing.
The method:

1. **Reproduce**: find a small input that gives a wrong answer.
2. **Inspect**: `print` the values inside the program to see where they
   stop being what you expect.
3. **Fix**, then check the original case *and* a few others.

```vyrn
create count_long_words(words):
    count = 0
    each w in words:
        print("  checking", w, len(w))
        if len(w) > 5: count += 1
    end
    return count
end

main:
    print(count_long_words(["planet", "sun", "comets"]))
end
```

```text
  checking planet 6
  checking sun 3
  checking comets 6
2
```

The extra `print` shows each step. Once the bug is found, remove it.

### Exercise

`sum_to(n)` should add the numbers from 1 to `n` (so `sum_to(4)` is 10),
but gives the wrong answer. Find and fix the bug.

```vyrn starter
create sum_to(n):
    total = 0
    each i in 1 until n:
        total += i
    end
    return total
end

main:
    print(sum_to(4))
    print(sum_to(100))
end
```

```text expect
10
5050
```



An answer that's wrong by exactly one step is so common it has a name: an
**off-by-one error**.

exercise.starter:
create sum_to(n):
    total = 0
    each i in 1 until n:
        total += i
    end
    return total
end

main:
    print(sum_to(4))
    print(sum_to(100))
end
exercise.solution:
create sum_to(n):
    total = 0
    each i in 1 to n:
        total += i
    end
    return total
end

main:
    print(sum_to(4))
    print(sum_to(100))
end
hints: Print `i` inside the loop: which number is missing?
`until` stops *before* the end; `to` includes it.

lessons.title: `attempt` and `catch`: recovering from failures
lessons.text:
Some errors can't be prevented by checking first: the user types `forty`
when asked for a number, or a file is missing. Wrap the risky code in
`attempt:`, and say what to do instead in `catch`:

```vyrn
create to_number(text):
    attempt:
        return int(text)
    catch ValueError:
        return -1
    end
end

main:
    each t in ["42", "forty", "7"]:
        print(t, "->", to_number(t))
    end
    attempt:
        print(10 / 0)
    catch DivisionByZero as e:
        print("Caught:", e.message)
    end
end
```

```text
42 -> 42
forty -> -1
7 -> 7
Caught: division by zero
```

- `catch ValueError:` handles only that kind of error; others still stop
  the program.
- `catch ValueError as e:` also names the error, so you can read
  `e.message`.
- `catch Error:` handles every kind.
- Several `catch` lines can follow one `attempt`; the first that matches
  runs.

### Exercise

Keep asking for an age until the answer is a whole number. The checker
types `twelve`, `12.5`, then `12`.

```vyrn starter
main:
    loop:
        text = input("Age: ")
    end
end
```

```text input
twelve
12.5
12
```

```text expect
Age: That's not a whole number, try again.
Age: That's not a whole number, try again.
Age: Next year you'll be 13.
```

exercise.starter:
main:
    loop:
        text = input("Age: ")
    end
end
exercise.expect:
Age: That's not a whole number, try again.
Age: That's not a whole number, try again.
Age: Next year you'll be 13.
exercise.solution:
main:
    age = 0
    loop:
        text = input("Age: ")
        attempt:
            age = int(text)
            stop
        catch ValueError:
            print("That's not a whole number, try again.")
        end
    end
    print("Next year you'll be {age + 1}.")
end
hints: Inside the loop: `attempt:` `age = int(text)` ... `stop` ... `catch ValueError:` print the message.
Create `age = 0` before the loop so it exists afterwards.

lessons.title: `always`: clean up no matter what
lessons.text:
`always:` runs whether the `attempt` succeeded, failed and was caught, or
failed and wasn't. It's for clean-up that must happen: closing a file,
saving progress, printing a final report.

```vyrn
create risky(n):
    attempt:
        print("  working on", n)
        return 100 // n
    catch DivisionByZero:
        print("  can't divide by zero")
        return 0
    always:
        print("  finished", n)
    end
end

main:
    print(risky(4))
    print(risky(0))
end
```

```text
  working on 4
  finished 4
25
  working on 0
  can't divide by zero
  finished 0
0
```

### Exercise

Add up the items in each order. One order is broken: instead of stopping
the whole program, print `skipped` for it and carry on with the rest.

```vyrn starter
main:
    orders = ["3", "5", "oops", "2"]
    total = 0
    each o in orders:
        total += int(o)
    end
    print("Total items:", total)
end
```

```text expect
skipped oops
Total items: 10
```

exercise.starter:
main:
    orders = ["3", "5", "oops", "2"]
    total = 0
    each o in orders:
        total += int(o)
    end
    print("Total items:", total)
end
exercise.solution:
main:
    orders = ["3", "5", "oops", "2"]
    total = 0
    each o in orders:
        attempt:
            total += int(o)
        catch ValueError:
            print("skipped", o)
        end
    end
    print("Total items:", total)
end
hints: Wrap `total += int(o)` in `attempt:` ... `catch ValueError:` ... `end`.

lessons.title: `fail`: raising your own errors
lessons.text:
Your functions can report problems too. `fail` stops the function and
sends an error up to whoever called it, until some `catch` handles it:

```vyrn
create withdraw(balance, amount):
    if amount <= 0: fail ValueError("the amount must be positive")
    if amount > balance: fail ValueError("not enough money: balance is {balance}")
    return balance - amount
end

main:
    var balance = 100
    each amount in [30, -5, 500, 20]:
        attempt:
            balance = withdraw(balance, amount)
            print("Withdrew {amount}, balance {balance}")
        catch ValueError as e:
            print("Refused {amount}: {e.message}")
        end
    end
end
```

```text
Withdrew 30, balance 70
Refused -5: the amount must be positive
Refused 500: not enough money: balance is 70
Withdrew 20, balance 50
```

Built-in kinds to fail with: `Error`, `ValueError`, `TypeError`,
`KeyError` and `IndexError`. On Day 30 you'll make your own kinds, which
carry extra information.

Why fail instead of printing a message? Because the function doesn't know
what the caller wants to do about it: show a message, try again, use a
default. Failing lets the caller decide.

### Exercise

Write `parse_percent(text)` that turns `"45%"` into `45`. Fail with a
`ValueError` if the text doesn't end with `%` or the number is not between
0 and 100.

```vyrn starter
create parse_percent(text):
    return 0
end

main:
    each t in ["45%", "120%", "abc", "7%"]:
        attempt:
            print(t, "->", parse_percent(t))
        catch ValueError as e:
            print(t, "->", "error:", e.message)
        end
    end
end
```

```text expect
45% -> 45
120% -> error: must be between 0 and 100
abc -> error: must end with %
7% -> 7
```

exercise.starter:
create parse_percent(text):
    return 0
end

main:
    each t in ["45%", "120%", "abc", "7%"]:
        attempt:
            print(t, "->", parse_percent(t))
        catch ValueError as e:
            print(t, "->", "error:", e.message)
        end
    end
end
exercise.expect:
45% -> 45
120% -> error: must be between 0 and 100
abc -> error: must end with %
7% -> 7
exercise.solution:
create parse_percent(text):
    if not text.endswith("%"): fail ValueError("must end with %")
    n = int(text[:-1])
    if n < 0 or n > 100: fail ValueError("must be between 0 and 100")
    return n
end

main:
    each t in ["45%", "120%", "abc", "7%"]:
        attempt:
            print(t, "->", parse_percent(t))
        catch ValueError as e:
            print(t, "->", "error:", e.message)
        end
    end
end
hints: `if not text.endswith("%"): fail ValueError("must end with %")`
`n = int(text[:-1])` drops the last character.

lessons.title: Project: the Bug Hunt
lessons.text:
This shopping-cart program has three bugs. It runs, but the totals are
wrong. Use the method from lesson 13.3: reproduce, inspect, fix.

### Exercise

```vyrn starter
const PRICES = {"apple": 0.5, "bread": 2.25, "milk": 1.2}

create line_total(item, quantity):
    return PRICES[item] + quantity
end

create cart_total(cart):
    total = 0.0
    each item, quantity in cart.items():
        total = line_total(item, quantity)
    end
    return total
end

create with_discount(total):
    if total > 10: return total * 0.1
    return total
end

main:
    cart = {"apple": 6, "bread": 2, "milk": 3}
    total = cart_total(cart)
    print("Total: {total:.2f}")
    print("To pay: {with_discount(total):.2f}")
end
```

```text expect
Total: 11.10
To pay: 9.99
```



**Day 13 done.** Errors are no longer scary: they're messages telling you
where to look. Tomorrow: a game built around data.

exercise.solution:
const PRICES = {"apple": 0.5, "bread": 2.25, "milk": 1.2}

create line_total(item, quantity):
    return PRICES[item] * quantity
end

create cart_total(cart):
    total = 0.0
    each item, quantity in cart.items():
        total += line_total(item, quantity)
    end
    return total
end

create with_discount(total):
    if total > 10: return total * 0.9
    return total
end

main:
    cart = {"apple": 6, "bread": 2, "milk": 3}
    total = cart_total(cart)
    print("Total: {total:.2f}")
    print("To pay: {with_discount(total):.2f}")
end
hints: A line's total is price **times** quantity.
`total = ...` replaces the running total each time; it should add.
A 10% discount means paying 90%: `total * 0.9`.

days.title: Day 14: Project: Bigger or Smaller
days.intro:
Today's game is driven by **data**: a list of records, each one a map with
the same keys. The player sees two mountains and guesses which is taller;
a correct guess scores a point and brings in a new challenger. Keeping the
facts in data, and the rules in code, means you can swap in rivers, cities
or planets without changing the program.

lessons.title: Records: a list of maps
lessons.text:
```vyrn
const MOUNTAINS = [
    {"name": "Everest", "height": 8849, "country": "Nepal"},
    {"name": "Kilimanjaro", "height": 5895, "country": "Tanzania"},
    {"name": "Denali", "height": 6190, "country": "USA"},
]

main:
    each m in MOUNTAINS:
        print("{m["name"]:<12} {m["height"]:>5} m  ({m["country"]})")
    end
end
```

```text
Everest       8849 m  (Nepal)
Kilimanjaro   5895 m  (Tanzania)
Denali        6190 m  (USA)
```

Each map is one **record**, and each key is a **field**. Day 17 shows
`struct`, Vyrn's way to declare a record's fields once, with their types.

### Exercise

Print the name of the tallest mountain in the list.

```vyrn starter
const MOUNTAINS = [

    {"name": "Kilimanjaro", "height": 5895, "country": "Tanzania"},
    {"name": "Denali", "height": 6190, "country": "USA"},
]

main:
end
```

```text expect
Everest
```

lessons.text:
A small function that turns a record into text keeps the game code tidy:

lessons.title: One round
lessons.text:
### Exercise

Write `check(a, b, answer)`: `answer` is `"a"` or `"b"`; return `true` if
the player picked the taller one.

```vyrn starter
create check(a, b, answer):
    return false
end

main:
    everest = {"name": "Everest", "height": 8849, "country": "Nepal"}
    denali = {"name": "Denali", "height": 6190, "country": "USA"}
    print(check(everest, denali, "a"))
    print(check(everest, denali, "b"))
    print(check(denali, everest, "b"))
end
```

```text expect
true
false
true
```

exercise.starter:
create check(a, b, answer):
    return false
end

main:
    everest = {"name": "Everest", "height": 8849, "country": "Nepal"}
    denali = {"name": "Denali", "height": 6190, "country": "USA"}
    print(check(everest, denali, "a"))
    print(check(everest, denali, "b"))
    print(check(denali, everest, "b"))
end
exercise.solution:
create check(a, b, answer):
    taller = "a" if a["height"] > b["height"] else "b"
    return answer == taller
end

main:
    everest = {"name": "Everest", "height": 8849, "country": "Nepal"}
    denali = {"name": "Denali", "height": 6190, "country": "USA"}
    print(check(everest, denali, "a"))
    print(check(everest, denali, "b"))
    print(check(denali, everest, "b"))
end
hints: Work out the right answer: `taller = "a" if a["height"] > b["height"] else "b"`.

lessons.title: The game
lessons.text:
The winner of each round stays as `a`; a new random mountain becomes `b`.
The game ends at the first wrong answer, or when the mountains run out.

### Exercise

The checker answers `a`, `a`, `b`, `a`, then makes a mistake with `b`.

```vyrn starter
use vyrn.random

const MOUNTAINS = [
    {"name": "Everest", "height": 8849, "country": "Nepal"},
    {"name": "K2", "height": 8611, "country": "Pakistan"},
    {"name": "Kilimanjaro", "height": 5895, "country": "Tanzania"},
    {"name": "Mont Blanc", "height": 4806, "country": "France"},
    {"name": "Denali", "height": 6190, "country": "USA"},
    {"name": "Aconcagua", "height": 6961, "country": "Argentina"},
    {"name": "Fuji", "height": 3776, "country": "Japan"},
]

create describe(m): return "{m["name"]}, in {m["country"]}"

create check(a, b, answer):
    taller = "a" if a["height"] > b["height"] else "b"
    return answer == taller
end

main:
    random.seed(14)
    pool = list(MOUNTAINS)
    random.shuffle(pool)
    a = pool.pop()
    score = 0
end
```

```text input
a
a
b
a
b
```

```text expect
A: Denali, in USA
B: Fuji, in Japan
Which is taller, a or b? Right! Score: 1
A: Denali, in USA
B: Mont Blanc, in France
Which is taller, a or b? Right! Score: 2
A: Denali, in USA
B: Everest, in Nepal
Which is taller, a or b? Right! Score: 3
A: Everest, in Nepal
B: K2, in Pakistan
Which is taller, a or b? Right! Score: 4
A: Everest, in Nepal
B: Kilimanjaro, in Tanzania
Which is taller, a or b? Wrong! Everest is 8849 m, Kilimanjaro is 5895 m.
Final score: 4
```



**Try it:** make a second data list (rivers and their lengths, planets and
their moons) and let the player choose which one to play.

**Day 14 done.** Data in, rules in code: a pattern you'll use in every
kind of program.

B: Fuji, in Japan
Which is taller, a or b? Right! Score: 1

B: Mont Blanc, in France
Which is taller, a or b? Right! Score: 2
A: Denali, in USA
B: Everest, in Nepal
Which is taller, a or b? Right! Score: 3

B: K2, in Pakistan
