exercise.solution:
use vyrn.random

const MOUNTAINS = [
    {"name": "Everest", "height": 8849, "country": "Nepal"},
    {"name": "K2", "height": 8611, "country": "Pakistan"},
    {"name": "Kilimanjaro", "height": 5895, "country": "Tanzania"},
    {"name": "Mont Blanc", "height": 4806, "country": "France"},
    {"name": "Denali", "height": 6190, "country": "USA"},
    {"name": "Aconcagua", "height": 6961, "country": "Argentina"},
    {"name": "Fuji", "height": 3776, "country": "Japan"},
]

create describe(m): return "{m["name"]}, in {m["country"]}"

create check(a, b, answer):
    taller = "a" if a["height"] > b["height"] else "b"
    return answer == taller
end

main:
    random.seed(14)
    pool = list(MOUNTAINS)
    random.shuffle(pool)
    a = pool.pop()
    score = 0
    loop len(pool) > 0:
        b = pool.pop()
        print("A: {describe(a)}")
        print("B: {describe(b)}")
        answer = input("Which is taller, a or b? ")
        if not check(a, b, answer):
            print("Wrong! {a["name"]} is {a["height"]} m, {b["name"]} is {b["height"]} m.")
            stop
        end
        score += 1
        print("Right! Score: {score}")
        if b["height"] > a["height"]: a = b
    end
    print("Final score: {score}")
end
hints: `loop len(pool) > 0:` take `b = pool.pop()`, show both, ask.
On a right answer, `score += 1` and, if `b` was taller, `a = b`. On a wrong one, show the heights and `stop`.

days.title: Day 15: Projects, Modules, Packages and Git
days.intro:
So far every program has been one file. Real programs are **projects**:
several files, each with one job, plus tests, settings and history. Today
you set up a project the way professionals do, split code into modules,
use other people's code, and save your work with Git. The day ends with a
smoothie bar that serves drinks and keeps track of stock and money.

lessons.title: Making a project
lessons.text:
In a terminal, in the folder where you keep your code:

```bash
vyrn new smoothies
```

```text
created smoothies/

    cd smoothies
    vyrn run
    vyrn test
```

Inside `smoothies/`:

| File | What it's for |
|---|---|
| `vyrn.toml` | the project's name and settings |
| `main.vyrn` | where the program starts (`main:`) |
| `greeting.vyrn` | an example module |
| `tests/test_greeting.vyrn` | an example test |
| `.gitignore` | files Git should not save (built programs) |

Inside the project, `vyrn run` runs `main.vyrn`, `vyrn test` runs the
tests, `vyrn check` checks every file, and `vyrn fmt` tidies them all.

**An editor.** Any text editor works, but one that knows Vyrn helps a lot:
install VS Code and the Vyrn extension (search "Vyrn" in its extensions
panel) to get colours, errors as you type, completion and "go to
definition". Open the project folder, not single files.

### Exercise

No project needed for this one: print the three commands you would type to
make a project called `quiz`, go into it, and run it, one per line.

```vyrn starter
main:
end
```

```text expect
vyrn new quiz
cd quiz
vyrn run
```

exercise.starter:
main:
end
exercise.expect:
vyrn new quiz
cd quiz
vyrn run
exercise.solution:
main:
    print("vyrn new quiz")
    print("cd quiz")
    print("vyrn run")
end
hints: Three `print`s.

lessons.title: Your own modules
lessons.text:
A **module** is simply another `.vyrn` file in your project. Here is
`greeting.vyrn`:

```vyrn check
create greet(name: str) -> str:
    return "Hello, {name}!"
end
```

and `main.vyrn` uses it:

```vyrn check
create greet(name: str) -> str:
    return "Hello, {name}!"
end

main:
    print(greet("world"))
end
```

In the real project, `main.vyrn` starts with `use greeting (greet)`
instead of repeating the function: `use greeting` finds `greeting.vyrn`,
and `(greet)` brings in the names you want. Without the brackets, you write
the module's name first: `use greeting` then `greeting.greet("world")`.

Split code into modules by topic: `menu.vyrn` for the menu, `stock.vyrn`
for the stock, `main.vyrn` to tie them together. Each file stays short and
easy to find your way around. Files in folders work too: `use shop.menu`
loads `shop/menu.vyrn`.

### Exercise

Library modules can be used the same two ways. Rewrite this program to
bring in `sqrt` and `pi` by name, so `math.` is no longer needed.

```vyrn starter
use vyrn.math

main:
    print(math.sqrt(2) * math.pi)
end
```

```text expect
4.442882938158366
```

exercise.starter:
use vyrn.math

main:
    print(math.sqrt(2) * math.pi)
end
exercise.solution:
use vyrn.math (sqrt, pi)

main:
    print(sqrt(2) * pi)
end
hints: `use vyrn.math (sqrt, pi)`

lessons.title: Using other people's code: packages
lessons.text:
Code someone else has shared is a **package**. Vyrn packages are fetched
straight from a Git host, at an exact version:

```bash
vyrn add github.com/someone/colours@v1.2.0
```

This downloads the package, and records the exact version in `vyrn.lock`
so everyone working on the project gets the same code. Then:

```vyrn check
main:
    # With the package added: use "github.com/someone/colours@v1.2.0" (shade)
    print("ready")
end
```

`vyrn fetch` downloads every locked package (for example on a new
computer, or before working offline).

Python programmers use `pip` and "virtual environments" to keep each
project's packages apart. Vyrn doesn't need virtual environments: packages
always belong to one project, listed in its `vyrn.lock`.

### Exercise

Print which file records the exact versions of a project's packages, and
which command downloads them all.

```vyrn starter
main:
end
```

```text expect
Versions: vyrn.lock
Download: vyrn fetch
```

exercise.starter:
main:
end
exercise.solution:
main:
    print("Versions: vyrn.lock")
    print("Download: vyrn fetch")
end
hints: Two `print`s.

lessons.title: Saving your history with Git
lessons.text:
**Git** records snapshots of your project, called **commits**. You can see
what changed, go back to an earlier version, and share the project.
**GitHub** is a website that stores Git projects online.

Once per project:

```bash
git init
```

Each time you reach a good point:

```bash
git add .
```

```bash
git commit -m "Serve smoothies and track stock"
```

| Command | Does |
|---|---|
| `git status` | what changed since the last commit |
| `git diff` | the changes, line by line |
| `git add .` | choose every change for the next commit |
| `git commit -m "message"` | save a snapshot with a description |
| `git log --oneline` | the list of snapshots |
| `git push` | send commits to GitHub (after linking the project with `git remote add origin <url>`) |

Commit small and often, with messages that say *what* changed and *why*.

### Exercise

Put the Git commands in the right order to save a first snapshot of a new
project, and print them.

```vyrn starter
main:
    steps = ["git commit -m \"First version\"", "git init", "git add ."]
end
```

```text expect
git init
git add .
git commit -m "First version"
```



`\"` puts a double quote inside a double-quoted string.

exercise.starter:
main:
    steps = ["git commit -m \"First version\"", "git init", "git add ."]
end
exercise.expect:
git init
git add .
git commit -m "First version"
exercise.solution:
main:
    steps = ["git commit -m \"First version\"", "git init", "git add ."]
    each i in [1, 2, 0]:
        print(steps[i])
    end
end
hints: Print `steps[1]`, `steps[2]`, `steps[0]`.

lessons.title: Project: the Smoothie Bar
lessons.text:
A smoothie bar has a menu, stock and a till. Each order needs the right
ingredients and enough money. The commands are a smoothie name, `report`
(show stock and takings) and `off` (close).

In a project you'd split this into `menu.vyrn`, `stock.vyrn` and
`main.vyrn`; here it's one file so it can be checked.

### Exercise

The checker orders a `berry` paying 5, a `mango` paying 3 (not enough), a
`green` paying 5, then `report` and `off`.

```vyrn starter
const MENU = {
    "berry": {"cost": 3.5, "needs": {"berries": 150, "yogurt": 100}},
    "mango": {"cost": 4.0, "needs": {"mango": 200, "yogurt": 50}},
    "green": {"cost": 4.5, "needs": {"spinach": 80, "mango": 100}},
}

create can_make(stock, needs):
    return true
end

create make(stock, needs):
end

main:
    stock = {"berries": 300, "yogurt": 200, "mango": 250, "spinach": 100}
    till = 0.0
end
```

```text input
berry
5
mango
3
green
5
report
off
```

```text expect
What would you like? (berry/mango/green) Insert money: Here is your berry smoothie! Change: 1.50
What would you like? (berry/mango/green) Insert money: That's not enough: 4.00 needed. Refunded.
What would you like? (berry/mango/green) Insert money: Here is your green smoothie! Change: 0.50
What would you like? (berry/mango/green) Stock: {"berries": 150, "yogurt": 100, "mango": 150, "spinach": 20}
Takings: 8.00
What would you like? (berry/mango/green) Closing up. Goodbye!
```



**Day 15 done.** You can organise code into projects and modules, use
packages, and keep your history in Git. Tomorrow: objects, which bundle
data and the code that works on it.

exercise.starter:
const MENU = {
    "berry": {"cost": 3.5, "needs": {"berries": 150, "yogurt": 100}},
    "mango": {"cost": 4.0, "needs": {"mango": 200, "yogurt": 50}},
    "green": {"cost": 4.5, "needs": {"spinach": 80, "mango": 100}},
}

create can_make(stock, needs):
    return true
end

create make(stock, needs):
end

main:
    stock = {"berries": 300, "yogurt": 200, "mango": 250, "spinach": 100}
    till = 0.0
end
exercise.expect:
What would you like? (berry/mango/green) Insert money: Here is your berry smoothie! Change: 1.50
What would you like? (berry/mango/green) Insert money: That's not enough: 4.00 needed. Refunded.
What would you like? (berry/mango/green) Insert money: Here is your green smoothie! Change: 0.50
What would you like? (berry/mango/green) Stock: {"berries": 150, "yogurt": 100, "mango": 150, "spinach": 20}
Takings: 8.00
What would you like? (berry/mango/green) Closing up. Goodbye!
exercise.solution:
const MENU = {
    "berry": {"cost": 3.5, "needs": {"berries": 150, "yogurt": 100}},
    "mango": {"cost": 4.0, "needs": {"mango": 200, "yogurt": 50}},
    "green": {"cost": 4.5, "needs": {"spinach": 80, "mango": 100}},
}

create can_make(stock, needs):
    each item, amount in needs.items():
        if stock[item] < amount:
            print("Sorry, not enough {item}.")
            return false
        end
    end
    return true
end

create make(stock, needs):
    each item, amount in needs.items(): stock[item] -= amount
end

main:
    stock = {"berries": 300, "yogurt": 200, "mango": 250, "spinach": 100}
    till = 0.0
    loop:
        order = input("What would you like? (berry/mango/green) ")
        if order == "off": stop
        if order == "report":
            print("Stock: {stock}")
            print("Takings: {till:.2f}")
            skip
        end
        if order not in MENU:
            print("We don't make {order}.")
            skip
        end
        drink = MENU[order]
        paid = float(input("Insert money: "))
        if paid < drink["cost"]:
            print("That's not enough: {drink["cost"]:.2f} needed. Refunded.")
            skip
        end
        if not can_make(stock, drink["needs"]): skip
        make(stock, drink["needs"])
        till += drink["cost"]
        print("Here is your {order} smoothie! Change: {paid - drink["cost"]:.2f}")
    end
    print("Closing up. Goodbye!")
end
hints: `can_make` loops over `needs.items()` and returns `false` (after saying what's missing) if `stock[item] < amount`.
`make` subtracts each amount: maps are shared, so `main` sees the change.
In `main`, a `loop:` reads `What would you like? (berry/mango/green) `; `off` stops; `report` prints and `skip`s.

days.title: Day 16: Objects
days.intro:
As programs grow, related data and the functions that work on it belong
together. A bank account has a balance *and* ways to deposit and withdraw;
a game character has health *and* ways to take damage and heal. An
**object** bundles both. (In Python, C++ and Java this is a *class*; Vyrn
calls it `object` because that's what it makes.)

lessons.title: Declaring an object
lessons.text:
```vyrn
object Dog:
    name: str
    age: int
end

main:
    rex = Dog("Rex", 3)
    print(rex.name, rex.age)
    rex.age += 1
    print(rex.age)
    print(rex)
end
```

```text
Rex 3
4
Dog(name="Rex", age=4)
```

- `object Dog:` declares a new **type**, named in CapitalCase by
  convention. Each line inside lists a **field**: a name and its type
  (`str`, `int`, `float`, `bool`, `list`, `map`, ...).
- `Dog("Rex", 3)` makes one dog, an **instance**, filling the fields in
  order. Calling the type like this is called its **constructor**.
- `rex.name` reads a field; `rex.age += 1` changes one.

### Exercise

Declare `object Book` with a `title`, an `author` and a number of `pages`,
make one, and print it as shown.

```vyrn starter
main:
end
```

```text expect
Dune by Frank Herbert, 412 pages
```

exercise.starter:
main:
end
exercise.solution:
object Book:
    title: str
    author: str
    pages: int
end

main:
    b = Book("Dune", "Frank Herbert", 412)
    print("{b.title} by {b.author}, {b.pages} pages")
end
hints: `object Book:` with three fields, above `main:`.
`b = Book("Dune", "Frank Herbert", 412)`

lessons.title: Default values and named fields
lessons.text:
Fields can have defaults, so they can be left out when making an instance.
Fields can also be given by name, in any order:

```vyrn
object Player:
    name: str
    health: int = 100
    level: int = 1
    items: list = []
end

main:
    a = Player("Ada")
    b = Player("Ben", level = 5)
    print(a)
    print(b)
    a.items.append("map")
    print(a.items, b.items)
end
```

```text
Player(name="Ada", health=100, level=1, items=[])
Player(name="Ben", health=100, level=5, items=[])
["map"] []
```

Each instance gets its **own** fresh list for `items`: adding to Ada's
doesn't touch Ben's.

### Exercise

Declare `object Order` with a `dish`, a `quantity` defaulting to 1, and
`spicy` defaulting to `false`. Make the two orders shown.

```vyrn starter broken
main:
    first = Order("curry", spicy = true)
    second = Order("rice", 2)
    print(first)
    print(second)
end
```

```text expect
Order(dish="curry", quantity=1, spicy=true)
Order(dish="rice", quantity=2, spicy=false)
```

exercise.starter:
main:
    first = Order("curry", spicy = true)
    second = Order("rice", 2)
    print(first)
    print(second)
end
exercise.expect:
Order(dish="curry", quantity=1, spicy=true)
Order(dish="rice", quantity=2, spicy=false)
exercise.solution:
object Order:
    dish: str
    quantity: int = 1
    spicy: bool = false
end

main:
    first = Order("curry", spicy = true)
    second = Order("rice", 2)
    print(first)
    print(second)
end
hints: `quantity: int = 1` and `spicy: bool = false`.

lessons.title: Methods: functions that belong to an object
lessons.text:
A function written inside the object is a **method**. Its first parameter,
`self`, is the instance it was called on:

```vyrn
object Rectangle:
    width: float
    height: float

    create area(self) -> float:
        return self.width * self.height
    end

    create is_square(self) -> bool:
        return self.width == self.height
    end
end

main:
    r = Rectangle(3.0, 4.0)
    print(r.area(), r.is_square())
    print(Rectangle(2.0, 2.0).is_square())
end
```

```text
12.0 false
true
```

`r.area()` calls `area` with `self` set to `r`. Inside, `self.width` is
that rectangle's width.

`-> float` after the parentheses says what the method returns. It's
optional, but it documents the method and lets `vyrn check` catch
mistakes.

### Exercise

Give `Circle` a method `area()` (pi times radius squared, use `3.14159`)
and `diameter()`.

```vyrn starter
object Circle:
    radius: float
end

main:
    c = Circle(2.0)
    print("{c.area():.2f} {c.diameter()}")
end
```

```text expect
12.57 4.0
```

exercise.starter:
object Circle:
    radius: float
end

main:
    c = Circle(2.0)
    print("{c.area():.2f} {c.diameter()}")
end
exercise.solution:
object Circle:
    radius: float

    create area(self) -> float:
        return 3.14159 * self.radius ** 2
    end

    create diameter(self) -> float:
        return self.radius * 2
    end
end

main:
    c = Circle(2.0)
    print("{c.area():.2f} {c.diameter()}")
end
hints: `create area(self) -> float: return 3.14159 * self.radius ** 2`

lessons.title: Methods that change the object
lessons.text:
The real power of objects: methods keep the object's **state** correct.
Instead of changing `balance` from anywhere, all changes go through
methods that check the rules:

```vyrn
object Account:
    owner: str
    balance: float = 0.0

    create deposit(self, amount: float):
        if amount <= 0: fail ValueError("deposits must be positive")
        self.balance += amount
    end

    create withdraw(self, amount: float) -> bool:
        if amount > self.balance: return false
        self.balance -= amount
        return true
    end
end

main:
    acct = Account("Ada")
    acct.deposit(100.0)
    print(acct.withdraw(30.0), acct.balance)
    print(acct.withdraw(500.0), acct.balance)
end
```

```text
true 70.0
false 70.0
```

### Exercise

Write a `Counter` object with a `count` starting at 0 and methods
`click()` (add one), `reset()` and `value()`.

```vyrn starter
object Counter:
    count: int = 0
end

main:
    c = Counter()
    c.click()
    c.click()
    c.click()
    print(c.value())
    c.reset()
    c.click()
    print(c.value())
end
```

```text expect
3
1
```

exercise.starter:
object Counter:
    count: int = 0
end

main:
    c = Counter()
    c.click()
    c.click()
    c.click()
    print(c.value())
    c.reset()
    c.click()
    print(c.value())
end
exercise.solution:
object Counter:
    count: int = 0

    create click(self): self.count += 1
    create reset(self): self.count = 0
    create value(self) -> int: return self.count
end

main:
    c = Counter()
    c.click()
    c.click()
    c.click()
    print(c.value())
    c.reset()
    c.click()
    print(c.value())
end
hints: `count: int = 0`, then three methods using `self.count`.

lessons.title: Choosing how an object prints
lessons.text:
By default an object prints all its fields. A method named `to_text`
decides instead, everywhere: in `print`, in `{...}`, in `str(...)`, and
inside printed lists:

```vyrn
object Money:
    cents: int

    create to_text(self) -> str:
        return "${self.cents // 100}.{self.cents % 100:02d}"
    end
end

main:
    price = Money(1999)
    print(price)
    print("Total: {price}")
    print([Money(5), Money(250)])
end
```

```text
$19.99
Total: $19.99
[$0.05, $2.50]
```

### Exercise

Give `Temperature` a `to_text` that shows one decimal and a degree sign.

```vyrn starter
object Temperature:
    celsius: float
end

main:
    print(Temperature(21.456))
    print([Temperature(-3.0), Temperature(30.25)])
end
```

```text expect
21.5°C
[-3.0°C, 30.2°C]
```

exercise.starter:
object Temperature:
    celsius: float
end

main:
    print(Temperature(21.456))
    print([Temperature(-3.0), Temperature(30.25)])
end
exercise.solution:
object Temperature:
    celsius: float

    create to_text(self) -> str:
        return "{self.celsius:.1f}°C"
    end
end

main:
    print(Temperature(21.456))
    print([Temperature(-3.0), Temperature(30.25)])
end
hints: `return "{self.celsius:.1f}°C"`

lessons.title: Objects are shared
lessons.text:
An important fact: assigning an object to another name does **not** copy
it. Both names refer to the same object:

```vyrn
object Box:
    contents: list = []
end

create fill(b: Box):
    b.contents.append("toy")
end

main:
    a = Box()
    b = a
    b.contents.append("book")
    fill(a)
    print(a.contents)
    print(b.contents)
end
```

```text
["book", "toy"]
["book", "toy"]
```

`b = a` gives the same box a second name, and `fill(a)` changes the box
the caller holds. That's usually what you want for things with an
identity: there is one bank account, one player, one game.

(C++ and Java programmers: an object variable behaves like a reference,
or a smart pointer, and the object is freed automatically once nothing
refers to it. There's no `new` or `delete`.)

Tomorrow you meet `struct`, which is the opposite: a value that is copied.

### Exercise

`add_points` should change the player it's given. Write it, and see both
names show the new score.

```vyrn starter
object Player:
    name: str
    score: int = 0
end

create add_points(player: Player, n: int):
end

main:
    p = Player("Ada")
    same = p
    add_points(p, 10)
    print(p.score, same.score)
end
```

```text expect
10 10
```

exercise.starter:
object Player:
    name: str
    score: int = 0
end

create add_points(player: Player, n: int):
end

main:
    p = Player("Ada")
    same = p
    add_points(p, 10)
    print(p.score, same.score)
end
exercise.solution:
object Player:
    name: str
    score: int = 0
end

create add_points(player: Player, n: int):
    player.score += n
end

main:
    p = Player("Ada")
    same = p
    add_points(p, 10)
    print(p.score, same.score)
end
hints: `create add_points(player: Player, n: int): player.score += n`

lessons.title: Project: the Pet Shelter
lessons.text:
A shelter keeps a list of pets. Each pet has a name, a species and a
hunger level from 0 (full) to 10 (starving). Feeding lowers hunger by 3
(never below 0); each day raises it by 2 (never above 10).

### Exercise

Write the `Pet` object with methods `feed()`, `next_day()` and `to_text()`
(`Rex the dog (hunger 4)`), then run the shelter for two days, feeding
only the hungriest pet each day.

```vyrn starter
object Pet:
    name: str
    species: str
    hunger: int = 5
end

main:
    pets = [Pet("Rex", "dog", 6), Pet("Tom", "cat", 2), Pet("Nemo", "fish")]
    each day in 1 to 2:
        print("Day {day}: {pets}")
    end
end
```

```text expect
Day 1: [Rex the dog (hunger 6), Tom the cat (hunger 2), Nemo the fish (hunger 5)]
Feeding Rex
Day 2: [Rex the dog (hunger 5), Tom the cat (hunger 4), Nemo the fish (hunger 7)]
Feeding Nemo
```



**Day 16 done.** You can design your own types with data and behaviour.
Tomorrow: values versus shared objects, keeping fields private, and a quiz
app built from objects.

exercise.starter:
object Pet:
    name: str
    species: str
    hunger: int = 5
end

main:
    pets = [Pet("Rex", "dog", 6), Pet("Tom", "cat", 2), Pet("Nemo", "fish")]
    each day in 1 to 2:
        print("Day {day}: {pets}")
    end
end
exercise.expect:
Day 1: [Rex the dog (hunger 6), Tom the cat (hunger 2), Nemo the fish (hunger 5)]
Feeding Rex
Day 2: [Rex the dog (hunger 5), Tom the cat (hunger 4), Nemo the fish (hunger 7)]
Feeding Nemo
exercise.solution:
object Pet:
    name: str
    species: str
    hunger: int = 5

    create feed(self): self.hunger = max(0, self.hunger - 3)
    create next_day(self): self.hunger = min(10, self.hunger + 2)

    create to_text(self) -> str:
        return "{self.name} the {self.species} (hunger {self.hunger})"
    end
end

main:
    pets = [Pet("Rex", "dog", 6), Pet("Tom", "cat", 2), Pet("Nemo", "fish")]
    each day in 1 to 2:
        print("Day {day}: {pets}")
        hungriest = max(pets, key = p => p.hunger)
        print("Feeding {hungriest.name}")
        hungriest.feed()
        each p in pets: p.next_day()
    end
end
hints: `feed`: `self.hunger = max(0, self.hunger - 3)`. `next_day`: `self.hunger = min(10, self.hunger + 2)`.
Each day: print, find `hungriest = max(pets, key = p => p.hunger)`, feed it, then call `next_day()` on every pet.

days.title: Day 17: Structs, Privacy, and a Quiz App
days.intro:
Yesterday's objects are **shared**: two names can point at one object.
Today you meet their partner, the **struct**, a value that is **copied**,
like a number. You'll learn when to use each, how to keep an object's
insides `private`, and you'll build a quiz app from both.

lessons.title: Structs are values
lessons.text:
A `struct` is declared like an object, but behaves like a number: assigning
or passing it makes a **copy**.

```vyrn
struct Point:
    x: int
    y: int
end

main:
    a = Point(1, 2)
    b = a
    b.x = 99
    print(a)
    print(b)
    print(a == Point(1, 2))
end
```

```text
Point(x=1, y=2)
Point(x=99, y=2)
true
```

Changing `b` left `a` alone: `b` was a copy. And two structs with the same
fields are equal (`==`), just as two `5`s are.

Compare objects: `b = a` shares, so changing `b` changes `a`, and `==`
asks "is this the very same object?".

### Exercise

Make a copy of the starting position, move the copy, and print both to show
the start was not changed.

```vyrn starter
struct Position:
    row: int
    col: int
end

main:
    start = Position(0, 0)
end
```

```text expect
start: Position(row=0, col=0)
moved: Position(row=2, col=3)
```

exercise.starter:
struct Position:
    row: int
    col: int
end

main:
    start = Position(0, 0)
end
exercise.expect:
start: Position(row=0, col=0)
moved: Position(row=2, col=3)
exercise.solution:
struct Position:
    row: int
    col: int
end

main:
    start = Position(0, 0)
    moved = start
    moved.row = 2
    moved.col = 3
    print("start:", start)
    print("moved:", moved)
end
hints: `moved = start`, then change `moved.row` and `moved.col`.

lessons.title: Struct or object?
lessons.text:
| Use a `struct` when... | Use an `object` when... |
|---|---|
| the thing *is* its values: a point, a colour, a date, a quiz question | the thing has an identity that changes over time: a player, an account, a game |
| two with the same values are interchangeable | two with the same values are still two different things |
| it's small | it may be large, or many places need to see its changes |

Python's dataclasses, Java's records and C++'s plain structs are all close
to Vyrn's `struct`. Python and Java classes, and C++ classes used through
pointers, are like Vyrn's `object`.

### Exercise

Decide: print `struct` or `object` for each, as `<thing>: <choice>`.

```vyrn starter
main:
    things = ["a colour (red, green, blue)", "a chat room with members", "a playing card"]
end
```

```text expect
a colour (red, green, blue): struct
a chat room with members: object
a playing card: struct
```

exercise.starter:
main:
    things = ["a colour (red, green, blue)", "a chat room with members", "a playing card"]
end
exercise.expect:
a colour (red, green, blue): struct
a chat room with members: object
a playing card: struct
exercise.solution:
main:
    things = ["a colour (red, green, blue)", "a chat room with members", "a playing card"]
    choices = ["struct", "object", "struct"]
    each i in 0 until len(things):
        print("{things[i]}: {choices[i]}")
    end
end
hints: Does it change over time, with others needing to see the change?

lessons.title: Methods on structs
lessons.text:
Structs have methods too. A method that gives back a **new** value is the
natural style for values:

```vyrn
struct Vec2:
    x: float
    y: float

    create plus(self, other: Vec2) -> Vec2:
        return Vec2(self.x + other.x, self.y + other.y)
    end

    create length(self) -> float:
        return (self.x ** 2 + self.y ** 2) ** 0.5
    end

    create scale(mut self, k: float):
        self.x *= k
        self.y *= k
    end
end

main:
    a = Vec2(3.0, 4.0)
    print(a.length(), a.plus(Vec2(1.0, 1.0)))
    var b = a
    b.scale(2.0)
    print(a, b)
end
```

```text
5.0 Vec2(x=4.0, y=5.0)
Vec2(x=3.0, y=4.0) Vec2(x=6.0, y=8.0)
```

A method that changes a struct in place says so with `mut self`, and works
on a `var`. Only that copy changes.

### Exercise

Give `Fraction` a method `times(other)` returning the product, and
`to_text` showing `3/8`.

```vyrn starter
struct Fraction:
    top: int
    bottom: int
end

main:
    half = Fraction(1, 2)
    three_quarters = Fraction(3, 4)
    print(half.times(three_quarters))
end
```

```text expect
3/8
```

exercise.starter:
struct Fraction:
    top: int
    bottom: int
end

main:
    half = Fraction(1, 2)
    three_quarters = Fraction(3, 4)
    print(half.times(three_quarters))
end
exercise.solution:
struct Fraction:
    top: int
    bottom: int

    create times(self, other: Fraction) -> Fraction:
        return Fraction(self.top * other.top, self.bottom * other.bottom)
    end

    create to_text(self) -> str:
        return "{self.top}/{self.bottom}"
    end
end

main:
    half = Fraction(1, 2)
    three_quarters = Fraction(3, 4)
    print(half.times(three_quarters))
end
hints: `return Fraction(self.top * other.top, self.bottom * other.bottom)`

lessons.title: `private`: keeping the insides inside
lessons.text:
An object's methods keep its rules: an account's balance only changes
through `deposit` and `withdraw`. But nothing stops other code writing
`acct.balance = 1000000`... unless the field is `private`:

```vyrn
object Account:
    owner: str
    private balance: float = 0.0

    create deposit(self, amount: float):
        if amount <= 0: fail ValueError("deposits must be positive")
        self.balance += amount
    end

    create current(self) -> float:
        return self.balance
    end
end

main:
    acct = Account("Ada")
    acct.deposit(50.0)
    print(acct.current())
    print(acct.balance)
end
```

```text
50.0
error: PrivateError: `balance` is private to `Account`: only its own methods can use it
```

`private` fields and methods can only be used inside the object's own
methods (and those of objects built on it, Day 21). Everything else goes
through the public methods. This is called **encapsulation**: you can
change how an object works inside without breaking the code that uses it.

### Exercise

Make `attempts` private, and add a method `attempts_left()` so `main`
doesn't need to touch the field.

```vyrn starter
object Lock:
    code: int
    attempts: int = 3

    create try_code(self, guess: int) -> bool:
        if self.attempts == 0: return false
        if guess == self.code: return true
        self.attempts -= 1
        return false
    end
end

main:
    lock = Lock(4321)
    print(lock.try_code(1111), lock.try_code(4321))
    print("Attempts left:", lock.attempts)
end
```

```text expect
false true
Attempts left: 2
```

exercise.starter:
object Lock:
    code: int
    attempts: int = 3

    create try_code(self, guess: int) -> bool:
        if self.attempts == 0: return false
        if guess == self.code: return true
        self.attempts -= 1
        return false
    end
end

main:
    lock = Lock(4321)
    print(lock.try_code(1111), lock.try_code(4321))
    print("Attempts left:", lock.attempts)
end
exercise.solution:
object Lock:
    code: int
    private attempts: int = 3

    create try_code(self, guess: int) -> bool:
        if self.attempts == 0: return false
        if guess == self.code: return true
        self.attempts -= 1
        return false
    end

    create attempts_left(self) -> int:
        return self.attempts
    end
end

main:
    lock = Lock(4321)
    print(lock.try_code(1111), lock.try_code(4321))
    print("Attempts left:", lock.attempts_left())
end
hints: `private attempts: int = 3`
`create attempts_left(self) -> int: return self.attempts`, and use it in `main`.

lessons.title: Private methods
lessons.text:
Helpers that only the object itself should call can be private too:

```vyrn
object Thermostat:
    private target: float = 20.0

    create set_target(self, value: float):
        self.target = self.clamp(value)
    end

    create target_now(self) -> float: return self.target

    private create clamp(self, value: float) -> float:
        return max(10.0, min(30.0, value))
    end
end

main:
    t = Thermostat()
    t.set_target(42.0)
    print(t.target_now())
    t.set_target(18.5)
    print(t.target_now())
end
```

```text
30.0
18.5
```

### Exercise

Add a private method `format_line(label, value)` to `Receipt`, used by
`show()`, so every line is formatted the same way.

```vyrn starter
object Receipt:
    items: map = {}

    create add(self, name: str, price: float):
        self.items[name] = price
    end

    create show(self):
        each name, price in self.items.items():
            print("{name:<10}{price:>7.2f}")
        end
        print("{"TOTAL":<10}{sum(self.items.values()):>7.2f}")
    end
end

main:
    r = Receipt()
    r.add("bread", 2.25)
    r.add("cheese", 6.5)
    r.show()
end
```

```text expect
bread        2.25
cheese       6.50
TOTAL        8.75
```

lessons.title: Project: the Quiz App
lessons.text:
The design, using the right tool for each part:

- `struct Question`: a question's text and its answer. A plain value.
- `object Quiz`: the list of questions, which one is next, and the score.
  It changes as the quiz goes on, so it's an object, with private state.

### Exercise

The checker answers `true`, `true`, `false`.

```vyrn starter
struct Question:
    text: str
    answer: bool
end

object Quiz:
    questions: list
    private next_index: int = 0
    private score: int = 0
end

main:
    let quiz = Quiz([
        Question("Octopuses have three hearts.", true),
        Question("Venus is the closest planet to the Sun.", false),
        Question("Honey can last for thousands of years.", true),
    ])
end
```

```text input
true
true
false
```

```text expect
Q1. Octopuses have three hearts. (true/false) Right!
Q2. Venus is the closest planet to the Sun. (true/false) Wrong: it's false.
Q3. Honey can last for thousands of years. (true/false) Wrong: it's true.
You scored 1/3.
```



**Try it:** load the questions from a list of maps with a comprehension:
`[Question(q["text"], q["answer"]) each q in data]`.

**Day 17 done.** You know values from shared objects, and how to protect
an object's insides. Tomorrow: pictures!

exercise.starter:
struct Question:
    text: str
    answer: bool
end

object Quiz:
    questions: list
    private next_index: int = 0
    private score: int = 0
end

main:
    let quiz = Quiz([
        Question("Octopuses have three hearts.", true),
        Question("Venus is the closest planet to the Sun.", false),
        Question("Honey can last for thousands of years.", true),
    ])
end
exercise.expect:
Q1. Octopuses have three hearts. (true/false) Right!
Q2. Venus is the closest planet to the Sun. (true/false) Wrong: it's false.
Q3. Honey can last for thousands of years. (true/false) Wrong: it's true.
You scored 1/3.
exercise.solution:
struct Question:
    text: str
    answer: bool
end

object Quiz:
    questions: list
    private next_index: int = 0
    private score: int = 0

    create has_more(self) -> bool:
        return self.next_index < len(self.questions)
    end

    create ask(self):
        let q = self.questions[self.next_index]
        self.next_index += 1
        let reply = input("Q{self.next_index}. {q.text} (true/false) ") == "true"
        if reply == q.answer:
            self.score += 1
            print("Right!")
        else:
            print("Wrong: it's {q.answer}.")
        end
    end

    create score_text(self) -> str:
        return "{self.score}/{len(self.questions)}"
    end
end

main:
    let quiz = Quiz([
        Question("Octopuses have three hearts.", true),
        Question("Venus is the closest planet to the Sun.", false),
        Question("Honey can last for thousands of years.", true),
    ])
    loop quiz.has_more(): quiz.ask()
    print("You scored {quiz.score_text()}.")
end
hints: Give `Quiz` methods `has_more()`, `ask()` and `score_text()`.
In `ask`, read the answer with `input(...) == "true"`, compare with the question's answer, then move `next_index` on.

days.title: Day 18: Drawing Pictures
days.intro:
Time for graphics! Today you draw shapes, use colours and coordinates, and
steer a turtle that draws as it moves. Every picture is saved as a PNG
file you can open in any image viewer. The day ends with a spot painting
in the style of modern art.

lessons.title: A canvas and coordinates
lessons.text:
`use vyrn.draw` brings in graphics. A **canvas** is a picture in memory,
made of **pixels** (tiny squares of colour). Positions are `(x, y)`
counted in pixels from the **top-left corner**: `x` grows to the right,
`y` grows **downwards**.

```vyrn
use vyrn.draw

main:
    pic = draw.canvas(200, 100)
    pic.clear("white")
    pic.rect(10, 10, 50, 30, "red")
    pic.save("first.png")
    print(pic.width, pic.height)
    print(pic.get_pixel(20, 20), pic.get_pixel(100, 50))
end
```

```text
200 100
#e53935 #ffffff
```

- `draw.canvas(200, 100)` makes a picture 200 pixels wide and 100 high.
- `pic.clear("white")` paints it all white.
- `pic.rect(x, y, width, height, colour)` draws a filled rectangle whose
  top-left corner is at `(x, y)`.
- `pic.save("first.png")` writes the picture to a file.
- `pic.get_pixel(x, y)` tells you the colour at a point, as a hex code.
  (That's how these lessons check your pictures.)

### Exercise

Draw a 40 by 40 blue square in the bottom-right corner of a 100 by 100
white canvas, and check two pixels.

```vyrn starter
use vyrn.draw

main:
    pic = draw.canvas(100, 100)
    pic.clear("white")
    print(pic.get_pixel(80, 80), pic.get_pixel(10, 10))
end
```

```text expect
#1e88e5 #ffffff
```

exercise.starter:
use vyrn.draw

main:
    pic = draw.canvas(100, 100)
    pic.clear("white")
    print(pic.get_pixel(80, 80), pic.get_pixel(10, 10))
end
exercise.solution:
use vyrn.draw

main:
    pic = draw.canvas(100, 100)
    pic.clear("white")
    pic.rect(60, 60, 40, 40, "blue")
    print(pic.get_pixel(80, 80), pic.get_pixel(10, 10))
end
hints: The square's top-left corner is at `(60, 60)`.

lessons.title: Colours
lessons.text:
A colour can be written three ways:

- a **name**: `"red"`, `"skyblue"`, `"gold"`, `"darkgreen"`, ...
- a **hex code**: `"#ff8800"`: two hex digits each for red, green and blue,
  from `00` (none) to `ff` (full)
- a **list** `[red, green, blue]` from 0 to 255, or `[r, g, b, alpha]`
  where alpha 0 is see-through and 255 solid

```vyrn
use vyrn.draw

main:
    pic = draw.canvas(30, 10)
    pic.rect(0, 0, 10, 10, "tomato")
    pic.rect(10, 0, 10, 10, "#00ff00")
    pic.rect(20, 0, 10, 10, [0, 0, 255])
    print(pic.get_pixel(5, 5), pic.get_pixel(15, 5), pic.get_pixel(25, 5))
    print(draw.rgb(255, 136, 0))
end
```

```text
#ff6347 #00ff00 #0000ff
#ff8800
```

Mixing light: red + green = yellow, all three = white, none = black.

### Exercise

51]`, white, and green `[19, 136, 8]`, then print the colour of each.

```vyrn starter

end
```

```text expect
#ff9933 #ffffff #138808
```

lessons.title: More shapes
lessons.text:
```vyrn check
use vyrn.draw

main:
    pic = draw.canvas(300, 200)
    pic.clear("white")
    pic.circle(60, 60, 40, "gold")
    pic.circle(60, 60, 40, "black", fill = false, width = 3)
    pic.line(120, 20, 280, 100, "navy", width = 4)
    pic.triangle(150, 180, 200, 110, 250, 180, "green")
    pic.polygon([[20, 190], [60, 130], [100, 190]], "purple")
    pic.text("Shapes!", 130, 150, "black")
    pic.save("shapes.png")
end
```

| Method | Draws |
|---|---|
| `rect(x, y, w, h, colour)` | a rectangle from its top-left corner |
| `circle(cx, cy, radius, colour)` | a circle around its centre |
| `line(x1, y1, x2, y2, colour)` | a line |
| `triangle(x1, y1, x2, y2, x3, y3, colour)` | a triangle |
| `polygon(points, colour)` | a shape through a list of points |
| `text(words, x, y, colour)` | text |
| `pixel(x, y, colour)` | one pixel |

Add `fill = false` for an outline only, and `width = n` for thicker lines.

### Exercise

40 red, 25 white, 10 red. Check the colours at distance 5, 15 and 30 from

lessons.title: Drawing with loops
lessons.text:
Loops and shapes together make patterns:

```vyrn
use vyrn.draw

main:
    pic = draw.canvas(200, 40)
    pic.clear("white")
    colours = ["red", "orange", "gold", "green", "blue"]
    each i in 0 until 5:
        pic.rect(i * 40, 0, 40, 40, colours[i])
    end
    pic.save("rainbow.png")
    print([pic.get_pixel(i * 40 + 20, 20) each i in 0 until 5])
end
```

```text
["#e53935", "#fb8c00", "#ffc107", "#43a047", "#1e88e5"]
```

### Exercise

Draw a chessboard: 8 by 8 squares of 10 pixels, black where `row + col` is
odd. Print the colours of the first two squares of the first two rows.

```vyrn starter
use vyrn.draw

main:
    board = draw.canvas(80, 80)
    board.clear("white")
end
```

```text expect
#ffffff #000000
#000000 #ffffff
```

exercise.starter:
use vyrn.draw

main:
    board = draw.canvas(80, 80)
    board.clear("white")
end
exercise.solution:
use vyrn.draw

main:
    board = draw.canvas(80, 80)
    board.clear("white")
    each row in 0 until 8:
        each col in 0 until 8:
            if (row + col) % 2 == 1:
                board.rect(col * 10, row * 10, 10, 10, "black")
            end
        end
    end
    print(board.get_pixel(5, 5), board.get_pixel(15, 5))
    print(board.get_pixel(5, 15), board.get_pixel(15, 15))
end

`if (row + col) % 2 == 1: board.rect(col * 10, row * 10, 10, 10, "black")`

lessons.title: The turtle
lessons.text:
A **turtle** is a pen you steer: it starts in the middle of the canvas,
facing right, and draws a line wherever it moves. Turtle positions are
measured from the centre, with `y` going **up**, like a maths graph.

```vyrn
use vyrn.draw

main:
    pic = draw.canvas(200, 200)
    pic.clear("white")
    t = draw.turtle(pic)
    t.color("blue")
    t.forward(50)
    t.left(90)
    t.forward(50)
    print(round(t.x), round(t.y), t.heading)
    pic.save("corner.png")
end
```

```text
50 50 90.0
```

| Command | Does |
|---|---|
| `forward(n)`, `back(n)` | move `n` pixels |
| `left(deg)`, `right(deg)` | turn |
| `goto(x, y)`, `home()` | jump to a point, or back to the middle |
| `pen_up()`, `pen_down()` | stop and start drawing |
| `color(c)`, `width(n)` | the pen's colour and thickness |
| `circle(r)`, `dot(size, colour)` | a circle, a dot |
| `begin_fill()`, `end_fill()` | fill the shape drawn in between |
| `x`, `y`, `heading` | where it is and which way it faces |

### Exercise

Draw a square with sides of 60 using a loop, and print where the turtle
ends and which way it faces.

```vyrn starter
use vyrn.draw

main:
    pic = draw.canvas(200, 200)
    t = draw.turtle(pic)
end
```

```text expect
0 0 0.0
```

exercise.starter:
use vyrn.draw

main:
    pic = draw.canvas(200, 200)
    t = draw.turtle(pic)
end
exercise.solution:
use vyrn.draw

main:
    pic = draw.canvas(200, 200)
    t = draw.turtle(pic)
    each _ in 1 to 4:
        t.forward(60)
        t.left(90)
    end
    print(round(t.x), round(t.y), t.heading)
end
hints: `each _ in 1 to 4:` forward 60, then left 90.
Print `round(t.x), round(t.y), t.heading`.

lessons.title: Turtle shapes and functions
lessons.text:
Any regular shape with `n` sides turns `360 / n` degrees at each corner.
A function makes it reusable:

```vyrn check
use vyrn.draw

create shape(t, sides, size, colour):
    t.color(colour)
    each _ in 1 to sides:
        t.forward(size)
        t.right(360 / sides)
    end
end

main:
    pic = draw.canvas(300, 300)
    pic.clear("white")
    t = draw.turtle(pic)
    colours = ["red", "orange", "gold", "green", "blue", "purple"]
    each sides in 3 to 8:
        shape(t, sides, 60, colours[sides - 3])
    end
    pic.save("shapes.png")
end
```

### Exercise

Draw a star: 5 lines of 100, turning right 144 degrees after each. Print
the heading at the end (it should face where it started).

```vyrn starter
use vyrn.draw

main:
    pic = draw.canvas(200, 200)
    t = draw.turtle(pic)
end
```

```text expect
0.0
```

exercise.starter:
use vyrn.draw

main:
    pic = draw.canvas(200, 200)
    t = draw.turtle(pic)
end
exercise.solution:
use vyrn.draw

main:
    pic = draw.canvas(200, 200)
    t = draw.turtle(pic)
    each _ in 1 to 5:
        t.forward(100)
        t.right(144)
    end

lessons.title: Project: a Spot Painting

Paint a 10 by 10 grid of dots in random colours from a palette, evenly

days.title: Day 19: Windows, Keys and Game State
days.intro:
Yesterday's pictures were saved to files. Today they come alive in a
**window** that redraws many times a second and reacts to the keyboard.
You'll learn the game loop, connect keys to functions, keep each
character's state in its own object, and finish with a turtle race.

lessons.title: A window and the game loop
lessons.text:
```vyrn check
use vyrn.draw

main:
    let win = draw.window(400, 300, "My first window")
    var x = 0
    loop win.open():
        x = (x + 2) % 400
        win.clear("white")
        win.circle(x, 150, 20, "tomato")
        win.show()
    end
end
```

Every game and animation has this shape, the **game loop**:

1. `loop win.open():` repeats until the window is closed.
2. **Update**: change the state (here, move `x`).
3. **Draw**: clear, then draw everything where it is now.
4. `win.show()` puts the frame on screen, and waits so the loop runs
   about 60 times a second.

A window has all the drawing methods of a canvas. Run it on your computer
with `vyrn run`: a ball glides across the window. (A window needs a
screen, so these lessons check the parts of a game that don't need one.)

### Exercise

The game loop's *update* step can be tested without a window. Write
`next_x(x, speed, width)`, which moves `x` by `speed` and wraps around the
width, then print the first positions.

```vyrn starter
create next_x(x, speed, width):
    return x
end

main:
    var x = 390
    each _ in 1 to 4:
        x = next_x(x, 4, 400)
        print(x)
    end
end
```

```text expect
394
398
2
6
```

exercise.starter:
create next_x(x, speed, width):
    return x
end

main:
    var x = 390
    each _ in 1 to 4:
        x = next_x(x, 4, 400)
        print(x)
    end
end
exercise.solution:
create next_x(x, speed, width):
    return (x + speed) % width
end

main:
    var x = 390
    each _ in 1 to 4:
        x = next_x(x, 4, 400)
        print(x)
    end
end
hints: `return (x + speed) % width`

lessons.title: Reading the keyboard
lessons.text:
```vyrn check
use vyrn.draw

main:
    let win = draw.window(400, 300, "Move the square")
    var x = 200
    var y = 150
    loop win.open():
        if win.key_down("left"): x -= 3
        if win.key_down("right"): x += 3
        if win.key_down("up"): y -= 3
        if win.key_down("down"): y += 3
        if win.key_pressed("space"):
            x = 200
            y = 150
        end
        win.clear("black")
        win.rect(x - 10, y - 10, 20, 20, "lime")
        win.show()
    end
end
```

- `win.key_down("left")` is true for every frame the key is **held**:
  good for movement.
- `win.key_pressed("space")` is true only on the frame the key **goes
  down**: good for actions like jumping or shooting.
- Keys are named `"left"`, `"right"`, `"up"`, `"down"`, `"space"`,
  `"enter"`, `"escape"`, letters `"a"` to `"z"` and digits `"0"` to `"9"`.
- The mouse: `win.mouse_x`, `win.mouse_y`, `win.mouse_down("left")`,
  `win.clicked()`.

### Exercise

Keep the square inside the window: write `clamp(value, low, high)` and use
it so moving never goes past the edges.

```vyrn starter
create clamp(value, low, high):
    return value
end

main:
    print(clamp(-5, 10, 390), clamp(200, 10, 390), clamp(450, 10, 390))
end
```

```text expect
10 200 390
```

exercise.starter:
create clamp(value, low, high):
    return value
end

main:
    print(clamp(-5, 10, 390), clamp(200, 10, 390), clamp(450, 10, 390))
end
exercise.solution:
create clamp(value, low, high):
    return max(low, min(high, value))
end

main:
    print(clamp(-5, 10, 390), clamp(200, 10, 390), clamp(450, 10, 390))
end
hints: `return max(low, min(high, value))`

lessons.title: Keys as data: event handlers
lessons.text:
Instead of a long list of `if`s, connect each key to a function in a map.
Each function is an **event handler**: code that runs when something
happens.

```vyrn check
use vyrn.draw

create forwards(t): t.forward(5)
create backwards(t): t.back(5)
create turn_left(t): t.left(10)
create turn_right(t): t.right(10)

main:
    let win = draw.window(500, 400, "Sketch")
    let pen = draw.turtle(win)
    let handlers = {"w": forwards, "s": backwards, "a": turn_left, "d": turn_right}
    win.clear("white")
    loop win.open():
        each key, handler in handlers.items():
            if win.key_down(key): handler(pen)
        end
        if win.key_pressed("c"): win.clear("white")
        win.show()
    end
end
```

Adding a new control now means adding one line to the map: the loop
doesn't change. Functions passed around like this are the
**higher-order functions** from Day 10 at work.

### Exercise

the handlers, and print where the pen ends.

```vyrn starter
end
```

```text expect
20 10 90.0
```

lessons.title: Each character keeps its own state
lessons.text:
With several moving things, give each its own object. Every instance
remembers its own position and speed:

```vyrn
object Ball:
    x: float
    speed: float

    create update(self, width: float):
        self.x += self.speed
        if self.x < 0 or self.x > width: self.speed = -self.speed
    end
end

main:
    balls = [Ball(10.0, 30.0), Ball(50.0, -20.0)]
    each frame in 1 to 3:
        each b in balls: b.update(100.0)
        print(frame, [b.x each b in balls])
    end
end
```

```text
1 [40.0, 30.0]
2 [70.0, 10.0]
3 [100.0, -10.0]
```

In a window, each frame calls `update` on every ball, then draws every
ball. That's the whole trick behind games with many moving parts.

### Exercise

Give `Ball` a vertical position too, with gravity: each update adds
`gravity` to the speed, then the speed to `y`. A ball that reaches the
floor (`y >= floor`) stops there with speed 0.

```vyrn starter
object Ball:
    y: float = 0.0
    speed: float = 0.0

    create update(self, gravity: float, floor: float):
    end
end

main:
    b = Ball()
    each _ in 1 to 5:
        b.update(4.0, 30.0)
        print(b.y, b.speed)
    end
end
```

```text expect
4.0 4.0
12.0 8.0
24.0 12.0
30.0 0.0
30.0 0.0
```

exercise.starter:
object Ball:
    y: float = 0.0
    speed: float = 0.0

    create update(self, gravity: float, floor: float):
    end
end

main:

        b.update(4.0, 30.0)
        print(b.y, b.speed)
    end
end
exercise.solution:
object Ball:
    y: float = 0.0
    speed: float = 0.0

    create update(self, gravity: float, floor: float):
        self.speed += gravity
        self.y += self.speed
        if self.y >= floor:
            self.y = floor
            self.speed = 0.0
        end
    end
end

main:
    b = Ball()
    each _ in 1 to 5:
        b.update(4.0, 30.0)
        print(b.y, b.speed)
    end
end
hints: `self.speed += gravity` then `self.y += self.speed`.
Then `if self.y >= floor:` set `self.y = floor` and `self.speed = 0.0`.

lessons.title: Project: the Turtle Race
lessons.text:
Five turtles line up on the left. Each round, each moves forward a random
distance; the first past the finish line wins. Each turtle is its own
instance with its own colour and position.

### Exercise

Run the race on a canvas (keep the seed) and print the winner.

```vyrn starter
use vyrn.draw
use vyrn.random

const COLOURS = ["red", "orange", "green", "blue", "purple"]
const FINISH = 200

main:
    random.seed(19)
    pic = draw.canvas(500, 300)
    pic.clear("white")
    racers = []
    each i in 0 until 5:
        t = draw.turtle(pic)
        t.color(COLOURS[i])
        t.pen_up()
        t.goto(-230, -100 + i * 50)
        t.pen_down()
        racers.append(t)
    end
end
```

```text expect
The purple turtle wins!
```



`enumerate(xs)` gives each item with its position: `each i, t in
enumerate(racers)`.

**Try it on screen:** draw the race in a window instead, calling
`win.show()` after each round, so you can watch it.

**Day 19 done.** Windows, keys, handlers and per-object state: you have
everything a game needs. Tomorrow: Snake.

days.title: Day 20: Snake, Part 1: The Game's Data
days.intro:
Snake is a classic: a snake slides around a grid, eats food, grows longer,
and must never bite itself. Today you design the game's **data** and
**rules** and test them without a window, then put them on screen. Tomorrow
adds scoring, levels and polish.

Designing data first is how real games are made: if the rules are right
as plain data, drawing them is easy.

lessons.title: Cells and the snake
lessons.text:
The grid is made of cells, each a `struct` with a column and a row. The
snake is a list of cells, **head first**.

```vyrn
struct Cell:
    x: int
    y: int
end

main:
    snake = [Cell(5, 3), Cell(4, 3), Cell(3, 3)]
    print("head:", snake[0])
    print("length:", len(snake))
    print(Cell(4, 3) in snake, Cell(9, 9) in snake)
end
```

```text
head: Cell(x=5, y=3)
length: 3
true false
```

Because `Cell` is a struct (a value), two cells with the same `x` and `y`
are equal, so `in` can ask "is this cell part of the snake?".

### Exercise

Write `occupied(snake, x, y)` returning whether the snake covers that cell.

```vyrn starter
struct Cell:
    x: int
    y: int
end

create occupied(snake, x, y):
    return false
end

main:
    snake = [Cell(5, 3), Cell(4, 3), Cell(3, 3)]
    print(occupied(snake, 4, 3), occupied(snake, 4, 4))
end
```

```text expect
true false
```

    print(occupied(snake, 4, 3), occupied(snake, 4, 4))
end

lessons.title: Moving
lessons.text:
To move, add a new head one cell in the direction of travel, and remove the
last cell. The body follows the head without moving each part separately.
The direction is a pair `(dx, dy)`: right is `(1, 0)`, up is `(0, -1)`.

### Exercise

list in place). Running off an edge wraps to the other side of a 10 by 8
grid.

```vyrn starter
    step(snake, 1, 0)
    print(snake)
    step(snake, 0, -1)
    print(snake)
end
```

```text expect
[Cell(x=0, y=3), Cell(x=9, y=3), Cell(x=8, y=3)]
[Cell(x=0, y=2), Cell(x=0, y=3), Cell(x=9, y=3)]
```

lessons.title: Eating and growing
lessons.text:
When the new head lands on the food, the snake **doesn't** lose its tail
that step, so it grows by one.

```vyrn starter
    end
end

```

lessons.title: Crashing
lessons.text:
The game ends when the head runs into the body.

### Exercise

Write `crashed(snake)`: whether the head is anywhere in the rest of the
snake.

```vyrn starter
    y: int
end

create crashed(snake):

end

main:
    print(crashed([Cell(1, 1), Cell(2, 1), Cell(3, 1)]))
    print(crashed([Cell(2, 1), Cell(2, 2), Cell(1, 2), Cell(1, 1), Cell(2, 1)]))
end
```

```text expect
false
true
```

lessons.title: Seeing it: a text picture
lessons.text:
Before any window, a text picture is a quick way to see the state:

### Exercise

Write `picture(snake, food)` returning the grid as lines: `@` for the
head, `o` for the body, `*` for food, `.` for empty.

```vyrn starter
const COLS = 8
const ROWS = 4

struct Cell:
    x: int
    y: int
end

create picture(snake, food):
    return ""
end

main:
    print(picture([Cell(3, 1), Cell(2, 1), Cell(1, 1)], Cell(6, 2)))
end
```

```text expect
........
.oo@....
......*.
........
```

exercise.starter:
const COLS = 8
const ROWS = 4

struct Cell:
    x: int
    y: int
end

create picture(snake, food):
    return ""
end

main:
    print(picture([Cell(3, 1), Cell(2, 1), Cell(1, 1)], Cell(6, 2)))
end
exercise.solution:
const COLS = 8
const ROWS = 4

struct Cell:
    x: int
    y: int
end

create picture(snake, food):
    lines = []
    each y in 0 until ROWS:
        line = ""
        each x in 0 until COLS:
            c = Cell(x, y)
            if c == snake[0]:
                line += "@"
            else if c in snake:
                line += "o"
            else if c == food:
                line += "*"
            else:
                line += "."
            end
        end
        lines.append(line)
    end
    return "\n".join(lines)
end

main:
    print(picture([Cell(3, 1), Cell(2, 1), Cell(1, 1)], Cell(6, 2)))
end
hints: Two loops: rows (`y`), then columns (`x`), building one line per row.
Check the head first: `if c == snake[0]:`, then `else if c in snake:`, then food.

lessons.title: On screen
lessons.text:
The same rules, drawn in a window. Each cell is a 20 by 20 square; the
arrow keys change direction (but never straight back into the body).

```vyrn check
use vyrn.draw
use vyrn.random

const CELL = 20
const COLS = 30
const ROWS = 20

struct Cell:
    x: int
    y: int
end

create random_cell() -> Cell:
    return Cell(random.int(0, COLS - 1), random.int(0, ROWS - 1))
end

create step(snake, dx, dy, food):
    head = Cell((snake[0].x + dx) % COLS, (snake[0].y + dy) % ROWS)
    snake.insert(0, head)
    if head == food: return true
    snake.pop()
    return false
end

main:
    let win = draw.window(COLS * CELL, ROWS * CELL, "Snake")
    win.set_fps(10)
    var snake = [Cell(5, 10), Cell(4, 10), Cell(3, 10)]
    var dx = 1
    var dy = 0
    var food = random_cell()
    loop win.open():
        if win.key_down("left") and dx == 0:
            dx = -1
            dy = 0
        else if win.key_down("right") and dx == 0:
            dx = 1
            dy = 0
        else if win.key_down("up") and dy == 0:
            dx = 0
            dy = -1
        else if win.key_down("down") and dy == 0:
            dx = 0
            dy = 1
        end
        if step(snake, dx, dy, food): food = random_cell()
        win.clear("#102018")
        win.rect(food.x * CELL, food.y * CELL, CELL, CELL, "red")
        each c in snake:
            win.rect(c.x * CELL + 1, c.y * CELL + 1, CELL - 2, CELL - 2, "lime")
        end
        win.show()
    end
end
```

`win.set_fps(10)` slows the loop to 10 frames a second, so the snake moves
at a playable speed.

### Exercise

The checks `and dx == 0` stop the snake reversing into itself. Write
`turn(dx, dy, key)` that returns the new direction for a key, ignoring a
turn straight back.

```vyrn starter
create turn(dx, dy, key):
    return (dx, dy)
end

main:
    print(turn(1, 0, "up"))
    print(turn(1, 0, "left"))
    print(turn(0, -1, "left"))
    print(turn(0, -1, "down"))
end
```

```text expect
(0, -1)
(1, 0)
(-1, 0)
(0, -1)
```



**Day 20 done, and Unit 2 with it!** You can design data, write and test
rules, use objects and structs, handle errors, organise projects, and draw
in windows. Unit 3 goes further: inheritance, files, comprehensions,
apps with buttons, and more games.

exercise.starter:
create turn(dx, dy, key):
    return (dx, dy)
end

main:
    print(turn(1, 0, "up"))
    print(turn(1, 0, "left"))
    print(turn(0, -1, "left"))
    print(turn(0, -1, "down"))
end
exercise.solution:
create turn(dx, dy, key):
    when key:
        is "left":
            if dx == 0: return (-1, 0)
        is "right":
            if dx == 0: return (1, 0)
        is "up":
            if dy == 0: return (0, -1)
        is "down":
            if dy == 0: return (0, 1)
    end
    return (dx, dy)
end

main:
    print(turn(1, 0, "up"))
    print(turn(1, 0, "left"))
    print(turn(0, -1, "left"))
    print(turn(0, -1, "down"))
end

`is "left": if dx == 0: return (-1, 0)`

days.title: Day 21: Inheritance, Polymorphism, and Snake Part 2
days.intro:
Often one kind of thing is a special case of another: a dog *is an*
animal, a savings account *is an* account. **Inheritance** lets one object
type build on another, reusing its fields and methods and changing only
what's different. Today you learn it, see why it matters, and use it to
finish Snake.

lessons.title: Building on another object
lessons.text:
```vyrn
object Animal:
    name: str
    legs: int = 4

    create describe(self) -> str:
        return "{self.name} has {self.legs} legs"
    end

    create speak(self) -> str:
        return "..."
    end
end

object Dog(Animal):
    tricks: list = []

    create speak(self) -> str:
        return "Woof!"
    end
end

main:
    rex = Dog("Rex", tricks = ["sit"])
    print(rex.describe())
    print(rex.speak())
    print(rex)
end
```

```text
Rex has 4 legs
Woof!
Dog(name="Rex", legs=4, tricks=["sit"])
```

`object Dog(Animal):` means a Dog is an Animal with extras:

- It **inherits** everything: `name`, `legs` and `describe()` come from
  `Animal` without being written again.
- It **adds** a field, `tricks`.
- It **overrides** `speak()` with its own version.

`Animal` is the **base** (or parent) type; `Dog` is **derived** from it
(the child).

### Exercise

Add `object Bird(Animal)` with 2 legs by default and a `speak` of
`Tweet!`.

```vyrn starter
    create describe(self) -> str:

    end
end

object Bird(Animal):
end

main:
    b = Bird("Tweety")
    print(b.describe(), b.speak())
end
```

```text expect
Tweety has 2 legs Tweet!
```

lessons.title: `super`: extending instead of replacing
lessons.text:
An overriding method can call the parent's version with `super`, and add to
it:

```vyrn
object Account:
    owner: str
    balance: float = 0.0

    create describe(self) -> str:
        return "{self.owner}: {self.balance:.2f}"
    end
end

object Savings(Account):
    rate: float = 0.02

    create describe(self) -> str:
        return super.describe() + " (saving at {self.rate:.0%})"
    end

    create add_interest(self):
        self.balance += self.balance * self.rate
    end
end

main:
    s = Savings("Ada", 1000.0)
    s.add_interest()
    print(s.describe())
end
```

```text
Ada: 1020.00 (saving at 2%)
```

### Exercise

`Manager` should describe itself as an employee plus its team size. Use
`super`.

```vyrn starter
object Employee:
    name: str
    salary: int

    create describe(self) -> str:
        return "{self.name} earns {self.salary}"
    end
end

object Manager(Employee):
    team: int = 0
end

main:
```

lessons.title: Polymorphism: one call, many behaviours
lessons.text:
The big payoff: code that works with the base type works with every
derived type, and each object uses its **own** version of a method. This
is called **polymorphism** ("many shapes"):

```vyrn
object Shape:
    name: str = "shape"
    create area(self) -> float: return 0.0
end

object Square(Shape):
    side: float = 1.0
    create area(self) -> float: return self.side * self.side
end

object Circle(Shape):
    radius: float = 1.0
    create area(self) -> float: return 3.14159 * self.radius ** 2
end

main:
    shapes = [Square("square", 2.0), Circle("circle", 1.0), Square("tile", 0.5)]
    each s in shapes:
        print("{s.name}: {s.area():.2f}")
    end
    print("total: {sum([s.area() each s in shapes]):.2f}")
end
```

```text
square: 4.00
circle: 3.14
tile: 0.25
total: 7.39
```

The loop never asks "is this a square or a circle?": each shape knows how
to compute its own area. Adding a `Triangle` later needs no change to the
loop. (C++ calls these *virtual* methods; in Vyrn every method can be
overridden.)

### Exercise

Add `object Triangle(Shape)` with `base` and `height` (area is half of
base times height), and include one in the list.

```vyrn starter
    name: str = "shape"
    create area(self) -> float: return 0.0
end

object Square(Shape):
    side: float = 1.0
    create area(self) -> float: return self.side * self.side
end

main:
    shapes = [Square("square", 2.0)]
    each s in shapes: print("{s.name}: {s.area():.2f}")
end
```

```text expect
square: 4.00
triangle: 6.00
```

lessons.title: `is`: asking what kind of thing it is
lessons.text:
Sometimes you do need to know the type. `value is Type` answers, and it
counts derived types: a `Dog` *is* an `Animal`.

```vyrn
object Animal:
    name: str
end

object Dog(Animal):
end

object Cat(Animal):
end

main:
    pets = [Dog("Rex"), Cat("Tom"), Dog("Fido")]
    print(pets[0] is Dog, pets[0] is Animal, pets[1] is Dog)
    dogs = [p.name each p in pets if p is Dog]
    print(dogs)
    print(5 is int, "hi" is str, none is none, pets[1] is not Dog)
end
```

```text
true true false
["Rex", "Fido"]
true true true true
```

Prefer overriding methods (lesson 21.3) when you can; use `is` when the
question really is about the type.

lessons.title: Setting up an object: `init`
lessons.text:
Sometimes an object needs to check its fields, or work something out, as
soon as it's made. A method called `init` runs automatically right after
the fields are filled in:

```vyrn
object Rectangle:
    width: float
    height: float
    area: float = 0.0

    create init(self):
        if self.width <= 0 or self.height <= 0:
            fail ValueError("sides must be positive")
        end
        self.area = self.width * self.height
    end
end

main:
    print(Rectangle(3.0, 4.0).area)
    attempt:
        Rectangle(-1.0, 2.0)
    catch ValueError as e:
        print("Refused:", e.message)
    end
end
```

```text
12.0
Refused: sides must be positive
```

Derived objects inherit `init` too. (This is what Python's `__init__` and
the constructors of Java and C++ are for.)

### Exercise

than 3 characters.

```vyrn starter

end

main:
    print(Username("AdaL").name)
    attempt:
        Username("Al")
    catch ValueError as e:
        print(e.message)
    end
end
```

```text expect
adal
too short
```

lessons.title: Project: Snake, Part 2
lessons.text:
The game becomes objects: a `Snake` that moves, grows and checks crashes,
and a `Scoreboard`. A `Game` ties them together. Slicing helps: the body
is `self.cells[1:]`.

### Exercise

Finish `Snake` and play a scripted game: the snake moves right, eats the
food at `(4, 2)`, then turns down.

```vyrn starter
const COLS = 10
const ROWS = 6

struct Cell:
    x: int
    y: int
end

object Snake:
    cells: list = [Cell(2, 2), Cell(1, 2), Cell(0, 2)]
    dx: int = 1
    dy: int = 0

    create head(self) -> Cell: return self.cells[0]
end

object Scoreboard:
    score: int = 0
    create add(self): self.score += 1
    create to_text(self) -> str: return "Score: {self.score}"
end

main:
    snake = Snake()
    board = Scoreboard()
    food = Cell(4, 2)
    moves = ["right", "right", "down", "down"]
end
```

```text expect
Cell(x=3, y=2) Score: 0
Cell(x=4, y=2) Score: 1
Cell(x=4, y=3) Score: 1
Cell(x=4, y=4) Score: 1
length 4, crashed: false
```



**Try it on screen:** replace the scripted moves with the window loop from
Day 20, calling `snake.turn` for the arrow keys, moving the food after each
meal, and ending the game when `snake.crashed()`.

**Day 21 done.** Inheritance, `super`, polymorphism and `is`: the core of
object-oriented programming. Tomorrow: Pong, with collisions.

exercise.expect:
Cell(x=3, y=2) Score: 0
Cell(x=4, y=2) Score: 1
Cell(x=4, y=3) Score: 1
Cell(x=4, y=4) Score: 1
length 4, crashed: false
exercise.solution:
const COLS = 10
const ROWS = 6

struct Cell:
    x: int
    y: int
end

object Snake:
    cells: list = [Cell(2, 2), Cell(1, 2), Cell(0, 2)]
    dx: int = 1
    dy: int = 0

    create head(self) -> Cell: return self.cells[0]

    create turn(self, key: str):
        when key:
            is "left":
                if self.dx == 0:
                    self.dx = -1
                    self.dy = 0
                end
            is "right":
                if self.dx == 0:
                    self.dx = 1
                    self.dy = 0
                end
            is "up":
                if self.dy == 0:
                    self.dx = 0
                    self.dy = -1
                end
            is "down":
                if self.dy == 0:
                    self.dx = 0
                    self.dy = 1
                end
        end
    end

    create step(self, food: Cell) -> bool:
        let h = self.head()
        let new_head = Cell((h.x + self.dx) % COLS, (h.y + self.dy) % ROWS)
        self.cells.insert(0, new_head)
        if new_head == food: return true
        self.cells.pop()
        return false
    end

    create crashed(self) -> bool:
        return self.head() in self.cells[1:]
    end
end

object Scoreboard:
    score: int = 0
    create add(self): self.score += 1
    create to_text(self) -> str: return "Score: {self.score}"
end

main:
    snake = Snake()
    board = Scoreboard()
    food = Cell(4, 2)
    moves = ["right", "right", "down", "down"]
    each key in moves:
        snake.turn(key)
        if snake.step(food): board.add()
        print(snake.head(), board)
    end
    print("length {len(snake.cells)}, crashed: {snake.crashed()}")
end
hints: Give `Snake` methods `turn(key)`, `step(food) -> bool` (true when it ate) and `crashed() -> bool`.
Each move: `snake.turn(key)`, then `if snake.step(food): board.add()`, then print the head and the board.

days.title: Day 22: Pong
days.intro:
Pong was one of the first video games: two paddles, one ball, and a lot of
bouncing. Building it teaches the two ideas at the heart of most games:
**movement** (position changes by velocity every frame) and **collision**
(noticing when two things touch).

lessons.title: Position and velocity
lessons.text:
Everything that moves has a position `(x, y)` and a **velocity**
`(vx, vy)`: how far it moves each frame. Each frame, add the velocity to
the position.

```vyrn
object Ball:
    x: float = 100.0
    y: float = 50.0
    vx: float = 3.0
    vy: float = -2.0

    create move(self):
        self.x += self.vx
        self.y += self.vy
    end
end

main:
    b = Ball()
    each frame in 1 to 3:
        b.move()
        print(frame, b.x, b.y)
    end
end
```

```text
1 103.0 48.0
2 106.0 46.0
3 109.0 44.0
```

### Exercise

Give `Ball` a `speed_up(factor)` method that multiplies both velocity
parts, then move it twice after speeding up by 1.5.

```vyrn starter
object Ball:
    x: float = 0.0
    y: float = 0.0
    vx: float = 2.0
    vy: float = 1.0

    create move(self):
        self.x += self.vx
        self.y += self.vy
    end
end

main:
    b = Ball()
    b.speed_up(1.5)
    b.move()
    b.move()
    print(b.x, b.y)
end
```

```text expect
6.0 3.0
```

lessons.title: Bouncing off walls
lessons.text:
When the ball reaches the top or bottom edge, flip the vertical velocity:
`vy = -vy`. The ball then heads back the other way.

### Exercise

Add `bounce_walls(height)`: if the ball is above 0 or below `height`, flip
`vy`. Watch the ball bounce off the top.

```vyrn starter

    y: float = 4.0
    vy: float = -3.0

    create move(self): self.y += self.vy
end

main:
    b = Ball()
    each _ in 1 to 4:
        b.move()
        b.bounce_walls(100.0)
        print(b.y, b.vy)
    end
end
```

```text expect
1.0 -3.0
-2.0 3.0
1.0 3.0
4.0 3.0
```

    vy: float = -3.0

    create move(self): self.y += self.vy
end

    each _ in 1 to 4:
        b.move()
        b.bounce_walls(100.0)
        print(b.y, b.vy)
    end
end

object Ball:
    y: float = 4.0
    vy: float = -3.0

    create move(self): self.y += self.vy

    create bounce_walls(self, height: float):
        if self.y < 0 or self.y > height: self.vy = -self.vy
    end
end

main:
    b = Ball()
    each _ in 1 to 4:
        b.move()
        b.bounce_walls(100.0)
        print(b.y, b.vy)

lessons.title: Collisions between rectangles
lessons.text:
Two rectangles touch when they overlap on **both** axes. For rectangles
given as `(x, y, width, height)`:

- they overlap horizontally when `a.x < b.x + b.width` and
  `b.x < a.x + a.width`;
- and vertically in the same way with `y` and `height`.

```vyrn
use vyrn.draw

create overlaps(ax, ay, aw, ah, bx, by, bw, bh):
    return ax < bx + bw and bx < ax + aw and ay < by + bh and by < ay + ah
end

main:
    print(overlaps(0, 0, 10, 10, 5, 5, 10, 10))
    print(overlaps(0, 0, 10, 10, 20, 0, 5, 5))
    print(draw.overlaps(0, 0, 10, 10, 5, 5, 10, 10))
end
```

```text
true
false
true
```

`draw.overlaps` is the same test, built in.

### Exercise

A paddle is at `x = 380`, `y = 120`, 10 wide and 60 tall. Print which of
the balls (each 8 by 8) hit it.

```vyrn starter
main:

end
```

```text expect
[true, false, false, false]
```

lessons.title: The full game
lessons.text:
Two players: `w`/`s` move the left paddle, the arrow keys the right one.
A ball past a paddle scores for the other side and restarts in the middle,
a little faster each time.

```vyrn check
use vyrn.draw

const WIDTH = 600
const HEIGHT = 400

object Paddle:
    x: float
    y: float = 170.0
    score: int = 0

    create move(self, dy: float):
        self.y = max(0.0, min(HEIGHT - 60.0, self.y + dy))
    end
end

object Ball:
    x: float = 300.0
    y: float = 200.0
    vx: float = 4.0
    vy: float = 3.0

    create reset(self, direction: float):
        self.x = 300.0
        self.y = 200.0
        self.vx = direction * (abs(self.vx) + 0.5)
    end
end

main:
    let win = draw.window(WIDTH, HEIGHT, "Pong")
    let left = Paddle(20.0)
    let right = Paddle(570.0)
    let ball = Ball()
    loop win.open():
        if win.key_down("w"): left.move(-6.0)
        if win.key_down("s"): left.move(6.0)
        if win.key_down("up"): right.move(-6.0)
        if win.key_down("down"): right.move(6.0)

        ball.x += ball.vx
        ball.y += ball.vy
        if ball.y < 0 or ball.y > HEIGHT - 10: ball.vy = -ball.vy
        each p in [left, right]:
            if draw.overlaps(ball.x, ball.y, 10, 10, p.x, p.y, 10, 60):
                ball.vx = -ball.vx
            end
        end
        if ball.x < 0:
            right.score += 1
            ball.reset(1.0)
        else if ball.x > WIDTH:
            left.score += 1
            ball.reset(-1.0)
        end

        win.clear("black")
        win.rect(left.x, left.y, 10, 60, "white")
        win.rect(right.x, right.y, 10, 60, "white")
        win.rect(ball.x, ball.y, 10, 10, "white")
        win.text("{left.score}   {right.score}", 280, 20, "white")
        win.show()
    end
end
```

### Exercise

The scoring rule is easy to get wrong, so test it on its own: write
`point_for(ball_x, width)` returning `"right"` when the ball leaves on the
left, `"left"` when it leaves on the right, and `""` otherwise.

```vyrn starter

    return ""
end

main:
    print([point_for(x, 600) each x in [-3, 300, 605]])
end
```

```text expect
["right", "", "left"]
```



**Day 22 done.** Movement, bouncing, collisions and scoring: the physics
of nearly every 2D game. Tomorrow: a game with many moving objects at
once.

days.title: Day 23: Many Objects at Once: the Road Crossing Game
days.intro:
A turtle tries to cross a busy road. Cars appear at random on the right
and drive left; each time the turtle reaches the far side, the cars speed
up. The new idea today is managing **many objects that come and go**:
creating them, updating all of them, and removing the ones you no longer
need.

lessons.title: A list of objects
lessons.text:
```vyrn
object Car:
    x: float
    lane: int
    speed: float = 5.0

    create update(self): self.x -= self.speed
end

main:
    cars = [Car(300.0, 0), Car(450.0, 2), Car(600.0, 1)]
    each _ in 1 to 2:
        each c in cars: c.update()
    end
    print([c.x each c in cars])
end
```

```text
[290.0, 440.0, 590.0]
```

Every frame, the game calls `update` on every car. Each car only knows
about itself.

### Exercise

Give `Car` a `speed_up(amount)` method, speed every car up by 2.5, and
update once more.

```vyrn starter
object Car:
    x: float
    lane: int
    speed: float = 5.0

    create update(self): self.x -= self.speed
end

main:
    cars = [Car(300.0, 0), Car(450.0, 2)]
    print([c.x each c in cars])
end
```


lessons.title: Making new objects at random
lessons.text:
Cars shouldn't all appear at once. Each frame, a new car appears with some
chance, in a random lane:

```vyrn
use vyrn.random

object Car:
    x: float
    lane: int
end

main:
    random.seed(23)
    cars = []
    each frame in 1 to 10:
        if random.int(1, 4) == 1:
            cars.append(Car(600.0, random.int(0, 5)))
        end
    end
    print(len(cars), "cars, in lanes", [c.lane each c in cars])
end
```

```text
2 cars, in lanes [5, 4]
```

`random.int(1, 4) == 1` is true about one time in four. Making the chance
smaller makes traffic lighter.

lessons.title: Removing what's gone
lessons.text:
Cars that have driven off the left edge should be removed, or the list
grows forever and the game slows down. Keep only the cars still on screen:

```vyrn
object Car:
    x: float
end

main:
    cars = [Car(-30.0), Car(100.0), Car(-5.0), Car(400.0)]
    cars = cars.filter(c => c.x > -20)
    print([c.x each c in cars])
end
```

```text
[100.0, -5.0, 400.0]
```

`xs.filter(test)` gives a new list of the items for which `test` is true.
Don't remove items from a list while looping over it with `each`: build
the new list instead, as here.

lessons.title: The player, levels and game over
lessons.text:
The turtle moves up one lane per key press. Reaching the top starts the
next level, with faster cars. Touching a car ends the game.

### Exercise

Write `Player` with `up()`, `at_top()` and `restart()`, and a `Level`
object that counts levels and gives the car speed (`3 + 2 * level`). Play
a scripted crossing of 3 lanes, twice.

```vyrn starter
const LANES = 3

object Player:
    lane: int = 0
end

object Level:
    number: int = 1
end

main:
    p = Player()
    level = Level()
    each _ in 1 to 6:
        p.up()
        if p.at_top():
            level.next()
            p.restart()
        end
        print("lane {p.lane}, level {level.number}, car speed {level.speed()}")
    end
end
```

```text expect
lane 1, level 1, car speed 5
lane 2, level 1, car speed 5
lane 0, level 2, car speed 7
lane 1, level 2, car speed 7
lane 2, level 2, car speed 7
lane 0, level 3, car speed 9
```

exercise.starter:

    level = Level()
    each _ in 1 to 6:
        p.up()

            level.next()

        end
