    each b in 1 to 3:
        print("box {b}: {len([w each w, box in boxes.items() if box == b])}")
    end
end

main:
    report({"chat": 1, "chien": 3, "maison": 2, "pomme": 1})
end
hints: `each b in 1 to 3:` and count the words whose box is `b`.

lessons.title: you built
lessons.text:
A study program with saved progress, smart repetition and forgiving
answers, out of pieces you already knew: CSV, maps, comprehensions, random
choice, JSON and error handling. Ideas to take it further:

- Read each answer with `input()` and stop when the player types `quit`.
- Show the cards in a window with buttons for "knew it" and "didn't"
  (Day 27).
- Load several CSV files and let the player choose a language.

days.title: Day 32: Dates and email
days.intro:
Today your programs learn the calendar: what day it is, how many days until
a holiday, which friends have a birthday today. Then they write
personalised letters and **send email**. The project is a birthday wisher
that checks a list of birthdays every morning and emails anyone whose day
it is.

lessons.title: Moments in time
lessons.text:
A computer stores a moment as a number: the seconds since the start of
1970. `time.make` builds one from a date, `time.date` takes one apart, and
`time.format` writes one the way people read dates:

```vyrn
use vyrn.time

main:
    moon = time.make(1969, 7, 20, 20, 17)
    print(moon)
    parts = time.date(moon)
    print(parts["year"], parts["month"], parts["day"], parts["weekday"])
    print(time.format(moon, "%A %d %B %Y at %H:%M"))
    print(time.format(moon, "%d/%m/%y"))
end
```

```text
-14182980.0
1969 7 20 Sunday
Sunday 20 July 1969 at 20:17
20/07/69
```

The moon landing was before 1970, so its number is negative, and that's
fine. The codes in `time.format`:

| Code | Means | Example |
|---|---|---|
| `%Y`, `%y` | year | 2026, 26 |
| `%m`, `%B`, `%b` | month | 03, March, Mar |
| `%d` | day of the month | 07 |
| `%A`, `%a` | weekday | Monday, Mon |
| `%H`, `%I`, `%p` | hour (24), hour (12), AM/PM | 15, 03, PM |
| `%M`, `%S` | minute, second | 09, 26 |

`time.now()` is the moment the program runs. Lessons use fixed dates instead,
so they print the same every day.

### Exercise

Print the day of the week you were born (use 14 March 2010 here).

```vyrn starter
use vyrn.time

main:
    born = time.make(2010, 3, 14)
end
```

```text expect
You were born on a Sunday
```

exercise.starter:
use vyrn.time

main:
    born = time.make(2010, 3, 14)
end
exercise.expect: You were born on a Sunday
exercise.solution:
use vyrn.time

main:
    born = time.make(2010, 3, 14)
    print("You were born on a", time.format(born, "%A"))
end
hints: `time.date(born)["weekday"]`, or `time.format(born, "%A")`.

lessons.title: Counting days
lessons.text:
Subtracting two moments gives seconds; divide by `86400` (seconds in a day)
for days. `time.add` moves a moment by days, months or years, keeping to the
calendar (adding a month to 31 January gives the last day of February):

```vyrn
use vyrn.time

main:
    today = time.make(2026, 11, 12)
    new_year = time.make(2027, 1, 1)
    print("days until new year:", (new_year - today) / 86400)
    next_week = time.add(today, days = 7)
    print("a week from now:", time.format(next_week, "%A %d %B"))
    print("in a month:", time.format(time.add(time.make(2026, 1, 31), months = 1), "%d %B"))
end
```

```text
days until new year: 50.0
a week from now: Thursday 19 November
in a month: 28 February
```

### Exercise

How old will someone born on 2 May 2011 be on 12 November 2026? A person's
age goes up on their birthday, so count the years and take one off if this
year's birthday hasn't happened yet.

```vyrn starter
use vyrn.time

create age_on(born: float, day: float) -> int:
    return 0
end

main:
    print(age_on(time.make(2011, 5, 2), time.make(2026, 11, 12)))
    print(age_on(time.make(2011, 12, 25), time.make(2026, 11, 12)))
end
```

```text expect
15
14
```

exercise.starter:
use vyrn.time

create age_on(born: float, day: float) -> int:
    return 0
end

main:
    print(age_on(time.make(2011, 5, 2), time.make(2026, 11, 12)))
    print(age_on(time.make(2011, 12, 25), time.make(2026, 11, 12)))
end
exercise.solution:
use vyrn.time

create age_on(born: float, day: float) -> int:
    let b = time.date(born)
    let d = time.date(day)
    var age = d["year"] - b["year"]
    if (d["month"], d["day"]) < (b["month"], b["day"]): age -= 1
    return age
end

main:
    print(age_on(time.make(2011, 5, 2), time.make(2026, 11, 12)))
    print(age_on(time.make(2011, 12, 25), time.make(2026, 11, 12)))
end
hints: `b = time.date(born)` and `d = time.date(day)`; the years are `d["year"] - b["year"]`.
the birthday hasn't happened if `(d["month"], d["day"]) < (b["month"], b["day"])`.

lessons.title: Time zones
lessons.text:
A moment is the same everywhere, but the clock on the wall differs. Give
`time.format` a `zone` to see the local time in another place:

```vyrn
use vyrn.time

main:
    meeting = time.make(2026, 6, 1, 15, 0, zone = "Europe/London")
    each zone in ["Europe/London", "America/New_York", "Asia/Tokyo", "Australia/Sydney"]:
        print(zone.split("/")[1].replace("_", " "), time.format(meeting, "%a %H:%M", zone = zone))
    end
end
```

```text
London Mon 15:00
New York Mon 10:00
Tokyo Mon 23:00
Sydney Tue 00:00
```

`zone = "local"` means wherever your computer is. Times saved in files
should be kept as these numbers (or in UTC), and only turned into a local
clock when shown to a person.

lessons.title: Personalised letters
lessons.text:
A **mail merge** fills a template with each person's details. Write the
template with markers, then replace each marker:

```vyrn
const TEMPLATE = """Dear [NAME],

Happy birthday! You are [AGE] today.

Best wishes,
Vyrn"""

create letter(name: str, age: int) -> str:
    return TEMPLATE.replace("[NAME]", name).replace("[AGE]", str(age))
end

main:
    print(letter("Ada", 12))
end
```

```text
Dear Ada,

Happy birthday! You are 12 today.

Best wishes,
Vyrn
```

Why `[NAME]` and not `{name}`? Because the template is data, often read
from a file, and the markers must stay as they are until you fill them.
For bigger templates, `vyrn.template` (Day 44) does the same with loops and
conditions.

lessons.title: Sending email
lessons.text:
`mail.send` sends a message through a mail server. Your email provider
tells you its server name; you log in with your address and an **app
password** (a password made just for programs, in your account's security
settings). Never write the password in the program: keep it in an
**environment variable** (Day 35 explains these):

```vyrn check
use vyrn.mail
use vyrn.os

main:
    mail.send(
        to = "friend@example.com",
        subject = "Happy birthday!",
        body = "Have a great day!",
        sender = "me@example.com",
        server = "smtp.example.com",
        user = "me@example.com",
        password = os.env("MAIL_PASSWORD"),
    )
    print("sent")
end
```

On Windows, set the variable in PowerShell before running:

```powershell
$env:MAIL_PASSWORD = "your-app-password"
```

and on macOS or Linux:

```bash
export MAIL_PASSWORD="your-app-password"
```

lessons.title: Project: the birthday wisher
lessons.text:
The birthdays live in a CSV file. Every morning the program finds today's
birthdays and sends each person a letter. Choosing *who* is a function of
the date, so it can be tested on any date; the sending is passed in, so a
test can pass a **fake** that only records what would have been sent
(Day 47 covers fakes fully):

```vyrn
use vyrn.csv
use vyrn.time

const TEMPLATE = "Dear [NAME],\nHappy birthday! You are [AGE] today."

create birthdays_on(rows: list, day: float) -> list:
    let d = time.date(day)
    return [row each row in rows if int(row["month"]) == d["month"] and int(row["day"]) == d["day"]]
end

create wish(rows: list, day: float, send: any) -> int:
    let year = time.date(day)["year"]
    let people = birthdays_on(rows, day)
    each person in people:
        let age = year - int(person["year"])
        let body = TEMPLATE.replace("[NAME]", person["name"]).replace("[AGE]", str(age))
        send(person["email"], "Happy birthday, {person["name"]}!", body)
    end
    return len(people)
end

main:
    write_text("birthdays.csv", "name,email,year,month,day\nAda,ada@example.com,2012,11,12\nKai,kai@example.com,2010,3,4\nMo,mo@example.com,2011,11,12\n")
    rows = csv.read("birthdays.csv")
    sent = fake(returns = true)
    count = wish(rows, time.make(2026, 11, 12), sent)
    print(count, "letters")
    each call in sent.calls:
        print("to", call[0], "-", call[2].lines()[1])
    end
end
```

```text
2 letters
to ada@example.com - Happy birthday! You are 14 today.
to mo@example.com - Happy birthday! You are 15 today.
```

For real, pass a function that calls `mail.send`, and run the program every
morning with your computer's scheduler (Task Scheduler on Windows, `cron` on
macOS and Linux).

### Exercise

People born on 29 February only get a real birthday every four years.
Change `birthdays_on` so that in a year without 29 February, their birthday
counts on 28 February.

```vyrn starter
use vyrn.time

create birthdays_on(rows: list, day: float) -> list:
    let d = time.date(day)
    return [row["name"] each row in rows if row["month"] == d["month"] and row["day"] == d["day"]]
end

main:
    rows = [{"name": "Leap", "month": 2, "day": 29}, {"name": "Ann", "month": 2, "day": 28}]
    print(birthdays_on(rows, time.make(2027, 2, 28)), birthdays_on(rows, time.make(2028, 2, 28)), birthdays_on(rows, time.make(2028, 2, 29)))
end
```

```text expect
["Leap", "Ann"] ["Ann"] ["Leap"]
```

exercise.starter:
use vyrn.time

create birthdays_on(rows: list, day: float) -> list:
    let d = time.date(day)
    return [row["name"] each row in rows if row["month"] == d["month"] and row["day"] == d["day"]]
end

main:
    rows = [{"name": "Leap", "month": 2, "day": 29}, {"name": "Ann", "month": 2, "day": 28}]
    print(birthdays_on(rows, time.make(2027, 2, 28)), birthdays_on(rows, time.make(2028, 2, 28)), birthdays_on(rows, time.make(2028, 2, 29)))
end
exercise.solution:
use vyrn.time

create has_leap_day(year: int) -> bool:
    return time.date(time.add(time.make(year, 2, 28), days = 1))["month"] == 2
end

create birthdays_on(rows: list, day: float) -> list:
    let d = time.date(day)
    let moved = not has_leap_day(d["year"]) and d["month"] == 2 and d["day"] == 28
    var found = []
    each row in rows:
        let today = row["month"] == d["month"] and row["day"] == d["day"]
        let leap = moved and row["month"] == 2 and row["day"] == 29
        if today or leap: found.append(row["name"])
    end
    return found
end

main:
    rows = [{"name": "Leap", "month": 2, "day": 29}, {"name": "Ann", "month": 2, "day": 28}]
    print(birthdays_on(rows, time.make(2027, 2, 28)), birthdays_on(rows, time.make(2028, 2, 28)), birthdays_on(rows, time.make(2028, 2, 29)))
end
hints: a year has 29 February if the day after 28 February is still in February: `time.date(time.add(time.make(year, 2, 28), days = 1))["month"] == 2`.
in a year without it, a row with month 2 and day 29 should match 28 February too.

lessons.title: you learned
lessons.text:
- A moment is a number of seconds; `time.make`, `time.date` and
  `time.format` build it, take it apart and write it.
- Subtract moments for durations; `time.add` moves along the calendar.
- `zone = "Asia/Tokyo"` shows the clock somewhere else.
- A mail merge fills `[MARKERS]` in a template with `replace`.
- `mail.send` sends email; keep passwords in environment variables.
- Pass the sending function in, so a fake can stand in for it in tests.

days.title: Day 33: Web APIs
days.intro:
Websites are for people; **APIs** are websites for programs. Instead of a
page, they answer with data, usually JSON: the weather, the position of the
space station, today's exchange rates, the time the sun rises. Today you ask
APIs questions, read their answers, and handle the times they say no. The
project tells you whether it is daytime anywhere in the world.

lessons.title: What an API is
lessons.text:
You ask an API a question by **requesting a URL**, just as a browser does:

```text
https://api.sunrise-sunset.org/json?lat=51.5&lng=-0.12&formatted=0
```

| Part | Here | Means |
|---|---|---|
| scheme | `https://` | how to talk to it (securely) |
| host | `api.sunrise-sunset.org` | which computer to ask |
| path | `/json` | which question |
| query | `?lat=51.5&lng=-0.12&formatted=0` | the details: `name=value`, joined by `&` |

The answer comes back with a **status code** saying how it went:

| Code | Means |
|---|---|
| 200 | OK: here is your data |
| 400 | Bad request: your question doesn't make sense |
| 401, 403 | Not allowed: you need a key, or the key is wrong |
| 404 | Not found: no such thing |
| 429 | Too many requests: slow down |
| 500 | The server broke: try later |

Build query strings with `http.query`, which makes any value safe to put in
a URL (spaces, `&` and accents need **encoding**):

```vyrn
use vyrn.http

main:
    params = http.query({"lat": 51.5, "lng": -0.12, "formatted": 0})
    print("https://api.sunrise-sunset.org/json?" + params)
    print(http.query({"q": "fish & chips", "city": "Zürich"}))
end
```

```text
https://api.sunrise-sunset.org/json?lat=51.5&lng=-0.12&formatted=0
q=fish%20%26%20chips&city=Z%C3%BCrich
```

lessons.title: Asking an API
lessons.text:
`http.get(url)` sends the request and waits for the answer. The response
has the status (`r.status`, and `r.ok`, true for 200 to 299), the body as
text (`r.text`) and, for JSON, the data (`r.json`):

```vyrn check
use vyrn.http

main:
    let r = http.get("http://api.open-notify.org/iss-now.json")
    if not r.ok:
        print("the API said", r.status)
        return
    end
    let where = r.json["iss_position"]
    print("The space station is over latitude {where["latitude"]}, longitude {where["longitude"]}")
end
```

Run it with `vyrn run`: it needs the internet, and prints where the space
station is right now (it moves 7.7 km every second).

Every example below that asks a real API uses a **recorded answer** instead,
so the lessons print the same each time and work offline. Programmers do this
all the time: you save one real answer and develop against it.

lessons.title: Reading the answer
lessons.text:
API answers nest maps and lists. Find your way in one step at a time:

```vyrn
use vyrn.json

const ANSWER = r'{"results": {"sunrise": "2026-11-12T07:12:40+00:00", "sunset": "2026-11-12T16:13:05+00:00", "day_length": 32425}, "status": "OK"}'

main:
    data = json.parse(ANSWER)
    print(data["status"])
    print(data["results"]["sunrise"])
    hours = data["results"]["day_length"] / 3600
    print("the day lasts {hours:.1f} hours")
end
```

```text
OK
2026-11-12T07:12:40+00:00
the day lasts 9.0 hours
```

When a field might be missing, `.get(key, default)` gives the default
instead of failing:

```vyrn
use vyrn.json

main:
    data = json.parse(r'{"name": "London", "population": 8982000}')
    print(data.get("population", "unknown"), data.get("mayor", "unknown"))
end
```

```text
8982000 unknown
```

### Exercise

The recorded answer is a weather forecast with a list of hours. Print the
highest temperature and the hour it happens.

```vyrn starter
use vyrn.json

const ANSWER = r'{"hourly": [{"time": "09:00", "temp": 11.5}, {"time": "12:00", "temp": 14.2}, {"time": "15:00", "temp": 13.8}]}'

main:
    data = json.parse(ANSWER)
end
```

```text expect
warmest: 14.2 at 12:00
```

exercise.starter:
use vyrn.json

const ANSWER = r'{"hourly": [{"time": "09:00", "temp": 11.5}, {"time": "12:00", "temp": 14.2}, {"time": "15:00", "temp": 13.8}]}'

main:
    data = json.parse(ANSWER)
end
exercise.solution:
use vyrn.json

const ANSWER = r'{"hourly": [{"time": "09:00", "temp": 11.5}, {"time": "12:00", "temp": 14.2}, {"time": "15:00", "temp": 13.8}]}'

main:
    data = json.parse(ANSWER)
    best = max(data["hourly"], key = h => h["temp"])
    print("warmest: {best["temp"]} at {best["time"]}")
end
hints: `hours = data["hourly"]` is a list of maps.
`best = max(hours, key = h => h["temp"])`

lessons.title: When the API says no
lessons.text:
Networks fail. Servers break, keys run out, Wi-Fi drops. A program that
talks to an API should check the status, and catch the failure when there
is no answer at all:

```vyrn check
use vyrn.http

create station_position() -> map?:
    attempt:
        let r = http.get("http://api.open-notify.org/iss-now.json")
        if r.status == 429:
            print("too many requests; wait a minute")
            return none
        end
        if not r.ok:
            print("the API said {r.status}")
            return none
        end
        return r.json["iss_position"]
    catch NetworkError as e:
        print("no connection:", e.message)
        return none
    end
end

main:
    print(station_position())
end
```

To test code like this without the internet, pass the fetching in as a
function. A test gives a **fake** that returns a recorded answer, or fails:

```vyrn
create describe(fetch: any) -> str:
    attempt:
        let data = fetch()
        return "over {data["latitude"]}, {data["longitude"]}"
    catch Error as e:
        return "unavailable ({e.kind})"
    end
end

main:
    print(describe(fake(returns = {"latitude": "47.6", "longitude": "-122.3"})))
    print(describe(fake(fails = NetworkError("timed out"))))
end
```

```text
over 47.6, -122.3
unavailable (NetworkError)
```

lessons.title: Project: is it daytime?
lessons.text:
The sunrise-sunset API gives sunrise and sunset in UTC, for any latitude
and longitude. Is it daytime there now? Compare the moment now with the
two times:

```vyrn
use vyrn.json
use vyrn.time

## A time from the API: "2026-11-12T07:12:40+00:00".
create api_time(text: str) -> float:
    return time.parse(text[:19], "%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S")
end

create is_daytime(answer: map, now: float) -> bool:
    let results = answer["results"]
    return api_time(results["sunrise"]) <= now and now < api_time(results["sunset"])
end

const LONDON = r'{"results": {"sunrise": "2026-11-12T07:12:40+00:00", "sunset": "2026-11-12T16:13:05+00:00"}, "status": "OK"}'
const SYDNEY = r'{"results": {"sunrise": "2026-11-11T18:46:05+00:00", "sunset": "2026-11-12T08:44:52+00:00"}, "status": "OK"}'

main:
    each hour in [6, 12, 20]:
        now = time.make(2026, 11, 12, hour, 0)
        london = "day" if is_daytime(json.parse(LONDON), now) else "night"
        sydney = "day" if is_daytime(json.parse(SYDNEY), now) else "night"
        print("{hour:02}:00 UTC: London {london}, Sydney {sydney}")
    end
end
```

```text
06:00 UTC: London night, Sydney day
12:00 UTC: London day, Sydney night
20:00 UTC: London night, Sydney night
```

At 20:00 UTC, it's 7 in the morning in Sydney the next day, so a new
sunrise has happened. That's why the program, for real, asks the API for
today's times each time, with `date=today`.

The live version:

```vyrn check
use vyrn.http
use vyrn.time

create api_time(text: str) -> float:
    return time.parse(text[:19], "%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S")
end

main:
    let query = http.query({"lat": -33.87, "lng": 151.21, "formatted": 0})
    let r = http.get("https://api.sunrise-sunset.org/json?" + query)
    if not r.ok:
        print("no answer:", r.status)
        return
    end
    let results = r.json["results"]
    let now = time.now()
    let day = api_time(results["sunrise"]) <= now and now < api_time(results["sunset"])
    print("It is", "day" if day else "night", "in Sydney")
end
```

### Exercise

Write `sun_hours(answer)`, which gives how many hours of daylight there are,
rounded to one decimal place, worked out from sunrise and sunset.

```vyrn starter
use vyrn.json
use vyrn.time

create api_time(text: str) -> float:
    return time.parse(text[:19], "%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S")
end

create sun_hours(answer: map) -> float:
    return 0.0
end

main:
    print(sun_hours(json.parse(r'{"results": {"sunrise": "2026-06-21T03:43:00+00:00", "sunset": "2026-06-21T20:21:00+00:00"}}')))
end
```

```text expect
16.6
```

exercise.starter:

use vyrn.time

create api_time(text: str) -> float:
    return time.parse(text[:19], "%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S")
end

create sun_hours(answer: map) -> float:
    return 0.0
end

main:
    print(sun_hours(json.parse(r'{"results": {"sunrise": "2026-06-21T03:43:00+00:00", "sunset": "2026-06-21T20:21:00+00:00"}}')))

exercise.solution:
use vyrn.json
use vyrn.time

create api_time(text: str) -> float:
    return time.parse(text[:19], "%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S")
end

create sun_hours(answer: map) -> float:
    let r = answer["results"]
    return round((api_time(r["sunset"]) - api_time(r["sunrise"])) / 3600, 1)
end

main:
    print(sun_hours(json.parse(r'{"results": {"sunrise": "2026-06-21T03:43:00+00:00", "sunset": "2026-06-21T20:21:00+00:00"}}')))
end
hints: subtract the two moments for seconds; divide by 3600.
`round(x, 1)` rounds to one place.

lessons.title: you learned
lessons.text:
- An API answers a URL with data, usually JSON; the query string carries
  the details, built safely with `http.query`.
- `http.get` gives a response with `status`, `ok`, `text` and `json`.
- Walk into nested answers one step at a time; `.get` copes with missing
  fields.
- Check the status, catch `NetworkError`, and test with recorded answers
  and fakes.

days.title: Day 34: An API in a window
days.intro:
Yesterday's programs printed what an API said. Today the answers go into a
window. The project is a trivia quiz: questions come from the Open Trivia
Database, the player clicks **True** or **False**, and the window keeps the
score. On the way you meet text that arrives *encoded* for web pages, and a
clean way to split a program into its data, its logic and its window.

lessons.title: The questions
lessons.text:
The Open Trivia Database gives questions as JSON. Ask for ten true-or-false
questions with:

```text
https://opentdb.com/api.php?amount=10&type=boolean
```

The answer looks like this (shortened to two questions):

```vyrn
use vyrn.json

const ANSWER = r'{"response_code": 0, "results": [{"category": "Science: Computers", "type": "boolean", "difficulty": "easy", "question": "The logo for Snapchat is a Bell.", "correct_answer": "False", "incorrect_answers": ["True"]}, {"category": "Geography", "type": "boolean", "difficulty": "easy", "question": "Greenland is covered with more than 50% of ice.", "correct_answer": "True", "incorrect_answers": ["False"]}]}'

main:
    data = json.parse(ANSWER)
    print("code", data["response_code"], "with", len(data["results"]), "questions")
    each q in data["results"]:
        print("-", q["question"], "->", q["correct_answer"])
    end
end
```

```text
code 0 with 2 questions
- The logo for Snapchat is a Bell. -> False
- Greenland is covered with more than 50% of ice. -> True
```

The API has its own `response_code` besides the HTTP status: `0` means
success, `1` means it doesn't have enough questions for what you asked.

lessons.title: Text made for web pages
lessons.text:
Ask the real API and some questions come back looking odd:

```text
The word "astronaut" comes from Greek words meaning "star sailor".
```

`"` is an **HTML entity**: how a web page writes `"` without confusing
it with the page's own quotes. `&` is `&`, `'` is `'`, `<` is
`<`. Turn them back with `html.unescape`:

```vyrn
use vyrn.html

main:
    raw = "The word "astronaut" comes from Greek words meaning "star sailor"."
    print(html.unescape(raw))
    print(html.unescape("Tom & Jerry's 5 < 6"))
end
```

```text
The word "astronaut" comes from Greek words meaning "star sailor".
Tom & Jerry's 5 < 6
```

`html.escape` goes the other way, for when you put text into a page
(Day 41).

### Exercise

Clean every question in the list, and print them numbered from 1.

```vyrn starter
use vyrn.html

main:
    questions = ["Pac-Man was first called "Puck Man".", "R&B stands for Rhythm and Blues."]
end
```

```text expect
1. Pac-Man was first called "Puck Man".
2. R&B stands for Rhythm and Blues.
```

exercise.starter:
use vyrn.html

main:
    questions = ["Pac-Man was first called "Puck Man".", "R&B stands for Rhythm and Blues."]
end
exercise.expect:
1. Pac-Man was first called "Puck Man".
2. R&B stands for Rhythm and Blues.
exercise.solution:
use vyrn.html

main:
    questions = ["Pac-Man was first called "Puck Man".", "R&B stands for Rhythm and Blues."]
    each i, q in enumerate(questions):
        print("{i + 1}. {html.unescape(q)}")
    end
end
hints: `each i, q in enumerate(questions):` and print `i + 1`.

lessons.title: The quiz logic, without a window
lessons.text:
Keep the rules of the game in an object that knows nothing about windows or
the internet. Then it can be tested with plain lists, and the same object
works with a window, a terminal, or a phone app later:

```vyrn
use vyrn.html

object Question:
    text: str
    answer: str
end

object Quiz:
    questions: list
    number: int = 0
    score: int = 0

    create has_more(self) -> bool:
        return self.number < len(self.questions)
    end

    create current(self) -> str:
        return "Q{self.number + 1}: {self.questions[self.number].text}"
    end

    ## Checks the answer, moves to the next question, and says how it went.
    create answer(mut self, guess: str) -> bool:
        let right = guess == self.questions[self.number].answer
        if right: self.score += 1
        self.number += 1
        return right
    end
end

create from_api(results: list) -> list:
    return [Question(html.unescape(r["question"]), r["correct_answer"]) each r in results]
end

main:
    results = [{"question": "The sun is a star.", "correct_answer": "True"}, {"question": "Spiders have six legs.", "correct_answer": "False"}, {"question": "Gold's symbol is Ag.", "correct_answer": "False"}]
    quiz = Quiz(from_api(results))
    each guess in ["True", "True", "False"]:
        print(quiz.current())
        print("  you said {guess}:", "right" if quiz.answer(guess) else "wrong")
    end
    print("score {quiz.score}/{len(quiz.questions)}; more? {quiz.has_more()}")
end
```

```text
Q1: The sun is a star.
  you said True: right
Q2: Spiders have six legs.
  you said True: wrong
Q3: Gold's symbol is Ag.
  you said False: right
score 2/3; more? false
```

### Exercise

Add a method `percent(self)` that gives the score as a whole-number
percentage of the questions answered so far (0 when none have been
answered).

```vyrn starter
object Quiz:
    answered: int = 0
    score: int = 0

    create percent(self) -> int:
        return 0
    end
end

main:
    print(Quiz().percent(), Quiz(answered = 3, score = 2).percent(), Quiz(answered = 4, score = 4).percent())
end
```

```text expect
0 67 100
```

exercise.starter:
object Quiz:
    answered: int = 0
    score: int = 0

    create percent(self) -> int:
        return 0
    end
end

main:
    print(Quiz().percent(), Quiz(answered = 3, score = 2).percent(), Quiz(answered = 4, score = 4).percent())
end
exercise.solution:
object Quiz:
    answered: int = 0
    score: int = 0

    create percent(self) -> int:
        if self.answered == 0: return 0
        return round(100 * self.score / self.answered)
    end
end

main:
    print(Quiz().percent(), Quiz(answered = 3, score = 2).percent(), Quiz(answered = 4, score = 4).percent())
end
hints: guard against dividing by zero first.
`round(100 * self.score / self.answered)`

lessons.title: Fetching the questions
lessons.text:
Fetching is one small function. It fails with a clear error when the API
doesn't deliver, so the window can show a message instead of crashing:

```vyrn check
use vyrn.http

create fetch_questions(amount: int = 10) -> list:
    let r = http.get("https://opentdb.com/api.php?" + http.query({"amount": amount, "type": "boolean"}))
    if not r.ok: fail NetworkError("the trivia server said {r.status}")
    if r.json["response_code"] != 0: fail ValueError("not enough questions")
    return r.json["results"]
end

main:
    each q in fetch_questions(3):
        print(q["question"])
    end
end
```

lessons.title: Long text in a window
lessons.text:
A window label is one line; a long question runs off the edge. **Wrap** it:
add words to a line until the next one wouldn't fit, then start a new line:

```vyrn
create wrap(text: str, width: int) -> list:
    var lines = [""]
    each word in text.split():
        if lines[-1] and len(lines[-1]) + 1 + len(word) > width:
            lines.append(word)
        else:
            lines[-1] = (lines[-1] + " " + word).strip()
        end
    end
    return lines
end

main:
    each line in wrap("The Great Wall of China is visible from the Moon with the naked eye.", 24):
        print("|" + line.ljust(24) + "|")
    end
end
```

```text
|The Great Wall of China |
|is visible from the Moon|
|with the naked eye.     |
```

With the window's text at its normal size, each letter is 16 pixels wide,
so a 520-pixel window fits about 28 letters a line after its margins.

lessons.title: Project: the trivia window
lessons.text:
The window draws whatever the quiz says now, and calls the quiz's methods
when a button is clicked. The whole program, run with `vyrn run` (it needs
the internet):

```vyrn check
use vyrn.draw
use vyrn.html
use vyrn.http

object Question:
    text: str
    answer: str
end

object Quiz:
    questions: list
    number: int = 0
    score: int = 0

    create has_more(self) -> bool:
        return self.number < len(self.questions)
    end

    create current(self) -> str:
        return self.questions[self.number].text
    end

    create answer(mut self, guess: str) -> bool:
        let right = guess == self.questions[self.number].answer
        if right: self.score += 1
        self.number += 1
        return right
    end
end

create wrap(text: str, width: int) -> list:
    var lines = [""]
    each word in text.split():
        if lines[-1] and len(lines[-1]) + 1 + len(word) > width:
            lines.append(word)
        else:
            lines[-1] = (lines[-1] + " " + word).strip()
        end
    end
    return lines
end

create fetch_questions() -> list:
    let r = http.get("https://opentdb.com/api.php?amount=10&type=boolean")
    if not r.ok: fail NetworkError("the trivia server said {r.status}")
    return [Question(html.unescape(q["question"]), q["correct_answer"]) each q in r.json["results"]]
end

main:
    let win = draw.window(520, 300, "Trivia")
    var quiz = Quiz([])
    var message = "Loading..."
    attempt:
        quiz = Quiz(fetch_questions())
        message = ""
    catch Error as e:
        message = "Could not load questions: {e.message}"
    end
    var flash = "#263238"
    loop win.open():
        win.clear(flash)
        win.layout(24, 24, gap = 16)
        win.label("Score: {quiz.score}/{quiz.number}", color = "#90caf9")
        if quiz.has_more():
            each line in wrap(quiz.current(), 28):
                win.label(line)
            end
            win.row()
            each choice in ["True", "False"]:
                if win.button(choice, w = 100):
                    flash = "#2e7d32" if quiz.answer(choice) else "#c62828"
                end
            end
            win.end_row()
        else:
            win.label(message or "Finished! {quiz.score} of {len(quiz.questions)}.")
        end
        win.show()
    end
end
```

The background flashes green or red after each answer. The window code has
almost no logic of its own: it asks the quiz what to show, and tells the
quiz what was clicked. That split, **logic** in one place and **display**
in another, is what lets you test the quiz on 34.3's plain lists.

### Exercise

The flash stays forever: once it turns green it never goes back. Make it
fade back after half a second. Write `background(since)`, which is given the
seconds since the last answer and the colour it flashed, and gives the
colour to clear the window with now.

```vyrn starter
create background(since: float, flash: str) -> str:
    return flash
end

main:
    print(background(0.1, "#2e7d32"), background(0.6, "#2e7d32"), background(0.2, "#c62828"))
end
```

```text expect
#2e7d32 #263238 #c62828
```

exercise.starter:
create background(since: float, flash: str) -> str:
    return flash
end

main:
    print(background(0.1, "#2e7d32"), background(0.6, "#2e7d32"), background(0.2, "#c62828"))
end
exercise.solution:
create background(since: float, flash: str) -> str:
    if since < 0.5: return flash
    return "#263238"
end

main:
    print(background(0.1, "#2e7d32"), background(0.6, "#2e7d32"), background(0.2, "#c62828"))
end
hints: under 0.5 seconds, keep the flash; after, give the normal `"#263238"`.
in the window, keep `answered_at = time.now()` when a button is clicked, and call `background(time.now() - answered_at, flash)`.

lessons.title: you learned
lessons.text:
- APIs can have their own success codes inside the JSON, besides the HTTP
  status.
- `html.unescape` turns `"`, `&` and friends back into text.
- Keep the rules in an object of their own, tested without a window or the
  internet; the window only shows what the object says and passes on clicks.

days.title: Day 35: Keys and secrets
days.intro:
Many APIs want to know who is asking. You sign up, and they give you an
**API key**: a long password that goes with every request. Keys are
secrets: anyone who has yours can use your account, and some APIs charge
for every request. Today you learn to keep keys out of your code with
**environment variables** and `.env` files. The project checks the weather
forecast every morning and warns you when you need an umbrella.

lessons.title: What a key looks like
lessons.text:
A weather API, OpenWeatherMap, takes its key in the query string as
`appid`:

```text
https://api.openweathermap.org/data/2.5/forecast?lat=51.5&lon=-0.12&appid=6c1b9a0f2e7d4c8a9b3e5f1d2c4a6b8e
```

Others want it in a **header**, a line of extra information sent with the
request:

```vyrn check
use vyrn.http

main:
    let r = http.get("https://api.example.com/v1/things", headers = {"Authorization": "Bearer 6c1b9a0f2e7d4c8a"})
    print(r.status)
end
```

The API's documentation says which. Either way the key is in your program
somewhere, and that is the problem: programs get shared, posted online,
and saved in Git, where old versions stay forever. Bots search GitHub for
keys all day long.

lessons.title: Environment variables
lessons.text:
Every running program gets a set of **environment variables** from whatever
started it: named pieces of text, like `HOME` or `PATH`. Put the key in one,
and the program reads it at run time; the code itself never contains it.

```vyrn
use vyrn.os

main:
    os.set_env("WEATHER_KEY", "6c1b9a0f")
    print(os.env("WEATHER_KEY"))
    print(os.env("NO_SUCH_VARIABLE"))
    print(os.env("UNITS", "metric"))
end
```

```text
6c1b9a0f
none
metric
```

`os.env(name)` gives `none` when the variable isn't set, or the default you
give. Here `os.set_env` stands in for you setting it before running; for
real you set it in the terminal, on Windows in PowerShell:

```powershell
$env:WEATHER_KEY = "6c1b9a0f2e7d4c8a9b3e5f1d2c4a6b8e"
vyrn run weather.vyrn
```

and on macOS or Linux:

```bash
WEATHER_KEY=6c1b9a0f2e7d4c8a9b3e5f1d2c4a6b8e vyrn run weather.vyrn
```

A missing key should stop the program with a message that says how to fix
it, not fail later with a confusing `401` from the API:

```vyrn
use vyrn.os

create need(name: str) -> str:
    let value = os.env(name)
    if value == none or value == "":
        fail ValueError("set the {name} environment variable first (see the README)")
    end
    return value
end

main:
    attempt:
        key = need("STOCKS_KEY")
    catch ValueError as e:
        print(e.message)
    end
end
```

```text
set the STOCKS_KEY environment variable first (see the README)
```

### Exercise

Write `settings()`, which gives a map of the city (from `CITY`, default
`"London"`) and the units (from `UNITS`, default `"metric"`).

```vyrn starter
use vyrn.os

create settings() -> map:
    return {}
end

main:
    print(settings())
    os.set_env("CITY", "Oslo")
    print(settings())
end
```

```text expect
{"city": "London", "units": "metric"}
{"city": "Oslo", "units": "metric"}
```

exercise.starter:
use vyrn.os

create settings() -> map:
    return {}
end

main:
    print(settings())
    os.set_env("CITY", "Oslo")
    print(settings())
end
exercise.solution:
use vyrn.os

create settings() -> map:
    return {"city": os.env("CITY", "London"), "units": os.env("UNITS", "metric")}
end

main:
    print(settings())
    os.set_env("CITY", "Oslo")
    print(settings())
end
hints: `{"city": os.env("CITY", "London"), ...}`

lessons.title: `.env` files
lessons.text:
Typing keys into the terminal every time gets old. The usual answer is a
file named `.env` next to the program, with one `NAME=value` per line, that
`os.load_env()` reads into the environment:

```vyrn
use vyrn.os

main:
    write_text(".env", "# my keys: never commit this file\nNEWS_KEY=e4f1a2b3c4d5\nPHONE=\"+44 7700 900123\"\n")
    print(os.load_env())
    print(os.env("NEWS_KEY"), os.env("PHONE"))
end
```

```text
["NEWS_KEY", "PHONE"]
e4f1a2b3c4d5 +44 7700 900123
```

Variables that are already set win over the file, so you can still override
one from the terminal. And the most important line of today: **tell Git to
ignore the file**, by adding it to `.gitignore`:

```text
.env
```

Then commit a `.env.example` instead, with the names but not the values, so
others know what to set:

```text
WEATHER_KEY=your-key-from-openweathermap.org
```

If a key ever does get committed, deleting the file isn't enough: the old
version is still in Git's history. **Revoke** the key on the API's website
and make a new one.

lessons.title: Project: the umbrella alert
lessons.text:
OpenWeatherMap's free forecast gives the weather every three hours for five
days. Each entry has a time and a list of conditions; every condition has
an **id**, and ids under 700 mean something falls from the sky (2xx
thunder, 3xx drizzle, 5xx rain, 6xx snow). Here is a recorded answer,
shortened:

```vyrn
use vyrn.json

const FORECAST = r'{"cod": "200", "list": [{"dt_txt": "2026-11-12 06:00:00", "weather": [{"id": 803, "main": "Clouds"}]}, {"dt_txt": "2026-11-12 09:00:00", "weather": [{"id": 500, "main": "Rain"}]}, {"dt_txt": "2026-11-12 12:00:00", "weather": [{"id": 501, "main": "Rain"}]}, {"dt_txt": "2026-11-12 15:00:00", "weather": [{"id": 800, "main": "Clear"}]}, {"dt_txt": "2026-11-12 18:00:00", "weather": [{"id": 800, "main": "Clear"}]}]}'

## The times today when something falls from the sky.
create wet_hours(forecast: map, hours: int) -> list:
    var wet = []
    each entry in forecast["list"][:hours // 3]:
        if any([c["id"] < 700 each c in entry["weather"]]):
            wet.append(entry["dt_txt"][11:16])
        end
    end
    return wet
end

main:
    let wet = wet_hours(json.parse(FORECAST), 12)
    if wet:
        print("Bring an umbrella: rain at", ", ".join(wet))
    else:
        print("No rain in the next 12 hours")
    end
end
```

```text
Bring an umbrella: rain at 09:00, 12:00
```

The live program puts it together: the key from `.env`, the forecast from
the API, and the alert by email (Day 32) or just printed:

```vyrn check
use vyrn.http
use vyrn.os

create wet_hours(forecast: map, hours: int) -> list:
    var wet = []
    each entry in forecast["list"][:hours // 3]:
        if any([c["id"] < 700 each c in entry["weather"]]):
            wet.append(entry["dt_txt"][11:16])
        end
    end
    return wet
end

main:
    os.load_env()
    let key = os.env("WEATHER_KEY")
    if key == none:
        print("Put WEATHER_KEY=... in a .env file first")
        return
    end
    let query = http.query({"lat": 51.5, "lon": -0.12, "appid": key})
    let r = http.get("https://api.openweathermap.org/data/2.5/forecast?" + query)
    if r.status == 401:
        print("The API doesn't accept this key (new keys take an hour to start working)")
        return
    end
    let wet = wet_hours(r.json, 12)
    print("Umbrella! Rain at " + ", ".join(wet) if wet else "No rain today")
end
```

Run it every morning with Task Scheduler (Windows) or `cron` (macOS and
Linux), and it becomes a small service of your own.

### Exercise

`dt_txt` is in UTC. Make `wet_hours` give the hours in a time zone instead,
using `time.parse` and `time.format(..., zone = ...)`. The forecast here has
rain at 09:00 and 12:00 UTC; in New York that is 04:00 and 07:00.

```vyrn starter
use vyrn.time

create wet_hours(entries: list, zone: str) -> list:
    return [e["dt_txt"][11:16] each e in entries if e["weather"][0]["id"] < 700]
end

main:
    entries = [{"dt_txt": "2026-11-12 09:00:00", "weather": [{"id": 500}]}, {"dt_txt": "2026-11-12 12:00:00", "weather": [{"id": 501}]}, {"dt_txt": "2026-11-12 15:00:00", "weather": [{"id": 800}]}]
    print(wet_hours(entries, "America/New_York"))
end
```

```text expect
["04:00", "07:00"]
```

exercise.starter:
use vyrn.time

create wet_hours(entries: list, zone: str) -> list:
    return [e["dt_txt"][11:16] each e in entries if e["weather"][0]["id"] < 700]
end

main:
    entries = [{"dt_txt": "2026-11-12 09:00:00", "weather": [{"id": 500}]}, {"dt_txt": "2026-11-12 12:00:00", "weather": [{"id": 501}]}, {"dt_txt": "2026-11-12 15:00:00", "weather": [{"id": 800}]}]
    print(wet_hours(entries, "America/New_York"))
end
exercise.solution:
use vyrn.time

create local_hour(text: str, zone: str) -> str:
    return time.format(time.parse(text, "%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S"), "%H:%M", zone = zone)
end

create wet_hours(entries: list, zone: str) -> list:
    return [local_hour(e["dt_txt"], zone) each e in entries if e["weather"][0]["id"] < 700]
end

main:
    entries = [{"dt_txt": "2026-11-12 09:00:00", "weather": [{"id": 500}]}, {"dt_txt": "2026-11-12 12:00:00", "weather": [{"id": 501}]}, {"dt_txt": "2026-11-12 15:00:00", "weather": [{"id": 800}]}]
    print(wet_hours(entries, "America/New_York"))
end
hints: `moment = time.parse(e["dt_txt"], "%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S")`
`time.format(moment, "%H:%M", zone = zone)`

lessons.title: you learned
lessons.text:
- API keys go in the query string or a header; they are passwords and must
  never be in your code.
- `os.env(name, default)` reads an environment variable; check for missing
  keys early with a helpful message.
- `os.load_env()` reads a `.env` file; put `.env` in `.gitignore` and commit
  a `.env.example`.
- A key that leaks must be revoked, not just deleted.

days.title: Day 36: Combining APIs
days.intro:
One API answers one kind of question. Interesting programs ask several and
put the answers together: the answer to the first decides what to ask the
second. Today's project watches a share price, and when it moves a lot,
fetches the news about that company to explain why, and sends you a short
**digest**. On the way you learn to **cache** answers so you don't ask the
same question twice, and to be polite to APIs that limit how often you ask.

lessons.title: One answer leads to the next
lessons.text:
A stock API gives the closing price for each day. The change from one day
to the next, as a percentage, tells you how much it moved:

```vyrn
use vyrn.json

const PRICES = r'{"Meta Data": {"2. Symbol": "TSLA"}, "Time Series (Daily)": {"2026-11-11": {"4. close": "312.40"}, "2026-11-10": {"4. close": "289.10"}, "2026-11-09": {"4. close": "291.50"}}}'

create change(prices: map) -> float:
    let days = prices["Time Series (Daily)"]
    let dates = sorted(days.keys(), reverse = true)
    let today = float(days[dates[0]]["4. close"])
    let before = float(days[dates[1]]["4. close"])
    return (today - before) / before * 100
end

main:
    let moved = change(json.parse(PRICES))
    print("TSLA moved {moved:+.1f}%")
    if abs(moved) >= 5: print("big move: fetch the news")
end
```

```text
TSLA moved +8.1%
big move: fetch the news
```

The prices come as text (`"312.40"`), so `float` turns them into numbers.
The dates are map keys; sorting them newest first finds today and the day
before. `{moved:+.1f}` shows the sign even when it's positive.

Only when the move is big does the program ask the second API, a news
search:

```vyrn
use vyrn.json

const NEWS = r'{"status": "ok", "totalResults": 3, "articles": [{"source": {"name": "Reuters"}, "title": "Tesla shares jump after record deliveries", "url": "https://example.com/a"}, {"source": {"name": "BBC"}, "title": "Electric car sales rise across Europe", "url": "https://example.com/b"}, {"source": {"name": "Bloomberg"}, "title": "Tesla opens new factory", "url": "https://example.com/c"}]}'

main:
    each a in json.parse(NEWS)["articles"][:2]:
        print("{a["source"]["name"]}: {a["title"]}")
    end
end
```

```text
Reuters: Tesla shares jump after record deliveries
BBC: Electric car sales rise across Europe
```

### Exercise

Write `headlines(news, words)`, which keeps only the articles whose title
contains one of the words (in any case), giving their titles.

```vyrn starter
create headlines(news: map, words: list) -> list:
    return []
end

main:
    news = {"articles": [{"title": "Tesla shares jump"}, {"title": "Rain expected all week"}, {"title": "Musk says TESLA will grow"}]}
    print(headlines(news, ["tesla", "musk"]))
end
```

```text expect
["Tesla shares jump", "Musk says TESLA will grow"]
```

exercise.starter:
create headlines(news: map, words: list) -> list:
    return []
end

main:
    news = {"articles": [{"title": "Tesla shares jump"}, {"title": "Rain expected all week"}, {"title": "Musk says TESLA will grow"}]}
    print(headlines(news, ["tesla", "musk"]))
end
exercise.expect: ["Tesla shares jump", "Musk says TESLA will grow"]
exercise.solution:
create mentions(title: str, words: list) -> bool:
    return any([w in title.lower() each w in words])
end

create headlines(news: map, words: list) -> list:
    return [a["title"] each a in news["articles"] if mentions(a["title"], words)]
end

main:
    news = {"articles": [{"title": "Tesla shares jump"}, {"title": "Rain expected all week"}, {"title": "Musk says TESLA will grow"}]}
    print(headlines(news, ["tesla", "musk"]))
end
hints: `any([w in title.lower() each w in words])`

lessons.title: Caching answers
lessons.text:
Free API plans allow only so many requests: Alpha Vantage, the stock API,
allows 25 a day. Run your program a few times while writing it and you've
used them up. A **cache** keeps each answer in a file, and gives the saved
copy while it's still fresh:

```vyrn
use vyrn.fs
use vyrn.json
use vyrn.time

## Gives the saved answer if it is younger than `max_age` seconds, or asks
## `fetch` for a new one and saves it.
create cached(path: str, max_age: float, fetch: any) -> any:
    if fs.exists(path) and time.now() - fs.modified(path) < max_age:
        return json.load(path)
    end
    let answer = fetch()
    json.save(path, answer)
    return answer
end

main:
    if fs.exists("prices.json"): fs.remove("prices.json")
    api = fake(returns = {"close": 312.4})
    each _ in 0 until 3:
        print(cached("prices.json", 3600, api))
    end
    print("the API was asked", len(api.calls), "time")
end
```

```text
{"close": 312.4}
{"close": 312.4}
{"close": 312.4}
the API was asked 1 time
```

Three answers, one request. Choose the age by how fast the data changes:
an hour for news, a day for yesterday's closing prices, never for history.

lessons.title: Being polite: rate limits
lessons.text:
An API that gets too many requests in a short time answers `429 Too Many
Requests`, often with a `Retry-After` header saying how many seconds to
wait. A program asking for many things should pause between requests, and
wait and try again when told to:

```vyrn
use vyrn.time

create polite_get(fetch: any, tries: int = 3) -> any:
    each attempt_number in 1 to tries:
        let r = fetch()
        if r["status"] != 429: return r
        let wait = float(r["headers"].get("retry-after", "1"))
        print("rate limited; waiting {wait} s (try {attempt_number})")
        time.sleep(wait / 100)
    end
    fail NetworkError("still rate limited after {tries} tries")
end

main:
    api = fake(returns_each = [{"status": 429, "headers": {"retry-after": "2"}}, {"status": 200, "headers": {}, "json": [1, 2]}])
    print(polite_get(api)["json"])
end
```

```text
rate limited; waiting 2.0 s (try 1)
[1, 2]
```

(The example divides the wait by 100 so the lesson doesn't take seconds to
run; the real one waits the full time.)

### Exercise

Many APIs say "wait longer each time": 1 second, then 2, then 4. Write
`backoff(try_number)` giving the wait for each try, never more than 30
seconds.

```vyrn starter
create backoff(try_number: int) -> int:
    return 1
end

main:
    print([backoff(n) each n in 1 to 7])
end
```

```text expect
[1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 30, 30]
```

exercise.starter:
create backoff(try_number: int) -> int:
    return 1
end

main:
    print([backoff(n) each n in 1 to 7])
end
exercise.solution:
create backoff(try_number: int) -> int:
    return min(2 ** (try_number - 1), 30)
end

main:
    print([backoff(n) each n in 1 to 7])
end
hints: `2 ** (try_number - 1)` doubles each time; `min` caps it.

lessons.title: Project: the stock news digest
lessons.text:
The whole program: for each share you follow, work out the move; for the
big movers, find the news; put it all in one message. The two APIs are
passed in as functions, so here they are fakes with recorded answers, and
for real they call `http.get`:

```vyrn
create change(closes: list) -> float:
    return (closes[0] - closes[1]) / closes[1] * 100
end

create digest(symbols: map, prices: any, news: any, threshold: float = 5) -> str:
    var lines = []
    each symbol, company in symbols.items():
        let moved = change(prices(symbol))
        let arrow = "▲" if moved > 0 else "▼"
        lines.append("{symbol} {arrow} {abs(moved):.1f}%")
        if abs(moved) >= threshold:
            each title in news(company)[:2]:
                lines.append("  - {title}")
            end
        end
    end
    return "\n".join(lines)
end

main:
    closes = {"TSLA": [312.4, 289.1], "AAPL": [228.0, 227.1], "NVDA": [131.2, 140.6]}
    stories = {"Tesla": ["Tesla shares jump after record deliveries", "Tesla opens new factory", "Old news"], "Nvidia": ["Chip stocks fall on export rules"]}
    prices = symbol => closes[symbol]
    news = company => stories.get(company, [])
    print(digest({"TSLA": "Tesla", "AAPL": "Apple", "NVDA": "Nvidia"}, prices, news))
end
```

```text
TSLA ▲ 8.1%
  - Tesla shares jump after record deliveries
  - Tesla opens new factory
AAPL ▲ 0.4%
NVDA ▼ 6.7%
  - Chip stocks fall on export rules
```

The live version fills in the two functions with real requests, keys from
`.env` (Day 35) and the cache from 36.2:

```vyrn check
use vyrn.fs
use vyrn.http
use vyrn.json
use vyrn.os
use vyrn.time

create cached(path: str, max_age: float, fetch: any) -> any:
    if fs.exists(path) and time.now() - fs.modified(path) < max_age:
        return json.load(path)
    end
    let answer = fetch()
    json.save(path, answer)
    return answer
end

create prices(symbol: str) -> list:
    let query = http.query({"function": "TIME_SERIES_DAILY", "symbol": symbol, "apikey": os.env("STOCK_KEY")})
    let data = cached("prices-{symbol}.json", 86400, () => http.get("https://www.alphavantage.co/query?" + query).json)
    let days = data["Time Series (Daily)"]
    return [float(days[d]["4. close"]) each d in sorted(days.keys(), reverse = true)[:2]]
end

create news(company: str) -> list:
    let query = http.query({"q": company, "sortBy": "publishedAt", "apiKey": os.env("NEWS_KEY")})
    let data = cached("news-{company}.json", 3600, () => http.get("https://newsapi.org/v2/everything?" + query).json)
    return [a["title"] each a in data["articles"]]
end

main:
    os.load_env()
    each symbol, company in {"TSLA": "Tesla", "NVDA": "Nvidia"}.items():
        let closes = prices(symbol)
        let moved = (closes[0] - closes[1]) / closes[1] * 100
        print("{symbol} {moved:+.1f}%")
        if abs(moved) >= 5:
            each title in news(company)[:3]: print("  - " + title)
        end
    end
end
```

### Exercise

Sort the digest so the biggest moves (up or down) come first. Write
`by_size(moves)`, which takes a map of symbol to move and gives the symbols
in that order.

```vyrn starter
create by_size(moves: map) -> list:
    return list(moves.keys())
end

main:
    print(by_size({"TSLA": 8.1, "AAPL": 0.4, "NVDA": -6.7}))
end
```

```text expect
["TSLA", "NVDA", "AAPL"]
```

exercise.starter:
create by_size(moves: map) -> list:
    return list(moves.keys())
end

main:
    print(by_size({"TSLA": 8.1, "AAPL": 0.4, "NVDA": -6.7}))
end
exercise.solution:
create by_size(moves: map) -> list:
    return sorted(moves.keys(), key = s => abs(moves[s]), reverse = true)
end

main:
    print(by_size({"TSLA": 8.1, "AAPL": 0.4, "NVDA": -6.7}))
end
hints: `sorted(moves.keys(), key = s => abs(moves[s]), reverse = true)`

lessons.title: you learned
lessons.text:
- Let one API's answer decide what to ask the next.
- Cache answers in files, and reuse them while they are fresh.
- Respect rate limits: pause, honour `Retry-After`, and back off.
- Pass the API calls in as functions so the whole program can run on
  recorded answers.

days.title: Day 37: Sending data to APIs
days.intro:
So far your programs only asked APIs questions. Today they **change**
things: create an account, add a record, update it, delete it. That means
new kinds of request (`POST`, `PUT`, `DELETE`), sending data in the
request's **body**, and proving who you are with **headers**. The project
is a habit tracker: every day you log how many minutes you practised, and a
graph website keeps the record.

lessons.title: The four verbs
lessons.text:
Every HTTP request has a **method** that says what it wants to do:

| Method | Means | `vyrn.http` |
|---|---|---|
| `GET` | give me something | `http.get(url, headers)` |
| `POST` | here is something new; create it | `http.post(url, body, headers)` |
| `PUT` | replace this thing with what I send | `http.put(url, body, headers)` |
| `DELETE` | remove this thing | `http.delete(url, headers)` |

The body of a `POST` or `PUT` is usually JSON: give `http.post` a map and it
is sent as JSON, with the header that says so. The answer's status says
how it went: `200 OK`, or `201 Created` for something new.

```vyrn check
use vyrn.http

main:
    let r = http.post("https://httpbin.org/post", {"habit": "piano", "minutes": 25})
    print(r.status)
    print(r.json["json"])
end
```

httpbin.org is a website for testing: it answers every request by showing
what it received. Run that and it prints `200` and the data you sent.

lessons.title: Headers and tokens
lessons.text:
**Headers** are the lines of extra information sent with a request: what
kind of data the body is, which language you'd like, and who you are. The
habit-tracking website Pixela gives each user a **token**, a password for
programs, that goes in a header with every request:

```vyrn check
use vyrn.http
use vyrn.os

main:
    let headers = {"X-USER-TOKEN": os.env("PIXELA_TOKEN")}
    let r = http.get("https://pixe.la/v1/users/ada/graphs/practice/stats", headers = headers)
    print(r.status, r.text)
end
```

Many APIs use the standard `Authorization` header instead, with the word
`Bearer` before the token: `{"Authorization": "Bearer " + token}`. Either
way, the token comes from the environment (Day 35), never from the code.

To keep a program testable, build each request as plain data first, and
send it in one place. The building is then a function you can check
without the internet:

```vyrn
create pixel_request(user: str, graph: str, day: str, minutes: int, token: str) -> map:
    return {
        "method": "POST",
        "url": "https://pixe.la/v1/users/{user}/graphs/{graph}",
        "headers": {"X-USER-TOKEN": token},
        "body": {"date": day, "quantity": str(minutes)},
    }
end

main:
    req = pixel_request("ada", "practice", "20261112", 25, "s3cret-token")
    print(req["method"], req["url"])
    print(req["body"])
end
```

```text
POST https://pixe.la/v1/users/ada/graphs/practice
{"date": "20261112", "quantity": "25"}
```

Pixela wants the date as `yyyyMMdd` and the quantity as text: every API has
its own little rules, written in its documentation. Read them carefully;
most API bugs are a format that's almost right.

### Exercise

Write `update_request(user, graph, day, minutes, token)` for changing a
day you already logged: Pixela wants a `PUT` to
`.../graphs/{graph}/{day}` with only the quantity in the body.

```vyrn starter
create update_request(user: str, graph: str, day: str, minutes: int, token: str) -> map:
    return {}
end

main:
    req = update_request("ada", "practice", "20261112", 40, "t0k")
    print(req["method"], req["url"], req["body"], req["headers"])
end
```

```text expect
PUT https://pixe.la/v1/users/ada/graphs/practice/20261112 {"quantity": "40"} {"X-USER-TOKEN": "t0k"}
```

exercise.starter:

    return {}
end

main:
    req = update_request("ada", "practice", "20261112", 40, "t0k")
    print(req["method"], req["url"], req["body"], req["headers"])
end
exercise.solution:
create update_request(user: str, graph: str, day: str, minutes: int, token: str) -> map:
    return {
        "method": "PUT",
        "url": "https://pixe.la/v1/users/{user}/graphs/{graph}/{day}",
        "headers": {"X-USER-TOKEN": token},
        "body": {"quantity": str(minutes)},
    }
end

main:
    req = update_request("ada", "practice", "20261112", 40, "t0k")
    print(req["method"], req["url"], req["body"], req["headers"])
end
hints: the same shape as `pixel_request`, with `"method": "PUT"` and the day at the end of the URL.

lessons.title: Sending a request
lessons.text:
One function sends any request built that way, choosing the `vyrn.http`
call by its method, and turns a failure status into an error:

```vyrn check
use vyrn.http

create send(req: map) -> any:
    let method = req["method"]
    var r = none
    if method == "GET":
        r = http.get(req["url"], headers = req["headers"])
    else if method == "POST":
        r = http.post(req["url"], req["body"], headers = req["headers"])
    else if method == "PUT":
        r = http.put(req["url"], req["body"], headers = req["headers"])
    else if method == "DELETE":
        r = http.delete(req["url"], headers = req["headers"])
    else:
        fail ValueError("unknown method {method}")
    end
    if not r.ok: fail NetworkError("{req["method"]} {req["url"]} said {r.status}: {r.text}")
    return r.json
end

main:
    print(send({"method": "GET", "url": "https://httpbin.org/get", "headers": {}}))
end
```

lessons.title: Dates for APIs
lessons.text:
APIs each want dates their own way. `time.format` writes them however
they're wanted, and `time.add` gives yesterday:

```vyrn
use vyrn.time

main:
    today = time.make(2026, 11, 12)
    print(time.format(today, "%Y%m%d"))
    print(time.format(time.add(today, days = -1), "%Y%m%d"))
    print(time.format(today, "%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ"))
end
```

```text
20261112
20261111
2026-11-12T00:00:00Z
```

lessons.title: Project: the habit tracker
lessons.text:
Setting up on Pixela takes three requests, done once: create a user, create
a graph, and after that, one pixel a day. The tracker asks how many minutes
you practised and logs them. Here `send` is a fake, so you can see exactly
what would go over the network:

```vyrn
use vyrn.time

const PIXELA = "https://pixe.la/v1/users"

object Tracker:
    user: str
    token: str
    graph: str
    send: any

    create setup(self):
        self.send({"method": "POST", "url": PIXELA, "headers": {}, "body": {"token": self.token, "username": self.user, "agreeTermsOfService": "yes", "notMinor": "yes"}})
        let graph = {"id": self.graph, "name": "Practice", "unit": "minutes", "type": "int", "color": "sora"}
        self.send({"method": "POST", "url": "{PIXELA}/{self.user}/graphs", "headers": self.auth(), "body": graph})
    end

    create log(self, day: float, minutes: int):
        let date = time.format(day, "%Y%m%d")
        self.send({"method": "POST", "url": "{PIXELA}/{self.user}/graphs/{self.graph}", "headers": self.auth(), "body": {"date": date, "quantity": str(minutes)}})
    end

    create auth(self) -> map:
        return {"X-USER-TOKEN": self.token}
    end
end

main:
    network = fake(returns = {"isSuccess": true})
    tracker = Tracker("ada", "s3cret-token", "practice", network)
    tracker.setup()
    tracker.log(time.make(2026, 11, 12), 25)
    each call in network.calls:
        let req = call[0]
        print(req["method"], req["url"].replace(PIXELA, "..."), req["headers"])
    end
end
```

```text
POST ... {}
POST .../ada/graphs {"X-USER-TOKEN": "s3cret-token"}
POST .../ada/graphs/practice {"X-USER-TOKEN": "s3cret-token"}
```

The first request has no token header because it is the one that *creates*
the user with that token. To run it for real, replace the fake with 37.3's
`send`, take the token from `.env`, and read the minutes with `input()`.
Your graph is then at `https://pixe.la/v1/users/<you>/graphs/practice.html`.

### Exercise

Add a `remove(day)` method that deletes a logged day: a `DELETE` to
`.../graphs/{graph}/{yyyyMMdd}` with the token header and no body.

```vyrn starter
use vyrn.time

object Tracker:
    user: str
    token: str
    graph: str
    send: any
end

main:
    network = fake(returns = {"isSuccess": true})
    tracker = Tracker("ada", "t0k", "practice", network)
    tracker.remove(time.make(2026, 11, 12))
    print(network.last_call[0])
end
```

```text expect
{"method": "DELETE", "url": "https://pixe.la/v1/users/ada/graphs/practice/20261112", "headers": {"X-USER-TOKEN": "t0k"}}
```

exercise.starter:
use vyrn.time

object Tracker:
    user: str
    token: str
    graph: str
    send: any
end

main:
    network = fake(returns = {"isSuccess": true})
    tracker = Tracker("ada", "t0k", "practice", network)
    tracker.remove(time.make(2026, 11, 12))

exercise.solution:
use vyrn.time

object Tracker:
    user: str
    token: str
    graph: str
    send: any

    create remove(self, day: float):
        let date = time.format(day, "%Y%m%d")
        let url = "https://pixe.la/v1/users/{self.user}/graphs/{self.graph}/{date}"
        self.send({"method": "DELETE", "url": url, "headers": {"X-USER-TOKEN": self.token}})
    end
end

main:
    network = fake(returns = {"isSuccess": true})
    tracker = Tracker("ada", "t0k", "practice", network)
    tracker.remove(time.make(2026, 11, 12))
    print(network.last_call[0])
end
hints: `create remove(self, day: float):` inside the object.
`self.send({"method": "DELETE", "url": ..., "headers": {"X-USER-TOKEN": self.token}})`

lessons.title: you learned
lessons.text:
- `POST` creates, `PUT` replaces, `DELETE` removes; `http.post` and
  `http.put` send a map as a JSON body.
- Headers carry tokens: `X-USER-TOKEN`, or `Authorization: Bearer ...`.
- Build requests as plain data, and send them in one place, so the building
  can be tested without the internet.
- Format dates exactly the way each API wants them.

days.title: Day 38: Databases
days.intro:
JSON and CSV files are fine for a few hundred records. When you have
thousands, want to search them quickly, or have several programs using the
same data at once, you want a **database**. Today you use SQLite, the
database inside every phone and web browser, which keeps everything in one
file. You will store records the easy way first, then learn **SQL**, the
language almost every database speaks. The project is a workout log that
answers questions like "how far did I run this month?".

lessons.title: Tables, rows and columns
lessons.text:
A database holds **tables**. A table is like a spreadsheet: each **row** is
one record, each **column** one kind of information, and every value in a
column has the same type.

| id | date | exercise | minutes |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 2026-11-10 | running | 30 |
| 2 | 2026-11-11 | swimming | 45 |

`db.open` opens a database file (making it if it isn't there);
`":memory:"` gives one that lives only while the program runs, which is
handy for trying things out. `create_table` makes a table from a map of
column names and types, adding an `id` column that numbers the rows:

```vyrn
use vyrn.db

main:
    let conn = db.open(":memory:")
    conn.create_table("workouts", {"date": "text", "exercise": "text", "minutes": "int"})
    print(conn.insert("workouts", {"date": "2026-11-10", "exercise": "running", "minutes": 30}))
    print(conn.insert("workouts", {"date": "2026-11-11", "exercise": "swimming", "minutes": 45}))
    print(conn.insert("workouts", {"date": "2026-11-12", "exercise": "running", "minutes": 25}))
    each row in conn.all("workouts"):
        print(row)
    end
end
```

```text
1
2
3
{"id": 1, "date": "2026-11-10", "exercise": "running", "minutes": 30}
{"id": 2, "date": "2026-11-11", "exercise": "swimming", "minutes": 45}
{"id": 3, "date": "2026-11-12", "exercise": "running", "minutes": 25}
```

`insert` gives the new row's `id`, and every row comes back as a map.

lessons.title: Records without SQL
lessons.text:
Finding, changing and deleting rows takes a `where` map: the rows whose
columns have all those values.

```vyrn
use vyrn.db

main:
    let conn = db.open(":memory:")
    conn.create_table("workouts", {"date": "text", "exercise": "text", "minutes": "int"})
    conn.insert("workouts", {"date": "2026-11-10", "exercise": "running", "minutes": 30})
    conn.insert("workouts", {"date": "2026-11-11", "exercise": "swimming", "minutes": 45})
    conn.insert("workouts", {"date": "2026-11-12", "exercise": "running", "minutes": 25})

    print(len(conn.find("workouts", {"exercise": "running"})), "runs")
    print(conn.find_one("workouts", {"date": "2026-11-11"})["exercise"])
    print(conn.update("workouts", {"id": 3}, {"minutes": 35}), "changed")
    print(conn.delete("workouts", {"exercise": "swimming"}), "deleted")
    print([r["minutes"] each r in conn.all("workouts")])
end
```

```text
2 runs
swimming
1 changed
1 deleted
[30, 35]
```

`update` and `delete` give how many rows they changed. `delete` insists on
a `where`, so you can't empty a table by accident.

### Exercise

Make a `books` table with a title, an author and a `read` flag (`int`, 0 or
1). Add the three books, mark *Dune* as read, and print the titles of the
books not read yet.

```vyrn starter
use vyrn.db

main:
    let conn = db.open(":memory:")
end
```

```text expect
["Emma", "Ubik"]
```

exercise.starter:
use vyrn.db

main:
    let conn = db.open(":memory:")
end

lessons.title: Asking in SQL
lessons.text:
`find` only matches exact values. To ask "workouts longer than 30
minutes", "the total per exercise" or "the five most recent", you write
**SQL** (Structured Query Language). `conn.query(sql)` runs a question and
gives the rows:

```vyrn
use vyrn.db

main:
    let conn = db.open(":memory:")
    conn.create_table("workouts", {"date": "text", "exercise": "text", "minutes": "int"})
    each date, exercise, minutes in [("2026-11-09", "cycling", 60), ("2026-11-10", "running", 30), ("2026-11-11", "swimming", 45), ("2026-11-12", "running", 25)]:
        conn.insert("workouts", {"date": date, "exercise": exercise, "minutes": minutes})
    end

    print(conn.query("select date, minutes from workouts where minutes > 30"))
    print(conn.query("select exercise from workouts order by minutes desc limit 2"))
    each row in conn.query("select exercise, sum(minutes) as total, count(*) as times from workouts group by exercise order by total desc"):
        print("{row["exercise"]:<10} {row["total"]:>4} min in {row["times"]}")
    end
    print(conn.value("select avg(minutes) from workouts"))
end
```

```text
[{"date": "2026-11-09", "minutes": 60}, {"date": "2026-11-11", "minutes": 45}]
[{"exercise": "cycling"}, {"exercise": "swimming"}]
cycling      60 min in 1
running      55 min in 2
swimming     45 min in 1
40.0
```

Read a `select` like a sentence:

| Part | Means |
|---|---|
| `select date, minutes` | which columns to give (`*` for all) |
| `from workouts` | which table |
| `where minutes > 30` | only rows where this is true (`and`, `or`, `=`, `!=`, `like`) |
| `group by exercise` | one result row per exercise, combining the rows with `sum`, `count`, `avg`, `min`, `max` |
| `order by total desc` | sorted, biggest first |
| `limit 2` | at most two rows |

`conn.value` gives just the first column of the first row: handy for a
single number.

### Exercise

How many minutes of running are there in total? Give the answer with one
`conn.value` call.

```vyrn starter
    conn.execute("create table workouts (exercise text, minutes int)")
    conn.execute("insert into workouts values ('running', 30), ('swimming', 45), ('running', 25)")
end
```

```text expect
55
```

lessons.title: Never build SQL from text
lessons.text:
The exercise wrote `'running'` straight into the SQL. With a value that
came from a user, **never** do that by joining text: a name like
`x' or '1'='1` would change the meaning of the statement. This is called
**SQL injection**, and it is one of the most common ways websites get
broken into. Instead, write `?` where a value goes and pass the values
separately; the database keeps them apart from the statement:

```vyrn
use vyrn.db

main:
    let conn = db.open(":memory:")
    conn.execute("create table users (name text, secret text)")
    conn.execute("insert into users values (?, ?)", ["ada", "piano"])
    conn.execute("insert into users values (?, ?)", ["alan", "chess"])

    let typed = "nobody' or '1'='1"
    let risky = conn.query("select name from users where name = '" + typed + "'")
    print("joined text found", len(risky), "users")
    let safe = conn.query("select name from users where name = ?", [typed])
    print("with ? found", len(safe), "users")
end
```

```text
joined text found 2 users
with ? found 0 users
```

The joined text matched *every* user. With `?` the typed text is just a
name nobody has. `insert`, `find` and the other record functions always
work this way, so they're safe too.

lessons.title: Project: the workout log
lessons.text:
The log keeps workouts in a file, `workouts.db`, so they're still there
next time. A small object wraps the database with the questions the app
asks, so the rest of the program never writes SQL:

```vyrn
use vyrn.db
use vyrn.fs

object Log:
    conn: any

    create add(self, date: str, exercise: str, minutes: int, km: float = 0.0) -> int:
        return self.conn.insert("workouts", {"date": date, "exercise": exercise, "minutes": minutes, "km": km})
    end

    create month(self, month: str) -> list:
        return self.conn.query("select exercise, sum(minutes) as minutes, sum(km) as km from workouts where date like ? group by exercise order by minutes desc", [month + "-%"])
    end

    create best(self, exercise: str) -> map?:
        return self.conn.query_one("select date, km from workouts where exercise = ? order by km desc limit 1", [exercise])
    end
end

create open_log(path: str) -> Log:
    let conn = db.open(path)
    if "workouts" not in conn.tables():
        conn.create_table("workouts", {"date": "text", "exercise": "text", "minutes": "int", "km": "real"})
    end
    return Log(conn)
end

main:
    if fs.exists("workouts.db"): fs.remove("workouts.db")
    var log = open_log("workouts.db")
    log.add("2026-10-30", "running", 40, 7.5)
    log.add("2026-11-02", "running", 30, 5.0)
    log.add("2026-11-05", "swimming", 45)
    log.add("2026-11-09", "running", 52, 10.2)
    log.conn.close()

    log = open_log("workouts.db")
    each row in log.month("2026-11"):
        print("{row["exercise"]}: {row["minutes"]} min, {row["km"]} km")
    end
    let best = log.best("running")
    print("longest run: {best["km"]} km on {best["date"]}")
end
```

```text
running: 82 min, 15.2 km
swimming: 45 min, 0.0 km
longest run: 10.2 km on 2026-11-09
```

The program closes the database and opens it again halfway, as if it were
run a second time: the workouts are still there. `like ?` with `"2026-11-%"`
matches every date that starts with `2026-11-`; `%` stands for any text.

lessons.title: you learned
lessons.text:
- A database holds tables of rows and columns; SQLite keeps one in a file.
- `create_table`, `insert`, `all`, `find`, `update` and `delete` handle
  records without SQL.
- SQL's `select ... from ... where ... group by ... order by ... limit`
  asks bigger questions; `query`, `query_one` and `value` run them.
- Always pass values with `?`, never by joining text: that's how SQL
  injection is stopped.

days.title: Day 39: Capstone: deal finder, part 1
days.intro:
The next two days are a **capstone**: one bigger program that uses
everything from this unit. The deal finder keeps a wishlist of games and
the price you'd be happy to pay for each. Every day it asks a deals API for
current prices, records them in a database, and emails you when something
on your list drops to your price. Today: the plan, the data, and the
prices. Tomorrow: alerts, commands, and running every day.

lessons.title: The plan
lessons.text:
Before writing code, write down what the program does and which pieces do
it. Small pieces that each do one thing are easier to write, test and fix:

| Piece | Job | From |
|---|---|---|
| `Wishlist` | games and target prices, in a database | Day 38 |
| `fetch_deals(title)` | current prices from the API | Days 33, 36 |
| `record(prices)` | keep a price history | Day 38 |
| `matches(...)` | which deals are at or under the target | Day 26 |
| `alert(...)` | one email listing the matches | Days 32, 35 |
| `main` | commands: `add`, `list`, `check` | Day 40 |

The API is CheapShark, which compares prices across game shops. It's free
and needs no key:

```text
https://www.cheapshark.com/api/1.0/deals?title=portal&upperPrice=15
```

lessons.title: The wishlist
lessons.text:
The wishlist is a table with a title and a target price. An object wraps
it, so nothing else in the program needs to know there is a database:

```vyrn
use vyrn.db

object Wishlist:
    conn: any

    create add(self, title: str, target: float):
        let existing = self.conn.find_one("wishes", {"title": title.lower()})
        if existing:
            self.conn.update("wishes", {"title": title.lower()}, {"target": target})
        else:
            self.conn.insert("wishes", {"title": title.lower(), "target": target})
        end
    end

    create remove(self, title: str) -> bool:
        return self.conn.delete("wishes", {"title": title.lower()}) > 0
    end

    create items(self) -> list:
        return self.conn.query("select title, target from wishes order by title")
    end
end

create open_wishlist(conn: any) -> Wishlist:
    if "wishes" not in conn.tables():
        conn.create_table("wishes", {"title": "text", "target": "real"})
    end
    return Wishlist(conn)
end

main:
    let wishes = open_wishlist(db.open(":memory:"))
    wishes.add("Portal 2", 5)
    wishes.add("Celeste", 8)
    wishes.add("portal 2", 4)
    print(wishes.remove("Doom"), wishes.items())
end
```

```text
false [{"title": "celeste", "target": 8.0}, {"title": "portal 2", "target": 4.0}]
```

Adding a game that's already there changes its target instead of adding it
twice. Titles are kept in lower case, so `Portal 2` and `portal 2` are the
same game.

lessons.title: Reading the deals
lessons.text:
CheapShark answers with a list of deals, one per shop that sells the game.
Prices are text, and searching for "portal" also finds "Portal 2" and
"Portal Stories", so the program keeps only exact title matches and the
cheapest shop:

```vyrn
use vyrn.json

const DEALS = r'[{"title": "Portal 2", "storeID": "1", "salePrice": "1.99", "normalPrice": "9.99", "savings": "80.08"}, {"title": "Portal 2", "storeID": "7", "salePrice": "2.49", "normalPrice": "9.99", "savings": "75.08"}, {"title": "Portal Stories: Mel", "storeID": "1", "salePrice": "0.00", "normalPrice": "0.00", "savings": "0"}]'

const STORES = {"1": "Steam", "7": "GOG", "11": "Humble"}

create best_deal(deals: list, title: str) -> map?:
    let exact = [d each d in deals if d["title"].lower() == title.lower()]
    if not exact: return none
    let best = min(exact, key = d => float(d["salePrice"]))
    return {
        "title": best["title"],
        "price": float(best["salePrice"]),
        "normal": float(best["normalPrice"]),
        "store": STORES.get(best["storeID"], "store " + best["storeID"]),
    }
end

main:
    let deals = json.parse(DEALS)
    print(best_deal(deals, "portal 2"))
    print(best_deal(deals, "half-life 3"))
end
```

```text
{"title": "Portal 2", "price": 1.99, "normal": 9.99, "store": "Steam"}
none
```

Turning the API's answer into a small map of exactly what the program needs
is worth doing right at the edge: everything after it works with clean
numbers and names, and if the API changes, only `best_deal` changes.

The live fetch, cached for an hour (Day 36) so testing doesn't hammer the
API:

```vyrn check
use vyrn.fs
use vyrn.http
use vyrn.json
use vyrn.time

create cached(path: str, max_age: float, fetch: any) -> any:
    if fs.exists(path) and time.now() - fs.modified(path) < max_age:
        return json.load(path)
    end
    let answer = fetch()
    json.save(path, answer)
    return answer
end

create fetch_deals(title: str) -> list:
    let url = "https://www.cheapshark.com/api/1.0/deals?" + http.query({"title": title, "pageSize": 20})
    let slug = title.lower().replace(" ", "-")
    return cached("deals-{slug}.json", 3600, () => http.get(url).json)
end

main:
    each d in fetch_deals("portal 2")[:3]:
        print(d["title"], d["salePrice"])
    end
end
```

lessons.title: Price history
lessons.text:
Each check stores today's best price, so the program can tell a real drop
from the usual price, and show how a price has changed:

```vyrn
use vyrn.db

create record(conn: any, day: str, deal: map):
    conn.execute("insert into prices (day, title, price, store) values (?, ?, ?, ?)", [day, deal["title"].lower(), deal["price"], deal["store"]])
end

create lowest(conn: any, title: str) -> float?:
    return conn.value("select min(price) from prices where title = ?", [title.lower()])
end

main:
    let conn = db.open(":memory:")
    conn.execute("create table prices (day text, title text, price real, store text)")
    record(conn, "2026-11-10", {"title": "Celeste", "price": 9.99, "store": "Steam"})
    record(conn, "2026-11-11", {"title": "Celeste", "price": 4.99, "store": "GOG"})
    record(conn, "2026-11-12", {"title": "Celeste", "price": 7.49, "store": "Steam"})
    print("lowest seen:", lowest(conn, "celeste"))
    print("never seen:", lowest(conn, "doom"))
    each row in conn.query("select day, price from prices where title = 'celeste' order by day"):
        print(row["day"], "#" * round(row["price"]))
    end
end
```

```text
lowest seen: 4.99
never seen: none
2026-11-10 ##########
2026-11-11 #####
2026-11-12 #######
```

A quick bar of `#`s is a chart you can print anywhere (Unit 6 draws real
ones).

### Exercise

every price recorded before, or when there is no history yet.

```vyrn starter
create is_new_low(conn: any, title: str, price: float) -> bool:

end

    print(is_new_low(conn, "celeste", 7.0))
    conn.execute("insert into prices values ('2026-11-11', 'celeste', 4.99, 'GOG')")
    print(is_new_low(conn, "celeste", 7.0), is_new_low(conn, "celeste", 3.99))
end
```

```text expect
true
false true
```

use vyrn.db

create is_new_low(conn: any, title: str, price: float) -> bool:
    let low = conn.value("select min(price) from prices where title = ?", [title.lower()])
    return low == none or price < low
