lessons.title: Putting today's pieces together
lessons.text:
One function checks the whole wishlist: fetch, pick the best deal, record
it, and collect the ones at or under target. The fetching is passed in, so
here a map of recorded answers stands in for the API:

```vyrn
use vyrn.db

create best_deal(deals: list, title: str) -> map?:
    let exact = [d each d in deals if d["title"].lower() == title.lower()]
    if not exact: return none
    let best = min(exact, key = d => float(d["salePrice"]))
    return {"title": best["title"], "price": float(best["salePrice"]), "store": "store " + best["storeID"]}
end

create check(conn: any, day: str, fetch: any) -> list:
    var hits = []
    each wish in conn.query("select title, target from wishes"):
        let deal = best_deal(fetch(wish["title"]), wish["title"])
        if deal == none: skip
        conn.execute("insert into prices values (?, ?, ?, ?)", [day, wish["title"], deal["price"], deal["store"]])
        if deal["price"] <= wish["target"]: hits.append(deal | {"target": wish["target"]})
    end
    return hits
end

main:
    let conn = db.open(":memory:")
    conn.execute("create table wishes (title text, target real)")
    conn.execute("create table prices (day text, title text, price real, store text)")
    conn.execute_many("insert into wishes values (?, ?)", [["celeste", 8], ["portal 2", 1.5], ["hades", 10]])
    let answers = {
        "celeste": [{"title": "Celeste", "salePrice": "4.99", "storeID": "7"}],
        "portal 2": [{"title": "Portal 2", "salePrice": "1.99", "storeID": "1"}],
        "hades": [],
    }
    each hit in check(conn, "2026-11-12", title => answers[title]):
        print("{hit["title"]}: {hit["price"]} at {hit["store"]} (wanted {hit["target"]})")
    end
    print(conn.value("select count(*) from prices"), "prices recorded")
end
```

```text
Celeste: 4.99 at store 7 (wanted 8.0)
2 prices recorded
```

Portal 2 is recorded but not a hit (1.99 is over the 1.50 target), and
nobody sells Hades today, so nothing is recorded for it.

lessons.title: you built
lessons.text:
The deal finder's data side: a wishlist in a database, deals read from an
API and cleaned at the edge, and a price history. Tomorrow it learns to
send alerts, take commands, and run by itself every day.

days.title: Day 40: Capstone: deal finder, part 2
days.intro:
Yesterday the deal finder learned to keep a wishlist, read prices and
remember them. Today it becomes a tool you actually use: you type commands
like `vyrn run deals.vyrn add celeste 8`, it sends one email when there are
deals (and doesn't nag you about the same deal every day), and it runs by
itself every morning.

lessons.title: Commands from the terminal
lessons.text:
`os.args()` gives the words typed after the file name. The program looks at
the first word to decide what to do. Keeping that in a function that takes
the words as a list means it can be tried without a terminal:

```vyrn
create run(args: list) -> int:
    if not args:
        print("usage: deals add <title> <price> | remove <title> | list | check")
        return 2
    end
    let command = args[0]
    if command == "add" and len(args) >= 3:
        let title = " ".join(args[1:-1])
        attempt:
            let price = float(args[-1])
            print("added {title} at {price:.2f}")
        catch ValueError:
            print("the price must be a number, like 7.50")
            return 2
        end
    else if command == "list":
        print("(the wishlist)")
    else:
        print("unknown command: {command}")
        return 2
    end
    return 0
end

main:
    print(run(["add", "portal", "2", "1.50"]))
    print(run(["add", "celeste", "cheap"]))
    print(run(["fly"]))
end
```

```text
added portal 2 at 1.50
0
the price must be a number, like 7.50
2
unknown command: fly
2
```

`args[1:-1]` is every word between the command and the price, so titles
with spaces work without quotes. The number `run` gives back is the
program's **exit code**: `0` means it worked, anything else that it didn't.
Scripts and schedulers read it; `os.exit(code)` hands it over:

```vyrn check
use vyrn.os

create run(args: list) -> int:
    print(args)
    return 0
end

main:
    os.exit(run(os.args()))
end
```

### Exercise

Add a `remove` command: `remove <title>` prints `removed <title>`, and
`remove` on its own prints `which game?` and gives exit code 2.

```vyrn starter
create run(args: list) -> int:
    let command = args[0]
    print("unknown command: {command}")
    return 2
end

main:
    print(run(["remove", "half-life", "3"]))
    print(run(["remove"]))
end
```

```text expect
removed half-life 3
0
which game?
2
```

exercise.starter:
create run(args: list) -> int:
    let command = args[0]
    print("unknown command: {command}")
    return 2
end

main:
    print(run(["remove", "half-life", "3"]))
    print(run(["remove"]))
end
exercise.solution:
create run(args: list) -> int:
    let command = args[0]
    if command == "remove":
        if len(args) < 2:
            print("which game?")
            return 2
        end
        print("removed", " ".join(args[1:]))
        return 0
    end
    print("unknown command: {command}")
    return 2
end

main:
    print(run(["remove", "half-life", "3"]))
    print(run(["remove"]))
end
hints: `if command == "remove":` then check `len(args) < 2`.
the title is `" ".join(args[1:])`.

lessons.title: Alerts that don't nag
lessons.text:
If a game stays at your price for a week, one email is enough. The program
remembers what it has told you in an `alerted` table, and only alerts again
when the price drops *further*:

```vyrn
use vyrn.db

create worth_telling(conn: any, title: str, price: float) -> bool:
    let told = conn.value("select min(price) from alerted where title = ?", [title])
    return told == none or price < told
end

create told(conn: any, title: str, price: float, day: str):
    conn.execute("insert into alerted values (?, ?, ?)", [title, price, day])
end

main:
    let conn = db.open(":memory:")
    conn.execute("create table alerted (title text, price real, day text)")
    each day, price in [("11-10", 4.99), ("11-11", 4.99), ("11-12", 3.99), ("11-13", 4.99)]:
        if worth_telling(conn, "celeste", price):
            told(conn, "celeste", price, day)
            print(day, "email: celeste is", price)
        else:
            print(day, "(already told)")
        end
    end
end
```

```text
11-10 email: celeste is 4.99
11-11 (already told)
11-12 email: celeste is 3.99
11-13 (already told)
```

lessons.title: One tidy email
lessons.text:
All the hits go in one email, sorted by how much you save, so the best deal
is on top:

```vyrn
create email_body(hits: list) -> str:
    var lines = ["Deals on your wishlist today:", ""]
    each hit in sorted(hits, key = h => h["target"] - h["price"], reverse = true):
        let saving = hit["target"] - hit["price"]
        lines.append("- {hit["title"]}: {hit["price"]:.2f} at {hit["store"]} ({saving:.2f} under your price)")
    end
    lines.append("")
    lines.append("Happy gaming!")
    return "\n".join(lines)
end

main:
    print(email_body([
        {"title": "Portal 2", "price": 1.49, "store": "Steam", "target": 1.5},
        {"title": "Celeste", "price": 3.99, "store": "GOG", "target": 8.0},
    ]))
end
```

```text
Deals on your wishlist today:

- Celeste: 3.99 at GOG (4.01 under your price)
- Portal 2: 1.49 at Steam (0.01 under your price)

Happy gaming!
```

### Exercise

The subject line should say how many deals there are: `1 deal on your
wishlist`, or `3 deals on your wishlist`. Write `subject(hits)`.

```vyrn starter
create subject(hits: list) -> str:
    return ""
end

main:
    print(subject([1]))
    print(subject([1, 2, 3]))
end
```

```text expect
1 deal on your wishlist
3 deals on your wishlist
```

exercise.starter:
create subject(hits: list) -> str:
    return ""
end

main:
    print(subject([1]))
    print(subject([1, 2, 3]))
end
exercise.expect:
1 deal on your wishlist
3 deals on your wishlist
exercise.solution:
create subject(hits: list) -> str:
    let word = "deal" if len(hits) == 1 else "deals"
    return "{len(hits)} {word} on your wishlist"
end

main:
    print(subject([1]))
    print(subject([1, 2, 3]))
end
hints: `"deal" if len(hits) == 1 else "deals"`

lessons.title: The whole program
lessons.text:
Here is the deal finder in one file. Every outside thing (the API, the
email, today's date) comes in through a `World` object, so the program can
be run against fakes, as below, or against the real world, as in the live
version after it:

```vyrn
use vyrn.db

object World:
    fetch: any
    send: any
    today: str
end

create best_deal(deals: list, title: str) -> map?:
    let exact = [d each d in deals if d["title"].lower() == title]
    if not exact: return none
    let best = min(exact, key = d => float(d["salePrice"]))
    return {"title": best["title"], "price": float(best["salePrice"]), "store": "store " + best["storeID"]}
end

create setup(conn: any):
    conn.execute("create table if not exists wishes (title text, target real)")
    conn.execute("create table if not exists prices (day text, title text, price real, store text)")
    conn.execute("create table if not exists alerted (title text, price real, day text)")
end

create check(conn: any, world: World) -> int:
    var hits = []
    each wish in conn.query("select title, target from wishes order by title"):
        let deal = best_deal(world.fetch(wish["title"]), wish["title"])
        if deal == none: skip
        conn.execute("insert into prices values (?, ?, ?, ?)", [world.today, wish["title"], deal["price"], deal["store"]])
        let told = conn.value("select min(price) from alerted where title = ?", [wish["title"]])
        if deal["price"] <= wish["target"] and (told == none or deal["price"] < told):
            conn.execute("insert into alerted values (?, ?, ?)", [wish["title"], deal["price"], world.today])
            hits.append("{deal["title"]}: {deal["price"]:.2f} at {deal["store"]}")
        end
    end
    let word = "deal" if len(hits) == 1 else "deals"
    if hits: world.send("{len(hits)} {word} on your wishlist", "\n".join(hits))
    print("checked; {len(hits)} new {word}")
    return 0
end

create run(args: list, conn: any, world: World) -> int:
    setup(conn)
    if not args:
        print("usage: deals add <title> <price> | remove <title> | list | check")
        return 2
    end
    let command = args[0]
    if command == "add" and len(args) >= 3:
        let title = " ".join(args[1:-1]).lower()
        conn.delete("wishes", {"title": title})
        conn.insert("wishes", {"title": title, "target": float(args[-1])})
        print("watching {title} for {float(args[-1]):.2f} or less")
    else if command == "remove" and len(args) >= 2:
        let gone = conn.delete("wishes", {"title": " ".join(args[1:]).lower()})
        print("removed" if gone else "not on the list")
    else if command == "list":
        each w in conn.query("select title, target from wishes order by title"):
            print("{w["title"]:<20} {w["target"]:>6.2f}")
        end
    else if command == "check":
        return check(conn, world)
    else:
        print("unknown command: {command}")
        return 2
    end
    return 0
end

main:
    let conn = db.open(":memory:")
    let mailbox = fake(returns = true)
    var prices = {"celeste": "4.99", "portal 2": "1.99"}
    let fetch = title => [{"title": title.title(), "salePrice": prices[title], "storeID": "1"}]
    var world = World(fetch, mailbox, "2026-11-12")
    run(["add", "Celeste", "8"], conn, world)
    run(["add", "Portal", "2", "1.50"], conn, world)
    run(["list"], conn, world)
    run(["check"], conn, world)
    world.today = "2026-11-13"
    prices["portal 2"] = "0.99"
    run(["check"], conn, world)
    each call in mailbox.calls:
        print("email:", call[0], "|", call[1].replace("\n", "; "))
    end
end
```

```text
watching celeste for 8.00 or less
watching portal 2 for 1.50 or less
celeste                8.00
portal 2               1.50
checked; 1 new deal
checked; 1 new deal
email: 1 deal on your wishlist | Celeste: 4.99 at store 1
email: 1 deal on your wishlist | Portal 2: 0.99 at store 1
```

On the second day Celeste is still 4.99, but you were already told, so only
Portal 2's new low price is in the email.

To make it real, replace `main` with the live version, which opens a file
database and fills `World` with the API (Day 39), `mail.send` (Day 32) and
today's date:

```vyrn check
use vyrn.db
use vyrn.http
use vyrn.mail
use vyrn.os
use vyrn.time

object World:
    fetch: any
    send: any
    today: str
end

create fetch(title: str) -> list:
    return http.get("https://www.cheapshark.com/api/1.0/deals?" + http.query({"title": title})).json
end

create send(subject: str, body: str):
    mail.send(to = os.env("DEALS_TO"), subject = subject, body = body, sender = os.env("MAIL_USER"),
              server = os.env("MAIL_SERVER"), user = os.env("MAIL_USER"), password = os.env("MAIL_PASSWORD"))
end

create run(args: list, conn: any, world: World) -> int:
    print(args, world.today)
    return 0
end

main:
    os.load_env()
    let world = World(fetch, send, time.format(time.now(), "%Y-%m-%d"))
    os.exit(run(os.args(), db.open("deals.db"), world))
end
```

lessons.title: Running every day
lessons.text:
A program that should run on its own needs a **scheduler**:

- **Windows**: open Task Scheduler, *Create Basic Task*, *Daily*, and as
  the action *Start a program*: `vyrn` with the arguments
  `run C:\path\to\deals.vyrn check`, starting in the program's folder.
- **macOS and Linux**: run `crontab -e` and add a line; this one runs at
  8:15 every morning:

```text
15 8 * * * cd /home/ada/deals && vyrn run deals.vyrn check >> deals.log 2>&1
```

`>> deals.log` keeps what it printed, so you can see later what happened.
Because the program records every price and every alert in its database,
it can be stopped, moved or run twice without sending duplicate emails.

lessons.title: you built
lessons.text:
A complete, useful tool: commands with exit codes, a database that remembers
prices and alerts, one tidy email, every outside thing passed in so the
whole program can be tested, and a scheduler to run it. Ideas to take it
further:

- A `history <title>` command that prints the price history as `#` bars.
- Send the email only on weekdays, or as HTML (`mail.send(html = ...)`).
- Watch something else: train tickets, a book, or a share price (Day 36).

days.title: Day 41: Web pages
days.intro:
Every web page is a text file written in **HTML**, the language browsers
read. Today you learn enough HTML to write pages by hand, then have Vyrn
write them for you: from data, safely, and served by a web server of your
own. The project is a personal home page made from a map of facts about
you.

lessons.title: Tags and elements
lessons.text:
HTML marks up text with **tags** in angle brackets. Most come in pairs, an opening `

` and a closing `

`, and everything between them is one **element**: ```text My page

Hello!

This is a web page.

``` - `` says "this is modern HTML". - `` holds facts *about* the page: its title (shown on the tab). - `` holds what you see. - Elements **nest**: the `` is inside the `

`, which is inside the ``. Indenting shows the nesting, like blocks in Vyrn. Save that text in a file called `page.html` and open it in a browser, and you have made a web page. Vyrn can save it for you, and also read it back the way a browser does with `vyrn.html`: ```vyrn use vyrn.html const PAGE = """ My page

Hello!

This is a web page.

""" main: write_text("page.html", PAGE) let page = html.parse(read_text("page.html")) print(page.title) print(page.select_one("h1").text) print(page.select_one("p").text) print(page.select_one("strong").parent.tag) end ``` ```text My page Hello! This is a web page. p ```

lessons.title: The tags you'll use most
lessons.text:
| Tag | Is | |---|---| | `

` ... `

` | headings, from biggest to smallest | | `

` | a paragraph | | `text` | a link | | `` | a picture (no closing tag) | | `

    ` with `
  • ` items | a bulleted list; `
      ` numbers them | | ``, `` | important, emphasised | | `
      `, `` | a box, a piece of text: no look of their own, used for layout and styling | | `
      ` | a line break (no closing tag) | `href`, `src` and `alt` are **attributes**: extra information inside the opening tag, as `name="value"`. `alt` describes a picture for people who can't see it, and for when it doesn't load: always include it. Writing HTML from data is a loop that builds text: ```vyrn main: let links = [("Vyrn", "https://vyrn.dev"), ("Wikipedia", "https://wikipedia.org")] var out = ["
        "] each name, url in links: out.append("
      • {name}
        • ") end out.append("
      ") print("\n".join(out)) end ``` ```text
      • Vyrn
      • Wikipedia
      ``` ### Exercise Write `table(rows)`, which gives an HTML table: ``, then one `` (table row) per row with a `
      ` (table cell) per value. ```vyrn starter create table(rows: list) -> str: return "" end main: print(table([["Ada", 36], ["Alan", 41]])) end ``` ```text expect
      Ada36
      Alan41
      ```

exercise.starter:
create table(rows: list) -> str:
    return ""
end

main:
    print(table([["Ada", 36], ["Alan", 41]]))
end
exercise.solution:
create table(rows: list) -> str: var lines = [""] each row in rows: let cells = "".join(["" each v in row]) lines.append("{cells}") end lines.append("
{v}
") return "\n".join(lines) end main: print(table([["Ada", 36], ["Alan", 41]])) end
hints: for each row, `"".join(["{v}" each v in row])`.
put `<tr>` around that, and `<table>` lines around everything.

lessons.title: Text that could be HTML
lessons.text:
What if the data has a `<` in it? A browser reads it as the start of a tag. Someone could type `" print("

" + html.escape(comment) + "

") print(html.escape("Tom & \"Jerry\"")) end ``` ```text

I <3 this! <script>steal()</script>

Tom & "Jerry" ``` The rule: **escape everything that came from outside the program** before putting it in a page. Day 44's templates do it for you.

lessons.title: Serving a page
lessons.text:
A browser gets pages from a **web server**. In Vyrn a server is a set of `route`s: each says which address it answers and gives back the page. Text that starts with `<` is sent as HTML: ```vyrn use vyrn.http route GET "/" (): return "Home

Welcome

About me

" end route GET "/about" (): return "About

About me

I'm learning Vyrn.

" end main: let r = http.test("GET", "/about") print(r.status, r.headers["content-type"]) print(r.text) print(http.test("GET", "/nowhere").status) end ``` ```text 200 text/html; charset=utf-8 About

About me

I'm learning Vyrn.

404 ``` `http.test` asks your own routes, without a network: perfect for trying them out (and for tests, Day 47). To open the pages in a real browser, end `main` with `http.serve(port = 8000)` instead and visit `http://localhost:8000`: ```vyrn check use vyrn.http route GET "/" (): return "Home

Welcome

" end main: print("open http://localhost:8000 (Ctrl+C stops it)") http.serve(port = 8000) end ``` `localhost` means "this computer". Nobody else can see it yet; Day 52 puts a site on the internet.

lessons.title: Project: your home page
lessons.text:
The page is made from a map of facts, so changing a fact never means editing HTML. Each part of the page is its own small function: ```vyrn use vyrn.html use vyrn.http const ME = { "name": "Ada", "tagline": "Learning to code, one day at a time", "likes": ["maths", "music", "engines"], "links": [("GitHub", "https://github.com/ada"), ("Blog", "https://ada.dev")], } create bullet_list(items: list) -> str: return "
    " + "".join(["
  • {html.escape(str(i))}
    • " each i in items]) + "
" end create link_list(links: list) -> str: return "
    " + "".join(["
  • {html.escape(n)}
    • " each n, u in links]) + "
" end create home(me: map) -> str: let name = html.escape(me["name"]) return "\n".join([ "", "{name}", "

{name}

", "

{html.escape(me["tagline"])}

", "

Things I like

", bullet_list(me["likes"]), "

Find me

", link_list(me["links"]), "", ]) end route GET "/" (): return home(ME) end main: let page = html.parse(http.test("GET", "/").text) print(page.title, "|", [li.text each li in page.select("li")]) print([a.attr("href") each a in page.select("a")]) write_text("index.html", home(ME)) end ``` ```text Ada | ["maths", "music", "engines", "GitHub", "Blog"] ["https://github.com/ada", "https://ada.dev"] ``` The program checks its own page by parsing it, then saves it as `index.html`: open that file in a browser to see it. Put in your own facts. ### Exercise Add a `"projects"` list to the facts, where each project is a map with a `name` and a `year`, and write `project_list(projects)` that shows them newest first as `
  • name (year)
    • `. ```vyrn starter create project_list(projects: list) -> str: return "
      " end main: print(project_list([{"name": "Snake", "year": 2025}, {"name": "Deal finder", "year": 2026}])) end ``` ```text expect
      • Deal finder (2026)
      • Snake (2025)
      ```

exercise.starter:
create project_list(projects: list) -> str: return "
    " end main: print(project_list([{"name": "Snake", "year": 2025}, {"name": "Deal finder", "year": 2026}])) end
exercise.solution:
create project_list(projects: list) -> str: let newest = sorted(projects, key = p => p["year"], reverse = true) return "
    " + "".join(["
  • {p["name"]} ({p["year"]})
    • " each p in newest]) + "
" end main: print(project_list([{"name": "Snake", "year": 2025}, {"name": "Deal finder", "year": 2026}])) end
hints: `sorted(projects, key = p => p["year"], reverse = true)`

lessons.title: you learned
lessons.text:
- HTML is text with nested elements: tags, attributes, `<head>` and
  `<body>`.
- Build HTML from data with loops and small functions, and read it back with
  `html.parse`.
- `html.escape` everything that came from outside the program.
- A `route` that returns HTML is a web page; `http.test` tries it,
  `http.serve` opens it to a browser.

days.title: Day 42: Styling pages with CSS
days.intro:
Yesterday's pages had the browser's plain black-on-white look. **CSS**
(Cascading Style Sheets) is the language that says how a page looks:
colours, fonts, spacing, sizes. HTML says *what* things are; CSS says *how
they look*. Today you write CSS, serve it from your own server, and build
it from a theme, so the whole site can change colour by changing one map.

lessons.title: Rules
lessons.text:
A CSS **rule** picks elements with a **selector**, then sets **properties** inside braces: ```text h1 { color: #1e88e5; font-family: Georgia, serif; } p { line-height: 1.6; max-width: 40em; } ``` The selectors you'll use most: | Selector | Picks | |---|---| | `h1` | every `

` | | `.card` | every element with `class="card"` | | `#top` | the element with `id="top"` | | `nav a` | every `` inside a `
` | | `a:hover` | a link while the mouse is over it | Classes are how you style *some* elements: `

` is styled by `.note { ... }`, and an element can have several, `class="card wide"`. CSS goes in a `

lessons.title: Colours, sizes and fonts
lessons.text:
```text
body {
  background: #fafafa;            /* a colour: #rrggbb, or a name like white */
  color: rgb(33, 33, 33);         /* the text colour */
  font-family: system-ui, sans-serif;
  font-size: 18px;                /* px: screen pixels */
}
h1 { font-size: 2.5rem; }         /* rem: times the page's font size */
.note { width: 50%; }             /* %: of the space it's in */
```

Text inside `/* */` is a comment. **Colours** are the same `#rrggbb` you
used in `vyrn.draw`: red, green and blue from `00` to `ff`. Vyrn can work
them out, for example to make a lighter shade of a theme colour:

```vyrn
create lighter(color: str, amount: float) -> str:
    var out = "#"
    each i in [1, 3, 5]:
        let c = int(color[i:i + 2], 16)
        let mixed = round(c + (255 - c) * amount)
        out += "{mixed:02x}"
    end
    return out
end

main:
    print(lighter("#1e88e5", 0.5))
    print(lighter("#000000", 0.25), lighter("#ff0000", 1))
end
```

```text
#8ec4f2
#404040 #ffffff
```

`int(text, 16)` reads hexadecimal, and `{x:02x}` writes it, two digits.

lessons.title: The box model
lessons.text:
Every element is a **box**. From the inside out: the **content**, then
**padding** (space inside the border), the **border**, and the **margin**
(space outside, between boxes):

```text
.card {
  padding: 16px;              /* inside */
  border: 1px solid #ddd;     /* width, style, colour */
  border-radius: 8px;         /* rounded corners */
  margin: 12px 0;             /* outside: 12px top and bottom, 0 at the sides */
  box-shadow: 0 2px 6px rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.15);
}
```

Two numbers mean top-and-bottom then sides; four go clockwise from the top:
`margin: 1px 2px 3px 4px`. Press F12 in a browser and click an element to
see its boxes drawn over the page.

lessons.title: Serving a stylesheet
lessons.text:
The stylesheet is just another route. Text that doesn't start with `<` is sent as plain text, so give the right **content type** with `http.Response`, or the browser ignores it: ```vyrn use vyrn.http const CSS = "body \{ font-family: system-ui; background: #fafafa; \}\nh1 \{ color: #1e88e5; \}" route GET "/style.css" (): return http.Response(200, CSS, {"Content-Type": "text/css"}) end route GET "/" (): return "

Styled

" end main: let r = http.test("GET", "/style.css") print(r.status, r.headers["content-type"]) print(r.text) end ``` ```text 200 text/css body { font-family: system-ui; background: #fafafa; } h1 { color: #1e88e5; } ``` Inside an ordinary Vyrn string `{` starts interpolation, so CSS braces are written `\{` and `\}`, or the CSS goes in a raw string `r"..."` or a file. ### Exercise Write `rule(selector, props)`, which turns a selector and a map of properties into a CSS rule on one line. ```vyrn starter create rule(selector: str, props: map) -> str: return "" end main: print(rule("h1", {"color": "#1e88e5", "font-size": "2rem"})) print(rule(".note", {"padding": "8px"})) end ``` ```text expect h1 { color: #1e88e5; font-size: 2rem; } .note { padding: 8px; } ```

exercise.starter:
create rule(selector: str, props: map) -> str:
    return ""
end

main:
    print(rule("h1", {"color": "#1e88e5", "font-size": "2rem"}))
    print(rule(".note", {"padding": "8px"}))
end
exercise.solution:
create rule(selector: str, props: map) -> str:
    let body = " ".join(["{k}: {v};" each k, v in props.items()])
    return selector + " \{ " + body + " \}"
end

main:
    print(rule("h1", {"color": "#1e88e5", "font-size": "2rem"}))
    print(rule(".note", {"padding": "8px"}))
end
hints: `"; ".join(["{k}: {v}" each k, v in props.items()])` gives the middle.
the braces: `"\{"` and `"\}"`.

lessons.title: Project: a themed site
lessons.text:
The theme is a map of colours and fonts. One function turns it into the
stylesheet, using the `rule` function from the exercise, and a **dark
mode**: a `@media` block whose rules only apply when the computer is set to
dark:

```vyrn
use vyrn.http

const THEME = {"accent": "#1e88e5", "text": "#212121", "page": "#fafafa", "font": "system-ui, sans-serif"}

create rule(selector: str, props: map) -> str:
    let body = " ".join(["{k}: {v};" each k, v in props.items()])
    return selector + " \{ " + body + " \}"
end

create stylesheet(t: map) -> str:
    return "\n".join([
        rule("body", {"font-family": t["font"], "color": t["text"], "background": t["page"], "max-width": "40em", "margin": "2em auto"}),
        rule("h1, h2", {"color": t["accent"]}),
        rule("a", {"color": t["accent"]}),
        rule(".card", {"padding": "16px", "border-radius": "8px", "box-shadow": "0 2px 6px rgba(0,0,0,.15)"}),
        "@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark) \{",
        "  " + rule("body", {"color": t["page"], "background": t["text"]}),
        "\}",
    ])
end

route GET "/style.css" ():
    return http.Response(200, stylesheet(THEME), {"Content-Type": "text/css"})
end

main:
    print(http.test("GET", "/style.css").text)
end
```

```text
body { font-family: system-ui, sans-serif; color: #212121; background: #fafafa; max-width: 40em; margin: 2em auto; }
h1, h2 { color: #1e88e5; }
a { color: #1e88e5; }
.card { padding: 16px; border-radius: 8px; box-shadow: 0 2px 6px rgba(0,0,0,.15); }
@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark) {
  body { color: #fafafa; background: #212121; }
}
```

Add `<link rel="stylesheet" href="/style.css">` to the head of yesterday's
home page, put the sections in `<div class="card">`, and serve both routes
with `http.serve(port = 8000)`. Change `"accent"` and every heading and
link changes with it.

`margin: 2em auto` is a classic trick: `auto` sides share the leftover
space, which centres the page.

### Exercise

Add a `"radius"` to the theme and use it for `.card`'s `border-radius`, so
a theme can choose square or round corners. Write `card_rule(theme)`.

```vyrn starter
create card_rule(t: map) -> str:
    return ".card \{ border-radius: 8px; \}"
end

main:
    print(card_rule({"radius": "0"}))
    print(card_rule({"radius": "16px"}))
end
```

```text expect
.card { border-radius: 0; }
.card { border-radius: 16px; }
```

exercise.starter:
create card_rule(t: map) -> str:
    return ".card \{ border-radius: 8px; \}"
end

main:
    print(card_rule({"radius": "0"}))
    print(card_rule({"radius": "16px"}))
end
exercise.solution:
create card_rule(t: map) -> str:
    return ".card \{ border-radius: " + t["radius"] + "; \}"
end

main:
    print(card_rule({"radius": "0"}))
    print(card_rule({"radius": "16px"}))
end
hints: `".card \{ border-radius: " + t["radius"] + "; \}"`

lessons.title: you learned
lessons.text:
- CSS rules pick elements with selectors (`h1`, `.class`, `#id`, `a b`) and
  set properties.
- Colours are `#rrggbb`; sizes are `px`, `rem` and `%`; every element is a
  box with padding, border and margin.
- Serve a stylesheet with `Content-Type: text/css`, and link it from every
  page.
- Write `\{` and `\}` for braces in Vyrn strings, and build CSS from a theme
  map so the look lives in one place.

days.title: Day 43: Forms and layout
days.intro:
So far your pages only *showed* things. **Forms** let visitors send
something back: a name, a message, a vote. Today you write forms, receive
what they send in your routes, check it, and answer. Then you arrange pages
into columns and grids with CSS **layout**. The project is a guestbook
where visitors leave messages.

lessons.title: A form
lessons.text:
A form is a `<form>` element holding **inputs** and a button. When the
button is pressed, the browser sends every input's `name` and value to the
form's `action` address, with the form's `method`:

```text
<form action="/sign" method="post">
  <label>Your name <input name="name" required maxlength="40"></label>
  <label>Message <textarea name="message" required></textarea></label>
  <label>Rating
    <select name="stars">
      <option>5</option><option>4</option><option>3</option>
    </select>
  </label>
  <button>Sign the guestbook</button>
</form>
```

| Input | Is |
|---|---|
| `<input name="x">` | one line of text; `type="email"`, `"number"`, `"password"`, `"date"`, `"checkbox"` change what it takes |
| `<textarea name="x">` | several lines |
| `<select name="x">` with `<option>`s | a choice from a list |
| `<label>` | the words for an input; clicking them focuses it |

`required` and `maxlength` make the browser check before sending. They
help honest visitors, but anyone can send anything to your server without
using your form, so **the server must check too**.

lessons.title: Receiving a form
lessons.text:
The browser sends the fields as `name=Ada&message=Hello+there&stars=5`.
A route receives each field as a parameter of the same name, converted to
the parameter's type:

```vyrn
use vyrn.http

route POST "/sign" (name: str, message: str, stars: int):
    return "Thanks {name}! {stars} stars for: {message}"
end

main:
    let r = http.test("POST", "/sign", form = {"name": "Ada", "message": "Hello there", "stars": "5"})
    print(r.status, r.text)
    print(http.test("POST", "/sign", form = {"name": "Ada"}).status)
    print(http.test("POST", "/sign", form = {"name": "Ada", "message": "x", "stars": "lots"}).status)
end
```

```text
200 Thanks Ada! 5 stars for: Hello there
400
400
```

A missing field, or `lots` where a number belongs, is answered with `400
Bad Request` before your code runs. `http.test(..., form = {...})` sends the
fields the way a browser does. The route can also take `request`, and read
every field from `request.form`, a map.

GET forms put the fields in the address instead, as a query string: right
for searches, which people like to bookmark.

```vyrn
use vyrn.http

route GET "/search" (q: str, page: int = 1):
    return "results for {q}, page {page}"
end

main:
    print(http.test("GET", "/search?q=green+tea").text)
    print(http.test("GET", "/search?q=tea&page=3").text)
end
```

```text
results for green tea, page 1
results for tea, page 3
```

lessons.title: Checking what arrives
lessons.text:
Types are checked for you; everything else is your job. Collect every
problem, so the visitor can fix them all at once:

```vyrn
create problems(name: str, message: str, stars: int) -> list:
    var found = []
    if name.strip() == "": found.append("Please give your name.")
    if len(name) > 40: found.append("Names are at most 40 letters.")
    if len(message.strip()) < 3: found.append("The message is too short.")
    if stars < 1 or stars > 5: found.append("Stars go from 1 to 5.")
    return found
end

main:
    print(problems("Ada", "Lovely site!", 5))
    print(problems("  ", "hi", 9))
end
```

```text
[]
["Please give your name.", "The message is too short.", "Stars go from 1 to 5."]
```

### Exercise

Add a check to `email_problems(email)`: an address needs exactly one `@`,
with something before it and a `.` somewhere after it.

```vyrn starter
create email_problems(email: str) -> list:
    return []
end

main:
    each e in ["ada@mail.com", "ada.mail.com", "@mail.com", "ada@mail", "a@b@c.com"]:
        print(e, email_problems(e))
    end
end
```

```text expect
ada@mail.com []
ada.mail.com ["That isn't an email address."]
@mail.com ["That isn't an email address."]
ada@mail ["That isn't an email address."]
a@b@c.com ["That isn't an email address."]
```

exercise.starter:
create email_problems(email: str) -> list:
    return []
end

main:
    each e in ["ada@mail.com", "ada.mail.com", "@mail.com", "ada@mail", "a@b@c.com"]:
        print(e, email_problems(e))
    end
end
exercise.expect:
ada@mail.com []
ada.mail.com ["That isn't an email address."]
@mail.com ["That isn't an email address."]
ada@mail ["That isn't an email address."]
a@b@c.com ["That isn't an email address."]
exercise.solution:
create email_problems(email: str) -> list:
    let parts = email.split("@")
    if len(parts) == 2 and parts[0] != "" and "." in parts[1]: return []
    return ["That isn't an email address."]
end

main:
    each e in ["ada@mail.com", "ada.mail.com", "@mail.com", "ada@mail", "a@b@c.com"]:
        print(e, email_problems(e))
    end
end
hints: `parts = email.split("@")` must have length 2.
then `parts[0] != ""` and `"." in parts[1]`.

lessons.title: Answering a form: redirect after POST
lessons.text:
After a successful POST, don't answer with a page: answer with a **redirect** to a normal page. Otherwise pressing the browser's refresh button sends the form again, and the message appears twice. A redirect is status `303 See Other` with a `Location` header. Both routes need the same list of messages. Vyrn has no global variables: instead, `main` **provides** a value under a name with `http.provide`, and any route with a parameter of that name receives it. A list is shared, not copied, so what one route appends the other sees: ```vyrn use vyrn.http route POST "/sign" (name: str, message: str, messages): messages.append((name, message)) return http.Response(303, "", {"Location": "/"}) end route GET "/" (messages): return "
    " + "".join(["
  • {n}: {m}
    • " each n, m in messages]) + "
" end main: http.provide("messages", []) let r = http.test("POST", "/sign", form = {"name": "Ada", "message": "Hi!"}) print(r.status, r.headers["location"]) print(http.test("GET", "/").text) end ``` ```text 303 /
  • Ada: Hi!
``` A browser follows the redirect by itself, so the visitor lands on the guestbook page and sees their message.

lessons.title: Layout: flexbox and grid
lessons.text:
Boxes normally stack one under another. Two CSS tools arrange them:

**Flexbox** lines up children in a row (or column), sharing the space:

```text
nav { display: flex; gap: 16px; justify-content: space-between; align-items: center; }
```

**Grid** places children in columns. This one makes as many 220-pixel-wide
columns as fit, so the page works on phones and wide screens alike:

```text
.cards { display: grid; grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fill, minmax(220px, 1fr)); gap: 16px; }
```

| Property | Does |
|---|---|
| `display: flex` | children in a row; `flex-direction: column` for a column |
| `gap` | space between children |
| `justify-content` | spacing along the row: `start`, `center`, `space-between` |
| `align-items` | alignment across it: `start`, `center`, `stretch` |
| `display: grid` | children in a grid; `grid-template-columns` says the columns |
| `1fr` | one share of the leftover space |

Pages must work on phones. Add this to every page's `<head>`, or phones
pretend to be a wide screen and shrink everything:

```text
<meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">
```

lessons.title: Project: the guestbook
lessons.text:
Everything together: a page with the form and the messages in a grid of cards, a POST route that checks the fields and either shows the problems or saves and redirects. Names and messages are escaped (Day 41), because visitors wrote them: ```vyrn use vyrn.html use vyrn.http const STYLE = r".cards { display: grid; grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fill, minmax(220px, 1fr)); gap: 16px; } .card { padding: 12px; border: 1px solid #ddd; border-radius: 8px; } .error { color: #c62828; }" const FORM = r'
' create page(entries: list, errors: list = []) -> str: let cards = "".join(["
{html.escape(n)}

{html.escape(m)}

" each n, m in entries]) let shown = "".join(["

{e}

" each e in errors]) return "Guestbook

Guestbook

{shown}{FORM}
{cards}
" end route GET "/" (entries): return page(entries) end route POST "/sign" (name: str, message: str, entries): var errors = [] if name.strip() == "": errors.append("Please give your name.") if len(message.strip()) < 3: errors.append("The message is too short.") if errors: return http.Response(400, page(entries, errors), {"Content-Type": "text/html"}) entries.append((name.strip(), message.strip())) return http.Response(303, "", {"Location": "/"}) end main: http.provide("entries", []) print(http.test("POST", "/sign", form = {"name": "Ada", "message": "Lovely site!"}).status) let bad = http.test("POST", "/sign", form = {"name": " ", "message": "hi"}) print(bad.status, [p.text each p in html.parse(bad.text).select(".error")]) let home = html.parse(http.test("GET", "/").text) print([c.select_one("p").text each c in home.select(".card")]) print("" in http.test("GET", "/").text) end ``` ```text 303 400 ["Please give your name.", "The message is too short."] ["Lovely site!"] false ``` The last line checks that the visitor's `` was escaped rather than sent as HTML. Serve it with `http.serve(port = 8000)` and sign it yourself. The messages live in a list, so they vanish when the server stops; Day 50 keeps them in a database. ### Exercise Show the newest message first, and number the cards: `#2`, `#1`. Write `card_titles(entries)` giving the strong text of each card in order. ```vyrn starter create card_titles(entries: list) -> list: return [n each n, m in entries] end main: print(card_titles([("Ada", "Hi"), ("Alan", "Hello"), ("Grace", "Hey")])) end ``` ```text expect ["#3 Grace", "#2 Alan", "#1 Ada"] ```

exercise.starter:
create card_titles(entries: list) -> list:
    return [n each n, m in entries]
end

main:
    print(card_titles([("Ada", "Hi"), ("Alan", "Hello"), ("Grace", "Hey")]))
end
exercise.solution:
create card_titles(entries: list) -> list:
    var titles = []
    each i, entry in enumerate(entries):
        titles.append("#{i + 1} {entry[0]}")
    end
    titles.reverse()
    return titles
end

main:
    print(card_titles([("Ada", "Hi"), ("Alan", "Hello"), ("Grace", "Hey")]))
end
hints: `each i, entry in enumerate(entries)` gives the position; the number is `i + 1`.
build the list, then `.reverse()` it, or use `reversed`.

lessons.title: you learned
lessons.text:
- A `<form>` sends its inputs' names and values to its `action` with its
  `method`; route parameters receive them by name.
- Check every field on the server, collect all the problems, and show them.
- After a successful POST, redirect with `303` and a `Location`.
- Routes share values that `main` gives them with `http.provide(name, value)`.
- Flexbox lines things up, grid places them in columns; add the viewport
  `<meta>` for phones.

days.title: Day 44: Templates
days.intro:
Building pages by joining strings works, but it gets messy fast: HTML mixed
into code, quotes inside quotes, and one forgotten `html.escape` is a
security hole. A **template** is the page written as HTML, with gaps for
the data. `vyrn.template` fills the gaps, and escapes everything by
default. The project generates a whole multi-page portfolio site from one
data file.

lessons.title: Filling gaps
lessons.text:
`{{name}}` is a gap. `template.render(text, data)` fills each one from a map (or a struct's fields): ```vyrn use vyrn.template main: let text = r"

{{title}}

By {{author.name}}, {{year}}

" print(template.render(text, {"title": "Dune", "year": 1965, "author": {"name": "Frank Herbert"}})) print(template.render(r"

{{comment}}

", {"comment": ""})) print(template.render(r"
{{{trusted}}}
", {"trusted": "mine"})) end ``` ```text

Dune

By Frank Herbert, 1965

<script>steal()</script>

mine
``` - `{{author.name}}` goes into maps and structs. - `{{x}}` is **escaped**: safe for anything a visitor typed. - `{{{x}}}` (three braces) is inserted as it is: only for HTML your own program made. Templates use `{{ }}`, and Vyrn strings use `{ }` for interpolation, so write templates in raw strings (`r"..."`, or `r"""..."""` for several lines) or, better, in their own files.

lessons.title: Lists and choices
lessons.text:
`{{#each list}}...{{/each}}` repeats its inside for every item; inside it, names are looked up in the item first, `{{this}}` is the item itself and `{{@index}}` its position. `{{#if x}}...{{else}}...{{/if}}` chooses; `{{#unless x}}` is the opposite. Anything "empty" (`false`, `none`, `0`, `""`, `[]`) counts as false: ```vyrn use vyrn.template const LIST = r"

{{title}}

{{#if items}}
    {{#each items}}
  1. {{name}}{{#if done}} ✓{{/if}}
    2. {{/each}}
{{else}}

Nothing to do!

{{/if}}" main: let todos = [{"name": "Learn templates", "done": true}, {"name": "Build a site", "done": false}] print(template.render(LIST, {"title": "Today", "items": todos})) print(template.render(LIST, {"title": "Tomorrow", "items": []})) print(template.render(r"{{#each tags}}#{{this}} {{/each}}", {"tags": ["vyrn", "web"]})) end ``` ```text

Today

  1. Learn templates ✓
  2. Build a site

Tomorrow

Nothing to do!

#vyrn #web ``` ### Exercise Write a template for a scoreboard: a `` with one row per player showing the position (counting from 1), the name and the score, and a `

No players yet

` when the list is empty. The positions come from the data, so number the players before rendering. ```vyrn starter use vyrn.template const BOARD = r"
" main: let players = [{"name": "Ada", "score": 30}, {"name": "Alan", "score": 25}] let numbered = players print(template.render(BOARD, {"players": numbered})) print(template.render(BOARD, {"players": []})) end ``` ```text expect
1Ada30
2Alan25

No players yet

```

exercise.starter:
use vyrn.template const BOARD = r"
" main: let players = [{"name": "Ada", "score": 30}, {"name": "Alan", "score": 25}] let numbered = players print(template.render(BOARD, {"players": numbered})) print(template.render(BOARD, {"players": []})) end
exercise.solution:
use vyrn.template const BOARD = r"{{#if players}}{{#each players}}{{/each}}
{{place}}{{name}}{{score}}
{{else}}

No players yet

{{/if}}" main: let players = [{"name": "Ada", "score": 30}, {"name": "Alan", "score": 25}] let numbered = [p | {"place": i + 1} each i, p in enumerate(players)] print(template.render(BOARD, {"players": numbered})) print(template.render(BOARD, {"players": []})) end
hints: `numbered = [p | {"place": i + 1} each i, p in enumerate(players)]` adds a `place` to each map.

`{{#if players}}{{#each players}}...{{/each}}
{{else}}...{{/if}}`

lessons.title: Template files and layouts
lessons.text:
Real templates live in files, usually in a `templates` folder, where your editor colours them as HTML. `template.render_file(path, data)` reads one. Every page of a site shares the same top and bottom: the ``, the menu, the footer. Put that in a **layout** template with a gap for the page's own content, render the page first, then put it in the layout with `{{{content}}}` (three braces: it's HTML your program made): ```vyrn use vyrn.fs use vyrn.template const LAYOUT = r""" {{title}} | My site
{{#each menu}}{{label}} {{/each}}
{{{content}}}
Made with Vyrn
""" const ABOUT = r"

About

{{bio}}

" const MENU = [{"url": "/", "label": "Home"}, {"url": "/about", "label": "About"}] create page(name: str, title: str, data: map) -> str: let content = template.render_file("templates/{name}.html", data) return template.render_file("templates/layout.html", {"title": title, "menu": MENU, "content": content}) end main: fs.mkdir("templates") write_text("templates/layout.html", LAYOUT) write_text("templates/about.html", ABOUT) print(page("about", "About", {"bio": "I like engines & music."})) end ``` ```text About | My site
Home About

About

I like engines & music.

Made with Vyrn
``` Change the layout once, and every page changes.

lessons.title: Templates in routes
lessons.text:
A route returning text that starts with `<` is a page, so a route is just `render_file` with the right data: ```vyrn check use vyrn.http use vyrn.template route GET "/" (): return template.render_file("templates/home.html", {"name": "Ada"}) end route GET "/hello/{name}" (name: str): return template.render(r"

Hello, {{name}}!

", {"name": name}) end main: http.serve(port = 8000) end ``` `/hello/

lessons.title: Project: a portfolio site generator
lessons.text:
Websites don't always need a server. A **static site** is a folder of finished HTML files, which free hosts like GitHub Pages serve as they are. This generator reads the projects from a JSON file and writes a home page plus one page per project: ```vyrn use vyrn.fs use vyrn.json use vyrn.template const LAYOUT = r'{{title}}
Home
{{{content}}}' const HOME = r'

{{name}}

{{intro}}

    {{#each projects}}
  • {{title}} ({{year}})
    • {{/each}}
' const PROJECT = r'

{{title}}

{{summary}}

{{#if tags}}

{{#each tags}}{{this}} {{/each}}

{{/if}}' create slug(title: str) -> str: return "-".join(title.lower().split()) end create build(data: map, out: str) -> list: fs.mkdir(out) let projects = [p | {"slug": slug(p["title"])} each p in sorted(data["projects"], key = p => p["year"], reverse = true)] var written = [] let home = template.render(HOME, data | {"projects": projects}) write_text("{out}/index.html", template.render(LAYOUT, {"title": data["name"], "content": home})) written.append("index.html") each p in projects: let body = template.render(PROJECT, p) write_text("{out}/{p["slug"]}.html", template.render(LAYOUT, {"title": p["title"], "content": body})) written.append(p["slug"] + ".html") end return written end main: json.save("portfolio.json", { "name": "Ada's projects", "intro": "Things I built while learning Vyrn.", "projects": [ {"title": "Snake Game", "year": 2025, "summary": "The classic, with a high-score table.", "tags": ["games"]}, {"title": "Deal Finder", "year": 2026, "summary": "Emails me when games go on sale.", "tags": ["apis", "databases"]}, ], }) print(build(json.load("portfolio.json"), "site")) print(read_text("site/index.html")) print(read_text("site/deal-finder.html").split("")[1]) end ``` ```text ["index.html", "deal-finder.html", "snake-game.html"] Ada's projects
Home

Ada's projects

Things I built while learning Vyrn.

  • Deal Finder (2026)
  • Snake Game (2025)
Home

Deal Finder

Emails me when games go on sale.

apis databases

``` Open `site/index.html` in a browser and click through. Adding a project is now one entry in the JSON file and running the generator again. (`'` is the escaped `'`, which the browser shows normally.) ### Exercise Add a "next project" link to the bottom of each project page. Write `with_next(projects)`, which gives each project map a `next` key holding the following project's slug, and the first project's slug for the last one, so the links go round in a circle. ```vyrn starter create with_next(projects: list) -> list: return projects end main: let ps = [{"slug": "a"}, {"slug": "b"}, {"slug": "c"}] print([p["next"] each p in with_next(ps)]) end ``` ```text expect ["b", "c", "a"] ```

exercise.starter:
create with_next(projects: list) -> list:
    return projects
end

main:
    let ps = [{"slug": "a"}, {"slug": "b"}, {"slug": "c"}]
    print([p["next"] each p in with_next(ps)])
end
exercise.solution:
create with_next(projects: list) -> list:
    let n = len(projects)
    return [p | {"next": projects[(i + 1) % n]["slug"]} each i, p in enumerate(projects)]
end

main:
    let ps = [{"slug": "a"}, {"slug": "b"}, {"slug": "c"}]
    print([p["next"] each p in with_next(ps)])
end
hints: the project after position `i` is at `(i + 1) % len(projects)`.
`p | {"next": ...}` makes a copy with the extra key.

lessons.title: you learned
lessons.text:
- `template.render(text, data)` fills `{{gaps}}`, escaping them; `{{{x}}}`
  inserts your own HTML as it is.
- `{{#each}}`, `{{#if}}`/`{{else}}` and `{{#unless}}` repeat and choose.
- Keep templates in files and share a layout with a `{{{content}}}` gap.
- A static site is a folder of HTML files: generate it from data.

days.title: Day 45: Web scraping
days.intro:
Not every website has an API. When the information is only on web pages,
a program can read the pages the way you do and pick out what it needs.
This is **web scraping**. Today you fetch pages, find things in them with
CSS selectors, follow links, and do it politely. The project collects every
book from a bookshop's catalogue into a CSV file.

lessons.title: Finding things in a page
lessons.text:
`html.parse` turns a page into elements you can search. `select(css)` gives every element a CSS selector matches (Day 42), `select_one` the first. Each element has its `text`, its `tag`, its attributes with `attr(name)`, and its own `select`, to search inside it: ```vyrn use vyrn.html const PAGE = r"""

Bookshop

Dune

£12.99

In stock

Emma

£7.50

Sold out

""" main: let page = html.parse(PAGE) print(page.select_one("h1").text) each book in page.select("article.book"): let link = book.select_one("h3 a") print(link.attr("title"), "|", book.select_one(".price").text, "|", link.attr("href")) end end ``` ```text Bookshop Dune | £12.99 | catalogue/dune.html Emma | £7.50 | catalogue/emma.html ``` The trick is finding the right selector. In a browser, right-click the thing you want and choose **Inspect**: the developer tools show its tag, classes and where it sits. Pick the shortest selector that finds exactly what you want: a class like `.price` is better than a long path like `body > div > article > p:nth-child(2)`, which breaks as soon as the page changes a little.

lessons.title: From elements to data
lessons.text:
Scraped text needs cleaning before it's useful: strip spaces, take off currency signs, turn "In stock" into `true`. Do it in one function per item, giving a clean map: ```vyrn use vyrn.html create book_from(el: any) -> map: let link = el.select_one("h3 a") let price = el.select_one(".price").text.strip().replace("£", "") return { "title": link.attr("title"), "price": float(price), "in_stock": "in stock" in el.select_one(".stock").text.lower(), } end main: let page = html.parse(r'

Dune

£12.99

In stock

') print([book_from(b) each b in page.select("article.book")]) end ``` ```text [{"title": "Dune", "price": 12.99, "in_stock": true}] ``` ### Exercise Pages often have tables. Write `table_rows(page)`, which gives each row of the table's body as a map from the header names to the cell texts. ```vyrn starter use vyrn.html create table_rows(page: any) -> list: return [] end main: let page = html.parse(r"
CityPeople
Oslo709000
Bergen291000
") print(table_rows(page)) end ``` ```text expect [{"City": "Oslo", "People": "709000"}, {"City": "Bergen", "People": "291000"}] ```

exercise.starter:
use vyrn.html create table_rows(page: any) -> list: return [] end main: let page = html.parse(r"
CityPeople
Oslo709000
Bergen291000
") print(table_rows(page)) end
exercise.solution:
use vyrn.html create table_rows(page: any) -> list: let headers = [th.text each th in page.select("thead th")] var rows = [] each tr in page.select("tbody tr"): let cells = [td.text each td in tr.select("td")] rows.append(dict(zip(headers, cells))) end return rows end main: let page = html.parse(r"
CityPeople
Oslo709000
Bergen291000
") print(table_rows(page)) end
hints: `headers = [th.text each th in page.select("thead th")]`
for each `tr` in `page.select("tbody tr")`, the cells are `[td.text each td in tr.select("td")]`; `dict(zip(headers, cells))` pairs them up.

lessons.title: Following links
lessons.text:
Links on a page are often **relative**: `catalogue/dune.html` means "next to this page", `../index.html` "one folder up", `/about` "from the top of the site". `http.join_url` turns them into full addresses, the way a browser does: ```vyrn use vyrn.http main: let here = "https://books.toscrape.com/catalogue/page-2.html" print(http.join_url(here, "page-3.html")) print(http.join_url(here, "../index.html")) print(http.join_url(here, "/static/style.css")) print(http.join_url(here, "https://other.site/x")) end ``` ```text https://books.toscrape.com/catalogue/page-3.html https://books.toscrape.com/index.html https://books.toscrape.com/static/style.css https://other.site/x ``` A catalogue split over several pages has a "next" link at the bottom. A scraper follows it until there isn't one: ```vyrn use vyrn.html use vyrn.http const SITE = { "https://shop.example/page-1.html": r'
  • Dune
  • Emma
  • next
    • ', "https://shop.example/page-2.html": r'
  • Ubik
    • ', } create crawl(start: str, fetch: any) -> list: var titles = [] var url = start loop url != none: let page = html.parse(fetch(url)) titles.extend([b.text each b in page.select("li.book")]) let next = page.select_one("li.next a") url = http.join_url(url, next.attr("href")) if next != none else none end return titles end main: print(crawl("https://shop.example/page-1.html", url => SITE[url])) end ``` ```text ["Dune", "Emma", "Ubik"] ``` As in the API days, fetching is passed in, so the crawler runs here on a recorded site; for real, `fetch` is `url => http.get(url).text`.

lessons.title: Scraping politely
lessons.text:
A scraper can ask for pages much faster than a person clicks. Be a good
guest:

1. **Check the rules.** Most sites have a `/robots.txt` file listing which
   paths programs should stay out of, and the site's terms may forbid
   scraping altogether. If there's an API, use it instead.
2. **Slow down.** Wait a second or so between pages (`time.sleep(1)`).
3. **Say who you are**, with a `User-Agent` header that names your program.
4. **Don't fetch the same page twice**: cache it (Day 36).
5. **Only take what you need**, and never collect people's personal
   information.

`robots.txt` is simple text. Here is a small reader for its most common
form, `Disallow` lines under `User-agent: *`:

```vyrn
create disallowed(robots: str) -> list:
    var rules = []
    var for_everyone = false
    each line in robots.lines():
        let parts = line.split("#")[0].split(":", 1)
        if len(parts) < 2: skip
        let field = parts[0].strip().lower()
        let value = parts[1].strip()
        if field == "user-agent": for_everyone = value == "*"
        if field == "disallow" and for_everyone and value != "": rules.append(value)
    end
    return rules
end

create allowed(robots: str, path: str) -> bool:
    return not any([path.startswith(rule) each rule in disallowed(robots)])
end

main:
    let robots = "User-agent: BadBot\nDisallow: /\n\nUser-agent: *\nDisallow: /checkout/\nDisallow: /account  # private\n"
    print(disallowed(robots))
    print(allowed(robots, "/catalogue/page-2.html"), allowed(robots, "/checkout/pay"))
end
```

```text
["/checkout/", "/account"]
true false
```

lessons.title: Project: the catalogue scraper
lessons.text:
books.toscrape.com is a pretend bookshop made for practising scraping. This program walks its whole catalogue, politely, and saves every book: ```vyrn check use vyrn.csv use vyrn.html use vyrn.http use vyrn.time const START = "https://books.toscrape.com/catalogue/page-1.html" const HEADERS = {"User-Agent": "vyrn-course-scraper (learning)"} create book_from(el: any, page_url: str) -> map: let link = el.select_one("h3 a") return { "title": link.attr("title"), "price": float(el.select_one(".price_color").text.replace("£", "")), "rating": el.select_one("p.star-rating").classes[1], "url": http.join_url(page_url, link.attr("href")), } end main: var books = [] var url = START loop url != none: let r = http.get(url, headers = HEADERS) if not r.ok: print("stopped: {url} said {r.status}") stop end let page = html.parse(r.text) books.extend([book_from(el, url) each el in page.select("article.product_pod")]) print("{len(books)} books so far") let next = page.select_one("li.next a") url = http.join_url(url, next.attr("href")) if next != none else none time.sleep(1) end csv.write("books.csv", books) print("saved", len(books), "books") end ``` It takes about a minute for the 50 pages. The rating is a class name on the stars (`

`), so it's the second class. ### Exercise The ratings are words. Write `stars(word)` turning `"One"` to `"Five"` into 1 to 5, and use it to find the average rating of the books given. ```vyrn starter create stars(word: str) -> int: return 0 end main: let books = [{"rating": "Three"}, {"rating": "Five"}, {"rating": "One"}, {"rating": "Five"}] print(stars("Four"), sum([stars(b["rating"]) each b in books]) / len(books)) end ``` ```text expect 4 3.5 ```

exercise.starter:
create stars(word: str) -> int:
    return 0
end

main:
    let books = [{"rating": "Three"}, {"rating": "Five"}, {"rating": "One"}, {"rating": "Five"}]
    print(stars("Four"), sum([stars(b["rating"]) each b in books]) / len(books))
end
exercise.solution:
create stars(word: str) -> int:
    return ["One", "Two", "Three", "Four", "Five"].index(word) + 1
end

main:
    let books = [{"rating": "Three"}, {"rating": "Five"}, {"rating": "One"}, {"rating": "Five"}]
    print(stars("Four"), sum([stars(b["rating"]) each b in books]) / len(books))
end
hints: `["One", "Two", "Three", "Four", "Five"].index(word) + 1`

lessons.title: you learned
lessons.text:
- `html.parse`, `select` and `select_one` find elements by CSS selector;
  `text`, `attr` and `classes` read them. Use the browser's Inspect to find
  selectors.
- Clean each item into a map at once; `http.join_url` resolves relative
  links; follow "next" links until there are none.
- Scrape politely: obey `robots.txt` and the site's terms, slow down, say
  who you are, cache, and take only what you need.

days.title: Day 46: Regular expressions
days.intro:
`split`, `find` and `replace` work when you know exactly what the text
says. When you only know its *shape*, "a number, then a dash, then four
digits", you need a **regular expression**: a tiny language for describing
patterns in text. Every programming language has them, written almost the
same way. Today you learn the pieces, then use them to read a web server's
log and find out which pages are popular and what went wrong.

lessons.title: Patterns
lessons.text:
`re.test(pattern, text)` says whether the pattern appears anywhere in the
text; `re.find_all` gives every piece that matches:

```vyrn
use vyrn.re

main:
    print(re.test(r"cat", "concatenate"))
    print(re.find_all(r"\d+", "3 cats, 12 dogs and 140 fish"))
    print(re.find_all(r"[A-Z]\w*", "Ada met Alan in London"))
end
```

```text
true
["3", "12", "140"]
["Ada", "Alan", "London"]
```

Write patterns in **raw strings** (`r"..."`), so a backslash stays a
backslash. The pieces:

| Pattern | Matches |
|---|---|
| `cat` | the letters c, a, t |
| `.` | any one character |
| `\d`, `\w`, `\s` | a digit; a letter, digit or `_`; a space, tab or newline |
| `\D`, `\W`, `\S` | anything *but* those |
| `[aeiou]`, `[a-z]`, `[^0-9]` | one of these; a range; anything not in it |
| `x*`, `x+`, `x?` | `x` zero or more times; one or more; maybe once |
| `x{3}`, `x{2,4}` | exactly 3; 2 to 4 |
| `^`, `$` | the start, the end of the text |
| `\b` | the edge of a word |
| `cat\|dog` | either |
| `\.`, `\(`, `\$` | a real `.`, `(` or `$` (a backslash takes away the special meaning) |

`+` and `*` are **greedy**: they take as much as they can. Add `?` to take
as little as possible: `<.+?>` matches one tag, `<.+>` from the first `<`
to the last `>`.

### Exercise

Write `is_postcode(text)` for a made-up postcode format: two capital
letters, one or two digits, a space, a digit, then two capital letters,
with nothing before or after.

```vyrn starter
use vyrn.re

create is_postcode(text: str) -> bool:
    return false
end

main:
    each t in ["SW1 2AB", "M4 9XY", "SW12 2AB", "sw1 2ab", "SW1 2AB please"]:
        print(t, is_postcode(t))
    end
end
```

```text expect
SW1 2AB true
M4 9XY false
SW12 2AB true
sw1 2ab false
SW1 2AB please false
```

exercise.starter:
use vyrn.re

create is_postcode(text: str) -> bool:
    return false
end

main:
    each t in ["SW1 2AB", "M4 9XY", "SW12 2AB", "sw1 2ab", "SW1 2AB please"]:
        print(t, is_postcode(t))
    end
end
exercise.expect:
SW1 2AB true
M4 9XY false
SW12 2AB true
sw1 2ab false
SW1 2AB please false
exercise.solution:
use vyrn.re

create is_postcode(text: str) -> bool:
    return re.test(r"^[A-Z]{2}\d{1,2} \d[A-Z]{2}$", text)
end

main:
    each t in ["SW1 2AB", "M4 9XY", "SW12 2AB", "sw1 2ab", "SW1 2AB please"]:
        print(t, is_postcode(t))
    end
end
hints: `[A-Z]{2}` is two capital letters; `\d{1,2}` one or two digits.
`^` and `$` make it the whole text.

lessons.title: Groups: taking a match apart
lessons.text:
Parentheses make a **group**, so you can take out just part of a match.
`re.find` gives the first match with its `text`, where it `start`s and
`end`s, and its `groups`; name a group with `(?P<name>...)` and it's in
`named` too:

```vyrn
use vyrn.re

main:
    let m = re.find(r"(\d{4})-(\d{2})-(\d{2})", "Due on 2026-11-12, paid late")
    print(m["text"], m["groups"], m["start"])
    let who = re.find(r"(?P<user>[\w.]+)@(?P<site>[\w.]+)", "write to ada.l@mail.com")
    print(who["named"]["user"], who["named"]["site"])
    print(re.find(r"\d+", "no numbers here"))
    print(re.find_all(r"(\w+)=(\d+)", "w=3 h=40 d=7"))
end
```

```text
2026-11-12 ["2026", "11", "12"] 7
ada.l mail.com
none
[("w", "3"), ("h", "40"), ("d", "7")]
```

With groups, `find_all` gives each match's groups as a tuple. `re.matches`
gives every match in full, like `re.find` does for the first.

lessons.title: Replacing and splitting
lessons.text:
`re.replace` replaces every match. In the replacement, `$1` is the first
group; or give a function, which is called with each match and gives its
replacement:

```vyrn
use vyrn.re

main:
    print(re.replace(r"(\d{2})/(\d{2})/(\d{4})", "Born 14/03/2010", "$3-$2-$1"))
    print(re.replace(r"\s+", "too    many   spaces", " "))
    print(re.replace(r"\d+", "3 apples and 12 pears", m => str(int(m["text"]) * 2)))
    print(re.split(r"[,;]\s*", "red, green;blue,  white"))
    print(re.replace(r"(?i)vyrn", "VYRN, Vyrn, vyrn!", "Vyrn"))
end
```

```text
Born 2010-03-14
too many spaces
6 apples and 24 pears
["red", "green", "blue", "white"]
Vyrn, Vyrn, Vyrn!
```

`(?i)` at the start makes a pattern ignore case.

### Exercise

Hide all but the last four digits of every card number in a text: a card
number here is four groups of four digits separated by spaces or dashes.

```vyrn starter
use vyrn.re

create mask(text: str) -> str:
    return text
end

main:
    print(mask("Paid with 4111 1111 1111 1234 and 5500-0000-0000-0004."))
end
```

```text expect
Paid with **** **** **** 1234 and **** **** **** 0004.
```

exercise.starter:
use vyrn.re

create mask(text: str) -> str:
    return text
end

main:
    print(mask("Paid with 4111 1111 1111 1234 and 5500-0000-0000-0004."))
end
exercise.solution:
use vyrn.re

create mask(text: str) -> str:
    return re.replace(r"\d{4}[ -]\d{4}[ -]\d{4}[ -](\d{4})", text, "**** **** **** $1")
end

main:
    print(mask("Paid with 4111 1111 1111 1234 and 5500-0000-0000-0004."))
end
hints: `\d{4}[ -]\d{4}[ -]\d{4}[ -](\d{4})` with the last group kept.
the replacement is `"**** **** **** $1"`.

lessons.title: When not to use them
lessons.text:
Regular expressions are powerful and hard to read. Some rules of thumb:

- If `split`, `startswith` or `in` does the job, use them.
- Don't parse HTML with regular expressions: use `html.parse`, which
  copes with everything real pages do.
- Don't try to fully check email addresses with one: the real rules are
  enormous. Check roughly, then send a confirmation email.
- Give a complicated pattern a name, as a constant, with a comment showing
  an example of what it matches.

lessons.title: Project: reading a server log
lessons.text:
Web servers write a line for every request. Each line has the visitor's
address, the time, the request, the status and the size:

```text
203.0.113.9 - - [12/Nov/2026:10:15:32 +0000] "GET /books/dune HTTP/1.1" 200 5120
```

One pattern with named groups takes a line apart; lines that don't match
are counted, not crashed on:

```vyrn
use vyrn.re

## 203.0.113.9 - - [12/Nov/2026:10:15:32 +0000] "GET /books HTTP/1.1" 200 5120
const LINE = r'^(?P<ip>\S+) \S+ \S+ \[(?P<time>[^\]]+)\] "(?P<method>[A-Z]+) (?P<path>\S+) [^"]*" (?P<status>\d{3}) (?P<size>\d+|-)$'

const LOG = """203.0.113.9 - - [12/Nov/2026:10:15:32 +0000] "GET /books/dune HTTP/1.1" 200 5120
198.51.100.4 - - [12/Nov/2026:10:15:40 +0000] "GET /books/emma HTTP/1.1" 200 4870
203.0.113.9 - - [12/Nov/2026:10:16:01 +0000] "POST /basket HTTP/1.1" 303 -
192.0.2.77 - - [12/Nov/2026:10:16:05 +0000] "GET /books/dune HTTP/1.1" 200 5120
192.0.2.77 - - [12/Nov/2026:10:16:09 +0000] "GET /wp-admin.php HTTP/1.1" 404 312
this line got cut off halfway
198.51.100.4 - - [12/Nov/2026:10:17:44 +0000] "GET /checkout HTTP/1.1" 500 230"""

create parse(log: str) -> (list, int):
    var hits = []
    var broken = 0
    each line in log.lines():
        let m = re.find(LINE, line)
        if m == none:
            broken += 1
        else:
            hits.append(m["named"])
        end
    end
    return (hits, broken)
end

main:
    let hits, broken = parse(LOG)
    print(len(hits), "requests,", broken, "unreadable")
    var pages = {}
    each h in hits:
        if h["method"] == "GET" and h["status"] == "200":
            pages[h["path"]] = pages.get(h["path"], 0) + 1
        end
    end
    print("popular:", sorted(pages.items(), key = kv => kv[1], reverse = true)[0])
    print("errors:", ["{h["status"]} {h["path"]}" each h in hits if int(h["status"]) >= 400])
    print("visitors:", len(set([h["ip"] each h in hits])))
end
```

```text
6 requests, 1 unreadable
popular: ("/books/dune", 2)
errors: ["404 /wp-admin.php", "500 /checkout"]
visitors: 3
```

The 404 for `/wp-admin.php` is a bot looking for a weak WordPress site;
every public server sees thousands of these. The 500 is a real bug in the
shop's checkout.

### Exercise

Add up the bytes sent per visitor (`size`, where `-` means 0), and give the
visitor who downloaded the most.

```vyrn starter
create biggest(hits: list) -> (str, int):
    return ("", 0)
end

main:
    let hits = [{"ip": "a", "size": "5120"}, {"ip": "b", "size": "4870"}, {"ip": "a", "size": "-"}, {"ip": "b", "size": "1000"}]
    print(biggest(hits))
end
```

```text expect
("b", 5870)
```

exercise.starter:
create biggest(hits: list) -> (str, int):
    return ("", 0)
end

main:
    let hits = [{"ip": "a", "size": "5120"}, {"ip": "b", "size": "4870"}, {"ip": "a", "size": "-"}, {"ip": "b", "size": "1000"}]
    print(biggest(hits))
end
exercise.solution:
create biggest(hits: list) -> (str, int):
    var totals = {}
    each h in hits:
        let size = 0 if h["size"] == "-" else int(h["size"])
        totals[h["ip"]] = totals.get(h["ip"], 0) + size
    end
    return max(totals.items(), key = kv => kv[1])
end

main:
    let hits = [{"ip": "a", "size": "5120"}, {"ip": "b", "size": "4870"}, {"ip": "a", "size": "-"}, {"ip": "b", "size": "1000"}]
    print(biggest(hits))
end
hints: keep a map from ip to total: `0 if h["size"] == "-" else int(h["size"])`.
`max(totals.items(), key = kv => kv[1])`

lessons.title: you learned
lessons.text:
- A regular expression describes the shape of text: characters, classes
  (`\d`, `[a-z]`), repeats (`+`, `*`, `{2,4}`), anchors (`^`, `$`).
- `re.test`, `re.find`, `re.find_all`, `re.matches`; groups `( )` and named
  groups `(?P<name> )` take matches apart.
- `re.replace` with `$1` or a function; `re.split` on a pattern; `(?i)`
  ignores case.
- Use simpler tools when they work, never parse HTML with patterns, and
  name complicated patterns.

days.title: Day 47: Testing
days.intro:
Every program so far, you checked by running it and reading what it
printed. That works once. But programs change: you fix one thing and break
another without noticing. **Automated tests** are small programs that
check your program, and run in a second every time you change anything.
Professional code has as much test code as program code, often more.
Today you write tests, learn what makes them good, test code that uses
the network or the clock with fakes, and test a web app's routes. The
project puts the deal finder from Day 40 under test.

lessons.title: A first test
lessons.text:
A test is a function whose name starts with `test_`, that uses `assert`
to check something is true. `assert` does nothing when it's true, and
fails, stopping the test, when it's false:

```vyrn
create price_with_vat(price: float) -> float:
    return round(price * 1.2, 2)
end

create test_vat_is_added():
    assert(price_with_vat(10) == 12.0)
end

create test_vat_rounds_to_pennies():
    assert(price_with_vat(0.99) == 1.19)
end

main:
    test_vat_is_added()
    test_vat_rounds_to_pennies()
    print("both passed")
end
```

```text
both passed
```

When a comparison in an `assert` is false, the error says what both sides
were, so you can see what went wrong without adding `print`s:

```vyrn
create price_with_vat(price: float) -> float:
    return round(price * 1.2, 2)
end

main:
    assert(price_with_vat(2.50) == 3.10, "VAT on 2.50")
end
```

```text
error: AssertionError: VAT on 2.50 (3.0 == 3.1 is false)
```

Here the *test* was wrong (20% of 2.50 is 0.50, not 0.60), which happens
too: a failing test means "these two disagree", and you decide which is
right.

lessons.title: `vyrn test`
lessons.text:
In a project, tests live in the `tests` folder, in files of their own, and
import what they test. `vyrn new shop` makes a project with one already:

```text
shop/
  vyrn.toml
  main.vyrn
  prices.vyrn             the code
  tests/
    test_prices.vyrn      the tests
```

`tests/test_prices.vyrn`:

```text
use prices (price_with_vat)

create test_vat_is_added():
    assert(price_with_vat(10) == 12.0)
end

create test_vat_rounds_to_pennies():
    assert(price_with_vat(0.99) == 1.19)
end
```

`vyrn test` finds every `test_` function in `tests/`, runs each one in a
fresh copy of the program (so tests can't affect each other), and reports.
If `price_with_vat` had a bug and rounded down, it would say:

```text
ok      tests/test_prices.vyrn::test_vat_is_added
FAILED  tests/test_prices.vyrn::test_vat_rounds_to_pennies
        AssertionError: 1.18 == 1.19 is false
  in test_vat_rounds_to_pennies at line 8

1 passed, 1 failed
```

It exits with code 1 when anything fails, so scripts and CI services
(Day 52) can refuse to publish broken code.

lessons.title: What to test
lessons.text:
Good tests check **behaviour**: what goes in and what comes out, not how
the function does it. Then you can rewrite the inside freely, and the
tests tell you whether it still works. For each function, test:

- a **typical** case;
- the **edges**: empty lists, zero, the first and last item, the largest
  allowed value;
- the **mistakes**: bad input should fail in the way you promised.

`assert_fails` checks that something fails, optionally with a particular
kind of error, and gives you the error to look at:

```vyrn
struct TooYoung:
    age: int
end

create ticket_price(age: int) -> float:
    if age < 0: fail ValueError("age can't be negative")
    if age < 3: fail TooYoung(age)
    if age < 16: return 5.0
    if age >= 65: return 7.0
    return 10.0
end

create test_prices_by_age():
    assert(ticket_price(10) == 5.0)
    assert(ticket_price(30) == 10.0)
    assert(ticket_price(70) == 7.0)
end

create test_edges():
    assert(ticket_price(3) == 5.0)
    assert(ticket_price(15) == 5.0)
    assert(ticket_price(16) == 10.0)
    assert(ticket_price(65) == 7.0)
end

create test_mistakes():
    assert_fails(() => ticket_price(-1), "ValueError")
    let e = assert_fails(() => ticket_price(2), "TooYoung")
    assert(e.age == 2)
end

main:
    test_prices_by_age()
    test_edges()
    test_mistakes()
    print("all passed")
end
```

```text
all passed
```

Edges are where bugs live: is 16 a child or an adult? The test decides,
and writes the decision down where everyone can see it.

lessons.title: Fixtures: shared setup
lessons.text:
Several tests often need the same starting point: a list of sample users,
a database with some rows. Put it in a helper function, a **fixture**, and
call it at the start of each test. Each test gets fresh data, so one test
changing it can't break another:

```vyrn
use vyrn.db

create sample_db() -> any:
    let conn = db.open(":memory:")
    conn.create_table("books", {"title": "text", "year": "int"})
    conn.insert("books", {"title": "Dune", "year": 1965})
    conn.insert("books", {"title": "Emma", "year": 1815})
    return conn
end

create older_than(conn: any, year: int) -> list[str]:
    return [r["title"] each r in conn.query("select title from books where year < ? order by title", [year])]
end

create test_finds_old_books():
    let conn = sample_db()
    assert(older_than(conn, 1900) == ["Emma"])
end

create test_after_deleting():
    let conn = sample_db()
    conn.delete("books", {"title": "Emma"})
    assert(older_than(conn, 1900) == [])
end

create test_finds_all():
    let conn = sample_db()
    assert(len(older_than(conn, 3000)) == 2)
end

main:
    test_finds_old_books()
    test_after_deleting()
    test_finds_all()
    print("3 passed")
end
```

```text
3 passed
```

`test_after_deleting` removed a book, but `test_finds_all` still sees two,
because each test made its own database with `sample_db()`.

lessons.title: Fakes: testing without the outside world
lessons.text:
Code that calls an API, sends email or reads the clock is hard to test:
the network is slow and changes, emails really get sent, the time is
different every run. Since Day 32 you've passed such things in as
functions. In a test, pass a **fake** instead: `fake(returns = ...)`
answers with a value you choose, `fake(returns_each = [...])` with a
different value each call, `fake(fails = ...)` fails, and every fake
remembers how it was called:

```vyrn
create remind(users: list[map], today: str, send: any) -> int:
    var sent = 0
    each u in users:
        if u["due"] == today:
            send(u["email"], "Your book is due today")
            sent += 1
        end
    end
    return sent
end

create test_only_due_users_are_emailed():
    let mail = fake(returns = true)
    let users = [{"email": "a@x.com", "due": "2026-11-12"}, {"email": "b@x.com", "due": "2026-11-20"}]
    assert(remind(users, "2026-11-12", mail) == 1)
    assert(mail.call_count == 1)
    assert(mail.last_call[0] == "a@x.com")
end

create test_a_failing_mail_server_is_reported():
    let broken = fake(fails = NetworkError("server down"))
    let users = [{"email": "a@x.com", "due": "2026-11-12"}]
    let e = assert_fails(() => remind(users, "2026-11-12", broken), "NetworkError")
    assert("down" in e.message)
end

main:
    test_only_due_users_are_emailed()
    test_a_failing_mail_server_is_reported()
    print("passed")
end
```

```text
passed
```

No email was sent and no network was used, yet the test proves that the
right person would be emailed, and what happens when the mail server is
down.

lessons.title: Testing a web app
lessons.text:
`http.test` (Day 41) sends a request to your own routes without a network,
so routes are as easy to test as functions:

```vyrn
use vyrn.http

route GET "/hello/{name}" (name: str):
    return {"greeting": "Hello, {name.title()}!"}
end

route POST "/signup" (email: str):
    if "@" not in email: return http.Response(400, {"error": "that isn't an email"})
    return 201, {"email": email}
end

create test_greets_by_name():
    let r = http.test("GET", "/hello/ada")
    assert(r.status == 200)
    assert(r.json["greeting"] == "Hello, Ada!")
end

create test_signup_checks_the_email():
    assert(http.test("POST", "/signup", form = {"email": "ada@mail.com"}).status == 201)
    let bad = http.test("POST", "/signup", form = {"email": "ada"})
    assert(bad.status == 400)
    assert(bad.json["error"] == "that isn't an email")
end

create test_unknown_pages_are_404():
    assert(http.test("GET", "/nowhere").status == 404)
end

main:
    test_greets_by_name()
    test_signup_checks_the_email()
    test_unknown_pages_are_404()
    print("routes passed")
end
```

```text
routes passed
```
