main:
    let full = table.from_csv("city,revenue
London,14
Leeds,7
London,35
York,10
Leeds,6.5
London,6
")
end
exercise.solution:
use vyrn.table

main:
    let full = table.from_csv("city,revenue\nLondon,14\nLeeds,7\nLondon,35\nYork,10\nLeeds,6.5\nLondon,6\n")
    let avg = full.group_by("city", "revenue", "mean").sort("revenue_mean", descending = true)
    each r in avg:
        print(r["city"], round(r["revenue_mean"], 2))
    end
end
hints: `group_by("city", "revenue", "mean")`, sorted descending.
`round(r["revenue_mean"], 2)`.

lessons.title: you learned
lessons.text:
- `group_by(column, value, how)` summarises each group; without a value it
  counts rows.
- Add computed columns with `add_column` and a comprehension.
- `join(other, key)` combines tables; an inner join drops unmatched rows,
  `how = "left"` keeps them. Compare row counts to catch bad keys.
- Analysis answers questions and finds data problems.

days.title: Day 56: Charts
days.intro:
A table of numbers answers a question for whoever reads it carefully; a
chart answers it at a glance. Today you make the four charts that cover
most needs, learn which one fits which question, and put charts into web
pages. The project charts a year of weather for two cities.

lessons.title: Your first chart
lessons.text:
`vyrn.chart` makes a chart from lists of numbers, and `save` writes it as
a PNG picture or an SVG drawing:

```vyrn
use vyrn.chart

main:
    let c = chart.bar(["North", "South", "East"], [57.5, 38, 24.5], title = "Revenue by region", y_label = "£")
    c.save("revenue.png")
    print(c)
end
```

```text
Chart(640x400)
```

Open `revenue.png` to see it: a bar per region, labelled, with a scale.
Every chart takes `title`, `x_label`, `y_label`, `width` and `height`.

lessons.title: Choosing the chart
lessons.text:
The right chart depends on the question:

| Question | Chart | `vyrn.chart` |
|---|---|---|
| How do categories compare? | bar | `chart.bar(labels, values)` |
| How does something change over time? | line | `chart.line(xs, ys)` |
| Are two measurements related? | scatter | `chart.scatter(xs, ys)` |
| How are values spread out? | histogram | `chart.hist(values, bins)` |
| What share is each part of a whole? | pie | `chart.pie(labels, values)` |

Give several **series** as a map from name to values, and they share one
chart with a legend:

```vyrn
use vyrn.chart

main:
    let months = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6]
    let temps = {"London": [5, 7, 11, 14, 17, 20], "Oslo": [-3, -2, 2, 7, 12, 16]}
    chart.line(months, temps, title = "Average temperature", x_label = "month", y_label = "°C").save("temps.png")
    print("saved temps.png")
end
```

```text
saved temps.png
```

A histogram groups values into **bins** and shows how many fall in each,
which reveals the shape of the data: where most values are, and whether
there are odd ones far away:

```vyrn
use vyrn.chart
use vyrn.random

main:
    random.seed(3)
    let heights = [round(random.float(150, 175) + random.float(0, 20), 1) each _ in 0 until 500]
    chart.hist(heights, 12, title = "Heights of 500 people", x_label = "cm").save("heights.png")
    print(min(heights), max(heights))
end
```

```text
151.7 193.1
```

lessons.title: Charts that tell the truth
lessons.text:
A chart can mislead without a single wrong number. Three rules:

- **Bars start at zero.** A bar's length *is* its value; cut off the bottom
  and a 5% difference looks like 50%.
- **Label everything**: what is measured, in which unit, over what time.
  A chart without labels is a picture, not information.
- **Don't use too many series.** Past about five lines, nobody can tell
  them apart; use several small charts instead.

Pie charts are the easiest to misread (people judge angles badly): use one
only for a few parts of a whole, and prefer bars when in doubt.

### Exercise

Make a scatter chart of hours studied against test score, titled "Study
and scores", with both axes labelled, saved as `study.png`. Then print how
many points it shows.

```vyrn starter
use vyrn.chart

main:
    let hours = [1, 2, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7]
    let scores = [52, 58, 61, 60, 70, 74, 79, 88]
end
```

```text expect
8 points
```

lessons.title: Charts in web pages
lessons.text:
`c.svg()` gives the chart as SVG text, which a web page can include directly: no picture file needed, and it stays sharp at any size. A route can draw a chart from live data every time the page is asked for: ```vyrn use vyrn.chart use vyrn.html use vyrn.http route GET "/report" (sales): let c = chart.bar(sales.keys(), sales.values(), title = "Sales this week", y_label = "units") return "

Weekly report

" + c.svg() + "

Total: {sum(sales.values())} units

" end main: http.provide("sales", {"Mon": 12, "Tue": 18, "Wed": 9}) let page = html.parse(http.test("GET", "/report").text) print(page.select_one("h1").text, "|", len(page.select("svg")), "chart |", page.select_one("p").text) end ``` ```text Weekly report | 1 chart | Total: 39 units ```

lessons.title: Project: a year of weather
lessons.text:
Monthly temperatures and rainfall for two cities, from a CSV file. The program makes three charts, each answering one question, and a small HTML report that holds them: ```vyrn use vyrn.chart use vyrn.table const WEATHER = "month,city,temp,rain\n1,London,5,55\n2,London,6,41\n3,London,9,42\n4,London,11,44\n5,London,14,49\n6,London,17,45\n7,London,19,45\n8,London,19,50\n9,London,16,49\n10,London,13,69\n11,London,9,59\n12,London,6,55\n1,Oslo,-3,49\n2,Oslo,-3,36\n3,Oslo,1,47\n4,Oslo,6,41\n5,Oslo,11,53\n6,Oslo,15,65\n7,Oslo,17,81\n8,Oslo,16,89\n9,Oslo,12,90\n10,Oslo,7,84\n11,Oslo,2,73\n12,Oslo,-2,55\n" main: let w = table.from_csv(WEATHER) let months = list(1 to 12) let cities = w.unique("city") let temps = {c: w.where("city", "==", c).column("temp") each c in cities} let rain = {c: w.where("city", "==", c).sum("rain") each c in cities} let charts = [ chart.line(months, temps, title = "Temperature through the year", x_label = "month", y_label = "°C"), chart.bar(cities, [rain[c] each c in cities], title = "Rain in a year", y_label = "mm"), chart.scatter(w.column("temp"), w.column("rain"), title = "Is warmer wetter?", x_label = "°C", y_label = "mm of rain"), ] let body = "".join(["
" + c.svg() + "
" each c in charts]) write_text("weather.html", "Weather

A year of weather

" + body) each c in cities: let t = temps[c] print("{c}: {min(t)} to {max(t)} °C, {rain[c]} mm of rain") end print("wrote weather.html with {len(charts)} charts") end ``` ```text London: 5 to 19 °C, 603 mm of rain Oslo: -3 to 17 °C, 763 mm of rain wrote weather.html with 3 charts ``` Open `weather.html` in a browser. Each chart answers one question, with its title phrased as that question or its answer. The scatter chart's "Is warmer wetter?" is the kind of question to ask of any two measurements; a pattern in a scatter chart is a clue, though not proof that one causes the other. ### Exercise Add a fourth chart: the temperature *range* (warmest month minus coldest) for each city, as bars. Print the ranges. ```vyrn starter use vyrn.chart main: let temps = {"London": [5, 6, 9, 11, 14, 17, 19, 19, 16, 13, 9, 6], "Oslo": [-3, -3, 1, 6, 11, 15, 17, 16, 12, 7, 2, -2]} end ``` ```text expect {"London": 14, "Oslo": 20} ```

use vyrn.chart

main:

    let ranges = {c: max(t) - min(t) each c, t in temps.items()}
    chart.bar(ranges.keys(), ranges.values(), title = "Temperature range", y_label = "°C").save("ranges.png")

`chart.bar(ranges.keys(), ranges.values(), ...)`

lessons.title: you learned
lessons.text:
- `chart.bar`, `line`, `scatter`, `hist` and `pie` draw charts; `save`
  writes PNG or SVG; a map of series adds a legend.
- Choose the chart by the question: compare, change over time, relation,
  spread, share.
- Bars start at zero, label everything, keep it simple.
- `c.svg()` puts a chart straight into a web page.

days.title: Day 57: SQL for analysis
days.intro:
On Day 38 you used SQL to store and find records. SQL is also one of the
most-used tools for *analysis*: companies keep their data in databases,
and analysts ask it questions in SQL directly, without loading everything
into a program first. Today you learn the SQL that answers questions:
joins, grouping with conditions, subqueries and views. The project answers
questions about a small music shop's database.

lessons.title: The shop
lessons.text:
Three tables, linked by ids, so each fact is stored once:

```text
artists (id, name, country)
albums  (id, artist_id, title, year, price)
sales   (id, album_id, day, copies)
```

This helper builds the database for the examples; every example below
starts from it:

```vyrn
use vyrn.db

create shop() -> any:
    let conn = db.open(":memory:")
    conn.execute("create table artists (id integer primary key, name text, country text)")
    conn.execute("create table albums (id integer primary key, artist_id int, title text, year int, price real)")
    conn.execute("create table sales (id integer primary key, album_id int, day text, copies int)")
    conn.execute_many("insert into artists values (?, ?, ?)", [[1, "Nina Simone", "US"], [2, "Kraftwerk", "DE"], [3, "Björk", "IS"], [4, "Fela Kuti", "NG"]])
    conn.execute_many("insert into albums values (?, ?, ?, ?, ?)", [[1, 1, "Pastel Blues", 1965, 9.99], [2, 2, "Autobahn", 1974, 11.5], [3, 2, "Computer World", 1981, 12.0], [4, 3, "Homogenic", 1997, 10.0], [5, 4, "Zombie", 1976, 8.5], [6, 3, "Vespertine", 2001, 10.0]])
    conn.execute_many("insert into sales (album_id, day, copies) values (?, ?, ?)", [[1, "2026-11-01", 3], [2, "2026-11-01", 1], [3, "2026-11-02", 4], [4, "2026-11-02", 2], [1, "2026-11-03", 2], [5, "2026-11-03", 5], [3, "2026-11-04", 1], [4, "2026-11-04", 3]])
    return conn
end

main:
    let conn = shop()
    print(conn.tables())
    print(conn.value("select count(*) from albums"), "albums,", conn.value("select sum(copies) from sales"), "copies sold")
end
```

```text
["albums", "artists", "sales"]
6 albums, 21 copies sold
```

lessons.title: Joins in SQL
lessons.text:
`join ... on` combines rows from two tables where the condition holds,
just like Day 55's table joins. Give tables short names (`al` for albums)
to keep the query readable:

```vyrn
use vyrn.db

create shop() -> any:
    let conn = db.open(":memory:")
    conn.execute("create table artists (id integer primary key, name text, country text)")
    conn.execute("create table albums (id integer primary key, artist_id int, title text, year int, price real)")
    conn.execute_many("insert into artists values (?, ?, ?)", [[1, "Nina Simone", "US"], [2, "Kraftwerk", "DE"], [3, "Björk", "IS"], [4, "Fela Kuti", "NG"]])
    conn.execute_many("insert into albums values (?, ?, ?, ?, ?)", [[1, 1, "Pastel Blues", 1965, 9.99], [2, 2, "Autobahn", 1974, 11.5], [3, 2, "Computer World", 1981, 12.0], [4, 3, "Homogenic", 1997, 10.0], [5, 4, "Zombie", 1976, 8.5], [6, 3, "Vespertine", 2001, 10.0]])
    return conn
end

main:
    let conn = shop()
    each row in conn.query("select ar.name, al.title, al.year from albums al join artists ar on al.artist_id = ar.id where al.year < 1980 order by al.year"):
        print("{row["year"]}  {row["title"]:<15} {row["name"]}")
    end
end
```

```text
1965  Pastel Blues    Nina Simone
1974  Autobahn        Kraftwerk
1976  Zombie          Fela Kuti
```

`left join` keeps rows from the first table with no match, filling the
other table's columns with `null` (`none` in Vyrn), exactly like
`how = "left"`.

lessons.title: Grouping with conditions
lessons.text:
`group by` makes one row per group, and the aggregate functions (`sum`,
`count`, `avg`, `min`, `max`) summarise each. `having` filters the groups
after they're made, where `where` filters rows before:

```vyrn
use vyrn.db

create shop() -> any:
    let conn = db.open(":memory:")
    conn.execute("create table artists (id integer primary key, name text, country text)")
    conn.execute("create table albums (id integer primary key, artist_id int, title text, year int, price real)")
    conn.execute("create table sales (id integer primary key, album_id int, day text, copies int)")
    conn.execute_many("insert into artists values (?, ?, ?)", [[1, "Nina Simone", "US"], [2, "Kraftwerk", "DE"], [3, "Björk", "IS"], [4, "Fela Kuti", "NG"]])
    conn.execute_many("insert into albums values (?, ?, ?, ?, ?)", [[1, 1, "Pastel Blues", 1965, 9.99], [2, 2, "Autobahn", 1974, 11.5], [3, 2, "Computer World", 1981, 12.0], [4, 3, "Homogenic", 1997, 10.0], [5, 4, "Zombie", 1976, 8.5], [6, 3, "Vespertine", 2001, 10.0]])
    conn.execute_many("insert into sales (album_id, day, copies) values (?, ?, ?)", [[1, "2026-11-01", 3], [2, "2026-11-01", 1], [3, "2026-11-02", 4], [4, "2026-11-02", 2], [1, "2026-11-03", 2], [5, "2026-11-03", 5], [3, "2026-11-04", 1], [4, "2026-11-04", 3]])
    return conn
end

main:
    let conn = shop()
    let sql = "select ar.name, sum(s.copies) as copies, round(sum(s.copies * al.price), 2) as revenue from sales s join albums al on s.album_id = al.id join artists ar on al.artist_id = ar.id group by ar.name having sum(s.copies) >= 5 order by revenue desc"
    each row in conn.query(sql):
        print("{row["name"]:<12} {row["copies"]:>3} copies  £{row["revenue"]}")
    end
end
```

```text
Kraftwerk      6 copies  £71.5
Björk          5 copies  £50.0
Nina Simone    5 copies  £49.95
Fela Kuti      5 copies  £42.5
```

The query joins three tables, works out revenue per sale line, adds it up
per artist, and keeps artists who sold at least 5 copies. Read it in the
order the database does: `from` and `join` (which rows), `where` (which
rows to keep), `group by` (which groups), `having` (which groups to
keep), `select` (which columns), `order by`.

### Exercise

total, biggest first, and print the top row.


`conn.query_one(...)` gives the first row as a map.

lessons.title: Subqueries and views
lessons.text:
A **subquery** is a query inside a query, used as a value or a list.
"Albums that never sold" asks for albums whose id is *not in* the list of
ids in `sales`:

```vyrn
use vyrn.db

main:
    let conn = db.open(":memory:")
    conn.execute("create table albums (id integer primary key, title text, price real)")
    conn.execute("create table sales (album_id int, copies int)")
    conn.execute_many("insert into albums values (?, ?, ?)", [[1, "Pastel Blues", 9.99], [2, "Autobahn", 11.5], [6, "Vespertine", 10.0]])
    conn.execute_many("insert into sales values (?, ?)", [[1, 3], [2, 1]])
    print(conn.query("select title from albums where id not in (select album_id from sales)"))
    print(conn.query("select title, price from albums where price > (select avg(price) from albums)"))
end
```

```text
[{"title": "Vespertine"}]
[{"title": "Autobahn", "price": 11.5}]
```

A **view** saves a query under a name, so it can be used like a table.
Put a complicated join in a view once, and every later question gets
simpler:

```vyrn
use vyrn.db

main:
    let conn = db.open(":memory:")
    conn.execute("create table albums (id integer primary key, title text, price real)")
    conn.execute("create table sales (album_id int, copies int)")
    conn.execute_many("insert into albums values (?, ?, ?)", [[1, "Pastel Blues", 9.99], [2, "Autobahn", 11.5]])
    conn.execute_many("insert into sales values (?, ?)", [[1, 3], [2, 1], [1, 2]])
    conn.execute("create view sale_lines as select al.title, s.copies, s.copies * al.price as revenue from sales s join albums al on s.album_id = al.id")
    print(conn.query("select title, sum(revenue) as total from sale_lines group by title order by total desc"))
end
```

```text
[{"title": "Pastel Blues", "total": 49.95}, {"title": "Autobahn", "total": 11.5}]
```

lessons.title: Project: questions for the shop
lessons.text:
The owner's questions, each answered by one query against a view of every
sale line with its album and artist:

```vyrn
use vyrn.db

create shop() -> any:
    let conn = db.open(":memory:")
    conn.execute("create table artists (id integer primary key, name text, country text)")
    conn.execute("create table albums (id integer primary key, artist_id int, title text, year int, price real)")
    conn.execute("create table sales (id integer primary key, album_id int, day text, copies int)")
    conn.execute_many("insert into artists values (?, ?, ?)", [[1, "Nina Simone", "US"], [2, "Kraftwerk", "DE"], [3, "Björk", "IS"], [4, "Fela Kuti", "NG"]])
    conn.execute_many("insert into albums values (?, ?, ?, ?, ?)", [[1, 1, "Pastel Blues", 1965, 9.99], [2, 2, "Autobahn", 1974, 11.5], [3, 2, "Computer World", 1981, 12.0], [4, 3, "Homogenic", 1997, 10.0], [5, 4, "Zombie", 1976, 8.5], [6, 3, "Vespertine", 2001, 10.0]])
    conn.execute_many("insert into sales (album_id, day, copies) values (?, ?, ?)", [[1, "2026-11-01", 3], [2, "2026-11-01", 1], [3, "2026-11-02", 4], [4, "2026-11-02", 2], [1, "2026-11-03", 2], [5, "2026-11-03", 5], [3, "2026-11-04", 1], [4, "2026-11-04", 3]])
    conn.execute("create view lines as select s.day, s.copies, al.title, al.year, al.price, ar.name as artist, ar.country, s.copies * al.price as revenue from sales s join albums al on s.album_id = al.id join artists ar on al.artist_id = ar.id")
    return conn
end

const QUESTIONS = [
    ("Total revenue", "select round(sum(revenue), 2) as answer from lines"),
    ("Best-selling album", "select title as answer from lines group by title order by sum(copies) desc, title limit 1"),
    ("Revenue by decade", "select (year / 10) * 10 as decade, round(sum(revenue), 2) as revenue from lines group by decade order by decade"),
    ("Countries never sold", "select country as answer from artists where country not in (select country from lines)"),
    ("Average sale (copies)", "select round(avg(copies), 2) as answer from lines"),
]

main:
    let conn = shop()
    each question, sql in QUESTIONS:
        let rows = conn.query(sql)
        if len(rows) == 1 and "answer" in rows[0]:
            print("{question}: {rows[0]["answer"]}")
        else:
            print("{question}:")
            each r in rows:
                print("   ", r)
            end
        end
    end
end
```

```text
Total revenue: 213.95
Best-selling album: Computer World
Revenue by decade:
    {"decade": 1960, "revenue": 49.95}
    {"decade": 1970, "revenue": 54.0}
    {"decade": 1980, "revenue": 60.0}
    {"decade": 1990, "revenue": 50.0}
Countries never sold:
Average sale (copies): 2.63
```

"Countries never sold" has no rows: every country has sold something. Four
albums tie for best-selling with 5 copies each, so that query breaks the tie
by title (`order by sum(copies) desc, title`); without a tie-breaker, which
one comes first is up to the database. Watch for ties in any "top" question.
Keeping questions as data (a list of name and SQL) makes adding the next
question one line, and the same list could feed a web dashboard (the
capstone).

### Exercise

```vyrn starter
    conn.execute_many("insert into albums values (?, ?, ?)", [[1, 1, "Pastel Blues"], [2, 2, "Autobahn"], [3, 2, "Computer World"], [4, 3, "Homogenic"], [5, 2, "Radio-Activity"]])
end

```

lessons.title: you learned
lessons.text:
- `join ... on` combines tables in SQL; `left join` keeps unmatched rows.
- `group by` with `sum`, `count`, `avg`, `min`, `max`; `having` filters
  groups, `where` filters rows.
- Subqueries use one query's result inside another (`in (select ...)`,
  `> (select avg(...))`).
- Views name a query so it can be used like a table.

days.title: Day 58: Capstone: a data dashboard, part 1
days.intro:
A **dashboard** is a page that answers the questions people ask every day,
with the newest data, at a glance: this month's sales, the trend, the best
products. The next two days build one for a small online shop. Today: the
data and the analysis, as functions that take a date range and return
numbers and charts. Tomorrow: the web page, with filters, served live.

lessons.title: The data
lessons.text:
A real shop's orders would come from its database. For the course, a
function makes a year of believable orders: busier at weekends and in
December, with some products more popular than others. The `random.seed`
makes it the same every run:

```vyrn
use vyrn.db
use vyrn.random
use vyrn.time

const PRODUCTS = [("Tea", 4.5, 5), ("Coffee", 6.0, 4), ("Mug", 9.0, 2), ("Teapot", 24.0, 1)]
const REGIONS = ["North", "South", "East", "West"]

create make_shop(seed: int) -> any:
    random.seed(seed)
    let conn = db.open(":memory:")
    conn.execute("create table orders (id integer primary key, day text, region text, product text, qty int, price real)")
    var pool = []
    each name, price, weight in PRODUCTS:
        each _ in 0 until weight: pool.append((name, price))
    end
    var rows = []
    each d in 0 until 365:
        let moment = time.add(time.make(2025, 1, 1), days = d)
        let parts = time.date(moment)
        var orders = 3 + (2 if parts["weekday"] in ["Saturday", "Sunday"] else 0) + (4 if parts["month"] == 12 else 0)
        each _ in 0 until orders + random.int(0, 3):
            let name, price = random.choice(pool)
            rows.append([time.format(moment, "%Y-%m-%d"), random.choice(REGIONS), name, random.int(1, 3), price])
        end
    end
    conn.execute_many("insert into orders (day, region, product, qty, price) values (?, ?, ?, ?, ?)", rows)
    return conn
end

main:
    let conn = make_shop(42)
    print(conn.value("select count(*) from orders"), "orders")
    print(conn.query_one("select min(day) as first, max(day) as last from orders"))
    print(conn.query("select * from orders limit 2"))
end
```

```text
2001 orders
{"first": "2025-01-01", "last": "2025-12-31"}
[{"id": 1, "day": "2025-01-01", "region": "West", "product": "Tea", "qty": 2, "price": 4.5}, {"id": 2, "day": "2025-01-01", "region": "South", "product": "Tea", "qty": 2, "price": 4.5}]
```

Dates are stored as `yyyy-mm-dd` text, which sorts correctly as text, so
`between` and `order by` work on them directly.

lessons.title: The questions as functions
lessons.text:
Each number on the dashboard is one function, taking the connection and a
date range. Keeping the range a parameter is what makes filters possible
tomorrow:

```vyrn
use vyrn.db

create totals(conn: any, start: str, end_day: str) -> map:
    return conn.query_one("select count(*) as orders, coalesce(sum(qty * price), 0) as revenue, coalesce(round(avg(qty * price), 2), 0) as average from orders where day between ? and ?", [start, end_day])
end

create by_month(conn: any, start: str, end_day: str) -> list:
    return conn.query("select substr(day, 1, 7) as month, round(sum(qty * price), 2) as revenue from orders where day between ? and ? group by month order by month", [start, end_day])
end

create top_products(conn: any, start: str, end_day: str, n: int = 3) -> list:
    return conn.query("select product, sum(qty) as units, round(sum(qty * price), 2) as revenue from orders where day between ? and ? group by product order by revenue desc, product limit ?", [start, end_day, n])
end

main:
    let conn = db.open(":memory:")
    conn.execute("create table orders (id integer primary key, day text, region text, product text, qty int, price real)")
    conn.execute_many("insert into orders (day, region, product, qty, price) values (?, ?, ?, ?, ?)", [["2025-01-05", "North", "Tea", 2, 4.5], ["2025-01-20", "South", "Mug", 1, 9.0], ["2025-02-02", "North", "Teapot", 1, 24.0]])
    print(totals(conn, "2025-01-01", "2025-12-31"))
    print(totals(conn, "2030-01-01", "2030-12-31"))
    print(by_month(conn, "2025-01-01", "2025-12-31"))
    print(top_products(conn, "2025-01-01", "2025-01-31"))
end
```

```text
{"orders": 3, "revenue": 42.0, "average": 14.0}
{"orders": 0, "revenue": 0, "average": 0}
[{"month": "2025-01", "revenue": 18.0}, {"month": "2025-02", "revenue": 24.0}]
[{"product": "Mug", "units": 1, "revenue": 9.0}, {"product": "Tea", "units": 2, "revenue": 9.0}]
```

Two details to copy:

- `coalesce(x, 0)` gives 0 instead of `none` when there are no orders in
  the range, so an empty month shows "£0" instead of crashing the page.
- Every "top" query has a tie-breaker (`, product`): Mug and Tea both made
  £9.

### Exercise

Add `by_region(conn, start, end_day)`, giving each region's revenue,
biggest first.

```vyrn starter

create by_region(conn: any, start: str, end_day: str) -> list:
    return []
end

main:
    let conn = db.open(":memory:")
    conn.execute("create table orders (day text, region text, qty int, price real)")
    conn.execute_many("insert into orders values (?, ?, ?, ?)", [["2025-01-05", "North", 2, 4.5], ["2025-01-20", "South", 1, 9.0], ["2025-02-02", "North", 1, 24.0], ["2026-01-01", "East", 9, 9.0]])
    print(by_region(conn, "2025-01-01", "2025-12-31"))
end
```

```text expect
[{"region": "North", "revenue": 33.0}, {"region": "South", "revenue": 9.0}]
```

lessons.title: From numbers to charts
lessons.text:
Each chart is drawn from one of the functions, so a chart can never
disagree with the numbers beside it:

```vyrn
use vyrn.chart
use vyrn.db

create by_month(conn: any, start: str, end_day: str) -> list:
    return conn.query("select substr(day, 1, 7) as month, round(sum(qty * price), 2) as revenue from orders where day between ? and ? group by month order by month", [start, end_day])
end

create month_chart(rows: list) -> any:
    let labels = [r["month"][5:] each r in rows]
    return chart.bar(labels, [r["revenue"] each r in rows], title = "Revenue by month", x_label = "month", y_label = "£")
end

main:
    let conn = db.open(":memory:")
    conn.execute("create table orders (id integer primary key, day text, region text, product text, qty int, price real)")
    conn.execute_many("insert into orders (day, region, product, qty, price) values (?, ?, ?, ?, ?)", [["2025-01-05", "North", "Tea", 2, 4.5], ["2025-02-02", "North", "Teapot", 1, 24.0], ["2025-03-09", "East", "Mug", 3, 9.0]])
    let rows = by_month(conn, "2025-01-01", "2025-12-31")
    let svg = month_chart(rows).svg()
    print(svg.startswith("<svg"), [r["month"][5:] each r in rows])
end
```

```text
true ["01", "02", "03"]
```

lessons.title: The whole analysis
lessons.text:
Putting the functions together over the generated year gives the report
the dashboard will show, here printed as text:

```vyrn
use vyrn.db
use vyrn.random
use vyrn.time

const PRODUCTS = [("Tea", 4.5, 5), ("Coffee", 6.0, 4), ("Mug", 9.0, 2), ("Teapot", 24.0, 1)]
const REGIONS = ["North", "South", "East", "West"]

create make_shop(seed: int) -> any:
    random.seed(seed)
    let conn = db.open(":memory:")
    conn.execute("create table orders (id integer primary key, day text, region text, product text, qty int, price real)")
    var pool = []
    each name, price, weight in PRODUCTS:
        each _ in 0 until weight: pool.append((name, price))
    end
    var rows = []
    each d in 0 until 365:
        let moment = time.add(time.make(2025, 1, 1), days = d)
        let parts = time.date(moment)
        var orders = 3 + (2 if parts["weekday"] in ["Saturday", "Sunday"] else 0) + (4 if parts["month"] == 12 else 0)
        each _ in 0 until orders + random.int(0, 3):
            let name, price = random.choice(pool)
            rows.append([time.format(moment, "%Y-%m-%d"), random.choice(REGIONS), name, random.int(1, 3), price])
        end
    end
    conn.execute_many("insert into orders (day, region, product, qty, price) values (?, ?, ?, ?, ?)", rows)
    return conn
end

create totals(conn: any, start: str, end_day: str) -> map:
    return conn.query_one("select count(*) as orders, coalesce(sum(qty * price), 0) as revenue, coalesce(round(avg(qty * price), 2), 0) as average from orders where day between ? and ?", [start, end_day])
end

create by_month(conn: any, start: str, end_day: str) -> list:
    return conn.query("select substr(day, 1, 7) as month, round(sum(qty * price), 2) as revenue from orders where day between ? and ? group by month order by month", [start, end_day])
end

create top_products(conn: any, start: str, end_day: str, n: int = 3) -> list:
    return conn.query("select product, sum(qty) as units, round(sum(qty * price), 2) as revenue from orders where day between ? and ? group by product order by revenue desc, product limit ?", [start, end_day, n])
end

main:
    let conn = make_shop(42)
    let t = totals(conn, "2025-01-01", "2025-12-31")
    print("2025: {t["orders"]:,} orders, £{t["revenue"]:,.2f}, £{t["average"]:.2f} per order")
    let months = by_month(conn, "2025-01-01", "2025-12-31")
    let best = max(months, key = m => m["revenue"])
    let worst = min(months, key = m => m["revenue"])
    print("best month {best["month"]} (£{best["revenue"]:,.2f}), quietest {worst["month"]} (£{worst["revenue"]:,.2f})")
    each p in top_products(conn, "2025-01-01", "2025-12-31"):
        print("  {p["product"]:<7} {p["units"]:>5} units  £{p["revenue"]:>9,.2f}")
    end
    let q4 = totals(conn, "2025-10-01", "2025-12-31")
    print("last quarter: £{q4["revenue"]:,.2f} ({100 * q4["revenue"] / t["revenue"]:.0f}% of the year)")
end
```

```text
2025: 2,001 orders, £29,023.50, £14.50 per order
best month 2025-12 (£4,042.50), quietest 2025-05 (£2,023.50)
  Tea      1787 units  £ 8,041.50
  Coffee   1318 units  £ 7,908.00
  Teapot    307 units  £ 7,368.00
last quarter: £8,437.50 (29% of the year)
```

December is the best month, as the data was made to be. And the teapot,
sold in a sixth as many units as tea, brings in nearly as much money: the
sort of thing a dashboard exists to make obvious.

lessons.title: you built
lessons.text:
The analysis behind the dashboard: data in a database, one function per
question, each taking a date range, with safe answers for empty ranges and
tie-breakers for rankings, and charts drawn from the same functions.
Tomorrow it goes on the web.

days.title: Day 59: Capstone: a data dashboard, part 2
days.intro:
Yesterday's functions answer the questions; today they go on a web page.
The dashboard shows the key numbers as large tiles, a chart of revenue by
month and a table of top products, with a form to choose the date range
and region. Everything is drawn from the database on each request, so the
page is always up to date. You'll use routes and query parameters
(Day 48), templates (Day 44), charts as SVG (Day 56) and tests (Day 47).

lessons.title: Filters as query parameters
lessons.text:
A dashboard's filters belong in the address, `/?start=2025-10-01&region=North`,
so a filtered view can be bookmarked and shared. Each filter is a route
parameter with a default, and is checked before it reaches SQL. The
region filter becomes part of the `where` clause, always through `?`:

```vyrn
use vyrn.time

struct BadRequest:
    message: str
end

const REGIONS = ["North", "South", "East", "West"]

create check_filters(start: str, end_day: str, region: str) -> (str, str, str):
    each d in [start, end_day]:
        attempt:
            time.parse(d, "%Y-%m-%d")
        catch ValueError:
            fail BadRequest("dates are written yyyy-mm-dd, not {d}")
        end
    end
    if start > end_day: fail BadRequest("the start is after the end")
    if region != "all" and region not in REGIONS: fail BadRequest("no region called {region}")
    return (start, end_day, region)
end

create region_sql(region: str) -> (str, list):
    if region == "all": return ("", [])
    return (" and region = ?", [region])
end

main:
    print(check_filters("2025-01-01", "2025-03-31", "North"))
    print(region_sql("all"), region_sql("East"))
    each start, end_day, region in [("2025-13-01", "2025-12-31", "all"), ("2025-06-01", "2025-01-01", "all"), ("2025-01-01", "2025-12-31", "Mars")]:
        attempt:
            check_filters(start, end_day, region)
        catch BadRequest as e:
            print(e.message)
        end
    end
end
```

```text
("2025-01-01", "2025-03-31", "North")
("", []) (" and region = ?", ["East"])
dates are written yyyy-mm-dd, not 2025-13-01
the start is after the end
no region called Mars
```

`region_sql` returns a piece of SQL *and* its values: the SQL text only
ever contains `?`, never the region itself, so the filter can't be used
for SQL injection (Day 51).

lessons.title: The page
lessons.text:
The template has three parts: tiles of key numbers, the chart, and the table, with the filter form at the top. Values are formatted before they reach the template: ```vyrn use vyrn.template const PAGE = r'Dashboard

Shop dashboard

{{#each tiles}}
{{label}}
{{value}}
{{/each}}
{{{chart}}}{{#each products}}{{else}}{{/each}}
ProductUnitsRevenue
{{product}}{{units}}{{revenue}}
No sales in this range
' main: let html_text = template.render(PAGE, { "start": "2025-01-01", "end_day": "2025-12-31", "regions": [{"name": r, "selected": r == "North"} each r in ["all", "North", "South"]], "tiles": [{"label": "Revenue", "value": "£1,234.00"}, {"label": "Orders", "value": "56"}], "chart": "", "products": [], }) print(len(html_text) > 500, "No sales in this range" in html_text, "" in html_text) end ``` ```text true true true ```

lessons.title: Project: the dashboard
lessons.text:
The whole program: the shop data from yesterday, the questions with the region filter added, the route, and tests that drive it through `http.test` and read the page with `html.parse`: ```vyrn use vyrn.chart use vyrn.db use vyrn.html use vyrn.http use vyrn.random use vyrn.template use vyrn.time const PRODUCTS = [("Tea", 4.5, 5), ("Coffee", 6.0, 4), ("Mug", 9.0, 2), ("Teapot", 24.0, 1)] const REGIONS = ["North", "South", "East", "West"] const PAGE = r'Dashboard

Shop dashboard

{{#each tiles}}
{{label}}
{{value}}
{{/each}}
{{{chart}}}{{#each products}}{{else}}{{/each}}
{{product}}{{units}}{{revenue}}
No sales in this range
' struct BadRequest: message: str end create make_shop(seed: int) -> any: random.seed(seed) let conn = db.open(":memory:") conn.execute("create table orders (id integer primary key, day text, region text, product text, qty int, price real)") var pool = [] each name, price, weight in PRODUCTS: each _ in 0 until weight: pool.append((name, price)) end var rows = [] each d in 0 until 365: let moment = time.add(time.make(2025, 1, 1), days = d) let parts = time.date(moment) var orders = 3 + (2 if parts["weekday"] in ["Saturday", "Sunday"] else 0) + (4 if parts["month"] == 12 else 0) each _ in 0 until orders + random.int(0, 3): let name, price = random.choice(pool) rows.append([time.format(moment, "%Y-%m-%d"), random.choice(REGIONS), name, random.int(1, 3), price]) end end conn.execute_many("insert into orders (day, region, product, qty, price) values (?, ?, ?, ?, ?)", rows) return conn end create check_filters(start: str, end_day: str, region: str): each d in [start, end_day]: attempt: time.parse(d, "%Y-%m-%d") catch ValueError: fail BadRequest("dates are written yyyy-mm-dd, not {d}") end end if start > end_day: fail BadRequest("the start is after the end") if region != "all" and region not in REGIONS: fail BadRequest("no region called {region}") end ## Runs `sql` (with `where {range}` in it) for the date range and region. create ask(conn: any, sql: str, start: str, end_day: str, region: str) -> list: var where = "day between ? and ?" var values = [start, end_day] if region != "all": where += " and region = ?" values.append(region) end return conn.query(sql.replace("\{range}", where), values) end route GET "/" (conn, start: str = "2025-01-01", end_day: str = "2025-12-31", region: str = "all"): check_filters(start, end_day, region) let t = ask(conn, "select count(*) as orders, coalesce(sum(qty * price), 0) as revenue from orders where \{range}", start, end_day, region)[0] let months = ask(conn, "select substr(day, 1, 7) as month, sum(qty * price) as revenue from orders where \{range} group by month order by month", start, end_day, region) let products = ask(conn, "select product, sum(qty) as units, sum(qty * price) as revenue from orders where \{range} group by product order by revenue desc, product limit 4", start, end_day, region) let average = t["revenue"] / t["orders"] if t["orders"] > 0 else 0 let chart_svg = chart.bar([m["month"][5:] each m in months], [m["revenue"] each m in months], title = "Revenue by month", y_label = "£").svg() if months else "" return template.render(PAGE, { "start": start, "end_day": end_day, "regions": [{"name": r, "selected": r == region} each r in ["all"] + REGIONS], "tiles": [{"label": "Revenue", "value": "£{t["revenue"]:,.2f}"}, {"label": "Orders", "value": "{t["orders"]:,}"}, {"label": "Average order", "value": "£{average:.2f}"}], "chart": chart_svg, "products": [p | {"revenue": "£{p["revenue"]:,.2f}"} each p in products], }) end create tiles(page: any) -> map: let labels = [d.text each d in page.select(".tile .label")] let values = [d.text each d in page.select(".tile .big")] return dict(zip(labels, values)) end create test_the_year_at_a_glance(): let page = html.parse(http.test("GET", "/").text) let t = tiles(page) assert(t["Orders"] == "2,001") assert(len(page.select("svg")) == 1) assert(page.select_one("td").text == "Tea") end create test_filters_change_the_numbers(): let all = tiles(html.parse(http.test("GET", "/").text)) let north = tiles(html.parse(http.test("GET", "/?region=North").text)) assert(all["Revenue"] != north["Revenue"]) let page = html.parse(http.test("GET", "/?region=North").text) assert(page.select_one("option[selected]").text == "North") end create test_an_empty_range_still_works(): let page = html.parse(http.test("GET", "/?start=2030-01-01&end_day=2030-12-31").text) assert(tiles(page)["Orders"] == "0") assert(page.select_one("td").text == "No sales in this range") assert(len(page.select("svg")) == 0) end create test_bad_filters_are_refused(): assert(http.test("GET", "/?region=Mars").status == 400) assert(http.test("GET", "/?start=2025-12-01&end_day=2025-01-01").status == 400) assert(http.test("GET", "/?region=North%27%20or%201=1--").status == 400) end main: http.provide("conn", make_shop(42)) each test in [test_the_year_at_a_glance, test_filters_change_the_numbers, test_an_empty_range_still_works, test_bad_filters_are_refused]: test() print("ok", test.name) end let page = html.parse(http.test("GET", "/?start=2025-12-01&end_day=2025-12-31®ion=East").text) print(tiles(page)) end ``` ```text ok test_the_year_at_a_glance ok test_filters_change_the_numbers ok test_an_empty_range_still_works ok test_bad_filters_are_refused {"Revenue": "£1,119.00", "Orders": "77", "Average order": "£14.53"} ``` The last test tries an SQL injection through the region filter; it never reaches SQL, because only the four real regions are allowed, and even if it did, `?` would make it harmless. `ask` builds the `where` part of each query in one place, so the date range and region filter can't be applied to one number on the page and forgotten for another. To use it, replace `make_shop(42)` with the real database and serve it (Day 52): ```vyrn check use vyrn.db use vyrn.http main: http.provide("conn", db.open("shop.db")) http.serve(port = 8000) end ``` ### Exercise Add a tile for the best day (the day with the most revenue) in the range. Write `best_day(rows)`, which takes the result of a "revenue per day" query and gives `"2025-12-20 (£96.00)"`, or `"none"` when there are no rows. ```vyrn starter create best_day(rows: list) -> str: return "none" end main: print(best_day([{"day": "2025-12-19", "revenue": 81.0}, {"day": "2025-12-20", "revenue": 96.0}])) print(best_day([])) end ``` ```text expect 2025-12-20 (£96.00) none ```

lessons.title: you built
lessons.text:
A live, filterable dashboard: numbers, a chart and a table from one
database, filters in the address checked before use, one place that
applies them, and tests that read the real page. That's the shape of
most internal tools in most companies. Ideas to take it further:

- Compare with the previous period: "£1,018 (+12% on November)".
- A download link giving the filtered rows as CSV (`t.to_csv()`).
- Refresh the numbers live with server-sent events (`stream` routes).

days.title: Day 60: Types and `vyrn check`
days.intro:
Since Day 6 you've been writing `name: str` and `-> int` on functions. This
unit is about the parts of Vyrn that make big programs safe and fast, and
types come first. Today you learn what Vyrn checks before your program
runs, how to describe lists, maps, optional values and functions as types,
and how to use `vyrn check` to find mistakes in a whole project at once.
The project is adding types to an untyped program and fixing what the
checker finds.

lessons.title: Checked before it runs
lessons.text:
Every `vyrn run` first **checks** the program: if a function wants text and
gets a number, the program doesn't start at all:

```vyrn
create shout(text: str) -> str:
    return text.upper() + "!"
end

main:
    print("this line never runs")
    print(shout(42))
end
```

```text
error: argument `text` of `shout` is str, but this is int
```

Python would print the first line and then crash on the second; C++ and
Java would refuse to compile. Vyrn refuses to run, which is the same thing
without a separate compile step. A mistake found before the program runs
can't reach the person using it.

`vyrn check file.vyrn` checks without running, and `vyrn check` on its own
checks a whole project: every problem in every file, with the line and a
hint. Run it before you commit.

lessons.title: Where types come from
lessons.text:
You don't have to write types everywhere. Vyrn works them out from values:

| You write | Vyrn knows |
|---|---|
| `let n = 5` | `n` is `int` |
| `let names = ["Ada", "Alan"]` | `names` is a list of `str` |
| `let p = Point(1, 2)` | `p` is a `Point` |
| `let total = price * 1.2` | `total` is `float` |

So mistakes are found even without annotations:

```vyrn
main:
    let names = ["Ada", "Alan"]
    let first = names[0]
    print(first + 1)
end
```

```text
error: cannot apply `+` to str and int
```

Where you *do* write types, they are promises the checker holds you to.
Function parameters and results are the important ones: they are the
contract between a function and everyone who calls it.

```vyrn
create half(n: int) -> int:
    return n / 2
end

main:
    print(half(7))
end
```

```text
error: `half` returns int, but this is float
```

`/` always gives a `float` (`7 / 2` is `3.5`). The function promised an
`int`, so the checker caught the broken promise. Fix it by changing the
promise (`-> float`) or the code (`n // 2`).

A `var` without a type can hold anything, like a Python variable; give it a
type and it can only hold that type:

```vyrn
main:
    var anything = 5
    anything = "five"
    var count: int = 5
    count = "five"
end
```

```text
error: `count` is int, but this is str
```

### Exercise

The function promises a `str` but can end without returning one (when the
list is empty). Make it always return text: `"nobody"` for an empty list.

```vyrn starter
create first_name(names: list[str]) -> str?:
    if names: return names[0]
    return none
end

main:
    print(first_name(["Ada", "Alan"]), first_name([]))
end
```

```text expect
Ada nobody
```

exercise.starter:
create first_name(names: list[str]) -> str?:
    if names: return names[0]
    return none
end

main:
    print(first_name(["Ada", "Alan"]), first_name([]))
end
exercise.solution:
create first_name(names: list[str]) -> str:
    if names: return names[0]
    return "nobody"
end

main:
    print(first_name(["Ada", "Alan"]), first_name([]))
end
hints: change the result type to `-> str` and return `"nobody"` instead of `none`.

lessons.title: Describing types
lessons.text:
| Type | Means | Example |
|---|---|---|
| `int`, `float`, `str`, `bool` | the basic values | `age: int` |
| `list[int]` (or `[int]`) | a list of ints | `scores: list[int]` |
| `map[str, float]` (or `{str: float}`) | a map from text to floats | `prices: map[str, float]` |
| `(int, str)` | a tuple: an int then a text | `-> (int, str)` |
| `int?` | an int, or `none` | `-> int?` |
| `Point` | a struct or object you declared | `p: Point` |
| `(int) -> str` | a function taking an int and giving text | `f: (int) -> str` |
| `any` | anything: switches checking off | `data: any` |

The item types are checked too:

```vyrn
main:
    let scores: list[int] = [90, 85]
    scores.append(77)
    scores.append("ninety")
end
```

```text
error: an item of this list[int] is int, but this is str
```

lessons.title: Optional values
lessons.text:
`int?` says "an int, or `none`". A function that might not find anything
returns one. The checker won't let you use it as an int until you've
checked:

```vyrn
create find(names: list[str], who: str) -> int?:
    each i, n in enumerate(names):
        if n == who: return i
    end
    return none
end

main:
    let i = find(["Ada", "Alan"], "Alan")
    print(i + 1)
end
```

```text
error: `i` may be none, so it cannot be used in arithmetic
```

After `if i != none:`, the checker knows it's an int inside the `if`. Or
give a default with `??`:

```vyrn
create find(names: list[str], who: str) -> int?:
    each i, n in enumerate(names):
        if n == who: return i
    end
    return none
end

main:
    let i = find(["Ada", "Alan"], "Alan")
    if i != none: print("position", i + 1)
    let j = find(["Ada"], "Grace") ?? -1
    print(j)
end
```

```text
position 2
-1
```

This removes the most common crash in Python and Java, using a missing
value (`NoneType has no attribute`, `NullPointerException`), by making you
handle it where it can happen. Day 61 has more tools for it.

lessons.title: Function types
lessons.text:
A function that takes another function says what kind with a function
type. A lambda passed to it gets its parameter types from it, so its body
is checked too:

```vyrn
create apply_all(xs: list[int], f: (int) -> int) -> list[int]:
    return [f(x) each x in xs]
end

create square(n: int) -> int:
    return n * n
end

main:
    print(apply_all([1, 2, 3], square))
    print(apply_all([1, 2, 3], n => n * 10))
    print(apply_all([1, 2, 3], n => n + "!"))
end
```

```text
error: cannot apply `+` to int and str
```

Here `n` in the last lambda is an `int` because `apply_all` said so, and
`int + str` is caught.

### Exercise

Write `count_if(xs, test)`, typed: it takes a list of ints and a function
from int to bool, and gives how many items pass the test.

```vyrn starter
create count_if(xs: list[int], test: any) -> any:
    return 0
end

main:
    print(count_if([3, 8, 12, 5], n => n > 4), count_if([], n => true))
end
```

```text expect
3 0
```

exercise.starter:
create count_if(xs: list[int], test: any) -> any:
    return 0
end

main:
    print(count_if([3, 8, 12, 5], n => n > 4), count_if([], n => true))
end
exercise.solution:
create count_if(xs: list[int], test: (int) -> bool) -> int:
    return len([x each x in xs if test(x)])
end

main:
    print(count_if([3, 8, 12, 5], n => n > 4), count_if([], n => true))
end
hints: `test: (int) -> bool` and `-> int`.
`len([x each x in xs if test(x)])`

lessons.title: Strict functions
lessons.text:
Ordinary functions may leave out types, which is handy while you're
exploring. A `strict create` must type every parameter and its result and
can't use `any`, so nothing in it goes unchecked. Strict, fully typed
functions are also the ones Vyrn can compile to machine code (Day 75):

```vyrn
strict create average(xs: list[float]) -> float:
    if not xs: return 0.0
    return sum(xs) / len(xs)
end

main:
    print(average([2.0, 4.0, 9.0]))
end
```

```text
5.0
```

```vyrn
strict create average(xs) -> float:
    return sum(xs) / len(xs)
end

main:
    print(average([1.0]))
end
```

```text
error: parameter `xs` needs a type in strict code
```

A good habit for growing programs: explore without types, then add types
to every function that others call, and make the busiest ones `strict`.

lessons.title: Project: typing an old program
lessons.text:
Here is a small program written without types, the way you'd write a quick
script. It runs, mostly:

```vyrn
create total(items):
    var sum = 0
    each item in items:
        sum += item["price"] * item["qty"]
    end
    return sum
end

create cheapest(items):
    var best = none
    each item in items:
        if best == none or item["price"] < best["price"]: best = item
    end
    return best
end

main:
    let basket = [{"name": "tea", "price": 3.5, "qty": 2}, {"name": "cake", "price": 2.25, "qty": 1}]
    print(total(basket), cheapest(basket)["name"])
    print(cheapest([])["name"])
end
```

```text
9.25 cake
error: TypeError: none cannot be indexed
```

The crash happens only when the basket is empty, which a quick test would
miss. Adding types, with a `struct` instead of maps, makes the checker
point at the problem before it can happen:

```vyrn
struct Item:
    name: str
    price: float
    qty: int
end

create total(items: list[Item]) -> float:
    return sum([i.price * i.qty each i in items])
end

create cheapest(items: list[Item]) -> Item?:
    if not items: return none
    return min(items, key = i => i.price)
end

main:
    let basket = [Item("tea", 3.5, 2), Item("cake", 2.25, 1)]
    print(total(basket), cheapest(basket)?.name)
    print(cheapest([])?.name ?? "the basket is empty")
end
```

```text
9.25 cake
the basket is empty
```

What changed, and why it's better:

- `Item` is a struct, so `item["prise"]` (a typo) would be an error found
  by the checker, not a `KeyError` found by a user.
- `cheapest` says it returns `Item?`, so every caller *must* deal with the
  empty case: `cheapest([]).name` would be an error ("may be none"). The
  crash from the untyped version can't be written any more.
- `total` and `cheapest` say what they take, so calling them with the wrong
  thing is caught where it is called.

`?.name` gives `none` instead of failing when the value is `none`, and `??`
gives a default (Day 61).

### Exercise

Type this function fully: it takes a map from names to scores and a pass
mark, and gives the names that passed, sorted.

```vyrn starter
create passed(scores, mark):
    return sorted([name each name, score in scores.items() if score >= mark])
end

main:
    print(passed({"Ada": 81, "Alan": 64, "Grace": 90}, 70))
end
```

```text expect
["Ada", "Grace"]
```

exercise.starter:
create passed(scores, mark):
    return sorted([name each name, score in scores.items() if score >= mark])
end

main:
    print(passed({"Ada": 81, "Alan": 64, "Grace": 90}, 70))
end
exercise.solution:
create passed(scores: map[str, int], mark: int) -> list[str]:
    return sorted([name each name, score in scores.items() if score >= mark])
end

main:
    print(passed({"Ada": 81, "Alan": 64, "Grace": 90}, 70))
end
hints: `scores: map[str, int]`, `mark: int`, and the result is `list[str]`.

lessons.title: you learned
lessons.text:
- Every run is checked first; `vyrn check` checks a whole project without
  running it.
- Types come from values; written types on parameters, results and `var`s
  are promises the checker enforces.
- `list[int]`, `map[str, float]`, `(int, str)`, `int?`, `(int) -> str` and
  `any` describe values; item types are checked too.
- An optional value must be checked (`if x != none`, `??`) before use.
- `strict create` functions are fully typed; type what others call, and
  make the busy parts strict.

days.title: Day 61: Enums, patterns and `none`
days.intro:
Many values can only be one of a few things. A traffic light is red, amber
or green. A payment is pending, paid or refunded. A shape is a circle *with
a radius* or a rectangle *with a width and height*. An **enum** says
exactly which forms a value can take, and `when` with **patterns** handles
each form, with the checker making sure none is forgotten. Today you also
finish the story of `none` from yesterday. The project is a parser that
turns typed commands into enums.

lessons.title: Enums
lessons.text:
An `enum` lists its **variants**. You name one with the enum's name, a dot,
and the variant:

```vyrn
enum Light:
    Red
    Amber
    Green
end

create next(light: Light) -> Light:
    when light:
        is Light.Red: return Light.Green
        is Light.Green: return Light.Amber
        is Light.Amber: return Light.Red
    end
end

main:
    var light = Light.Red
    each _ in 0 until 4:
        print(light)
        light = next(light)
    end
    print(light == Light.Red)
end
```

```text
Light.Red
Light.Green
Light.Amber
Light.Red
false
```

Why not just use text, `"red"`? Because `"rde"` is also text: a typo would
be a silent bug. `Light.Rde` is an error before the program runs.

And if a `when` forgets a variant, the checker says which:

```vyrn
enum Light:
    Red
    Amber
    Green
end

create must_stop(light: Light) -> bool:
    when light:
        is Light.Red: return true
        is Light.Green: return false
    end
end

main:
    print(must_stop(Light.Amber))
end
```

```text
error: this `when` does not handle `Light.Amber`
```

Add a variant to an enum later, and the checker finds every `when` that
must now handle it. In a big program that's a lifesaver.

lessons.title: Variants that carry data
lessons.text:
A variant can carry values, like a small struct. Each variant has its own:

```vyrn
enum Shape:
    Circle(radius: float)
    Rect(width: float, height: float)
    Point
end

create area(s: Shape) -> float:
    when s:
        is Shape.Circle(r): return 3.14159 * r * r
        is Shape.Rect(w, h): return w * h
        is Shape.Point: return 0.0
    end
end

main:
    let shapes = [Shape.Circle(1.0), Shape.Rect(2.0, 3.5), Shape.Point]
    each s in shapes:
        print(s, area(s))
    end
end
```

```text
Shape.Circle(radius=1.0) 3.14159
Shape.Rect(width=2.0, height=3.5) 7.0
Shape.Point 0.0
```

`is Shape.Rect(w, h)` does two things: checks the variant, and takes its
values out into `w` and `h`. This is what other languages call a *tagged
union*, *sum type* or *sealed class*: one type, several shapes, and the
compiler knows them all.

### Exercise

Add a `Triangle(base: float, height: float)` variant (area: half of base
times height) and handle it in `area`.

```vyrn starter
enum Shape:
    Circle(radius: float)
    Rect(width: float, height: float)
end

create area(s: Shape) -> float:
    when s:
        is Shape.Circle(r): return 3.14159 * r * r
        is Shape.Rect(w, h): return w * h
    end
end

main:
    print(area(Shape.Rect(2.0, 3.0)))
end
```

```text expect
6.0
12.0
```

exercise.starter:
enum Shape:
    Circle(radius: float)
    Rect(width: float, height: float)
end

create area(s: Shape) -> float:
    when s:
        is Shape.Circle(r): return 3.14159 * r * r
        is Shape.Rect(w, h): return w * h
    end
end

main:
    print(area(Shape.Rect(2.0, 3.0)))
end
exercise.solution:
enum Shape:
    Circle(radius: float)
    Rect(width: float, height: float)
    Triangle(base: float, height: float)
end

create area(s: Shape) -> float:
    when s:
        is Shape.Circle(r): return 3.14159 * r * r
        is Shape.Rect(w, h): return w * h
        is Shape.Triangle(b, h): return b * h / 2
    end
end

main:
    print(area(Shape.Rect(2.0, 3.0)))
    print(area(Shape.Triangle(4.0, 6.0)))
end
hints: add the variant to the enum, then `is Shape.Triangle(b, h): return b * h / 2`.
in `main`, also print `area(Shape.Triangle(4.0, 6.0))`.

lessons.title: Patterns
lessons.text:
`when` can match much more than enum variants. Each `is` line is a
**pattern**, tried top to bottom; the first that fits wins:

| Pattern | Matches |
|---|---|
| `is 0`, `is "hi"` | that exact value |
| `is 1 to 9` | a number from 1 to 9 |
| `is "y" or "yes"` | any of several |
| `is (x, y)` | a tuple of two, naming its parts |
| `is [first, rest...]` | a list with at least one item |
| `is []` | an empty list |
| `is Shape.Rect(w, h)` | that variant, naming its values |
| `is n if n > 100` | anything, but only if the **guard** after `if` is true |
| `is _` or `else:` | anything else |

```vyrn
create describe(x: any) -> str:
    when x:
        is 0: return "zero"
        is 1 to 9: return "between 1 and 9"
        is n if n is int and n < 0: return "negative"
        is "y" or "yes": return "agreement"
        is []: return "an empty list"
        is [only]: return "a list of just {only}"
        is [first, rest...]: return "a list starting {first}, {len(rest)} more"
        is (a, b): return "a pair: {a} and {b}"
        else: return "something else"
    end
end

main:
    each value in [0, 7, -3, "yes", [], [4], [1, 2, 3], ("x", 2), 12.5]:
        print(describe(value))
    end
end
```

```text
zero
between 1 and 9
negative
agreement
an empty list
a list of just 4
a list starting 1, 2 more
a pair: x and 2
something else
```

Order matters: `is 0` must come before a pattern that would also match 0.

### Exercise

Write `fizz(n)` with a single `when` on the tuple `(n % 3, n % 5)`:
`(0, 0)` is `"FizzBuzz"`, `(0, _)` is `"Fizz"`, `(_, 0)` is `"Buzz"`, and
anything else is the number as text.

```vyrn starter
create fizz(n: int) -> str:
    return str(n)
end

main:
    print([fizz(n) each n in 1 to 15])
end
```

```text expect
["1", "2", "Fizz", "4", "Buzz", "Fizz", "7", "8", "Fizz", "Buzz", "11", "Fizz", "13", "14", "FizzBuzz"]
```

exercise.starter:
create fizz(n: int) -> str:
    return str(n)
end

main:
    print([fizz(n) each n in 1 to 15])
end
exercise.solution:
create fizz(n: int) -> str:
    when (n % 3, n % 5):
        is (0, 0): return "FizzBuzz"
        is (0, _): return "Fizz"
        is (_, 0): return "Buzz"
        else: return str(n)
    end
end

main:
    print([fizz(n) each n in 1 to 15])
end
hints: `when (n % 3, n % 5):` then `is (0, 0): return "FizzBuzz"`.
`_` in a pattern matches anything without naming it.

lessons.title: `if let`: one pattern
lessons.text:
When you only care about one variant, `if let` tries a single pattern and
names its parts if it fits:

```vyrn
enum Reply:
    Found(value: int)
    Missing(reason: str)
end

main:
    each reply in [Reply.Found(42), Reply.Missing("no such user")]:
        if let Reply.Found(v) = reply:
            print("got", v)
        else:
            print("nothing:", reply)
        end
    end
end
```

```text
got 42
nothing: Reply.Missing(reason="no such user")
```

An enum like `Reply` is a good way to return "a value, or why there isn't
one": the caller can't use the value without first checking which it got.

lessons.title: Living with `none`
lessons.text:
Yesterday you met `int?`: a value that may be `none`, which must be checked
before it's used. Three tools make the checking short:

| Write | Means |
|---|---|
| `if x != none:` | inside, `x` is known not to be none |
| `x ?? fallback` | `x`, or `fallback` when `x` is none |
| `x?.name`, `x?.method()` | `none` if `x` is none, otherwise `x.name` |

```vyrn
struct User:
    name: str
    email: str?
end

create find(users: list[User], name: str) -> User?:
    each u in users:
        if u.name == name: return u
    end
    return none
end

main:
    let users = [User("ada", "ada@mail.com"), User("alan", none)]
    print(find(users, "ada")?.email)
    print(find(users, "alan")?.email ?? "no email")
    print(find(users, "grace")?.email ?? "no such user")
    print(find(users, "grace")?.email?.upper())
end
```

```text
ada@mail.com
no email
no such user
none
```

`?.` stops at the first `none` and gives `none` for the whole chain; `??`
then turns it into something useful. Without them, each step would need its
own `if`.

### Exercise

Write `city_of(people, name)`, giving the person's city in capitals, or
`"UNKNOWN"` when there's no such person or they have no address. Use `?.`
and `??`, no `if`.

```vyrn starter
struct Address:
    city: str
end

struct Person:
    name: str
    address: Address?
end

create find(people: list[Person], name: str) -> Person?:
    each p in people:
        if p.name == name: return p
    end
    return none
end

create city_of(people: list[Person], name: str) -> str:
    return "UNKNOWN"
end

main:
    let people = [Person("ada", Address("London")), Person("alan", none)]
    print(city_of(people, "ada"), city_of(people, "alan"), city_of(people, "grace"))
end
```

```text expect
LONDON UNKNOWN UNKNOWN
```
