```vyrn
        let _, m = merge_count(xs)
        print("{n:>6} {bubble_count(xs):>9,} {m:>9,}")
    end
end
```

```text
     n    bubble     merge
    10        45        23
   100     4,950       537
  1000   499,500     8,701
  2000 1,999,000    19,421
```

Doubling *n* from 1,000 to 2,000 quadruples bubble sort's work (n²) but
only a little more than doubles merge sort's (n log n). At a million items,
bubble sort would need half a million million comparisons; merge sort,
about twenty million.

### Exercise

Two loops over the same list are O(n) each; a loop *inside* a loop is
O(n²). This function finds whether any two numbers add up to a target,
with nested loops. Rewrite it to be O(n) with a set: for each number, check
whether the number it needs has already been seen.

```vyrn starter
create has_pair(xs: list[int], target: int) -> bool:
    each i in 0 until len(xs):
        each j in i + 1 until len(xs):
            if xs[i] + xs[j] == target: return true
        end
    end
    return false
end

main:
    print(has_pair([8, 3, 5, 11], 16), has_pair([8, 3, 5, 11], 9), has_pair([], 1))
end
```

```text expect
true false false
```

exercise.starter:
create has_pair(xs: list[int], target: int) -> bool:
    each i in 0 until len(xs):
        each j in i + 1 until len(xs):
            if xs[i] + xs[j] == target: return true
        end
    end
    return false
end

main:
    print(has_pair([8, 3, 5, 11], 16), has_pair([8, 3, 5, 11], 9), has_pair([], 1))
end
exercise.solution:
create has_pair(xs: list[int], target: int) -> bool:
    var seen = set()
    each x in xs:
        if target - x in seen: return true
        seen.add(x)
    end
    return false
end

main:
    print(has_pair([8, 3, 5, 11], 16), has_pair([8, 3, 5, 11], 9), has_pair([], 1))
end
hints: `var seen = set()`; for each `x`, if `target - x in seen` you've found a pair; then `seen.add(x)`.

lessons.title: you learned
lessons.text:
- Measure algorithms by how their step count grows with the input size.
- Linear search is O(n); binary search on sorted data is O(log n).
- Big-O: O(1), O(log n), O(n), O(n log n), O(n²), O(2ⁿ). Map and set
  lookups are O(1); `in` on a list is O(n).
- Bubble sort is O(n²); merge sort and quicksort divide and conquer in
  O(n log n).
- Dynamic programming solves overlapping sub-problems once and remembers
  them.

days.title: Day 69: Capstone: an expression evaluator
days.intro:
This unit's capstone builds a small piece of a programming language: a
calculator that understands `2 * (3 + 4) - x / 2`, with variables and
clear error messages. It's how `vyrn` itself works, in miniature: text
becomes **tokens**, tokens become a **tree**, and the tree is **evaluated**.
You'll use enums and patterns (Day 61), types (Day 60), traits (Day 62),
recursion (Day 68) and your own errors (Day 30).

lessons.title: Tokens
lessons.text:
The first step reads the text and cuts it into **tokens**: numbers,
names, operators and brackets, skipping spaces. Each kind of token is an
enum variant:

```vyrn
enum Token:
    Num(value: float)
    Name(text: str)
    Op(symbol: str)
end

struct SyntaxError:
    message: str
end

create tokenize(text: str) -> list[Token]:
    var tokens = []
    var i = 0
    loop i < len(text):
        let c = text[i]
        if c == " ":
            i += 1
        else if c.isdigit() or c == ".":
            var j = i
            loop j < len(text) and (text[j].isdigit() or text[j] == "."): j += 1
            tokens.append(Token.Num(float(text[i:j])))
            i = j
        else if c.isalpha():
            var j = i
            loop j < len(text) and text[j].isalnum(): j += 1
            tokens.append(Token.Name(text[i:j]))
            i = j
        else if c in "+-*/^()":
            tokens.append(Token.Op(c))
            i += 1
        else:
            fail SyntaxError("I don't know the character '{c}' at position {i + 1}")
        end
    end
    return tokens
end

main:
    print(tokenize("2 * (x + 3.5)"))
    attempt:
        tokenize("2 # 3")
    catch SyntaxError as e:
        print(e.message)
    end
end
```

```text
[Token.Num(value=2.0), Token.Op(symbol="*"), Token.Op(symbol="("), Token.Name(text="x"), Token.Op(symbol="+"), Token.Num(value=3.5), Token.Op(symbol=")")]
I don't know the character '#' at position 3
```

lessons.title: The tree
lessons.text:
`2 * (x + 3.5)` isn't really a flat list: the `+` happens first, and its
result is multiplied. A **syntax tree** shows that structure. Each node is
a number, a variable, or an operation with the nodes it combines:

```text
      *
     / \
    2   +
       / \
      x   3.5
```

As an enum, a node that holds other nodes is a variant with node fields:

```vyrn
enum Node:
    Num(value: float)
    Var(name: str)
    Neg(inner: Node)
    BinOp(op: str, left: Node, right: Node)
end

create show(n: Node) -> str:
    when n:
        is Node.Num(v): return str(v)
        is Node.Var(name): return name
        is Node.Neg(inner): return "-{show(inner)}"
        is Node.BinOp(op, a, b): return "({show(a)} {op} {show(b)})"
    end
end

main:
    let tree = Node.BinOp("*", Node.Num(2.0), Node.BinOp("+", Node.Var("x"), Node.Num(3.5)))
    print(show(tree))
end
```

```text
(2.0 * (x + 3.5))
```

`show` is recursive because the tree is: to show an operation, show its
two sides. Almost every function on a tree has this shape.

lessons.title: Parsing: from tokens to a tree
lessons.text:
The **parser** builds the tree, and it must know that `*` binds tighter
than `+`. The classic method is **recursive descent**: one function per
level of priority, each calling the next level for its parts:

| Function | Handles | Example |
|---|---|---|
| `expression` | `+` and `-`, between terms | `a + b - c` |
| `term` | `*` and `/`, between factors | `a * b / c` |
| `power` | `^`, right to left | `2 ^ 3 ^ 2` |
| `factor` | a number, a name, `-x`, or `( expression )` | `3`, `x`, `(a + b)` |

```vyrn
enum Token:
    Num(value: float)
    Name(text: str)
    Op(symbol: str)
end

enum Node:
    Num(value: float)
    Var(name: str)
    Neg(inner: Node)
    BinOp(op: str, left: Node, right: Node)
end

struct SyntaxError:
    message: str
end

object Parser:
    tokens: list[Token]
    pos: int = 0

    create peek(self) -> str:
        if self.pos >= len(self.tokens): return "end"
        if let Token.Op(s) = self.tokens[self.pos]: return s
        return "value"
    end

    create expression(self) -> Node:
        var left = self.term()
        loop self.peek() in ["+", "-"]:
            let op = self.peek()
            self.pos += 1
            left = Node.BinOp(op, left, self.term())
        end
        return left
    end

    create term(self) -> Node:
        var left = self.power()
        loop self.peek() in ["*", "/"]:
            let op = self.peek()
            self.pos += 1
            left = Node.BinOp(op, left, self.power())
        end
        return left
    end

    create power(self) -> Node:
        let base = self.factor()
        if self.peek() == "^":
            self.pos += 1
            return Node.BinOp("^", base, self.power())
        end
        return base
    end

    create factor(self) -> Node:
        if self.pos >= len(self.tokens): fail SyntaxError("the expression ends too early")
        let t = self.tokens[self.pos]
        self.pos += 1
        when t:
            is Token.Num(v): return Node.Num(v)
            is Token.Name(n): return Node.Var(n)
            is Token.Op("-"): return Node.Neg(self.factor())
            is Token.Op("("):
                let inside = self.expression()
                if self.peek() != ")": fail SyntaxError("a '(' is never closed")
                self.pos += 1
                return inside
            is Token.Op(s): fail SyntaxError("'{s}' can't start a value")
        end
    end
end

create show(n: Node) -> str:
    when n:
        is Node.Num(v): return str(v)
        is Node.Var(name): return name
        is Node.Neg(inner): return "-{show(inner)}"
        is Node.BinOp(op, a, b): return "({show(a)} {op} {show(b)})"
    end
end

main:
    let tokens = [Token.Num(1.0), Token.Op("+"), Token.Num(2.0), Token.Op("*"), Token.Name("x"), Token.Op("^"), Token.Num(2.0)]
    print(show(Parser(tokens).expression()))
end
```

```text
(1.0 + (2.0 * (x ^ 2.0)))
```

The tree shows `^` bound tightest, then `*`, then `+`, without a single
priority table: the order of the function calls *is* the priority.

lessons.title: Evaluating
lessons.text:
Evaluating is one more recursive `when`: a number is itself, a variable is
looked up, an operation evaluates both sides and combines them. Errors
get their own type so the user sees a clear message:

```vyrn
enum Node:
    Num(value: float)
    Var(name: str)
    Neg(inner: Node)
    BinOp(op: str, left: Node, right: Node)
end

struct MathError:
    message: str
end

create evaluate(n: Node, vars: map[str, float]) -> float:
    when n:
        is Node.Num(v): return v
        is Node.Var(name):
            if name not in vars: fail MathError("'{name}' has no value")
            return vars[name]
        is Node.Neg(inner): return -evaluate(inner, vars)
        is Node.BinOp(op, a, b):
            let x = evaluate(a, vars)
            let y = evaluate(b, vars)
            when op:
                is "+": return x + y
                is "-": return x - y
                is "*": return x * y
                is "/":
                    if y == 0: fail MathError("division by zero")
                    return x / y
                is "^": return x ** y
                else: fail MathError("unknown operator {op}")
            end
    end
end

main:
    let tree = Node.BinOp("*", Node.Num(2.0), Node.BinOp("+", Node.Var("x"), Node.Num(3.5)))
    print(evaluate(tree, {"x": 1.5}))
    attempt:
        evaluate(tree, {})
    catch MathError as e:
        print(e.message)
    end
end
```

```text
10.0
'x' has no value
```

### Exercise

Add a `%` (remainder) operator to `evaluate`: `7 % 4` is `3`, and a
remainder by zero is a `MathError`.

```vyrn starter
enum Node:
    Num(value: float)
    BinOp(op: str, left: Node, right: Node)
end

struct MathError:
    message: str
end

create evaluate(n: Node) -> float:
    when n:
        is Node.Num(v): return v
        is Node.BinOp(op, a, b):
            let x = evaluate(a)
            let y = evaluate(b)
            when op:
                is "+": return x + y
                else: fail MathError("unknown operator {op}")
            end
    end
end

main:
    print(evaluate(Node.BinOp("%", Node.Num(7.0), Node.Num(4.0))))
    attempt:
        evaluate(Node.BinOp("%", Node.Num(7.0), Node.Num(0.0)))
    catch MathError as e:
        print(e.message)
    end
end
```

```text expect
3.0
remainder by zero
```

exercise.starter:
enum Node:
    Num(value: float)
    BinOp(op: str, left: Node, right: Node)
end

struct MathError:
    message: str
end

create evaluate(n: Node) -> float:
    when n:
        is Node.Num(v): return v
        is Node.BinOp(op, a, b):
            let x = evaluate(a)
            let y = evaluate(b)
            when op:
                is "+": return x + y
                else: fail MathError("unknown operator {op}")
            end
    end
end

main:
    print(evaluate(Node.BinOp("%", Node.Num(7.0), Node.Num(4.0))))
    attempt:
        evaluate(Node.BinOp("%", Node.Num(7.0), Node.Num(0.0)))
    catch MathError as e:
        print(e.message)
    end
end
exercise.solution:
enum Node:
    Num(value: float)
    BinOp(op: str, left: Node, right: Node)
end

struct MathError:
    message: str
end

create evaluate(n: Node) -> float:
    when n:
        is Node.Num(v): return v
        is Node.BinOp(op, a, b):
            let x = evaluate(a)
            let y = evaluate(b)
            when op:
                is "+": return x + y
                is "%":
                    if y == 0: fail MathError("remainder by zero")
                    return x % y
                else: fail MathError("unknown operator {op}")
            end
    end
end

main:
    print(evaluate(Node.BinOp("%", Node.Num(7.0), Node.Num(4.0))))
    attempt:
        evaluate(Node.BinOp("%", Node.Num(7.0), Node.Num(0.0)))
    catch MathError as e:
        print(e.message)
    end
end
hints: `is "%":` then check `y == 0` before `return x % y`.

lessons.title: The whole calculator
lessons.text:
All three stages together, with variables set by `name = expression`
lines, so it can run a little script:

```vyrn
enum Token:
    Num(value: float)
    Name(text: str)
    Op(symbol: str)
end

enum Node:
    Num(value: float)
    Var(name: str)
    Neg(inner: Node)
    BinOp(op: str, left: Node, right: Node)
end

struct SyntaxError:
    message: str
end

struct MathError:
    message: str
end

create tokenize(text: str) -> list[Token]:
    var tokens = []
    var i = 0
    loop i < len(text):
        let c = text[i]
        if c == " ":
            i += 1
        else if c.isdigit() or c == ".":
            var j = i
            loop j < len(text) and (text[j].isdigit() or text[j] == "."): j += 1
            tokens.append(Token.Num(float(text[i:j])))
            i = j
        else if c.isalpha():
            var j = i
            loop j < len(text) and text[j].isalnum(): j += 1
            tokens.append(Token.Name(text[i:j]))
            i = j
        else if c in "+-*/^()":
            tokens.append(Token.Op(c))
            i += 1
        else:
            fail SyntaxError("I don't know the character '{c}'")
        end
    end
    return tokens
end

object Parser:
    tokens: list[Token]
    pos: int = 0

    create peek(self) -> str:
        if self.pos >= len(self.tokens): return "end"
        if let Token.Op(s) = self.tokens[self.pos]: return s
        return "value"
    end

    create parse(self) -> Node:
        let tree = self.expression()
        if self.pos < len(self.tokens): fail SyntaxError("unexpected '{self.peek()}' after the end")
        return tree
    end

    create expression(self) -> Node:
        var left = self.term()
        loop self.peek() in ["+", "-"]:
            let op = self.peek()
            self.pos += 1
            left = Node.BinOp(op, left, self.term())
        end
        return left
    end

    create term(self) -> Node:
        var left = self.power()
        loop self.peek() in ["*", "/"]:
            let op = self.peek()
            self.pos += 1
            left = Node.BinOp(op, left, self.power())
        end
        return left
    end

    create power(self) -> Node:
        let base = self.factor()
        if self.peek() == "^":
            self.pos += 1
            return Node.BinOp("^", base, self.power())
        end
        return base
    end

    create factor(self) -> Node:
        if self.pos >= len(self.tokens): fail SyntaxError("the expression ends too early")
        let t = self.tokens[self.pos]
        self.pos += 1
        when t:
            is Token.Num(v): return Node.Num(v)
            is Token.Name(n): return Node.Var(n)
            is Token.Op("-"): return Node.Neg(self.factor())
            is Token.Op("("):
                let inside = self.expression()
                if self.peek() != ")": fail SyntaxError("a '(' is never closed")
                self.pos += 1
                return inside
            is Token.Op(s): fail SyntaxError("'{s}' can't start a value")
        end
    end
end

create evaluate(n: Node, vars: map[str, float]) -> float:
    when n:
        is Node.Num(v): return v
        is Node.Var(name):
            if name not in vars: fail MathError("'{name}' has no value")
            return vars[name]
        is Node.Neg(inner): return -evaluate(inner, vars)
        is Node.BinOp(op, a, b):
            let x = evaluate(a, vars)
            let y = evaluate(b, vars)
            when op:
                is "+": return x + y
                is "-": return x - y
                is "*": return x * y
                is "/":
                    if y == 0: fail MathError("division by zero")
                    return x / y
                else: return x ** y
            end
    end
end

create run_line(line: str, vars: map[str, float]) -> str:
    attempt:
        var name = none
        var text = line
        if "=" in line:
            let parts = line.split("=", 1)
            name = parts[0].strip()
            text = parts[1]
        end
        let value = evaluate(Parser(tokenize(text)).parse(), vars)
        if name != none:
            vars[name] = value
            return "{name} = {value}"
        end
        return str(value)
    catch SyntaxError as e:
        return "syntax error: {e.message}"
    catch MathError as e:
        return "math error: {e.message}"
    end
end

main:
    var vars = {"pi": 3.14159}
    each line in ["r = 2", "area = pi * r ^ 2", "-(area - 12) / 2", "2 ^ 3 ^ 2", "(1 + 2", "1 / (r - 2)", "speed * 3", "4 $ 5"]:
        print("> {line:<20} {run_line(line, vars)}")
    end
end
```

```text
> r = 2                r = 2.0
> area = pi * r ^ 2    area = 12.56636
> -(area - 12) / 2     -0.28317999999999977
> 2 ^ 3 ^ 2            512.0
> (1 + 2               syntax error: a '(' is never closed
> 1 / (r - 2)          math error: division by zero
> speed * 3            math error: 'speed' has no value
> 4 $ 5                syntax error: I don't know the character '$'
```

`2 ^ 3 ^ 2` is 512 (2 to the 9th), not 64, because `power` calls itself
for its right side, so powers group from the right as in maths. The long
`-0.28317999...` is a float being honest about rounding (Day 63): print
it with `{value:.4f}` for people.

### Exercise

Add functions of one argument: `sqrt(x)` and `abs(x)`. A name followed by
`(` is a call. Write just the new `factor` case and `evaluate` case in this
cut-down version, where the tree has a `Call(name, arg)` variant.

```vyrn starter
enum Node:
    Num(value: float)
    Call(name: str, arg: Node)
end

struct MathError:
    message: str
end

create evaluate(n: Node) -> float:
    when n:
        is Node.Num(v): return v
        is Node.Call(name, arg): fail MathError("no function {name}")
    end
end

main:
    print(evaluate(Node.Call("sqrt", Node.Num(16.0))), evaluate(Node.Call("abs", Node.Num(-3.0))))
    attempt:
        evaluate(Node.Call("cube", Node.Num(2.0)))
    catch MathError as e:
        print(e.message)
    end
end
```

```text expect
4.0 3.0
no function cube
```

exercise.starter:
enum Node:
    Num(value: float)
    Call(name: str, arg: Node)
end

struct MathError:
    message: str
end

create evaluate(n: Node) -> float:
    when n:
        is Node.Num(v): return v
        is Node.Call(name, arg): fail MathError("no function {name}")
    end
end

main:
    print(evaluate(Node.Call("sqrt", Node.Num(16.0))), evaluate(Node.Call("abs", Node.Num(-3.0))))
    attempt:
        evaluate(Node.Call("cube", Node.Num(2.0)))
    catch MathError as e:
        print(e.message)
    end
end
exercise.solution:
enum Node:
    Num(value: float)
    Call(name: str, arg: Node)
end

struct MathError:
    message: str
end

create evaluate(n: Node) -> float:
    when n:
        is Node.Num(v): return v
        is Node.Call(name, arg):
            let x = evaluate(arg)
            when name:
                is "sqrt": return x ** 0.5
                is "abs": return abs(x)
                else: fail MathError("no function {name}")
            end
    end
end

main:
    print(evaluate(Node.Call("sqrt", Node.Num(16.0))), evaluate(Node.Call("abs", Node.Num(-3.0))))
    attempt:
        evaluate(Node.Call("cube", Node.Num(2.0)))
    catch MathError as e:
        print(e.message)
    end
end
hints: evaluate the argument first, then `when name:` with `is "sqrt": return x ** 0.5`.

lessons.title: you built
lessons.text:
A working interpreter for arithmetic: a tokenizer, a recursive-descent
parser that gets priorities right, a tree as a recursive enum, an
evaluator, and clear errors at every stage. Every programming language,
Vyrn included, is built from these same three stages. Ideas to take it
further:

- Comparisons (`<`, `==`) and `if ... else ...` expressions.
- Functions with several arguments, or functions the user defines:
  `f(x) = x ^ 2 + 1`.
- Show where an error is with a `^` under the position in the line, as
  `vyrn` does.

days.title: Day 70: Stacks, queues, lists and trees
days.intro:
Lists and maps cover most needs, but some problems are much simpler (or
much faster) with a structure built for them. Today you build four
classic **data structures**: stacks, queues, linked lists and binary
search trees. Each is an object with a few methods, and with Day 63's
`len`, `contains` and `iter` they feel built in. The project adds undo to
a text editor and builds a word index.

lessons.title: Stacks: last in, first out
lessons.text:
A **stack** is like a pile of plates: you add to the top and take from the
top. The last thing in is the first out. A list does it, with `append`
and `pop`:

```vyrn
object Stack[T]:
    items: list[T] = []

    create push(self, item: T):
        self.items.append(item)
    end
    create pop(self) -> T:
        if not self.items: fail IndexError("the stack is empty")
        return self.items.pop()
    end
    create peek(self) -> T?:
        return self.items[-1] if self.items else none
    end
    create len(self) -> int:
        return len(self.items)
    end
end

main:
    let s = Stack()
    each x in ["a", "b", "c"]: s.push(x)
    print(s.pop(), s.pop(), s.peek(), len(s))
end
```

```text
c b a 1
```

Stacks are everywhere: the "back" button, undo, and the calls your program
is in the middle of (the trace in an error message is the call stack).
A classic use, checking that brackets match:

```vyrn
create balanced(text: str) -> bool:
    let pairs = {")": "(", "]": "[", "}": "\{"}
    var stack = []
    each c in text:
        if c in "([\{":
            stack.append(c)
        else if c in pairs:
            if not stack or stack.pop() != pairs[c]: return false
        end
    end
    return not stack
end

main:
    each t in ["(a[b]c)", "(a[b)c]", "((", "f(x) = [1, 2]"]:
        print(t, balanced(t))
    end
end
```

```text
(a[b]c) true
(a[b)c] false
(( false
f(x) = [1, 2] true
```

lessons.title: Queues: first in, first out
lessons.text:
A **queue** is a line at a shop: join at the back, leave from the front.
Taking from the front of a list (`pop(0)`) moves every other item along,
which is slow for long lists. A queue that keeps a moving start index
avoids that:

```vyrn
object Queue[T]:
    items: list[T] = []
    start: int = 0

    create add(self, item: T):
        self.items.append(item)
    end
    create take(self) -> T:
        if self.start == len(self.items): fail IndexError("the queue is empty")
        let item = self.items[self.start]
        self.start += 1
        if self.start > 64 and self.start * 2 > len(self.items):
            self.items = self.items[self.start:]
            self.start = 0
        end
        return item
    end
    create len(self) -> int:
        return len(self.items) - self.start
    end
end

main:
    let q = Queue()
    each name in ["Ada", "Alan", "Grace"]: q.add(name)
    print(q.take(), q.take(), len(q))
    q.add("Mo")
    print(q.take(), q.take(), len(q))
end
```

```text
Ada Alan 1
Grace Mo 0
```

Every so often it drops the items already taken, so it doesn't grow
forever. Queues hold work waiting to be done: print jobs, messages,
requests, and (Day 71) places still to explore.

### Exercise

A printer queue: jobs arrive as `(name, pages)`; the printer prints 10
pages a minute. Using a queue, print when each job finishes.

```vyrn starter
main:
    let jobs = [("report", 25), ("photo", 2), ("thesis", 120)]
end
```

```text expect
report done after 2.5 minutes
photo done after 2.7 minutes
thesis done after 14.7 minutes
```

exercise.starter:
main:
    let jobs = [("report", 25), ("photo", 2), ("thesis", 120)]
end
exercise.expect:
report done after 2.5 minutes
photo done after 2.7 minutes
thesis done after 14.7 minutes
exercise.solution:
main:
    var jobs = [("report", 25), ("photo", 2), ("thesis", 120)]
    var minutes = 0.0
    loop jobs:
        let name, pages = jobs.pop(0)
        minutes += pages / 10
        print("{name} done after {minutes:.1f} minutes")
    end
end
hints: a list used as a queue is fine for three jobs: `jobs.pop(0)` takes the first.
keep a running total of minutes: `pages / 10` each.

lessons.title: Linked lists
lessons.text:
A **linked list** stores each item in a node that points to the next.
Adding at the front is instant, whatever the length, because nothing
moves; finding the 500th item means walking 500 steps. It's the simplest
structure built from objects pointing at objects:

```vyrn
object Node:
    value: any
    next: Node? = none
end

object LinkedList:
    head: Node? = none
    size: int = 0

    create push_front(self, value):
        self.head = Node(value, self.head)
        self.size += 1
    end
    create iter(self):
        var node = self.head
        loop node != none:
            yield node.value
            node = node.next
        end
    end
    create len(self) -> int:
        return self.size
    end
    create reverse(self):
        var previous = none
        var node = self.head
        loop node != none:
            let next = node.next
            node.next = previous
            previous = node
            node = next
        end
        self.head = previous
    end
end

main:
    let l = LinkedList()
    each x in [3, 2, 1]: l.push_front(x)
    print([x each x in l], len(l))
    l.reverse()
    print([x each x in l])
end
```

```text
[1, 2, 3] 3
[3, 2, 1]
```

Reversing a linked list in place, by turning each arrow around, is a
classic interview question: draw the nodes on paper and follow the three
variables through the loop.

lessons.title: Binary search trees
lessons.text:
A **binary search tree** keeps items sorted as they're added. Each node
has a value, a left branch with everything smaller, and a right branch
with everything bigger. Finding a value means going left or right at each
node, like binary search (Day 68), so a balanced tree of a million items
needs about 20 steps:

```text
          8
        /   \
       3     10
      / \      \
     1   6      14
        / \    /
       4   7  13
```

```vyrn
object TreeNode:
    value: int
    left: TreeNode? = none
    right: TreeNode? = none
end

object Tree:
    root: TreeNode? = none
    size: int = 0

    create add(self, value: int):
        if self.root == none:
            self.root = TreeNode(value)
        else:
            insert(self.root, value)
        end
        self.size += 1
    end
    create contains(self, value: int) -> bool:
        var node = self.root
        loop node != none:
            if value == node.value: return true
            node = node.left if value < node.value else node.right
        end
        return false
    end
    create iter(self):
        each v in in_order(self.root): yield v
    end
    create len(self) -> int:
        return self.size
    end
end

create insert(node: TreeNode, value: int):
    if value < node.value:
        if node.left == none:
            node.left = TreeNode(value)
        else:
            insert(node.left, value)
        end
    else:
        if node.right == none:
            node.right = TreeNode(value)
        else:
            insert(node.right, value)
        end
    end
end

## Left branch, then the node, then the right branch: sorted order.
create in_order(node: TreeNode?):
    if node == none: return
    each v in in_order(node.left): yield v
    yield node.value
    each v in in_order(node.right): yield v
end

create height(node: TreeNode?) -> int:
    if node == none: return 0
    return 1 + max(height(node.left), height(node.right))
end

main:
    let t = Tree()
    each x in [8, 3, 10, 1, 6, 14, 4, 7, 13]: t.add(x)
    print([x each x in t], len(t))
    print(6 in t, 5 in t, height(t.root))
    let sorted_in = Tree()
    each x in 1 to 9: sorted_in.add(x)
    print(height(sorted_in.root))
end
```

```text
[1, 3, 4, 6, 7, 8, 10, 13, 14] 9
true false 4
9
```

The last line shows the catch: adding items that are already sorted gives
a "tree" that is just a long line, height 9 for 9 items, as slow as a
list. Real libraries use **self-balancing** trees that reorganise
themselves to stay short. In Vyrn, a map is usually the right tool for
"find by key"; a tree when you also need the items in order.

### Exercise

Add a method `smallest(self)` giving the smallest value in the tree (keep
going left), or `none` for an empty tree.

```vyrn starter
object TreeNode:
    value: int
    left: TreeNode? = none
    right: TreeNode? = none
end

object Tree:
    root: TreeNode? = none

    create smallest(self) -> int?:
        return none
    end
end

main:
    let t = Tree(TreeNode(8, TreeNode(3, TreeNode(1)), TreeNode(10)))
    print(t.smallest(), Tree().smallest())
end
```

```text expect
1 none
```

exercise.starter:
object TreeNode:
    value: int
    left: TreeNode? = none
    right: TreeNode? = none
end

object Tree:
    root: TreeNode? = none

    create smallest(self) -> int?:
        return none
    end
end

main:
    let t = Tree(TreeNode(8, TreeNode(3, TreeNode(1)), TreeNode(10)))
    print(t.smallest(), Tree().smallest())
end
exercise.solution:
object TreeNode:
    value: int
    left: TreeNode? = none
    right: TreeNode? = none
end

object Tree:
    root: TreeNode? = none

    create smallest(self) -> int?:
        if self.root == none: return none
        var node = self.root
        loop node.left != none:
            node = node.left
        end
        return node.value
    end
end

main:
    let t = Tree(TreeNode(8, TreeNode(3, TreeNode(1)), TreeNode(10)))
    print(t.smallest(), Tree().smallest())
end
hints: `if self.root == none: return none`, then follow `.left` while it isn't `none`.

lessons.title: Project: undo, and a word index
lessons.text:
**Undo** is two stacks: every change goes on the undo stack; undoing moves
it to the redo stack; a new change clears redo:

```vyrn
object Editor:
    text: str = ""
    undo_stack: list[str] = []
    redo_stack: list[str] = []

    create type_text(self, more: str):
        self.undo_stack.append(self.text)
        self.redo_stack = []
        self.text += more
    end
    create undo(self):
        if not self.undo_stack: return
        self.redo_stack.append(self.text)
        self.text = self.undo_stack.pop()
    end
    create redo(self):
        if not self.redo_stack: return
        self.undo_stack.append(self.text)
        self.text = self.redo_stack.pop()
    end
end

main:
    let e = Editor()
    e.type_text("Hello")
    e.type_text(", world")
    e.type_text("!!!")
    e.undo()
    print(repr(e.text))
    e.undo()
    print(repr(e.text))
    e.redo()
    print(repr(e.text))
    e.type_text("?")
    e.redo()
    print(repr(e.text))
end
```

```text
"Hello, world"
"Hello"
"Hello, world"
"Hello, world?"
```

A **word index** (the back of a book: each word with the pages it's on)
is a map from word to a set of pages, printed in sorted order:

```vyrn
create index(pages: list[str]) -> map:
    var found = {}
    each number, text in enumerate(pages):
        each word in text.lower().split():
            let w = word.strip(".,!?;:")
            if len(w) < 4: skip
            if w not in found: found[w] = set()
            found[w].add(number + 1)
        end
    end
    return found
end

main:
    let book = ["The engine computes numbers.", "Numbers become music, said Ada.", "The engine weaves patterns like a loom weaves flowers."]
    let idx = index(book)
    each word in sorted(idx.keys()):
        print("{word:<10} {", ".join([str(p) each p in sorted(idx[word])])}")
    end
end
```

```text
become     2
computes   1
engine     1, 3
flowers    3
like       3
loom       3
music      2
numbers    1, 2
patterns   3
said       2
weaves     3
```

### Exercise

Write `page_list(pages)`, which turns a set of page numbers into the text
the index prints: sorted, separated by commas.

```vyrn starter
create page_list(pages: any) -> str:
    return ""
end

main:
    print(page_list({3, 1}), page_list({2}))
end
```

```text expect
1, 3 2
```

exercise.starter:
create page_list(pages: any) -> str:
    return ""
end

main:
    print(page_list({3, 1}), page_list({2}))
end
exercise.solution:
create page_list(pages: any) -> str:
    return ", ".join([str(p) each p in sorted(pages)])
end

main:
    print(page_list({3, 1}), page_list({2}))
end
hints: `", ".join([str(p) each p in sorted(pages)])`

lessons.title: you learned
lessons.text:
- A stack is last in, first out (undo, brackets, the call stack); a queue
  is first in, first out (jobs waiting).
- A linked list is nodes pointing to the next: instant to add at the front,
  slow to index.
- A binary search tree keeps items sorted for fast search, but must stay
  balanced to stay fast.
- Give data structures `len`, `contains` and `iter` and they work like
  built-in ones.

days.title: Day 71: Graphs, and bits
days.intro:
A **graph** is a set of things and the connections between them: towns and
roads, people and friendships, web pages and links, tasks and what each
depends on. Many problems that look different are the same graph problem
underneath: "can I get from here to there?", "what's the shortest way?",
"in what order must these be done?". Today you store graphs, search them
two ways, and find shortest routes. Then a short tour of **bits**, the
ones and zeros under every number. The project is a route planner.

lessons.title: Storing a graph
lessons.text:
The things are **nodes**; the connections are **edges**. The handiest way
to store a graph is an **adjacency map**: each node, with the list of
nodes it connects to:

```vyrn
create add_edge(graph: map, a: str, b: str):
    graph[a] = graph.get(a, []) + [b]
    graph[b] = graph.get(b, []) + [a]
end

main:
    var g = {}
    each a, b in [("Home", "Shop"), ("Home", "Park"), ("Shop", "School"), ("Park", "School"), ("School", "Library")]:
        add_edge(g, a, b)
    end
    each node, near in g.items():
        print("{node:<8} -> {near}")
    end
end
```

```text
Home     -> ["Shop", "Park"]
Shop     -> ["Home", "School"]
Park     -> ["Home", "School"]
School   -> ["Shop", "Park", "Library"]
Library  -> ["School"]
```

Roads go both ways, so `add_edge` adds each edge in both directions. For
one-way connections (a link from page A to page B, task B needing task A),
add only one direction: that's a **directed** graph.

lessons.title: Breadth-first search
lessons.text:
To find the way from one node to another with the fewest steps, explore in
**rings**: first every neighbour, then their neighbours, and so on. A
queue (Day 70) keeps the order: nodes are explored in the order they were
found. Remembering where each node was reached *from* lets you trace the
path back:

```vyrn
create add_edge(graph: map, a: str, b: str):
    graph[a] = graph.get(a, []) + [b]
    graph[b] = graph.get(b, []) + [a]
end

create shortest_path(graph: map, start: str, goal: str) -> list?:
    var came_from = {start: none}
    var queue = [start]
    loop queue:
        let node = queue.pop(0)
        if node == goal:
            var path = []
            var at = goal
            loop at != none:
                path.insert(0, at)
                at = came_from[at]
            end
            return path
        end
        each next in graph.get(node, []):
            if next not in came_from:
                came_from[next] = node
                queue.append(next)
            end
        end
    end
    return none
end

main:
    var g = {}
    each a, b in [("Home", "Shop"), ("Home", "Park"), ("Shop", "School"), ("Park", "School"), ("School", "Library"), ("Pond", "Woods")]:
        add_edge(g, a, b)
    end
    print(shortest_path(g, "Home", "Library"))
    print(shortest_path(g, "Library", "Park"))
    print(shortest_path(g, "Home", "Woods"))
end
```

```text
["Home", "Shop", "School", "Library"]
["Library", "School", "Park"]
none
```

`came_from` doubles as the record of what's been seen, so no node is
explored twice and the search can't go round in circles. "Pond" and
"Woods" aren't connected to the rest, so there's no path. This is
**breadth-first search** (BFS): it always finds a path with the fewest
edges.

### Exercise

How many steps away is every place from Home? Write `distances(graph,
start)` with the same BFS, recording each node's distance (its parent's
distance plus one).

```vyrn starter
create distances(graph: map, start: str) -> map:
    return {start: 0}
end

main:
    let g = {"Home": ["Shop", "Park"], "Shop": ["Home", "School"], "Park": ["Home", "School"], "School": ["Shop", "Park", "Library"], "Library": ["School"]}
    print(distances(g, "Home"))
end
```

```text expect
{"Home": 0, "Shop": 1, "Park": 1, "School": 2, "Library": 3}
```

exercise.starter:
create distances(graph: map, start: str) -> map:
    return {start: 0}
end

main:
    let g = {"Home": ["Shop", "Park"], "Shop": ["Home", "School"], "Park": ["Home", "School"], "School": ["Shop", "Park", "Library"], "Library": ["School"]}
    print(distances(g, "Home"))
end
exercise.solution:
create distances(graph: map, start: str) -> map:
    var dist = {start: 0}
    var queue = [start]
    loop queue:
        let node = queue.pop(0)
        each next in graph.get(node, []):
            if next not in dist:
                dist[next] = dist[node] + 1
                queue.append(next)
            end
        end
    end
    return dist
end

main:
    let g = {"Home": ["Shop", "Park"], "Shop": ["Home", "School"], "Park": ["Home", "School"], "School": ["Shop", "Park", "Library"], "Library": ["School"]}
    print(distances(g, "Home"))
end
hints: start with `var dist = {start: 0}` and `var queue = [start]`.
for each unseen neighbour, `dist[next] = dist[node] + 1` and add it to the queue.

lessons.title: Depth-first search
lessons.text:
**Depth-first search** (DFS) goes as far as it can down one path before
backing up and trying the next, like exploring a maze by keeping one hand
on the wall. It's naturally recursive. It doesn't find shortest paths, but
it's the tool for "what can I reach?" and for ordering tasks that depend
on each other:

```vyrn
## Tasks in an order where each comes after everything it needs.
create task_order(needs: map) -> list[str]:
    var done = []
    var visiting = set()
    create visit(task: str):
        if task in done: return
        if task in visiting: fail ValueError("tasks depend on each other in a circle at {task}")
        visiting.add(task)
        each before in needs.get(task, []): visit(before)
        visiting.discard(task)
        done.append(task)
    end
    each task in needs.keys(): visit(task)
    return done
end

main:
    let recipe = {
        "serve": ["bake", "make icing"],
        "bake": ["mix", "heat oven"],
        "mix": ["buy eggs"],
        "make icing": ["buy sugar"],
    }
    print(task_order(recipe))
    attempt:
        task_order({"a": ["b"], "b": ["a"]})
    catch ValueError as e:
        print(e.message)
    end
end
```

```text
["buy eggs", "mix", "heat oven", "bake", "buy sugar", "make icing", "serve"]
tasks depend on each other in a circle at a
```

This ordering is a **topological sort**. Build tools use it to compile
files in the right order, and package managers (like `vyrn add`) to
install dependencies before what needs them. The `visiting` set catches
circles, where no order is possible.

lessons.title: Shortest routes with distances
lessons.text:
Real roads have lengths. The path with the fewest roads isn't always the
shortest drive. **Dijkstra's algorithm** handles this: always continue
from the closest place not yet settled. For a small graph, picking the
closest from a map is fine:

```vyrn
create dijkstra(roads: map, start: str) -> (map, map):
    var dist = {start: 0}
    var came_from = {start: none}
    var settled = set()
    loop len(settled) < len(dist):
        let node = min([n each n in dist.keys() if n not in settled], key = n => dist[n])
        settled.add(node)
        each next, km in roads.get(node, {}).items():
            let through = dist[node] + km
            if next not in dist or through < dist[next]:
                dist[next] = through
                came_from[next] = node
            end
        end
    end
    return (dist, came_from)
end

create route(came_from: map, goal: str) -> list[str]:
    var path = []
    var at = goal
    loop at != none:
        path.insert(0, at)
        at = came_from[at]
    end
    return path
end

main:
    let roads = {
        "A": {"B": 7, "C": 2},
        "B": {"A": 7, "D": 1},
        "C": {"A": 2, "B": 3, "D": 8},
        "D": {"B": 1, "C": 8},
    }
    let dist, came_from = dijkstra(roads, "A")
    print(dist)
    print(route(came_from, "D"), dist["D"], "km")
end
```

```text
{"A": 0, "B": 5, "C": 2, "D": 6}
["A", "C", "B", "D"] 6 km
```

Going A → C → B → D is three roads but 6 km; A → C → D is two roads but
10 km. Maps apps, network routers and games all run versions of this.

lessons.title: Bits
lessons.text:
Under the hood every number is **binary**: ones and zeros, called
**bits**. `bin` and `hex` show them; `int(text, 2)` reads them back:

```vyrn
main:
    print(bin(13), hex(255), int("1101", 2), int("ff", 16))
    print(13 & 6, 13 | 6, 13 ^ 6, 1 << 4, 200 >> 3)
end
```

```text
0b1101 0xff 13 255
4 15 11 16 25
```

| Operator | Name | Each bit of the answer is 1 when |
|---|---|---|
| `a & b` | and | both bits are 1 |
| `a \| b` | or | either bit is 1 |
| `a ^ b` | xor | the bits differ |
| `a << n` | shift left | (moves bits up: multiplies by 2ⁿ) |
| `a >> n` | shift right | (moves bits down: divides by 2ⁿ) |

Their everyday use is **flags**: several yes/no settings packed into one
number, one bit each. Files' permissions, game controller buttons and
network packets all work this way:

```vyrn
const READ = 1 << 0
const WRITE = 1 << 1
const SHARE = 1 << 2

create describe(perms: int) -> str:
    var names = []
    each flag, name in [(READ, "read"), (WRITE, "write"), (SHARE, "share")]:
        if perms & flag != 0: names.append(name)
    end
    return ", ".join(names) or "nothing"
end

main:
    var p = READ | WRITE
    print(p, bin(p), describe(p))
    p = p | SHARE
    p = p & ~WRITE
    print(p, bin(p), describe(p))
end
```

```text
3 0b11 read, write
5 0b101 read, share
```

`| flag` turns a bit on, `& ~flag` turns it off, `& flag != 0` tests it.

### Exercise

A colour is often stored as one number, `0xRRGGBB`. Write `channels(c)`
giving the red, green and blue parts by shifting and masking with `0xff`.

```vyrn starter
create channels(c: int) -> (int, int, int):
    return (0, 0, 0)
end

main:
    print(channels(0x1e88e5), channels(0xff0000))
end
```

```text expect
(30, 136, 229) (255, 0, 0)
```

exercise.starter:
create channels(c: int) -> (int, int, int):
    return (0, 0, 0)
end

main:
    print(channels(0x1e88e5), channels(0xff0000))
end
exercise.solution:
create channels(c: int) -> (int, int, int):
    return ((c >> 16) & 0xff, (c >> 8) & 0xff, c & 0xff)
end

main:
    print(channels(0x1e88e5), channels(0xff0000))
end
hints: red is `(c >> 16) & 0xff`, green `(c >> 8) & 0xff`, blue `c & 0xff`.

lessons.title: Project: a route planner
lessons.text:
A small rail network with travel times in minutes. The planner gives the
fastest route between any two stations, with the time of each leg:

```vyrn
const LINES = [
    ("Kings Cross", "Euston", 4), ("Euston", "Warren Street", 2), ("Warren Street", "Oxford Circus", 2),
    ("Kings Cross", "Angel", 3), ("Angel", "Old Street", 3), ("Old Street", "Bank", 4),
    ("Oxford Circus", "Bond Street", 2), ("Oxford Circus", "Tottenham Court Road", 2),
    ("Tottenham Court Road", "Bank", 9), ("Kings Cross", "Farringdon", 4), ("Farringdon", "Bank", 6),
]

create network() -> map:
    var roads = {}
    each a, b, minutes in LINES:
        if a not in roads: roads[a] = {}
        if b not in roads: roads[b] = {}
        roads[a][b] = minutes
        roads[b][a] = minutes
    end
    return roads
end

create plan(roads: map, start: str, goal: str) -> list?:
    var dist = {start: 0}
    var came_from = {start: none}
    var settled = set()
    loop len(settled) < len(dist):
        let node = min([n each n in dist.keys() if n not in settled], key = n => dist[n])
        if node == goal: stop
        settled.add(node)
        each next, minutes in roads[node].items():
            if next not in dist or dist[node] + minutes < dist[next]:
                dist[next] = dist[node] + minutes
                came_from[next] = node
            end
        end
    end
    if goal not in dist: return none
    var legs = []
    var at = goal
    loop came_from[at] != none:
        let before = came_from[at]
        legs.insert(0, (before, at, roads[before][at]))
        at = before
    end
    return legs
end

main:
    let roads = network()
    each start, goal in [("Kings Cross", "Bank"), ("Bond Street", "Angel")]:
        let legs = plan(roads, start, goal)
        print("{start} to {goal}: {sum(m each _, _, m in legs)} minutes")
        each a, b, m in legs:
            print("  {a} -> {b} ({m} min)")
        end
    end
end
```

```text
Kings Cross to Bank: 10 minutes
  Kings Cross -> Farringdon (4 min)
  Farringdon -> Bank (6 min)
Bond Street to Angel: 13 minutes
  Bond Street -> Oxford Circus (2 min)
  Oxford Circus -> Warren Street (2 min)
  Warren Street -> Euston (2 min)
  Euston -> Kings Cross (4 min)
  Kings Cross -> Angel (3 min)
```

The planner stops as soon as the goal is settled: its distance can't get
any shorter after that, so there's no need to explore the rest.

### Exercise

Write `legs_text(legs)`
that joins the stations of a route with arrows, like
`"Kings Cross → Angel → Old Street → Bank"`.

```vyrn starter
create legs_text(legs: list) -> str:
    return ""
end

main:
    print(legs_text([("Kings Cross", "Angel", 3), ("Angel", "Old Street", 3), ("Old Street", "Bank", 4)]))
end
```

```text expect
Kings Cross → Angel → Old Street → Bank
```

exercise.starter:
create legs_text(legs: list) -> str:
    return ""
end

main:
    print(legs_text([("Kings Cross", "Angel", 3), ("Angel", "Old Street", 3), ("Old Street", "Bank", 4)]))
end
exercise.expect: Kings Cross → Angel → Old Street → Bank
exercise.solution:
create legs_text(legs: list) -> str:
    let stations = [legs[0][0]] + [b each _, b, _ in legs]
    return " → ".join(stations)
end

main:
    print(legs_text([("Kings Cross", "Angel", 3), ("Angel", "Old Street", 3), ("Old Street", "Bank", 4)]))
end
hints: the stations are the first leg's start, then every leg's end.

lessons.title: you learned
lessons.text:
- Graphs are nodes and edges; store them as a map from each node to its
  neighbours.
- Breadth-first search finds the fewest steps; depth-first search explores
  and orders tasks (topological sort), catching circles.
- Dijkstra's algorithm finds the shortest route when edges have lengths.
- Numbers are bits: `&`, `|`, `^`, `~`, `<<`, `>>`, and flags packed into
  one number.

days.title: Day 72: Doing several things at once
days.intro:
Most of the time a program that talks to the network is **waiting**: for
a web page, a database, a file. Fetching ten pages one after another means
waiting ten times; fetching them all at once means waiting about as long
as the slowest one. Today you learn Vyrn's **tasks**: functions that can
pause while they wait and let others run. The project downloads many
pages at once, politely.

lessons.title: `async` and `await`
lessons.text:
A function marked `async` runs as a **task**. Calling it starts it and
gives back the task straight away; `await` waits for its result. While a
task waits (for `sleep`, a download, a message), other tasks run:

```vyrn
async create make_tea(name: str, minutes: float) -> str:
    print("{name}: kettle on")
    await sleep(minutes / 100)
    print("{name}: ready")
    return "{name}'s tea"
end

main:
    let ada = make_tea("Ada", 3)
    let alan = make_tea("Alan", 1)
    print("both started")
    print(await ada, "and", await alan)
end
```

```text
Ada: kettle on
Alan: kettle on
both started
Alan: ready
Ada: ready
Ada's tea and Alan's tea
```

Both kettles boil at the same time: Alan's tea (1 "minute") is ready
before Ada's (3). Without `async`, Alan would wait for Ada's tea to finish
first. (The example divides by 100 so it runs in hundredths of a second.)

Tasks take turns on one thread. A task only lets others run where it
waits (`await`), so code between two `await`s runs without interruption:
no two tasks ever change the same variable at the same moment. That makes
tasks much easier to get right than threads in most languages.

lessons.title: Waiting for many
lessons.text:
`join(a, b, ...)` waits for all of several tasks and gives their results
in order. A **task group** does the same for any number of tasks, and
makes sure none outlives the block:

```vyrn
use vyrn.task
use vyrn.time

async create fetch(page: int) -> str:
    await sleep(0.05)
    return "page {page}"
end

main:
    let start = time.now()
    var one_by_one = []
    each p in 1 to 5:
        one_by_one.append(await fetch(p))
    end
    let slow = time.now() - start

    let start2 = time.now()
    using task.group() as g:
        each p in 1 to 5: g.spawn(fetch(p))
        print(await g.wait())
    end
    let fast = time.now() - start2
    print("one by one took about 5 waits; together about 1:", fast < slow / 2)
end
```

```text
["page 1", "page 2", "page 3", "page 4", "page 5"]
one by one took about 5 waits; together about 1: true
```

The results come back in the order the tasks were added, whatever order
they finished in.

### Exercise

Three friends each take a different time to arrive. Start all three
`arrive` tasks at once, and print the names in the order they arrived
(the order of the "here" lines shows it), then all three results with
`join`.

```vyrn starter
async create arrive(name: str, minutes: int) -> str:
    await sleep(minutes / 1000)
    print(name, "is here")
    return name
end

main:
    print(await arrive("Ada", 30))
end
```

```text expect
Grace is here
Alan is here
Ada is here
("Ada", "Alan", "Grace")
```

exercise.starter:
async create arrive(name: str, minutes: int) -> str:
    await sleep(minutes / 1000)
    print(name, "is here")
    return name
end

main:
    print(await arrive("Ada", 30))
end
exercise.expect:
Grace is here
Alan is here
Ada is here
("Ada", "Alan", "Grace")
exercise.solution:
async create arrive(name: str, minutes: int) -> str:
    await sleep(minutes / 1000)
    print(name, "is here")
    return name
end

main:
    print(await join(arrive("Ada", 30), arrive("Alan", 20), arrive("Grace", 10)))
end
hints: `print(await join(arrive("Ada", 30), arrive("Alan", 20), arrive("Grace", 10)))`

lessons.title: When tasks fail, or take too long
lessons.text:
A task that fails passes its error to whoever awaits it, like a function
call. `task.timeout` gives up on work that takes too long, and stops it:

```vyrn
use vyrn.task

async create flaky(n: int) -> int:
    await sleep(0.01)
    if n == 2: fail ValueError("item {n} is broken")
    return n * 10
end

async create stuck() -> str:
    await sleep(10)
    return "never"
end

main:
    each n in 1 to 3:
        attempt:
            print(await flaky(n))
        catch ValueError as e:
            print("failed:", e.message)
        end
    end
    attempt:
        await task.timeout(0.05, stuck())
    catch Timeout as e:
        print(e.message)
    end
end
```

```text
10
failed: item 2 is broken
30
the work took longer than 0.05 seconds
```

Always put a timeout on anything that talks to the network: a server that
never answers would otherwise freeze that part of your program forever.

lessons.title: Not too many at once
lessons.text:
Starting a thousand downloads at once overloads the other server and your
own connection. Limit how many run together. A **channel** (tomorrow's
topic) is one way; the simplest is to work through the list in batches.
`0 until n by 3` counts 0, 3, 6, ...: the start of each batch.

```vyrn
use vyrn.task

async create fetch(page: int) -> str:
    await sleep(0.01)
    return "p{page}"
end

async create fetch_all(pages: list[int], at_once: int) -> list[str]:
    var results = []
    each start in 0 until len(pages) by at_once:
        let batch = pages[start:start + at_once]
        using task.group() as g:
            each p in batch: g.spawn(fetch(p))
            results.extend(await g.wait())
        end
        print("batch done:", batch)
    end
    return results
end

main:
    print(await fetch_all(list(1 to 7), 3))
end
```

```text
batch done: [1, 2, 3]
batch done: [4, 5, 6]
batch done: [7]
["p1", "p2", "p3", "p4", "p5", "p6", "p7"]
```

lessons.title: Project: downloading many pages
lessons.text:
A real downloader with everything above: at most a few downloads at once,
a timeout on each, and failures reported without stopping the others. The
fetching function is passed in, so here it's a stand-in that sleeps and
sometimes fails; for real it would call `http.get`.

```vyrn
use vyrn.task

async create fake_fetch(url: str) -> str:
    let n = int(url.split("/")[-1])
    await sleep(0.01 * (n % 3 + 1))
    if n == 4: fail NetworkError("connection reset")
    if n == 6: await sleep(1)
    return "<html>page {n}</html>"
end

async create safe_fetch(fetch: any, url: str, seconds: float) -> (str, str):
    attempt:
        let page = await task.timeout(seconds, fetch(url))
        return (url, "ok, {len(page)} characters")
    catch Timeout:
        return (url, "too slow")
    catch Error as e:
        return (url, "failed: {e.message}")
    end
end

async create download_all(urls: list[str], fetch: any, at_once: int = 3) -> list:
    var report = []
    each start in 0 until len(urls) by at_once:
        using task.group() as g:
            each url in urls[start:start + at_once]: g.spawn(safe_fetch(fetch, url, 0.2))
            report.extend(await g.wait())
        end
    end
    return report
end

main:
    let urls = ["https://example.com/page/{n}" each n in 1 to 7]
    each url, outcome in await download_all(urls, fake_fetch):
        print("{url.split("/")[-1]}: {outcome}")
    end
end
```

```text
1: ok, 19 characters
2: ok, 19 characters
3: ok, 19 characters
4: failed: connection reset
5: ok, 19 characters
6: too slow
7: ok, 19 characters
```

`safe_fetch` turns every outcome into a value, so one broken page can't
stop the group, and the report lists every page whatever happened to it.
That's a good pattern for any batch of independent work.

### Exercise

Add a summary line: write `summary(report)` counting how many pages were
ok and how many weren't.

```vyrn starter
create summary(report: list) -> str:
    return ""
end

main:
    print(summary([("a", "ok, 23 characters"), ("b", "too slow"), ("c", "ok, 9 characters")]))
end
```

```text expect
2 ok, 1 problems
```

exercise.starter:
create summary(report: list) -> str:
    return ""
end

main:
    print(summary([("a", "ok, 23 characters"), ("b", "too slow"), ("c", "ok, 9 characters")]))
end
exercise.solution:
create summary(report: list) -> str:
    let ok = len([o each _, o in report if o.startswith("ok")])
    return "{ok} ok, {len(report) - ok} problems"
end

main:
    print(summary([("a", "ok, 23 characters"), ("b", "too slow"), ("c", "ok, 9 characters")]))
end
hints: count the outcomes that start with `"ok"`.

lessons.title: you learned
lessons.text:
- `async` functions run as tasks; calling one starts it, `await` waits for
  its result; other tasks run while one waits.
- Tasks switch only at `await`, so code between awaits never runs at the
  same moment as other tasks' code.
- `join` and `task.group()` wait for many tasks, giving results in order.
- Failures travel to whoever awaits; `task.timeout` stops work that takes
  too long. Limit how many run at once.

days.title: Day 73: Channels, and work that fails
days.intro:
Yesterday's tasks each did one job and returned. Bigger programs have
tasks that run for a long time and pass work between them: one reads
orders, several process them, one writes the results. Today you connect
tasks with **channels**, wait on whichever thing happens first with
`task.select`, and make work survive failures with **retries**. The
project is a reliable worker that keeps going when things go wrong.

lessons.title: Channels
lessons.text:
A **channel** is a pipe between tasks: one end `send`s values, the other
receives them with `await ch`, or with `async each x in ch` until the
channel is closed. A channel with a **capacity** holds at most that many
values; a sender waits while it's full, so a fast producer can't run far
ahead of a slow consumer:

```vyrn
async create producer(ch: any, n: int):
    each i in 1 to n:
        ch.send(i)
        print("sent", i)
    end
    ch.close()
end

async create consumer(ch: any, name: str) -> int:
    var total = 0
    async each x in ch:
        print("  {name} got {x}")
        total += x
        await sleep(0.01)
    end
    return total
end

main:
    let ch = channel(capacity = 2)
    let p = producer(ch, 5)
    let a = consumer(ch, "A")
    let b = consumer(ch, "B")
    await p
    print("total", await a + await b)
end
```

```text
sent 1
sent 2
  A got 1
  B got 2
sent 3
sent 4
  A got 3
  B got 4
sent 5
  A got 5
total 15
```

Two consumers share the work: each value goes to exactly one of them.
`ch.close()` tells receivers no more is coming, which ends their
`async each` loops. This **producer and consumers** shape (a queue of jobs
with several workers) is how web servers, print spoolers and build tools
spread work.

lessons.title: Whichever comes first
lessons.text:
`task.select(a, b, ...)` waits for the first of several tasks or channels
and gives `(position, value)`. Combined with a channel of messages, it
lets a task react to whatever happens next: new work, or being told to
stop:

```vyrn
use vyrn.task

async create worker(jobs: any, quit: any) -> int:
    var done = 0
    loop:
        let which, value = await task.select(jobs, quit)
        if which == 1 or value == none:
            print("worker stopping after", done, "jobs")
            return done
        end
        print("doing", value)
        done += 1
    end
end

main:
    let jobs = channel()
    let quit = channel()
    let w = worker(jobs, quit)
    jobs.send("wash")
    jobs.send("dry")
    await sleep(0.01)
    quit.send(true)
    print(await w)
end
```

```text
doing wash
doing dry
worker stopping after 2 jobs
2
```

lessons.title: Retrying
lessons.text:
Networks fail for a moment and then work again: a dropped connection, a
busy server. Trying again after a short wait fixes most of these.
**Exponential backoff** (Day 36) waits longer each time, so a struggling
server gets room to recover:

```vyrn
async create with_retries(work: any, tries: int = 4, wait: float = 0.01) -> any:
    var delay = wait
    each attempt_number in 1 to tries:
        attempt:
            return await work()
        catch NetworkError as e:
            if attempt_number == tries: fail e
            print("try {attempt_number} failed ({e.message}); waiting {delay}")
            await sleep(delay)
            delay *= 2
        end
    end
end

main:
    var calls = 0
    async create flaky_fetch() -> str:
        calls += 1
        if calls < 3: fail NetworkError("connection reset")
        return "the page"
    end
    print(await with_retries(flaky_fetch))
    async create always_down() -> str:
        fail NetworkError("server down")
    end
    attempt:
        await with_retries(always_down, tries = 2)
    catch NetworkError as e:
        print("gave up:", e.message)
    end
end
```

```text
try 1 failed (connection reset); waiting 0.01
try 2 failed (connection reset); waiting 0.02
the page
try 1 failed (server down); waiting 0.01
gave up: server down
```

Retry only what might work next time. A `NetworkError` might; a
`ValueError` from bad input never will, so `with_retries` lets those
through at once. And only retry things that are safe to do twice: fetching
a page is, but charging a card twice is not.

### Exercise

Some services say *when* to try again. Write `wait_before(try_number,
retry_after)`, giving the server's `retry_after` when it gave one (not
`none`), or else the backoff `0.5 * 2 ** (try_number - 1)`, never more
than 8.

```vyrn starter
create wait_before(try_number: int, retry_after: float?) -> float:
    return 0.0
end

main:
    print(wait_before(1, none), wait_before(3, none), wait_before(10, none), wait_before(2, 5.0))
end
```

```text expect
0.5 2.0 8.0 5.0
```

exercise.starter:
create wait_before(try_number: int, retry_after: float?) -> float:
    return 0.0
end

main:
    print(wait_before(1, none), wait_before(3, none), wait_before(10, none), wait_before(2, 5.0))
end
exercise.solution:
create wait_before(try_number: int, retry_after: float?) -> float:
    if retry_after != none: return retry_after
    return min(0.5 * 2 ** (try_number - 1), 8.0)
end

main:
    print(wait_before(1, none), wait_before(3, none), wait_before(10, none), wait_before(2, 5.0))
end
hints: `if retry_after != none: return retry_after`

lessons.title: Failing well: circuit breakers
lessons.text:
When a service is really down, retrying every request makes things worse:
every request now waits through all its retries, and the struggling
service is hammered. A **circuit breaker** notices repeated failures and
stops calling for a while, failing at once instead, then lets one request
through to see if the service has recovered:

```vyrn
object Breaker:
    failures: int = 0
    limit: int = 3
    open_until: float = 0.0
    cool_down: float = 30.0

    create allow(self, now: float) -> bool:
        return now >= self.open_until
    end
    create record(self, ok: bool, now: float):
        if ok:
            self.failures = 0
        else:
            self.failures += 1
            if self.failures >= self.limit: self.open_until = now + self.cool_down
        end
    end
end

main:
    let b = Breaker()
    each now, ok in [(0, false), (1, false), (2, false), (3, true), (20, true), (40, true), (41, false)]:
        if not b.allow(now):
            print("t={now}: not calling, the breaker is open")
            skip
        end
        b.record(ok, now)
        print("t={now}: called, {"ok" if ok else "failed"} (failures {b.failures})")
    end
end
```

```text
t=0: called, failed (failures 1)
t=1: called, failed (failures 2)
t=2: called, failed (failures 3)
t=3: not calling, the breaker is open
t=20: not calling, the breaker is open
t=40: called, ok (failures 0)
t=41: called, failed (failures 1)
```

After three failures, calls stop for 30 seconds, then resume. Large
systems of services that call each other ("microservices") use timeouts,
retries and breakers together, so one failing part doesn't drag down the
rest.

lessons.title: Project: a reliable worker
lessons.text:
Jobs arrive on a channel. Several workers take them, each with a timeout
and retries; jobs that fail for good go to a **dead-letter** list for a
person to look at, instead of being lost:

```vyrn
use vyrn.task

async create process(job: int) -> str:
    await sleep(0.005)
    if job % 5 == 0: fail ValueError("job {job} has bad data")
    if job == 3: await sleep(1)
    return "job {job} done"
end

async create worker(name: str, jobs: any, results: list, dead: list):
    async each job in jobs:
        attempt:
            let r = await task.timeout(0.1, process(job))
            results.append(r)
        catch Timeout:
            dead.append((job, "too slow"))
        catch ValueError as e:
            dead.append((job, e.message))
        end
    end
end

main:
    let jobs = channel(capacity = 3)
    var results = []
    var dead = []
    let workers = [worker("w{i}", jobs, results, dead) each i in 1 to 3]
    each job in 1 to 10: jobs.send(job)
    jobs.close()
    each w in workers: await w
    print(len(results), "done:", sorted(results))
    print("dead letters:", sorted(dead))
end
```

```text
7 done: ["job 1 done", "job 2 done", "job 4 done", "job 6 done", "job 7 done", "job 8 done", "job 9 done"]
dead letters: [(3, "too slow"), (5, "job 5 has bad data"), (10, "job 10 has bad data")]
```

Every one of the ten jobs is accounted for: done, or in the dead letters
with the reason. The slow job didn't hold up the others, because the other
workers kept taking jobs while one waited for its timeout.

### Exercise

Count each worker's jobs. Write `tally(log)`, which takes a list of
`(worker, job)` pairs and gives a map from worker to how many jobs it did.

```vyrn starter
create tally(log: list) -> map:
    return {}
end

main:
    print(tally([("w1", 1), ("w2", 2), ("w1", 3), ("w3", 4), ("w1", 5)]))
end
```

```text expect
{"w1": 3, "w2": 1, "w3": 1}
```

exercise.starter:
create tally(log: list) -> map:
    return {}
end

main:
    print(tally([("w1", 1), ("w2", 2), ("w1", 3), ("w3", 4), ("w1", 5)]))
end
exercise.solution:
create tally(log: list) -> map:
    var counts = {}
    each w, _ in log:
        counts[w] = counts.get(w, 0) + 1
    end
    return counts
end

main:
    print(tally([("w1", 1), ("w2", 2), ("w1", 3), ("w3", 4), ("w1", 5)]))
end
hints: `counts[w] = counts.get(w, 0) + 1` for each pair.

lessons.title: you learned
lessons.text:
- Channels pass values between tasks; a capacity makes fast senders wait;
  `close` ends receivers' `async each` loops.
- `task.select` waits for whichever task or channel is ready first.
- Retry with growing waits, only what might succeed later and is safe to
  repeat.
- Circuit breakers stop calling a service that keeps failing; dead letters
  keep failed work for a person.

days.title: Day 74: Design patterns
days.intro:
Programmers keep meeting the same problems: "the program must work with
several kinds of payment", "many parts must react when something
happens", "this object is complicated to build". The well-known solutions
have names, **design patterns**, so people can say "use an observer here"
and be understood. Today you meet five of the most useful, each solving a
real problem, in Vyrn's style: traits, closures and maps often make them
shorter than in Java, where most were first described. The project is a
small plugin system that uses several at once.

lessons.title: Strategy: swap the method
lessons.text:
**Problem:** a shop works out shipping differently for standard, express
and collection. A chain of `if`s grows with every new option.
**Pattern:** make each method an object (or function) with the same shape,
and choose one:

```vyrn
trait Shipping:
    create cost(self, weight_kg: float) -> float
    create name(self) -> str
end

struct Standard:
end

struct Express:
    surcharge: float
end

struct Collect:
end

impl Shipping for Standard:
    create cost(self, weight_kg: float) -> float:
        return 3.0 + 0.5 * weight_kg
    end
    create name(self) -> str:
        return "standard"
    end
end

impl Shipping for Express:
    create cost(self, weight_kg: float) -> float:
        return 3.0 + 0.5 * weight_kg + self.surcharge
    end
    create name(self) -> str:
        return "express"
    end
end

impl Shipping for Collect:
    create cost(self, weight_kg: float) -> float:
        return 0.0
    end
    create name(self) -> str:
        return "collect in store"
    end
end

create checkout(total: float, weight: float, shipping: Shipping) -> str:
    return "£{total + shipping.cost(weight):.2f} with {shipping.name()}"
end

main:
    each s in [Standard(), Express(7.5), Collect()]:
        print(checkout(20.0, 4.0, s))
    end
end
```

```text
£25.00 with standard
£32.50 with express
£20.00 with collect in store
```

`checkout` never changes when a shipping method is added. When the
strategy is just one function, a function value is enough: `sorted(xs,
key = ...)` takes a strategy for comparing.

lessons.title: Factory: build the right thing
lessons.text:
**Problem:** code receives `"express"` from a form and must make the right
object. **Pattern:** one function, the **factory**, knows how to turn a
name into an object, so the rest of the program never does:

```vyrn
struct Standard:
end

struct Express:
    surcharge: float
end

create shipping_from(name: str) -> any:
    let makers = {
        "standard": () => Standard(),
        "express": () => Express(7.5),
    }
    if name not in makers: fail ValueError("no shipping called {name}; choose from {sorted(makers.keys())}")
    return makers[name]()
end

main:
    print(shipping_from("express"))
    attempt:
        shipping_from("drone")
    catch ValueError as e:
        print(e.message)
    end
end
```

```text
Express(surcharge=7.5)
no shipping called drone; choose from ["express", "standard"]
```

A map from names to functions is the factory's whole table; adding a
method is one line, and the error message lists the choices for free.

lessons.title: Observer: tell everyone who's interested
lessons.text:
**Problem:** when an order is placed, the stock must go down, an email must
be sent and a counter must go up, and you don't want the order code to
know about all of them. **Pattern:** the order code **publishes** an
event; anything interested **subscribes** a function to it:

```vyrn
object Events:
    handlers: map = {}

    create on(self, name: str, handler: any):
        self.handlers[name] = self.handlers.get(name, []) + [handler]
    end
    create emit(self, name: str, data: any):
        each h in self.handlers.get(name, []):
            h(data)
        end
    end
end

main:
    let events = Events()
    var stock = {"tea": 10}
    var emails = []
    create take_stock(o: map):
        stock[o["item"]] -= o["qty"]
    end
    events.on("order", take_stock)
    events.on("order", o => emails.append("Thanks for ordering {o["item"]}!"))
    events.emit("order", {"item": "tea", "qty": 3})
    events.emit("refund", {"item": "tea"})
    print(stock, emails)
end
```

```text
{"tea": 7} ["Thanks for ordering tea!"]
```

Nobody listens for "refund" yet, so emitting it does nothing, and that's
fine. (A lambda holds one expression, so the handler that changes `stock`
is a small named function.) Buttons in a GUI, webhooks, and the middleware you wrote on Day 49
are all observers.

### Exercise

Add `once(name, handler)` to `Events`: a handler that runs the first time
the event happens, and never again.

```vyrn starter
object Events:
    handlers: map = {}

    create on(self, name: str, handler: any):
        self.handlers[name] = self.handlers.get(name, []) + [handler]
    end
    create emit(self, name: str, data: any):
        each h in self.handlers.get(name, []):
            h(data)
        end
    end
end

main:
    let e = Events()
    e.on("tick", n => print("every", n))
    e.emit("tick", 1)
    e.emit("tick", 2)
end
```

```text expect
every 1
first 1
every 2
```

exercise.starter:
object Events:
    handlers: map = {}

    create on(self, name: str, handler: any):
        self.handlers[name] = self.handlers.get(name, []) + [handler]
    end
    create emit(self, name: str, data: any):
        each h in self.handlers.get(name, []):
            h(data)
        end
    end
end

main:
    let e = Events()
    e.on("tick", n => print("every", n))
    e.emit("tick", 1)
    e.emit("tick", 2)
end
exercise.solution:
object Events:
    handlers: map = {}

    create on(self, name: str, handler: any):
        self.handlers[name] = self.handlers.get(name, []) + [handler]
    end
    create once(self, name: str, handler: any):
        var done = false
        create wrapper(data):
            if done: return
            done = true
            handler(data)
        end
        self.on(name, wrapper)
    end
    create emit(self, name: str, data: any):
        each h in self.handlers.get(name, []):
            h(data)
        end
    end
end

main:
    let e = Events()
    e.on("tick", n => print("every", n))
    e.once("tick", n => print("first", n))
    e.emit("tick", 1)
    e.emit("tick", 2)
end
hints: in `once`, wrap the handler in a closure with `var done = false` that does nothing once `done` is true.
in `main`, add `e.once("tick", n => print("first", n))` after the `on` line.

lessons.title: Decorator: add behaviour around something
lessons.text:
**Problem:** some shipping costs need a weekend surcharge, some a
discount, some both, and making a type for every combination explodes.
**Pattern:** wrap an object in another with the same shape that adds one
thing; wrappers stack. (Vyrn's `@decorator` for functions, Day 64, is the
same idea.)

```vyrn
trait Price:
    create amount(self) -> float
    create label(self) -> str
end

struct Base:
    value: float
    what: str
end

struct Discount:
    inner: Price
    percent: float
end

struct Surcharge:
    inner: Price
    extra: float
end

impl Price for Base:
    create amount(self) -> float:
        return self.value
    end
    create label(self) -> str:
        return self.what
    end
end

impl Price for Discount:
    create amount(self) -> float:
        return self.inner.amount() * (1 - self.percent / 100)
    end
    create label(self) -> str:
        return "{self.inner.label()}, {self.percent}% off"
    end
end

impl Price for Surcharge:
    create amount(self) -> float:
        return self.inner.amount() + self.extra
    end
    create label(self) -> str:
        return "{self.inner.label()}, +£{self.extra:.2f}"
    end
end

main:
    let p = Surcharge(Discount(Base(40.0, "concert ticket"), 25), 2.5)
    print("{p.label()}: £{p.amount():.2f}")
end
```

```text
concert ticket, 25% off, +£2.50: £32.50
```

lessons.title: Singleton, and why to avoid it
lessons.text:
**Problem:** there must be exactly one of something, such as the settings
or the database connection. The classic **singleton** pattern hides it in
a global that everything reaches for. Vyrn has no global variables, on
purpose: code that secretly reaches for shared state is hard to test
(you can't give it a fake) and hard to follow. Instead, make the one
object in `main` and **pass it in**, to functions as an argument or to
routes with `http.provide`. That is what every project in this course has
done, and why fakes could replace databases and email so easily. This
approach has a name too: **dependency injection**.

lessons.title: Project: a plugin system
lessons.text:
A text tool whose features are plugins: each is registered by name
(factory), transforms the text (strategy), and announces what it did
(observer). New plugins need no change to the tool:

```vyrn
trait Plugin:
    create apply(self, text: str) -> str
end

struct Upper:
end

struct Replace:
    old: str
    new: str
end

struct Trim:
end

impl Plugin for Upper:
    create apply(self, text: str) -> str:
        return text.upper()
    end
end

impl Plugin for Replace:
    create apply(self, text: str) -> str:
        return text.replace(self.old, self.new)
    end
end

impl Plugin for Trim:
    create apply(self, text: str) -> str:
        return " ".join(text.split())
    end
end

object Tool:
    makers: map = {}
    listeners: list = []

    create register(self, name: str, maker: any):
        self.makers[name] = maker
    end
    create on_step(self, listener: any):
        self.listeners.append(listener)
    end
    create run(self, text: str, steps: list[str]) -> str:
        var result = text
        each step in steps:
            let parts = step.split(":")
            if parts[0] not in self.makers: fail ValueError("no plugin {parts[0]}")
            let before = result
            result = self.makers[parts[0]](parts[1:]).apply(result)
            each l in self.listeners: l(parts[0], before, result)
        end
        return result
    end
end

main:
    let tool = Tool()
    tool.register("upper", args => Upper())
    tool.register("trim", args => Trim())
    tool.register("replace", args => Replace(args[0], args[1]))
    var log = []
    tool.on_step((name, before, after) => log.append("{name}: {len(before)} -> {len(after)} chars"))
    print(tool.run("  hello   wide   world  ", ["trim", "replace:world:Vyrn", "upper"]))
    each line in log: print(" ", line)
end
```

```text
HELLO WIDE VYRN
  trim: 24 -> 16 chars
  replace: 16 -> 15 chars
  upper: 15 -> 15 chars
```

Adding a plugin is one `struct`, one `impl` and one `register` line.

### Exercise

Add a `reverse` plugin that reverses the text, register it, and run
`["reverse", "upper"]` on `"abc"`.

```vyrn starter
trait Plugin:
    create apply(self, text: str) -> str
end

main:
    print("nothing yet")
end
```

```text expect
CBA
```

exercise.starter:
trait Plugin:
    create apply(self, text: str) -> str
end

main:
    print("nothing yet")
end
exercise.solution:
trait Plugin:
    create apply(self, text: str) -> str
end

struct Reverse:
end

struct Upper:
end

impl Plugin for Reverse:
    create apply(self, text: str) -> str:
        return text[::-1]
    end
end

impl Plugin for Upper:
    create apply(self, text: str) -> str:
        return text.upper()
    end
end

main:
    var text = "abc"
    each p in [Reverse(), Upper()]:
        text = p.apply(text)
    end
    print(text)
end
hints: `struct Reverse:` with `impl Plugin for Reverse:` whose `apply` returns `text[::-1]`.
no tool needed for the exercise: `Upper().apply(Reverse().apply("abc"))` works, given both plugins.

lessons.title: you learned
lessons.text:
- Strategy: interchangeable ways of doing one job, behind a trait or a
  function value.
- Factory: one place that turns a name into the right object.
- Observer: publish events; subscribers react without the publisher
  knowing them.
- Decorator: wrap an object to add behaviour, keeping its shape.
- Prefer passing shared objects in (dependency injection) to singletons.

days.title: Day 75: Making programs fast
days.intro:
Most programs are fast enough. When one isn't, guessing where the time
goes is almost always wrong: measure first. Today you measure with the
**profiler**, then speed up the slow part three ways, in order of how much
they usually help: a better algorithm, types that let Vyrn compile the
code to machine code, and using every core of the processor. The project
speeds up an image filter.

lessons.title: Measure first
lessons.text:
`vyrn run --profile file.vyrn` runs the program and then lists the time
spent in each function:

```bash
vyrn run --profile report.vyrn
```

```text
function                              calls       own ms  ms per call
match_names                               1      812.441     812.4410
load_rows                                 1       41.020      41.0200
main                                      1        2.301       2.3010
```

"Own ms" is time spent in that function itself, not in functions it
calls. Here `match_names` is 95% of the time: speeding up anything else
would be wasted effort. To time one part of a program yourself, take
`time.now()` before and after:

```vyrn
use vyrn.time

main:
    let start = time.now()
    let total = sum(i * i each i in 0 until 200000)
    let took = time.now() - start
    print(total, took < 5.0)
end
```

```text
2666646666700000 true
```

(The lesson prints only whether it took under five seconds, so it shows
the same on every computer.)

lessons.title: A better algorithm beats everything
lessons.text:
Day 68's lesson in practice: the biggest speed-ups come from doing less
work, not doing the same work faster. Finding which names in one list
appear in another, with a list (O(n²)) and with a set (O(n)):

```vyrn
use vyrn.time

create common_slow(a: list[str], b: list[str]) -> int:
    return len([x each x in a if x in b])
end

create common_fast(a: list[str], b: list[str]) -> int:
    let seen = set(b)
    return len([x each x in a if x in seen])
end

main:
```
