```vyrn
    let a = ["user{i}" each i in 0 until 3000]
    let b = ["user{i * 2}" each i in 0 until 3000]
    var start = time.now()
    let slow = common_slow(a, b)
    let slow_time = time.now() - start
    start = time.now()
    let fast = common_fast(a, b)
    let fast_time = time.now() - start
    print(slow, fast, "set version more than 10 times faster:", fast_time * 10 < slow_time)
end
```

```text
1500 1500 set version more than 10 times faster: true
```

Same answer; with 3,000 names the set version is hundreds of times faster,
and the gap grows with the data. Before anything else, ask: am I searching
a list inside a loop? Recomputing something that doesn't change? Reading a
file over and over?

lessons.title: Types make code fast
lessons.text:
A function whose parameters and result are typed with numbers, and that
uses only numbers and lists of numbers inside, is **compiled to machine
code** when the program loads, the way C is. Untyped code runs in Vyrn's
interpreter, which has to check what each value is as it goes:

```vyrn
use vyrn.time

create typed_sum(n: int) -> int:
    var t = 0
    each i in 0 until n:
        t += i % 7
    end
    return t
end

create untyped_sum(n):
    var t = 0
    each i in 0 until n:
        t += i % 7
    end
    return t
end

main:
    var start = time.now()
    let a = untyped_sum(2000000)
    let untyped_time = time.now() - start
    start = time.now()
    let b = typed_sum(2000000)
    let typed_time = time.now() - start
    print(a == b, "typed more than 5 times faster:", typed_time * 5 < untyped_time)
end
```

```text
true typed more than 5 times faster: true
```

The two functions differ only in `n: int` and `-> int`. On a typical
computer the typed one is around twenty times faster. That's why Day 60
suggested typing the functions others call, and making the busiest ones
`strict`: strict functions are guaranteed fully typed, so they always
compile.

What compiles: numbers (`int`, `float`, `bool`), lists of numbers,
structs of numbers, arithmetic, comparisons, loops, `if`, and calls to
other compiled functions. Anything else (text, maps, objects, printing)
runs in the interpreter, which is still plenty fast for most work. A good
design keeps the number-crunching in small typed functions, and the rest
of the program untyped and comfortable.

### Exercise

Make this function compile to machine code by giving it types, and check
the answer is unchanged.

```vyrn starter
create count_primes(limit):
    var count = 0
    each n in 2 until limit:
        var prime = true
        var d = 2
        loop d * d <= n:
            if n % d == 0:
                prime = false
                stop
            end
            d += 1
        end
        if prime: count += 1
    end
    return count
end

main:
    print(count_primes(20000))
end
```

```text expect
2262
```

exercise.starter:

exercise.solution:
create count_primes(limit: int) -> int:
    var count = 0
    each n in 2 until limit:
        var prime: bool = true
        var d = 2
        loop d * d <= n:
            if n % d == 0:
                prime = false
                stop
            end
            d += 1
        end
        if prime: count += 1
    end
    return count
end

main:
    print(count_primes(20000))
end
hints: `create count_primes(limit: int) -> int:`, and `var prime: bool = true`.

lessons.title: Using every core
lessons.text:
A modern processor has several **cores**, each able to run a program at
the same time. `task.parallel(work, items)` runs `work(x)` for every item,
spread over all the cores, and gives the results in order. Each core runs
its own copy of the program, so nothing is shared and nothing can clash;
`work` must be a top-level function, and items and results plain data:

```vyrn
use vyrn.task

create collatz_steps(start: int) -> int:
    var n = start
    var steps = 0
    loop n != 1:
        n = n // 2 if n % 2 == 0 else 3 * n + 1
        steps += 1
    end
    return steps
end

create longest(chunk: list[int]) -> (int, int):
    var best = (0, 0)
    each n in chunk:
        let s = collatz_steps(n)
        if s > best[1]: best = (n, s)
    end
    return best
end

main:
    let chunks = [list(start until start + 25000) each start in 1 until 200001 by 25000]
    let results = task.parallel(longest, chunks)
    print(max(results, key = r => r[1]))
end
```

```text
(156159, 382)
```

The search is split into 8 chunks, each searched on its own core; the
best of the chunks' bests is the answer. Splitting work into independent
pieces like this is called **data parallelism**. On a machine with 8
cores it's up to 8 times faster. It only helps with work that needs the
processor: waiting for the network is Day 72's job, not this one's.

lessons.title: Project: a faster image filter
lessons.text:
A blur replaces each pixel with the average of itself and its neighbours.
An image is a grid of brightness values; a real photo has millions. Here
is the plain version, then a typed version working on one row at a time,
then the rows spread over every core:

```vyrn
use vyrn.task
use vyrn.time

const W = 300
const H = 200

create make_image() -> list:
    return [[(x * 7 + y * 13) % 256 each x in 0 until W] each y in 0 until H]
end

create blur_plain(img: list) -> list:
    var out = []
    each y in 0 until H:
        var row = []
        each x in 0 until W:
            var total = 0
            var count = 0
            each dy in -1 to 1:
                each dx in -1 to 1:
                    let yy = y + dy
                    let xx = x + dx
                    if 0 <= yy < H and 0 <= xx < W:
                        total += img[yy][xx]
                        count += 1
                    end
                end
            end
            row.append(total // count)
        end
        out.append(row)
    end
    return out
end

## One output row from the rows above, at and below it.
create blur_row(above: list[int], here: list[int], below: list[int], has_above: bool, has_below: bool) -> list[int]:
    var row: list[int] = []
    let w = len(here)
    each x in 0 until w:
        var total = 0
        var count = 0
        each dx in -1 to 1:
            let xx = x + dx
            if 0 <= xx < w:
                total += here[xx]
                count += 1
                if has_above:
                    total += above[xx]
                    count += 1
                end
                if has_below:
                    total += below[xx]
                    count += 1
                end
            end
        end
        row.append(total // count)
    end
    return row
end

create blur_job(job: list) -> list[int]:
    return blur_row(job[0], job[1], job[2], job[3], job[4])
end

create jobs_for(img: list) -> list:
    return [[img[max(y - 1, 0)], img[y], img[min(y + 1, H - 1)], y > 0, y < H - 1] each y in 0 until H]
end

main:
    let img = make_image()
    var start = time.now()
    let a = blur_plain(img)
    let plain = time.now() - start
    start = time.now()
    let b = [blur_job(j) each j in jobs_for(img)]
    let typed = time.now() - start
    start = time.now()
    let c = task.parallel(blur_job, jobs_for(img))
    let parallel = time.now() - start
    print("same result:", a == b and b == c)
    print("typed rows faster than plain:", typed < plain)
    print("a pixel before and after:", img[50][50], a[50][50])
end
```

```text
same result: true
typed rows faster than plain: true
a pixel before and after: 232 232
```

All three give the same image. The typed row function compiles to machine
code; spreading rows over cores helps most on big photos, where the time
saved outweighs the cost of sending rows to each core. Measure with your
own images before deciding: that's the whole lesson of today.

### Exercise

`blur_plain` checks `0 <= yy < H and 0 <= xx < W` nine times per pixel.
Write `clamp(v, low, high)` (a typed function) giving `v` pushed into the
range, the building block for an "edge pixels repeat" blur that needs no
checks.

```vyrn starter
create clamp(v: int, low: int, high: int) -> int:
    return v
end

main:
    print(clamp(-1, 0, 9), clamp(5, 0, 9), clamp(12, 0, 9))
end
```

```text expect
0 5 9
```

exercise.starter:
create clamp(v: int, low: int, high: int) -> int:
    return v
end

main:
    print(clamp(-1, 0, 9), clamp(5, 0, 9), clamp(12, 0, 9))
end
exercise.solution:
create clamp(v: int, low: int, high: int) -> int:
    return max(low, min(v, high))
end

main:
    print(clamp(-1, 0, 9), clamp(5, 0, 9), clamp(12, 0, 9))
end
hints: `max(low, min(v, high))`

lessons.title: you learned
lessons.text:
- Measure before optimising: `vyrn run --profile`, and `time.now()`.
- A better algorithm (a set instead of a list) beats any other speed-up.
- Typed numeric functions are compiled to machine code: often 10 to 50
  times faster.
- `task.parallel` spreads independent work over every core.
- Keep the number-crunching small and typed; keep the rest simple.

days.title: Day 76: Borrowing other languages' libraries
days.intro:
No language has a library for everything. Python has decades of science
and machine-learning libraries; C has fast, battle-tested libraries for
compression, images, audio and more, and is the language operating
systems speak. Vyrn can call both directly. Today you learn when that's
worth it, how to call C functions and Python modules, and the simplest
bridge of all, running another program. The project uses a Python library
from a Vyrn program.

lessons.title: Three ways to borrow
lessons.text:
| Way | Use when | Cost |
|---|---|---|
| run another program (`os.run`) | a tool already does the job from the command line | slowest per call; simplest; nothing to build |
| `use python.x` | a Python library does the job (NumPy, pandas, scikit-learn, ...) | needs Python installed; values are converted at the boundary |
| `extern "c"` | a C library does the job, or you need the operating system | fastest; you must describe each function exactly; mistakes can crash |

Try them in that order. Running a program is often all you need, and it
can't crash yours.

lessons.title: Running another program
lessons.text:
`os.run(command)` runs a program and gives back its exit code and what it
printed. A list (`["git", "log", "-1"]`) passes each argument exactly as
written, with no shell to misread spaces or quotes; use that form for
anything that includes outside data:

```vyrn check
use vyrn.os

main:
    let r = os.run(["git", "log", "-1", "--format=%an: %s"])
    if r.ok:
        print("last commit by", r.out.strip())
    else:
        print("git failed:", r.err.strip())
    end
end
```

Programs that can print JSON are easiest to use this way, since the output
is data, not text to pick apart:

```vyrn
use vyrn.json

create disk_report(output: str) -> list[str]:
    let data = json.parse(output)
    return ["{d["name"]}: {d["used_pct"]}% used" each d in data["disks"] if d["used_pct"] > 80]
end

main:
    let recorded = r'{"disks": [{"name": "/", "used_pct": 91}, {"name": "/data", "used_pct": 40}]}'
    print(disk_report(recorded))
end
```

```text
["/: 91% used"]
```

lessons.title: Python libraries
lessons.text:
`use python.numpy as np` imports a Python module, and from then on it's
used like a Vyrn module. Numbers, text, lists and maps are converted both
ways; Python objects stay Python objects, with their attributes and methods
available. Vyrn tensors and NumPy arrays share memory, so big arrays cross
without being copied:

```vyrn check
use python.statistics
use python.numpy as np

main:
    let marks = [62, 71, 75, 80, 88, 94]
    print(statistics.median(marks), statistics.stdev(marks))
    let a = np.array([[1, 2], [3, 4]])
    print(np.linalg.det(a))
    let t = a.to_tensor()
    print(t * 2)
end
```

This needs a Vyrn built with Python support, and Python installed with the
libraries you use:

```bash
cargo build --release --features python
```

The standard downloads of Vyrn leave Python support out, so that Vyrn
doesn't need Python on every computer. Without it, a program that uses
Python stops with a clear message saying how to get it.

lessons.title: C libraries
lessons.text:
C functions are described in an `extern "c"` block: their names, the types
of their parameters and their result. Vyrn finds them in the library named
by `@link` (or in the standard C library without one) and calls them
directly, as fast as C calls C:

```vyrn check
extern "c":
    create abs(x: i32) -> i32
    create strlen(s: str) -> u64
end

@link("m")
extern "c":
    create cbrt(x: f64) -> f64
end

main:
    print(abs(-7), strlen("hello"), cbrt(27.0))
end
```

The types must match the C declaration *exactly*: `i32` is C's `int`,
`i64` is `long long`, `f64` is `double`, `str` is a `const char*`. Get one
wrong and the result is garbage, or a crash, which is why calling C needs
care. Functions that take or return raw pointers (`ptr u8`) can only be
called inside an `unsafe:` block: by writing `unsafe`, you promise the C
code only touches what it's given. This needs the `ffi` build feature:

```bash
cargo build --release --features ffi
```

lessons.title: Wrapping a library
lessons.text:
Whatever the bridge, keep it at the edge of your program, behind a few
plain Vyrn functions. The rest of the program then doesn't know or care
that Python or C is involved, can be tested with fakes, and keeps working
if you later swap the library for another:

```vyrn
## The only place that knows how sentiment is scored. For real, `score`
## calls a Python library; tests pass a fake.
create sentiment(texts: list[str], score: any) -> list[str]:
    var labels = []
    each t in texts:
        let s = score(t)
        labels.append("positive" if s > 0.2 else ("negative" if s < -0.2 else "neutral"))
    end
    return labels
end

main:
    let fake_score = fake(returns_each = [0.9, -0.6, 0.0])
    print(sentiment(["I love it", "awful service", "it arrived"], fake_score))
end
```

```text
["positive", "negative", "neutral"]
```

lessons.title: Project: a Python library from Vyrn
lessons.text:
The project uses Python's `difflib` to find the closest match for a
mistyped word, a feature that would take a page of code to write well.
The bridge is one small function; everything else is Vyrn:

```vyrn check
use python.difflib

create closest(word: str, choices: list[str]) -> str?:
    let found = difflib.get_close_matches(word, choices, n = 1, cutoff = 0.6)
    return found[0] if found else none
end

main:
    let commands = ["list", "add", "remove", "check", "help"]
    each typed in ["lsit", "remvoe", "chek", "xyzzy"]:
        let guess = closest(typed, commands)
        print(typed, "->", "did you mean {guess}?" if guess != none else "unknown command")
    end
end
```

With a Python-enabled Vyrn it prints `lsit -> did you mean list?` and so
on. Vyrn's own error messages do the same thing (misspell a variable and
it says "`totl` is not defined ... did you mean `total`?"), with code
written in Rust: the same idea, from another language's library.

### Exercise

Without Python, write the core of `closest` yourself: the number of
positions where two equal-length words differ, then pick the command with
the fewest differences (only among commands of the same length as the
typed word).

```vyrn starter
create differences(a: str, b: str) -> int:
    return 0
end

create closest(word: str, choices: list[str]) -> str?:
    return none
end

main:
    print(closest("lsit", ["list", "add", "help"]), closest("hepl", ["list", "add", "help"]), closest("x", ["list"]))
end
```

```text expect
list help none
```

exercise.starter:
create differences(a: str, b: str) -> int:
    return 0
end

create closest(word: str, choices: list[str]) -> str?:
    return none
end

main:
    print(closest("lsit", ["list", "add", "help"]), closest("hepl", ["list", "add", "help"]), closest("x", ["list"]))
end
exercise.solution:
create differences(a: str, b: str) -> int:
    return len([i each i in 0 until len(a) if a[i] != b[i]])
end

create closest(word: str, choices: list[str]) -> str?:
    let same_length = [c each c in choices if len(c) == len(word)]
    if not same_length: return none
    return min(same_length, key = c => differences(word, c))
end

main:
    print(closest("lsit", ["list", "add", "help"]), closest("hepl", ["list", "add", "help"]), closest("x", ["list"]))
end
hints: `differences` counts `i` where `a[i] != b[i]`.
in `closest`, keep choices with `len(c) == len(word)`; give `none` if there are none, else `min(same_length, key = c => differences(word, c))`.

lessons.title: you learned
lessons.text:
- Borrow before you build: run a program (`os.run` with a list), use a
  Python module (`use python.x`), or call C (`extern "c"`), in that order
  of simplicity.
- Python and C support are build features (`--features python`,
  `--features ffi`); without them Vyrn says how to get them.
- C types must match exactly; raw pointers need `unsafe:`.
- Keep the bridge in a few small functions at the edge, so the rest can be
  tested with fakes.

days.title: Day 77: A platformer
days.intro:
Unit 2 made games where things slide around a screen: Snake, Pong, a road
crossing. This unit makes games that feel physical, starting with the
most loved kind of 2D game: a **platformer**, where a character runs and
jumps between ledges. You'll write gravity, jumping that feels good, and
collision with a level made of tiles. The game logic is plain functions
on plain data, so every rule can be tested without opening a window; the
window code at the end only draws it.

lessons.title: Velocity and gravity
lessons.text:
A thing that moves has a **position** and a **velocity** (how far it moves
each second). Gravity changes the velocity; the velocity changes the
position. Each frame lasts `dt` seconds (Day 19, and the game-dev guide):

```vyrn
struct Body:
    x: float
    y: float
    vx: float
    vy: float
end

const GRAVITY = 1500.0

create step(b: Body, dt: float) -> Body:
    let vy = b.vy + GRAVITY * dt
    return Body(b.x + b.vx * dt, b.y + vy * dt, b.vx, vy)
end

main:
    var ball = Body(0.0, 0.0, 200.0, -600.0)
    each frame in 0 until 50:
        ball = step(ball, 1.0 / 60)
        if frame % 10 == 9: print("t={(frame + 1) / 60:.2f}s  x={ball.x:.0f}  y={ball.y:.0f}")
    end
end
```

```text
t=0.17s  x=33  y=-77
t=0.33s  x=67  y=-112
t=0.50s  x=100  y=-106
t=0.67s  x=133  y=-58
t=0.83s  x=167  y=31
```

Screen coordinates grow *downwards*, so a negative `vy` is upwards. The
ball rises, slows, and falls: a curve, from two lines of arithmetic. Every
physics engine, from Mario to Unreal, starts here.

lessons.title: A level made of tiles
lessons.text:
Platformer levels are usually grids of **tiles**: each cell is empty or
solid. Writing the level as text makes it easy to draw by hand and easy to
read:

```vyrn
const LEVEL = """
..........
..........
....###...
..........
#........#
##########
"""

const TILE = 32

create load(text: str) -> list[str]:
    return [line each line in text.strip().split("\n")]
end

create solid(level: list[str], px: float, py: float) -> bool:
    let col = int(px // TILE)
    let row = int(py // TILE)
    if row < 0 or row >= len(level) or col < 0 or col >= len(level[0]): return true
    return level[row][col] == "#"
end

main:
    let level = load(LEVEL)
    print(len(level), "rows of", len(level[0]))
    print(solid(level, 5 * 32 + 3, 2 * 32 + 10), solid(level, 40.0, 40.0), solid(level, -1.0, 0.0))
end
```

```text
6 rows of 10
true false true
```

`px // TILE` turns a pixel position into a tile column. Outside the level
counts as solid, so nothing can fall out of the world.

lessons.title: Colliding with tiles
lessons.text:
The classic method: move along one axis at a time, and if the box ends up
inside a solid tile, push it back to the tile's edge and stop that part of
its velocity. Moving x and y separately is what lets a character slide
along a wall or land on a floor cleanly:

```vyrn
const TILE = 32

struct Player:
    x: float
    y: float
    vx: float
    vy: float
    on_ground: bool
end

const W = 20.0
const H = 28.0

create solid(level: list[str], px: float, py: float) -> bool:
    let col = int(px // TILE)
    let row = int(py // TILE)
    if row < 0 or row >= len(level) or col < 0 or col >= len(level[0]): return true
    return level[row][col] == "#"
end

create hits(level: list[str], x: float, y: float) -> bool:
    return solid(level, x, y) or solid(level, x + W - 1, y) or solid(level, x, y + H - 1) or solid(level, x + W - 1, y + H - 1)
end

create move(level: list[str], p: Player, dt: float) -> Player:
    ## Across: if the new place is inside a wall, stay put and stop.
    var x = p.x + p.vx * dt
    var vx = p.vx
    if hits(level, x, p.y):
        x = p.x
        vx = 0.0
    end
    ## Down or up: when landing, stand exactly on top of the tile hit.
    var y = p.y + p.vy * dt
    var vy = p.vy
    if hits(level, x, y):
        y = int((y + H - 1) // TILE) * TILE - H if p.vy > 0 else p.y
        vy = 0.0
    end
    ## Standing means solid ground one pixel below the feet.
    return Player(x, y, vx, vy, hits(level, x, y + 1))
end

main:
    let level = ["........", "........", "........", "########"]
    var p = Player(40.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0, false)
    each _ in 0 until 60:
        p = move(level, Player(p.x, p.y, p.vx, p.vy + 1500.0 / 60, p.on_ground), 1.0 / 60)
    end
    print("landed:", p.on_ground, "feet at", round(p.y + H), "floor at", 3 * TILE)
end
```

```text
landed: true feet at 96 floor at 96
```

The player falls, hits the floor, and stands on it, with their feet
exactly on the floor's top edge.

lessons.title: Jumping that feels good
lessons.text:
Jumping is only allowed on the ground, or the player could fly. Two small
tricks make it feel far better, and nearly every good platformer uses
them:

- **Coyote time:** you can still jump for a moment (a tenth of a second)
  after running off a ledge, because people press jump a fraction late.
- **Jump buffering:** a jump pressed a moment *before* landing still
  happens when you land.

```vyrn
object JumpControl:
    since_ground: float = 1.0
    since_press: float = 1.0
    window: float = 0.1

    create update(self, dt: float, on_ground: bool, pressed: bool) -> bool:
        self.since_ground = 0.0 if on_ground else self.since_ground + dt
        self.since_press = 0.0 if pressed else self.since_press + dt
        if self.since_ground <= self.window and self.since_press <= self.window:
            self.since_ground = 1.0
            self.since_press = 1.0
            return true
        end
        return false
    end
end

main:
    let dt = 1.0 / 60
    let late = JumpControl()
    late.update(dt, true, false)
    each _ in 0 until 4: late.update(dt, false, false)
    print("pressed 4 frames after leaving the ledge:", late.update(dt, false, true))
    let early = JumpControl()
    early.update(dt, false, true)
    each _ in 0 until 3: early.update(dt, false, false)
    print("pressed 4 frames before landing:", early.update(dt, true, false))
    let flying = JumpControl()
    each _ in 0 until 30: flying.update(dt, false, false)
    print("pressed in mid-air long after:", flying.update(dt, false, true))
end
```

```text
pressed 4 frames after leaving the ledge: true
pressed 4 frames before landing: true
pressed in mid-air long after: false
```

### Exercise

**Variable jump height:** if the player lets go of jump while still
rising, cut their upward speed in half, so a tap gives a small hop and a
hold a full jump. Write `release(vy, holding)`.

```vyrn starter
create release(vy: float, holding: bool) -> float:
    return vy
end

main:
    print(release(-600.0, true), release(-600.0, false), release(200.0, false))
end
```

```text expect
-600.0 -300.0 200.0
```

exercise.starter:
create release(vy: float, holding: bool) -> float:
    return vy
end

main:
    print(release(-600.0, true), release(-600.0, false), release(200.0, false))
end
exercise.solution:
create release(vy: float, holding: bool) -> float:
    if not holding and vy < 0: return vy / 2
    return vy
end

main:
    print(release(-600.0, true), release(-600.0, false), release(200.0, false))
end
hints: only change it when not holding *and* still going up (`vy < 0`).

lessons.title: Project: the platformer
lessons.text:
The game: a level with ledges and coins, a player who runs and jumps, a
camera that follows them. The rules live in one `update` function that
takes the input as data, so a test can play the game by "pressing keys"
with a list:

```vyrn
const TILE = 32
const W = 20.0
const H = 28.0
const GRAVITY = 1500.0
const RUN = 180.0
const JUMP = -560.0

const LEVEL = [
    "....................",
    "............o.......",
    "..........#####.....",
    "....o...............",
    "...####........o....",
    "..............###...",
    "#..................#",
    "####################",
]

object Game:
    level: list[str]
    x: float = 40.0
    y: float = 150.0
    vx: float = 0.0
    vy: float = 0.0
    on_ground: bool = false
    coins: set = set()

    create solid(self, px: float, py: float) -> bool:
        let col = int(px // TILE)
        let row = int(py // TILE)
        if row < 0 or row >= len(self.level) or col < 0 or col >= len(self.level[0]): return true
        return self.level[row][col] == "#"
    end

    create hits(self, x: float, y: float) -> bool:
        return self.solid(x, y) or self.solid(x + W - 1, y) or self.solid(x, y + H - 1) or self.solid(x + W - 1, y + H - 1)
    end

    create update(self, dt: float, left: bool, right: bool, jump: bool):
        self.vx = (RUN if right else 0.0) - (RUN if left else 0.0)
        if jump and self.on_ground: self.vy = JUMP
        self.vy += GRAVITY * dt
        let nx = self.x + self.vx * dt
        if not self.hits(nx, self.y): self.x = nx
        let ny = self.y + self.vy * dt
        if self.hits(self.x, ny):
            if self.vy > 0: self.y = int((ny + H - 1) // TILE) * TILE - H
            self.vy = 0.0
        else:
            self.y = ny
        end
        self.on_ground = self.hits(self.x, self.y + 1)
        let col = int((self.x + W / 2) // TILE)
        let row = int((self.y + H / 2) // TILE)
        if 0 <= row < len(self.level) and self.level[row][col] == "o": self.coins.add((col, row))
    end
end

## Plays a script of (keys held, number of frames): "L", "R", "J" for left,
## right and jump.
create play(game: Game, script: list):
    each keys, frames in script:
        each _ in 0 until frames:
            game.update(1.0 / 60, "L" in keys, "R" in keys, "J" in keys)
        end
    end
end

main:
    let g = Game(LEVEL)
    play(g, [("", 20), ("RJ", 16), ("R", 20), ("", 40)])
    print("x={g.x:.0f} y={g.y:.0f} on ground: {g.on_ground}, coins: {sorted(g.coins)}")
    let still = Game(LEVEL)
    play(still, [("", 90)])
    print("standing still: y={still.y:.0f}, on ground: {still.on_ground}, coins: {len(still.coins)}")
end
```

```text
x=130 y=100 on ground: true, coins: [(4, 3)]
standing still: y=196, on ground: true, coins: 0
```

Waiting, then running right while jumping, lands the player on the first
ledge with its coin; standing still, they settle on the floor. Scripts like
these are the game's tests: change the jump strength and you'll see at
once whether that ledge can still be reached.

The window version draws the same `Game`: tiles as squares, coins as
circles, and a camera that keeps the player in the middle of the screen
by drawing everything shifted by the camera's position:

```vyrn check
use vyrn.draw

const TILE = 32

main:
    let level = ["....................", "....o...............", "...####.............", "####################"]
    let win = draw.window(480, 256, "Platformer")
    var x = 40.0
    var dt = 0.016
    loop win.open():
        if win.key_down("right"): x += 180 * dt
        if win.key_down("left"): x -= 180 * dt
        let camera = max(0.0, x - 240)
        win.clear("#87ceeb")
        each row, line in enumerate(level):
            each col, c in enumerate(line):
                let sx = col * TILE - camera
                if c == "#": win.rect(sx, row * TILE, TILE, TILE, "#5d4037")
                if c == "o": win.circle(sx + 16, row * TILE + 16, 8, "gold")
            end
        end
        win.rect(x - camera, 2 * TILE + 4, 20, 28, "crimson")
        dt = win.show()
    end
end
```

Put the `Game` object and this drawing together, read the arrow keys and
space into `update`, and you have a playable game. Because `update` is
tested on its own, you can change the jump height, add enemies or design
levels and check the rules still hold without playing through every time.

### Exercise

Add a **goal**: the level is finished when the player touches a `G` tile.
Write `at_goal(level, x, y)` that checks the tile under the player's
centre.

```vyrn starter
const TILE = 32

create at_goal(level: list[str], x: float, y: float) -> bool:
    return false
end

main:
    let level = ["....G", "#####"]
    print(at_goal(level, 4 * 32 + 5, 2.0), at_goal(level, 10.0, 2.0))
end
```

```text expect
true false
```

exercise.starter:
const TILE = 32

create at_goal(level: list[str], x: float, y: float) -> bool:
    return false
end

main:
    let level = ["....G", "#####"]
    print(at_goal(level, 4 * 32 + 5, 2.0), at_goal(level, 10.0, 2.0))

exercise.solution:
const TILE = 32

create at_goal(level: list[str], x: float, y: float) -> bool:
    let col = int((x + 10) // TILE)
    let row = int((y + 14) // TILE)
    if row < 0 or row >= len(level) or col < 0 or col >= len(level[0]): return false
    return level[row][col] == "G"
end

main:
    let level = ["....G", "#####"]
    print(at_goal(level, 4 * 32 + 5, 2.0), at_goal(level, 10.0, 2.0))
end
hints: centre column `int((x + 10) // TILE)`, row `int((y + 14) // TILE)`.

lessons.title: you learned
lessons.text:
- Gravity changes velocity, velocity changes position, scaled by `dt`.
- Tile levels written as text; pixel to tile with `//`.
- Collide one axis at a time, push back to the tile edge, stop that
  velocity.
- Coyote time, jump buffering and variable jump height make jumping feel
  good.
- Keep game rules in an `update` function that tests can drive with
  recorded input; the window only draws.

days.title: Day 78: A 3D maze
days.intro:
Yesterday's platformer was flat. Today the game gets a third dimension:
you walk through a maze in first person, with lights, fog and a minimap.
3D sounds hard, but a 3D game is the same loop as a 2D one (input,
update, draw), with a **camera** that decides what the screen shows. The
rules of the maze (where the walls are, where you can walk, how to reach
the exit) are still a grid and still plain, testable functions. The
`game-dev.md` guide goes much further, to a full shooter; this lesson is
the first step.

lessons.title: Coordinates in 3D
lessons.text:
A 3D position has three numbers. In Vyrn's 3D, **x** is right, **y** is up
and **z** is forward. A flat maze lives on the ground, so walls sit at
grid cells `(column, row)` with x = column and z = row, and y is height:

```vyrn
const MAZE = """
#########
#S..#...#
#.#.#.#.#
#.#...#.#
#.#####.#
#...#..E#
#########
"""

create load(text: str) -> list[str]:
    return text.strip().split("\n")
end

create find(maze: list[str], c: str) -> (int, int):
    each row, line in enumerate(maze):
        let col = line.find(c)
        if col >= 0: return (col, row)
    end
    fail ValueError("no {c} in the maze")
end

main:
    let maze = load(MAZE)
    print(len(maze[0]), "by", len(maze), "cells")
    print("start", find(maze, "S"), "exit", find(maze, "E"))
    let walls = [(col, row) each row, line in enumerate(maze) each col, c in enumerate(line) if c == "#"]
    print(len(walls), "wall blocks")
end
```

```text
9 by 7 cells
start (1, 1) exit (7, 5)
40 wall blocks
```

Each `#` becomes a cube one unit wide in the world, standing on the
ground at x = column + 0.5, z = row + 0.5.

lessons.title: Turning and walking
lessons.text:
The player has a position and a **yaw**: the direction they face, in
degrees. Walking forward moves along that direction, worked out with sine
and cosine; turning just changes the yaw:

```vyrn
use vyrn.math

create ahead(x: float, z: float, yaw: float, distance: float) -> (float, float):
    let r = math.radians(yaw)
    return (x + distance * math.sin(r), z + distance * math.cos(r))
end

main:
    each yaw in [0, 90, 180, 45]:
        let nx, nz = ahead(0.0, 0.0, yaw, 1.0)
        print("yaw {yaw:>3}: ({nx:.2f}, {nz:.2f})")
    end
end
```

```text
yaw   0: (0.00, 1.00)
yaw  90: (1.00, 0.00)
yaw 180: (0.00, -1.00)
yaw  45: (0.71, 0.71)
```

Yaw 0 looks along +z, yaw 90 along +x. `draw.camera` does exactly this
for you (`cam.forward(d)`, `cam.turn(degrees)`); knowing the maths lets
you move other things, such as enemies, the same way.

lessons.title: Not walking through walls
lessons.text:
The player is a small circle on the floor plan. Before moving, check the
cells the circle would touch; as on Day 77, try each axis separately, so
walking into a wall at an angle slides along it instead of stopping dead:

```vyrn
const RADIUS = 0.25

create is_wall(maze: list[str], x: float, z: float) -> bool:
    let col = int(x // 1)
    let row = int(z // 1)
    if row < 0 or row >= len(maze) or col < 0 or col >= len(maze[0]): return true
    return maze[row][col] == "#"
end

create blocked(maze: list[str], x: float, z: float) -> bool:
    each dx, dz in [(-RADIUS, -RADIUS), (RADIUS, -RADIUS), (-RADIUS, RADIUS), (RADIUS, RADIUS)]:
        if is_wall(maze, x + dx, z + dz): return true
    end
    return false
end

create slide(maze: list[str], x: float, z: float, dx: float, dz: float) -> (float, float):
    let nx = x if blocked(maze, x + dx, z) else x + dx
    let nz = z if blocked(maze, nx, z + dz) else z + dz
    return (nx, nz)
end

main:
    let maze = ["#####", "#...#", "#...#", "#####"]
    print(slide(maze, 1.5, 1.5, 0.3, 0.0))
    print(slide(maze, 3.5, 1.5, 0.3, 0.0))
    print(slide(maze, 3.5, 1.5, 0.3, 0.3))
end
```

```text
(1.8, 1.5)
(3.5, 1.5)
(3.5, 1.8)
```

Against the right-hand wall, the move to the right is refused, but the
part of a diagonal move that goes along the wall still happens.

### Exercise

Write `at_exit(maze, x, z)`: true when the player stands in the `E` cell.

```vyrn starter
create at_exit(maze: list[str], x: float, z: float) -> bool:
    return false
end

main:
    let maze = ["####", "#.E#", "####"]
    print(at_exit(maze, 2.5, 1.5), at_exit(maze, 1.5, 1.5))
end
```

```text expect
true false
```

exercise.starter:
create at_exit(maze: list[str], x: float, z: float) -> bool:
    return false
end

main:
    let maze = ["####", "#.E#", "####"]
    print(at_exit(maze, 2.5, 1.5), at_exit(maze, 1.5, 1.5))
end
exercise.solution:
create at_exit(maze: list[str], x: float, z: float) -> bool:
    return maze[int(z // 1)][int(x // 1)] == "E"
end

main:
    let maze = ["####", "#.E#", "####"]
    print(at_exit(maze, 2.5, 1.5), at_exit(maze, 1.5, 1.5))
end
hints: the cell is `maze[int(z // 1)][int(x // 1)]`.

lessons.title: A hint: the way out
lessons.text:
Lost in a maze? Breadth-first search (Day 71) finds the shortest way out
on the grid, step by step. The game can draw it on a minimap, or point an
arrow at the next cell:

```vyrn
create way_out(maze: list[str], start: (int, int), goal: (int, int)) -> list?:
    var came_from = {start: none}
    var queue = [start]
    loop queue:
        let cell = queue.pop(0)
        if cell == goal:
            var path = []
            var at = goal
            loop at != none:
                path.insert(0, at)
                at = came_from[at]
            end
            return path
        end
        let col, row = cell
        each next in [(col + 1, row), (col - 1, row), (col, row + 1), (col, row - 1)]:
            let c, r = next
            if maze[r][c] != "#" and next not in came_from:
                came_from[next] = cell
                queue.append(next)
            end
        end
    end
    return none
end

main:
    let maze = ["#########", "#S..#...#", "#.#.#.#.#", "#.#...#.#", "#.#####.#", "#...#..E#", "#########"]
    let path = way_out(maze, (1, 1), (7, 5))
    print(len(path) - 1, "steps")
    each row, line in enumerate(maze):
        print("".join(["*" if (col, row) in path and c == "." else c each col, c in enumerate(line)]))
    end
end
```

```text
14 steps
#########
#S**#***#
#.#*#*#*#
#.#***#*#
#.#####*#
#...#..E#
#########
```

lessons.title: Project: the maze in 3D
lessons.text:
Putting it on screen: a camera at the player's eyes, a cube per wall, a
floor, a sun and a little ambient light so the shadows aren't black, and
fog to make the far end of the corridor fade out (which looks good and
hides how small the maze really is). The arrow keys turn and walk; the
movement goes through `slide`, so walls stop you:

```vyrn check
use vyrn.draw
use vyrn.math

const RADIUS = 0.25

create is_wall(maze: list[str], x: float, z: float) -> bool:
    let col = int(x // 1)
    let row = int(z // 1)
    if row < 0 or row >= len(maze) or col < 0 or col >= len(maze[0]): return true
    return maze[row][col] == "#"
end

create blocked(maze: list[str], x: float, z: float) -> bool:
    each dx, dz in [(-RADIUS, -RADIUS), (RADIUS, -RADIUS), (-RADIUS, RADIUS), (RADIUS, RADIUS)]:
        if is_wall(maze, x + dx, z + dz): return true
    end
    return false
end

main:
    let maze = ["#########", "#S..#...#", "#.#.#.#.#", "#.#...#.#", "#.#####.#", "#...#..E#", "#########"]
    let win = draw.window(800, 500, "Maze")
    let cam = draw.camera(1.5, 0.6, 1.5)
    var dt = 0.016
    var spin = 0.0
    loop win.open():
        spin += 90 * dt
        if win.key_down("left"): cam.turn(-120 * dt, 0)
        if win.key_down("right"): cam.turn(120 * dt, 0)
        var step = 0.0
        if win.key_down("up"): step = 2.5 * dt
        if win.key_down("down"): step = -2.5 * dt
        let r = math.radians(cam.yaw)
        let dx = step * math.sin(r)
        let dz = step * math.cos(r)
        let nx = cam.x if blocked(maze, cam.x + dx, cam.z) else cam.x + dx
        let nz = cam.z if blocked(maze, nx, cam.z + dz) else cam.z + dz
        cam.move_to(nx, 0.6, nz)

        win.clear("#202830")
        win.ambient(0.35, "white")
        win.light([0.4, -1, 0.3], "white", 0.8)
        win.fog("#202830", 3, 9)
        win.box(cam, [4.5, -0.05, 3.5, 9, 0.1, 7], "#4a4a4a")
        each row, line in enumerate(maze):
            each col, c in enumerate(line):
                if c == "#": win.cube(cam, col + 0.5, 0.5, row + 0.5, 1, "#8d6e63")
                if c == "E": win.cube(cam, col + 0.5, 0.2, row + 0.5, 0.3, "gold", rotation = [0, spin, 0])
            end
        end
        if maze[int(cam.z // 1)][int(cam.x // 1)] == "E": win.text("You escaped!", 320, 230, "gold", 3)
        dt = win.show()
    end
end
```

The rules are the functions you tested above; the window loop only reads
keys, moves the camera through `slide`'s logic, and draws. The spinning
gold cube at the exit uses `rotation`, with `spin` growing by 90 degrees
a second.

### Exercise

A minimap: write `minimap(maze, col, row)` giving the maze as text with an
`@` where the player is.

```vyrn starter
create minimap(maze: list[str], col: int, row: int) -> str:
    return "\n".join(maze)
end

main:
    print(minimap(["#####", "#...#", "#####"], 2, 1))
end
```

```text expect
#####
#.@.#
#####
```

exercise.starter:
create minimap(maze: list[str], col: int, row: int) -> str:
    return "\n".join(maze)
end

main:
    print(minimap(["#####", "#...#", "#####"], 2, 1))
end
exercise.solution:
create minimap(maze: list[str], col: int, row: int) -> str:
    var lines = []
    each r, line in enumerate(maze):
        lines.append("".join(["@" if (c, r) == (col, row) else ch each c, ch in enumerate(line)]))
    end
    return "\n".join(lines)
end

main:
    print(minimap(["#####", "#...#", "#####"], 2, 1))
end
hints: build each line with `"@" if (c, r) == (col, row) else ch`.

lessons.title: you learned
lessons.text:
- 3D positions are x (right), y (up), z (forward); a flat maze is a grid
  on the x–z plane.
- Facing is a yaw angle; forward is `(sin, cos)` of it.
- Collide on the floor plan, one axis at a time, so walls slide.
- Breadth-first search gives hints; the camera, cubes, lights and fog draw
  the world.

days.title: Day 79: Finishing a game
days.intro:
A game that runs isn't yet a game people can play: it needs a title
screen, a pause button, sound, a "game over" with the score, a table of
high scores that's still there tomorrow, and a way to give it to a friend.
These are the last 20% of a game that take 50% of the time, and today you
do them properly. The project turns a small dodging game into a finished
one.

lessons.title: Screens as states
lessons.text:
A finished game has several **screens**: the title menu, playing, paused,
game over. Exactly one is active at a time. That's an enum (Day 61), and
the game is a **state machine**: each screen decides, from the input,
which screen comes next:

```vyrn
enum Screen:
    Title
    Playing
    Paused
    GameOver(score: int)
end

create next_screen(s: Screen, key: str, crashed: bool, score: int) -> Screen:
    when s:
        is Screen.Title:
            if key == "enter": return Screen.Playing
        is Screen.Playing:
            if crashed: return Screen.GameOver(score)
            if key == "p": return Screen.Paused
        is Screen.Paused:
            if key == "p": return Screen.Playing
            if key == "escape": return Screen.Title
        is Screen.GameOver(_):
            if key == "enter": return Screen.Title
    end
    return s
end

main:
    var s = Screen.Title
    each key, crashed in [("", false), ("enter", false), ("p", false), ("x", false), ("p", false), ("", true), ("enter", false)]:
        s = next_screen(s, key, crashed, 42)
        print("{key:<6} -> {s}")
    end
end
```

```text
       -> Screen.Title
enter  -> Screen.Playing
p      -> Screen.Paused
x      -> Screen.Paused
p      -> Screen.Playing
       -> Screen.GameOver(score=42)
enter  -> Screen.Title
```

Every possible move between screens is in one function, readable at a
glance and tested by a list of key presses. Because `Screen` is an enum,
the checker complains if a new screen (say `Settings`) is added and
`next_screen` forgets it.

lessons.title: High scores that last
lessons.text:
High scores live in a file, so they survive closing the game. Keep the top
five, newest first among equal scores, and never crash because the file is
missing or damaged (Day 30):

```vyrn
use vyrn.fs
use vyrn.json

const FILE = "scores.json"

create load_scores() -> list:
    if not fs.exists(FILE): return []
    attempt:
        let data = json.load(FILE)
        if data is list: return data
    catch ValueError:
        print("(scores file damaged; starting fresh)")
    end
    return []
end

create add_score(name: str, score: int) -> int?:
    var scores = load_scores()
    scores.insert(0, {"name": name, "score": score})
    scores = sorted(scores, key = s => s["score"], reverse = true)[:5]
    json.save(FILE, scores)
    each i, s in enumerate(scores):
        if s["name"] == name and s["score"] == score: return i + 1
    end
    return none
end

main:
    if fs.exists(FILE): fs.remove(FILE)
    each name, score in [("ADA", 120), ("BOB", 80), ("CY", 200), ("DEE", 95), ("ED", 60), ("FAY", 10), ("GUS", 150)]:
        let place = add_score(name, score)
        print(name, score, "-> place", place ?? "not in the top 5")
    end
    print([s["name"] each s in load_scores()])
    write_text(FILE, r"[{broken")
    print(load_scores())
end
```

```text
ADA 120 -> place 1
BOB 80 -> place 2
CY 200 -> place 1
DEE 95 -> place 3
ED 60 -> place 5
FAY 10 -> place not in the top 5
GUS 150 -> place 2
["CY", "GUS", "ADA", "DEE", "BOB"]
(scores file damaged; starting fresh)
[]
```

### Exercise

Arcade games ask for exactly three letters. Write `clean_name(typed)`:
keep only letters, in capitals, at most three; `"???"` if none are left.

```vyrn starter
create clean_name(typed: str) -> str:
    return typed
end

main:
    print(clean_name("ada"), clean_name("  Ab1c2d "), clean_name("42!"))
end
```

```text expect
ADA ABC ???
```

exercise.starter:
create clean_name(typed: str) -> str:
    return typed
end

main:
    print(clean_name("ada"), clean_name("  Ab1c2d "), clean_name("42!"))
end
exercise.solution:
create clean_name(typed: str) -> str:
    let letters = "".join([c.upper() each c in typed if c.isalpha()])[:3]
    return letters if letters else "???"
end

main:
    print(clean_name("ada"), clean_name("  Ab1c2d "), clean_name("42!"))
end
hints: `"".join([c.upper() each c in typed if c.isalpha()])[:3]`

lessons.title: Sound
lessons.text:
Sound makes a game feel alive far more than its size suggests. `vyrn.sound`
plays files (WAV, Ogg, MP3), and can also **make** simple sounds from
waves, which is handy before you have real sound files:

```vyrn check
use vyrn.sound

main:
    let jump = sound.tone(660, 0.12, "square", 0.3)
    let crash = sound.tone(110, 0.4, "noise", 0.4)
    let music = sound.load("assets/theme.ogg")
    let playing = music.play(volume = 0.5, loop = true)
    jump.play()
    crash.play(speed = 0.8)
    playing.set_volume(0.2)
end
```

Without a sound device (on a server, in a test), playing is silent rather
than an error, so the game still runs. Two habits: keep effects short and
quiet compared with the music, and give the player a way to turn sound
off, saved with their settings.

lessons.title: Project: a finished dodging game
lessons.text:
Blocks fall; the player moves left and right to dodge them; the score is
how long you survive. The game rules are a `Game` object with an
`update(dt, left, right)` method, so they can be tested without a window,
as on Day 77. The screen logic and high scores are 79.1 and 79.2:

```vyrn
use vyrn.random

const WIDTH = 400.0
const HEIGHT = 500.0

struct Block:
    x: float
    y: float
    speed: float
end

object Game:
    x: float = 200.0
    blocks: list = []
    time: float = 0.0
    next_block: float = 0.0
    crashed: bool = false

    create update(self, dt: float, left: bool, right: bool):
        if self.crashed: return
        self.time += dt
        if left: self.x = max(20.0, self.x - 300 * dt)
        if right: self.x = min(WIDTH - 20, self.x + 300 * dt)
        self.next_block -= dt
        if self.next_block <= 0:
            self.blocks.append(Block(random.float(0, WIDTH - 40), -40.0, 150 + self.time * 10))
            self.next_block = max(0.25, 0.9 - self.time * 0.02)
        end
        var kept = []
        each b in self.blocks:
            let moved = Block(b.x, b.y + b.speed * dt, b.speed)
            if moved.y < HEIGHT: kept.append(moved)
            let px = self.x - 15
            let py = HEIGHT - 50
            if moved.x < px + 30 and px < moved.x + 40 and moved.y < py + 30 and py < moved.y + 40:
                self.crashed = true
            end
        end
        self.blocks = kept
    end

    create score(self) -> int:
        return int(self.time * 10)
    end
end

create survive(seed: int, policy: any) -> int:
    random.seed(seed)
    let g = Game()
    var frames = 0
    loop not g.crashed and frames < 60 * 120:
        let left, right = policy(g)
        g.update(1.0 / 60, left, right)
        frames += 1
    end
    return g.score()
end

## Moves away from the nearest block that's coming down near the player.
create dodge(g: Game) -> (bool, bool):
    let near = [b each b in g.blocks if b.y > HEIGHT - 250 and abs(b.x + 20 - g.x) < 60]
    if not near: return (false, false)
    let b = near[0]
    let go_left = b.x + 20 > g.x and g.x > 60 or g.x > WIDTH - 60
    return (go_left, not go_left)
end

main:
    print("standing still scores", survive(1, g => (false, false)))
    print("dodging scores", survive(1, dodge))
end
```

```text
standing still scores 51
dodging scores 462
```

The two lines test the game by playing it automatically. The "dodging"
player isn't clever, but it should do better than standing still; if a
change to the rules ever made dodging useless, this would show it at
once. Game studios run thousands of such automated players to test
balance.

The window version adds the screens, drawing and sound around the same
`Game`:

```vyrn check
use vyrn.draw
use vyrn.sound

enum Screen:
    Title
    Playing
    GameOver(score: int)
end

main:
    let win = draw.window(400, 500, "Dodge")
    let crash = sound.tone(110, 0.4, "noise", 0.4)
    var screen = Screen.Title
    var time = 0.0
    var dt = 0.016
    loop win.open():
        win.clear("#101820")
        when screen:
            is Screen.Title:
                win.text("DODGE", 130, 180, "white", 5)
                win.text("press Enter", 135, 260, "#9e9e9e", 2)
                if win.key_pressed("enter"):
                    time = 0.0
                    screen = Screen.Playing
                end
            is Screen.Playing:
                time += dt
                win.text("score {int(time * 10)}", 10, 10, "white", 2)
                if win.key_pressed("escape"):
                    crash.play()
                    screen = Screen.GameOver(int(time * 10))
                end
            is Screen.GameOver(score):
                win.text("GAME OVER", 95, 200, "tomato", 4)
                win.text("score {score}", 140, 260, "white", 2)
                if win.key_pressed("enter"): screen = Screen.Title
        end
        dt = win.show()
    end
end
```

(In this sketch Escape stands in for crashing; put the `Game` object's
`update` in the `Playing` screen, draw its blocks, and switch to
`GameOver` when `crashed` is true.)

lessons.title: Giving it to people
lessons.text:
`vyrn build` makes a single program file (Day 52). A game also has
**assets**: pictures, sounds, levels. Keep them in an `assets` folder next
to the game and load them with paths relative to it:

```text
dodge/
  vyrn.toml
  main.vyrn
  game.vyrn
  assets/
    theme.ogg
    font.png
  tests/
    test_game.vyrn
```

```bash
vyrn build -o dodge
```

Zip `build/dodge` together with the `assets` folder, and anyone on the same
kind of computer can unzip it and play. Build once on each system you want
to support (Windows, macOS, Linux); a GitHub Actions workflow (Day 52) can
build all three on every release. Before sharing, play it all the way
through once more: menus, pause, game over, high scores, sound off.

### Exercise

Write `stars(score, thresholds)`, giving a rating of 1 to 3 stars: one
star for any score, two for reaching `thresholds[0]`, three for
`thresholds[1]`, shown as `"★★☆"`.

```vyrn starter
create stars(score: int, thresholds: list[int]) -> str:
    return ""
end

main:
    print(stars(10, [100, 250]), stars(120, [100, 250]), stars(400, [100, 250]))
end
```

```text expect
★☆☆ ★★☆ ★★★
```

exercise.starter:
create stars(score: int, thresholds: list[int]) -> str:
    return ""
end

main:
    print(stars(10, [100, 250]), stars(120, [100, 250]), stars(400, [100, 250]))
end
exercise.solution:
create stars(score: int, thresholds: list[int]) -> str:
    let n = 1 + len([t each t in thresholds if score >= t])
    return "★" * n + "☆" * (3 - n)
end

main:
    print(stars(10, [100, 250]), stars(120, [100, 250]), stars(400, [100, 250]))
end
hints: count `n = 1 + len([t each t in thresholds if score >= t])`, then `"★" * n + "☆" * (3 - n)`.

lessons.title: you learned
lessons.text:
- Screens are an enum and the game a state machine, all moves in one
  tested function.
- Save high scores to a file, keep the top few, survive a damaged file.
- `sound.tone` and `sound.load` for effects and music; silent without a
  device; let players turn it off.
- Test a game by letting simple automatic players play it.
- Ship with `vyrn build` plus an `assets` folder.

days.title: Day 80: Portfolio project: a command-line tool
days.intro:
The last five days are yours. Each is a **project brief**: what to build,
what "done" means, and a suggested route, but no step-by-step code. Build
it in a project of its own (`vyrn new`), commit as you go, and put it on
GitHub when it's finished: these are the programs to show people.

Today's brief: a **command-line tool** that does one job well, the way
`git`, `curl` and `vyrn` itself do.

lessons.title: The brief
lessons.text:
Pick a job you actually have. Some ideas:

- `notes`: quick notes from the terminal (`notes add "buy milk"`,
  `notes list`, `notes search milk`).
- `tidy`: sort a downloads folder into subfolders by file type.
- `budget`: read a bank's CSV export and report spending by category.
- `rename`: rename many files at once by a pattern (`IMG_0042.jpg` to
  `2026-11-12 holiday 042.jpg`).

lessons.title: Done means
lessons.text:
- [ ] Commands and options from `os.args()`, with a `help` command that
      lists them, and a clear message for anything unknown.
- [ ] Exit code 0 on success, not 0 on failure (`os.exit`), so scripts can
      use it.
- [ ] Never loses data: anything destructive asks first, or has a
      `--dry-run` that shows what would happen.
- [ ] Settings or data stored in a file in the user's home folder
      (`path.home()`), surviving a damaged file.
- [ ] Tests (`vyrn test`) for every command, with the file system or
      clock passed in where needed.
- [ ] `vyrn check` and `vyrn fmt --check` are clean.
- [ ] Built with `vyrn build`, and a README saying what it does, how to
      install it, and an example of each command.

lessons.title: A suggested route
lessons.text:
1. Write the README first, with examples of using the tool. It's the
   design.
2. Parse the arguments into an enum of commands (Day 61), tested on its
   own: `parse(["add", "buy milk"])` gives `Command.Add("buy milk")`.
3. One function per command, taking what it needs (a storage object, the
   clock) as parameters.
4. `main` is three lines: parse, run, exit with the code.

lessons.title: Warm-up
lessons.text:
Most tools take flags like `--dry-run` and `--limit=5`. Write
`split_flags(args)`, separating flags from the other words, as a map and
a list.

```vyrn starter
create split_flags(args: list[str]) -> (map, list[str]):
    return ({}, args)
end

main:
    print(split_flags(["tidy", "--dry-run", "Downloads", "--limit=5"]))
end
```

```text expect
({"dry-run": true, "limit": "5"}, ["tidy", "Downloads"])
```

exercise.starter:
create split_flags(args: list[str]) -> (map, list[str]):
    return ({}, args)
end

main:
    print(split_flags(["tidy", "--dry-run", "Downloads", "--limit=5"]))
end
hints: a word starting with `--` is a flag; split it on the first `=` for a value, else its value is `true`.

lessons.title: Going further
lessons.text:
- Colour in the output, and a `--quiet` flag for scripts.
- Publish it as a package (`vyrn publish`) so others can `vyrn add` it.
- Shell completion: a `completions` command that prints a script for bash.

days.title: Day 81: Portfolio project: a full-stack web app
days.intro:
Today's brief is a complete web application with accounts and a database,
the kind of project that shows you can build something real end to end.
Day 53's todo app is the pattern; this one should be your own idea.

lessons.title: The brief
lessons.text:
Some ideas:

- A **reading tracker**: books you're reading, pages per day, a chart of
  your year.
- A **club organiser**: events, who's coming, a reminder email the day
  before.
- A **recipe box**: recipes with ingredients, scaling servings, a shopping
  list for the week.
- A **shared expenses** app: who paid what, and who owes whom.

lessons.title: Done means
lessons.text:
- [ ] Sign up, log in, log out, with hashed passwords and sessions
      (Day 49).
- [ ] Each user sees and changes only their own data: every query includes
      the owner (Day 53).
- [ ] At least three kinds of record in the database, with at least one
      join in a real page.
- [ ] Pages from templates with a shared layout; works on a phone.
- [ ] Forms checked on the server, with errors shown next to the form;
      CSRF tokens on every POST (Day 51).
- [ ] A JSON API for at least one resource (Day 48).
- [ ] Tests through `http.test` for the main promises, including "another
      user can't see this".
- [ ] Settings from the environment, a `/health` route, a Dockerfile, and
      a GitHub Actions workflow running the tests (Day 52).
- [ ] Deployed somewhere people can visit, with HTTPS.

lessons.title: A suggested route
lessons.text:
1. Sketch the pages on paper, and the tables they need.
2. Data layer first, with tests, using an in-memory database.
3. Routes and templates for one resource, end to end, before the next.
4. Logins last but one; deployment last, early enough to fix surprises.

lessons.title: Warm-up
lessons.text:
Shared expenses need "who owes whom". Write `balances(payments)`: given
`(payer, amount)` pairs shared equally by everyone listed, give each
person's balance (positive: they're owed money).

```vyrn starter
create balances(payments: list) -> map:
    return {}
end

main:
    print(balances([("ada", 30.0), ("bob", 0.0), ("cy", 15.0)]))
end
```

```text expect
{"ada": 15.0, "bob": -15.0, "cy": 0.0}
```

exercise.starter:
create balances(payments: list) -> map:
    return {}
end

main:
    print(balances([("ada", 30.0), ("bob", 0.0), ("cy", 15.0)]))
end
exercise.solution:
create balances(payments: list) -> map:
    let share = sum(a each _, a in payments) / len(payments)
    return {name: paid - share each name, paid in payments}
end

main:
    print(balances([("ada", 30.0), ("bob", 0.0), ("cy", 15.0)]))
end
hints: everyone's share is the total divided by the number of people; each balance is what they paid minus the share.

lessons.title: Going further
lessons.text:
- Live updates with server-sent events or WebSockets.
- Uploading pictures, kept safely outside the web folder (Day 51).
- An admin page, behind a role check, with usage charts.

days.title: Day 82: Portfolio project: a report every morning
days.intro:
Today's brief is an **automated report**: a program that runs by itself
every day, gathers data, analyses it, and delivers the result as an email
or a web page. It combines the API days (Unit 4) with the data days
(Unit 6).

lessons.title: The brief
lessons.text:
Some ideas:

- **Your city today**: weather, air quality and public transport delays,
  with a chart of the week.
- **Market watch**: your chosen shares or currencies, with the biggest
  moves and the news behind them (Day 36).
- **Project pulse**: commits, open issues and pull requests across your
  GitHub repositories.
- **Habit report**: from your habit tracker's data (Day 37), streaks and
  trends.

lessons.title: Done means
lessons.text:
- [ ] Fetches from at least two sources, with keys from the environment,
      timeouts and retries (Days 35, 73).
- [ ] Keeps a history in a database, so it can say "compared with last
      week".
- [ ] At least two charts and one table, with honest axes (Day 56).
- [ ] Delivered as an HTML email or a page on a static site (Day 44).
- [ ] Runs on a schedule (Task Scheduler, cron, or a GitHub Actions
      `schedule`), and logs each run.
- [ ] If a source is down, the report still goes out, saying what's
      missing.
- [ ] Tested with recorded API answers and a fake clock; no test touches
      the network.

lessons.title: A suggested route
lessons.text:
1. Record one real answer from each API into files, and build everything
   against those.
2. One function per section of the report, each returning data, then one
   that renders it all.
3. Only at the end, swap the recorded answers for live calls, behind the
   same function signatures.

lessons.title: Warm-up
lessons.text:
Reports often compare with the past. Write `change(now, before)` giving a
short phrase: `"up 12%"`, `"down 5%"`, `"no change"`, or `"new"` when there
was nothing before.

```vyrn starter
create change(now: float, before: float?) -> str:
    return ""
end

main:
    print(change(112.0, 100.0), "|", change(95.0, 100.0), "|", change(100.0, 100.0), "|", change(7.0, none))
end
```

```text expect
up 12% | down 5% | no change | new
```

exercise.starter:
create change(now: float, before: float?) -> str:
    return ""
end

main:
    print(change(112.0, 100.0), "|", change(95.0, 100.0), "|", change(100.0, 100.0), "|", change(7.0, none))
end
exercise.solution:
create change(now: float, before: float?) -> str:
    if before == none or before == 0: return "new"
    let pct = round(100 * (now - before) / before)
    if pct > 0: return "up {pct}%"
    if pct < 0: return "down {-pct}%"
    return "no change"
end

main:
    print(change(112.0, 100.0), "|", change(95.0, 100.0), "|", change(100.0, 100.0), "|", change(7.0, none))
end
hints: deal with `none` (and zero) first; then the percentage is `round(100 * (now - before) / before)`.

lessons.title: Going further
lessons.text:
- A small dashboard (Days 58 and 59) beside the email, for exploring the
  history.
- Alerts only when something unusual happens, instead of every day.
- Run each source in parallel with tasks (Day 72), so one slow API doesn't
  delay the rest.

days.title: Day 83: Portfolio project: a game of your own
days.intro:
Today's brief is a complete game, designed by you. Not a copy of a famous
game: take an idea you like and make it your own, with your rules, your
look and your twist. Days 77 to 79 are the toolkit.

lessons.title: The brief
lessons.text:
Pick a size you can finish: a small finished game beats a large
unfinished one. Some starting points:

- A **one-screen arcade** game with a single clever mechanic: gravity
  that flips, a weapon that rebounds, a timer that rewinds.
- A **puzzle** game on a grid with ten hand-made levels of rising
  difficulty.
- A **3D explorer**: a small world to wander, with something to find
  (Day 78 and the game-dev guide).
- A **two-player** game on one keyboard, or over the network (`vyrn.net`).

lessons.title: Done means
lessons.text:
- [ ] Title screen, playing, pause and game over, as a state machine
      (Day 79).
- [ ] Rules in `update` functions tested without a window, including an
      automatic player that checks the game can be won (Day 79).
- [ ] Movement scaled by `dt`, so it plays the same on any computer.
- [ ] Sound effects, and music that can be turned off.
- [ ] High scores (or level progress) saved, surviving a damaged file.
- [ ] Someone else has played it and you changed something because of what
      you saw.
- [ ] Built with `vyrn build`, zipped with its assets, with a README and a
      screenshot or short video.

lessons.title: A suggested route
lessons.text:
1. Make the core mechanic fun with squares and circles before drawing any
   art. If it isn't fun as squares, art won't save it.
2. Then levels or difficulty, then screens and scores, then sound and art,
   in that order.
3. Watch someone play without helping them. Note every moment they're
   confused.

lessons.title: Warm-up
lessons.text:
Games feel smoother when things **ease** instead of moving at constant
speed. Write `ease_out(t)`: for `t` from 0 to 1, give `1 - (1 - t)²`,
which starts fast and slows into place.

```vyrn starter
create ease_out(t: float) -> float:
    return t
end

main:
    print([round(ease_out(t / 4), 3) each t in 0 to 4])
end
```

```text expect
[0.0, 0.438, 0.75, 0.938, 1.0]
```

exercise.starter:
create ease_out(t: float) -> float:
    return t
end

main:
    print([round(ease_out(t / 4), 3) each t in 0 to 4])
end
exercise.solution:
create ease_out(t: float) -> float:
    return 1 - (1 - t) ** 2
end

main:
    print([round(ease_out(t / 4), 3) each t in 0 to 4])
end

lessons.title: Going further
lessons.text:
- A level editor: levels as text files the game loads, made in the game.
- Gamepad support (`draw.gamepad()`).
- Put it in a browser: Vyrn runs on WebAssembly (the playground in
  `playground/` shows how).

days.title: Day 84: Your own project
days.intro:
The last day of the course, and the start of everything after it. Today's
brief is the one you write: a project of your own choosing, built,
tested, packaged and deployed like a professional's. Everything from the
last 83 days is available to you; the hard part now is choosing what to
build and seeing it through.

lessons.title: Choosing
lessons.text:
The best project is one you'd use yourself, or one for someone you know:
a tool for a club, a game for a younger sibling, a dashboard for a family
business. Real users give real feedback, and a reason to finish. Write one
paragraph answering:

- Who is it for, and what problem does it solve for them?
- What is the smallest version that would already be useful?
- How will you know it works?

Then cut the smallest version down by half. That's your first milestone.

lessons.title: Done means
lessons.text:
- [ ] A README: what it is, a screenshot, how to install and use it.
- [ ] Organised in modules, with types on the functions others call
      (Day 60).
- [ ] Tests for its promises, run by GitHub Actions on every push, with
      `vyrn check` and `vyrn fmt --check`.
- [ ] Errors handled: clear messages, no lost data, nothing secret in the
      code.
- [ ] Packaged for its users: `vyrn build`, a container, a package
      (`vyrn publish`), or a website.
- [ ] Used by at least one person other than you, and improved from what
      they said.

lessons.title: How to keep going
lessons.text:
- **Small steps, always working.** Commit each time something works. Never
  be more than a day away from a working version.
- **When stuck,** shrink the problem: a tiny program that shows just the
  part you don't understand. Half of all bugs are found while writing
  that tiny program.
- **Read other people's code.** The Vyrn examples (`examples/`), the
  standard library's documentation (`docs/stdlib.md`), and packages from
  `vyrn search` all show how others solved problems you'll meet.

lessons.title: A last warm-up
lessons.text:
Plan the project as milestones. Write `plan(tasks, days)`: given tasks
with an estimate in days, give the tasks that fit into the days available,
in order, and the ones that don't (for version 2).

```vyrn starter
create plan(tasks: list, days: int) -> (list, list):
    return (tasks, [])
end

main:
    print(plan([("login", 2), ("data model", 1), ("charts", 3), ("export", 2)], 5))
end
```

```text expect
(["login", "data model"], ["charts", "export"])
```

exercise.starter:
create plan(tasks: list, days: int) -> (list, list):
    return (tasks, [])
end

main:
    print(plan([("login", 2), ("data model", 1), ("charts", 3), ("export", 2)], 5))
end
exercise.solution:
create plan(tasks: list, days: int) -> (list, list):
    var now = []
    var later = []
    var used = 0
    each name, estimate in tasks:
        if not later and used + estimate <= days:
            now.append(name)
            used += estimate
        else:
            later.append(name)
        end
    end
    return (now, later)
end

main:
    print(plan([("login", 2), ("data model", 1), ("charts", 3), ("export", 2)], 5))
end
hints: walk the tasks in order, adding each estimate to a running total; once one doesn't fit, everything after goes to version 2.

lessons.title: Where next
lessons.text:
You can now write programs that are typed and tested, that talk to the
web, keep data in databases, analyse it, draw it, run tasks in parallel,
and run as games, tools, servers and reports. The same ideas carry over
to every other language: Python, JavaScript, Go, Rust, C#, Swift. Learning
the next one will take weeks, not months, because you already know what
programs are made of. Pick the one your next project needs, and keep
building.
